`SurpriseRolledEvent`s and the reaction
roll's kernel event, both at referee visibility. The two surprise outcomes are here,
because the party knows when it's caught off guard.

An encounter can open with more than one group, like goblins and the orcs they march with.
`monster_name` and `monster_name_plural` name the first group, and `count` counts the
creatures of every group. `group_labels`, `group_labels_plural`, and `group_counts` give
each group in the encounter's order, so a line like "2 goblins and 3 orcs" can name them all.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
How the encounter started: `"wandering"` from the wandering-monster check, `"keyed"` from an
area the adventure placed monsters in, or `"spawned"` from a referee command.

area_ref.title: Area Ref
area_ref.description:
The keyed area's reference, when `kind` is `"keyed"`. When every monster in the encounter is
slain or routed, `end_encounter` marks the area's
encounter resolved, so entering the area again doesn't start another fight. When the party gets
past the monsters some other way, `EndEncounter` with
`resolve_area=True` marks it resolved too.

groups.title: Groups
groups.description:
The monster groups, each an `EncounterGroup`, in the
order they were spawned. There's always at least one.

stance.title: Stance
stance.description:
The monsters' current attitude toward the party, as a
`ReactionResult` value: `"attacks"`, `"hostile"`,
`"uncertain"`, `"indifferent"`, or `"friendly"`. It's None only while the encounter opens,
before the reaction is rolled.

round.title: Round
round.description:
The number of encounter rounds run so far. `Wait` and
`Parley` each add one when the encounter goes on. A chase counts
its rounds in `pursuit` instead.

started_round.title: Started Round
started_round.description:
The session clock's round count when the encounter opened.
`end_encounter` uses it to make the encounter cost at
least one turn.

party_surprised.title: Party Surprised
party_surprised.description: True when the party lost the surprise roll and gave up a round.

monsters_surprised.title: Monsters Surprised
monsters_surprised.description:
True when the monsters lost the surprise roll. When both sides are surprised, neither side gains
anything.

monsters_skip_rounds.title: Monsters Skip Rounds
monsters_skip_rounds.description:
The rounds the monsters still have to sit out because they were surprised. Each round they sit
out reduces it by one. A battle that starts while any remain gives the party a free round.

hostile_deadline.title: Hostile Deadline
hostile_deadline.description:
The encounter round at which hostile monsters attack. The session sets it each time the stance
becomes hostile, and it's None until then. It applies only while the stance is hostile, so once a
parley improves the stance, the deadline no longer applies.

evading.title: Evading
evading.description:
True once the party has tried to evade. While it's True, hostile monsters don't attack at
`hostile_deadline`.

pursuit.description: The `PursuitState` while a chase is on, or None.

EncounterState.title: EncounterState
EncounterState.description:
An open encounter: the monster groups, the stance, the surprise result, and any chase.

You get this from `session.encounter`, which is None whenever no encounter is open. A save
contains it with the session, so a saved game restores in the middle of an encounter. Read it to show the
encounter, and change it only through commands: the session's encounter and battle commands
update its fields.

id.title: Id
id.description: The table's id, like `"level_1"`, `"level_4_5"`, or `"level_8_plus"`.

label.title: Label
label.description: The table's printed heading, like `"Level 1"` or `"Level 8+"`, for display.

min_level.title: Min Level
min_level.description: The shallowest dungeon level this table is for.

max_level.title: Max Level
max_level.description: The deepest dungeon level this table is for, or `null` on the last table, which is for every deeper level.

rows.title: Rows
rows.description: A row for each d20 result, in order, so `rows[roll - 1]` is the row for a roll.

overrides_applied.title: Overrides Applied
overrides_applied.description:
The fields osrlib corrected when it compiled this table from the SRD, as dotted paths. Empty when none were.

`"rows.1.name"` means the name in `rows[1]`, the row for a d20 roll of 2, was corrected. Read it when you check
osrlib's data against the SRD.

EncounterTable.title: EncounterTable
EncounterTable.description:
The wandering monster table for one dungeon level, or for a range of levels.

Get the table for a level with
`EncounterTables.for_level`, then roll a
d20 and read `rows[roll - 1]`. The tables for deeper levels have more dangerous monsters.

roll.title: Roll
roll.description: The d20 result this row is for, from 1 to 20. A table's rows are in this order.

name.title: Name
name.description: The name the SRD prints in the row, like `"Acolyte"`, for display.

entry.title: Entry
entry.description: What appears: monsters, or a party of NPC adventurers. Check its `kind`.

count_dice.title: Count Dice
count_dice.description:
A dice expression for how many appear, like `"1d6"`, or `null` when the row has a fixed number.

Roll it with `roll`. Use this count rather than the number appearing in the monster's
description, as the SRD's note on the dungeon tables says. Exactly one of this and `count_fixed` is set. The
expression's highest total must be at most 100, so `"1d100"` is legal and `"1d100+1"` isn't.

count_fixed.title: Count Fixed
count_fixed.description:
A fixed number of individuals from 1 to 100, or `null` when the row has a dice expression instead.

Exactly one of this and `count_dice` is set.

EncounterTableRow.title: EncounterTableRow
EncounterTableRow.description:
One d20 result on a wandering monster table: what appears, and how many.

Roll a d20 and take `rows[roll - 1]`. Roll `count_dice`, or take `count_fixed`, for how
many appear. For a `MonsterEncounterEntry`,
pass the entry and the count to
`select_encounter_individuals`. For an
`NpcPartyEncounterEntry`, pass them to
`generate_npc_party`.

A row creates at most 100 monsters or adventurers, so an adventure's own wandering monster
table can't spawn more at once than a
`SpawnMonsters` command can.

tables.title: Tables
tables.description: The wandering monster tables, shallowest first. Together they cover every dungeon level from 1 down.

npc_class_levels.title: Npc Class Levels
npc_class_levels.description: The rows of the d8 table that gives each NPC adventurer a class and a level, in d8 order.

npc_alignment.title: Npc Alignment
npc_alignment.description: The bands of the d6 table that gives an NPC adventuring party its alignment.

npc_compositions.title: Npc Compositions
npc_compositions.description: The dice for how many adventurers a party has: one entry for `"basic"` parties and one for `"expert"`.

EncounterTables.title: EncounterTables
EncounterTables.description:
Every wandering monster table, and the tables for generating an NPC adventuring party.

Get it from `load_encounter_tables`. Start with
`for_level`, which returns the table for
a dungeon level.

A `GameSession` rolls wandering monsters for you, and
an adventure's dungeon level can replace these tables with a different table in
`WanderingSpec.table`. Use this model
yourself to stock rooms or roll wandering monsters outside a session.

groups.title: Groups
groups.description:
The monster groups in the encounter, in the order the session's encounter state lists
them.

stance.title: Stance
stance.description:
How the monsters are behaving, as a `ReactionResult`
serialized value: `"attacks"`, `"hostile"`, `"uncertain"`, `"indifferent"`, or `"friendly"`.
`null` before the reaction roll has settled it.

in_battle.title: In Battle
in_battle.description: Whether the encounter has become a battle with rounds and declarations.

battle_round.title: Battle Round
battle_round.description: The current battle round, counting from the first. `null` outside a battle.

pursuit_gap_feet.title: Pursuit Gap Feet
pursuit_gap_feet.description:
How far ahead of its nearest pursuer the fleeing party is, in feet. `null` when the party
isn't being pursued. A pursuing group's `distance_feet` in `groups` shows the same chase, so the
nearest pursuer's distance is this value.

declarers.title: Declarers
declarers.description:
Every member who has to declare this round, in marching order: the ones living and
able to act. A `ResolveBattleRound` with any
other roster, a slept or paralysed member included, is rejected whole with
`battle.declaration.roster_mismatch`.

front_rank.title: Front Rank
front_rank.description:
The first row of the party's ranks toward the nearest group, in marching order.

The nearest group is the group that hasn't fled and has a living member, and that stands closest
to any living member. When two are equally near, it's the one that comes first in `groups`. The
ranks toward a group are the living members sorted by their distance to it and cut into rows of
`formation_width`, and this is the first row, however far away it stands. With the ruleset's
`formation_width_limit` flag off, the row holds every living member at the nearest distance.
Outside a battle, every member stands on the party line, so it's the party's first rank in
marching order.

In a fight with one group, before any member has moved, it's the members who can attack that
group in melee once it's within 5'. As soon as members stand at different distances, or the party
fights more than one group, read each group's
`front_rank` instead, which says exactly who
can attack that group in melee this round.

immobile.title: Immobile
immobile.description:
The declarers who can't move this round. In practice they're the entangled members,
because the other conditions that stop a move stop every declaration as well. A `move`
declaration of any kind from one of them is rejected with
`battle.declaration.cannot_move`, and so is an `attack` from one of them that sets
`move="close"`.

reloading.title: Reloading
reloading.description:
The members who may not fire a `reload` weapon this round, because they fired one
last round (`combat.attack.reload`). Empty when the ruleset's `weapon_reload` flag is
off, so you can combine this list with the weapon's qualities and never read the flag.

can_hide.title: Can Hide
can_hide.description:
The declarers who can declare `hide` this round, in marching order: those whose class has
thief skills, as the thief's does, and who don't stand in the party's front rank, the first row
of the ranks toward any group that hasn't fled and has a living member. Empty outside a battle.

It reads the battle as it stands, as each group's `front_rank` does. The session judges a
`hide` where the members will stand once the round's declared moves are made, so a member in
this list who would end up in the front rank because of another member's move is refused with
`battle.declaration.hide_in_front_rank`. A member outside it gets
`battle.declaration.hide_not_a_thief` or `battle.declaration.hide_in_front_rank`. To learn who
can hide beside the declarations planned so far, read
`BattleRoundPreview.can_hide`.

hiding.title: Hiding
hiding.description:
The members who are hiding, in marching order: each has declared a `hide` that resolved, and
the attempt hasn't ended since. Empty outside a battle.

A member here can declare an `attack` with
`BattleDeclaration.back_stab` in any round
without a place in the front rank, as long as their class has the `back_stab` ability and they
can act, and `can_back_stab` lists them. The
back-stab still needs a melee weapon, or bare hands, and a group within 5' of the member, as
each group's `member_distance_feet`
shows, or a `close` that brings one within 5'. The list doesn't say
whether a hide worked: the session rolls the skills in secret, and the attack's
`AttackRolledEvent.back_stab` tells the players
whether it was a back-stab. A member leaves the list when the attempt ends, which
`BattleDeclaration.back_stab` describes.

can_back_stab.title: Can Back Stab
can_back_stab.description:
The declarers who can declare an `attack` with
`BattleDeclaration.back_stab` this round, in
marching order: those whose class has the `back_stab` ability, as the thief's does, in the
party's free round (see `party_free_round`) or while they're in `hiding`. Empty outside a battle.

The session refuses a back-stab by any other declarer with `battle.declaration.back_stab_no_ability`
or `battle.declaration.back_stab_target_aware`, and never refuses one by a member here with
either code. A member who can't act isn't a declarer, so they aren't here, even while they're in
`hiding`. Like `hiding`, the list holds every member who has hidden, whatever the secret hide in
shadows roll was, so it never tells the players whether a hide worked.

The list doesn't read the declaration, so the session can still refuse a back-stab by a member
here for what the declaration says: `battle.declaration.back_stab_not_attack` when the action
isn't `attack`, `battle.declaration.back_stab_not_melee` for a missile weapon, or a dagger aimed
at a group more than 5' from the member after their `close`, and the checks every attack takes,
like `battle.declaration.unknown_group`, `battle.declaration.weapon_not_wielded`,
`combat.attack.out_of_reach`, and `combat.attack.attacker_blind`. In the free round, a back-stab
takes the melee checks of any attack, so a member outside the group's front rank gets
`battle.declaration.not_in_front_rank`. In any other round, a member here is hiding and needs no
place in the front rank. To
learn who can back-stab beside the declarations planned so far, read
`BattleRoundPreview.can_back_stab`.

advance_feet.title: Advance Feet
advance_feet.description:
Each living member's place on the range track, keyed by member id, in feet forward of the party
line. Empty outside a battle.

The party line is where the party stood when the encounter opened. Each group's `distance_feet`
is measured from it. Every member starts a battle on the line, at zero. A member who closes on a
group moves forward, and a member who falls back alone moves back, below zero once they're behind
the line. When every member the monsters can see is behind the line, the line moves back to the
foremost of them. This field and each group's `distance_feet` then show the moved values, and no
distance between a member and a group changes. Use it to draw where each member stands. Each group's
`member_distance_feet` gives the
distance it leaves between the member and that group.

formation_width.title: Formation Width
formation_width.description:
How many members can fight side by side where the party stands, or `null` when the ruleset's
`formation_width_limit` flag is off and a rank has no width limit.

The width is the side of the largest square of open cells that includes the party's cell, times
10', divided by 5' for each combatant
(`FIGHTER_FRONTAGE_FEET`). The square holds only
cells of the space the party stands in, so a door or the edge of a room bounds it. A one-cell
corridor gives 2, and so does a crossroads of one-cell corridors. A room gives twice its shorter
side in cells: a 4 by 4 room gives 8, and a 2 by 8 room gives 4. The width comes from the party's
cell, so it's set in an encounter before a battle starts, and it stays the same for the whole
fight. The ranks toward each group are rows this wide, so
a group's `front_rank` never holds more members
than this. Compare the two to show how many places are left in a group's front rank.

The width limits the monsters too. Each group's front rank of monsters is its first living
monsters, as many as this, and only they make melee attacks on the party.

party_free_round.title: Party Free Round
party_free_round.description:
True in the round the party gets free after it surprised the monsters, while the monsters can't
act. False in every other round, and outside a battle.

It's the round in which any thief's back-stab is legal: an `attack` that sets
`BattleDeclaration.back_stab`. In other
rounds, only the members in `hiding` can back-stab. `can_back_stab` lists the members who can
back-stab in this round, in either case. It's true while
`BattleState.monsters_hold_rounds` is above
zero.

evade_rejections.title: Evade Rejections
evade_rejections.description:
Why the session would refuse an `Evade` now, for each value of
`Evade.drop`, keyed by that value: `"none"`, `"treasure"`, and `"food"`.

Read it to disable a choice on your flee menu that the session would refuse, and to show the reason. Each value is a
tuple of `Rejection` models with the `code` and `params` that an `Evade` with
that `drop` gets. An empty tuple means that the session accepts it. An accepted `Evade` can still end in a pursuit
or a battle, because the outcome depends on the monsters, and the view makes no prediction of it.

The codes you'll meet are these:

- `encounter.evade.already_evading`, for every value, while a pursuit is running, as `pursuit_gap_feet` shows.
  Each round of a pursuit comes from a `Wait` or a
  `DropItems` instead.
- `encounter.evade.nobody_able_to_act`, for every value, when no living member can act, because each one is
  paralysed, petrified, or asleep.
- `encounter.evade.cannot_move`, for every value, with the `character` param, when that living member is caught in
  a *web*.
- `encounter.evade.cannot_move`, with the `reason` param `"overloaded"`, when a living member would still carry
  more than the maximum load after the drop. The `"treasure"` drop scatters every coin before the party runs, so
  an overloaded party can get the rejection for `"none"` and `"food"` and none for `"treasure"`.
- `encounter.evade.nothing_to_drop`, with the `drop` param `"treasure"`, when no living member has a coin in
  their purse.
- `encounter.evade.nothing_to_drop`, with the `drop` param `"food"`, when no living member carries a
  `rations_standard` or a `rations_iron`.

A dead member's coins and rations don't count. A member who is alive but can't act, such as one who is asleep or
paralysed, counts, as long as another member can act.

While the session is in the `encounter` mode and no pursuit is running, the `"none"` entry is empty unless the party
can't run: nobody can act, a member is caught in a *web*, or a member carries too much to move. Only the overload
can clear with a drop, so read the `"treasure"` entry before you tell the player that the party can't evade.

The map has an entry for every value while the session is in the `encounter` mode. In a battle, the map is empty,
because the session refuses every `Evade` there with `session.command.wrong_mode`. An `EncounterView` that osrlib
2.10.0 built, such as one in a stored feed entry, has no `evade_rejections`, and it validates with the map empty.

EncounterView.title: EncounterView
EncounterView.description:
The current encounter or battle's public state.

You get one from `PlayerView.encounter`, which
is `null` when the party isn't in an encounter.

In a battle, each party member stands at their own place on the range track, the
one-dimensional measure of distance a battle uses. `advance_feet` gives each member's place, and
each group in `groups` gives every member's distance to it and the members who can reach it in
melee. Read those to draw the fight and to offer each member the moves and attacks they can make.

The id tuples `declarers`, `immobile`, `reloading`, `can_hide`, `hiding`, and `can_back_stab`
describe the battle round as the players see it at the table: who is able to act, who is held
fast, who is still reloading a crossbow, who can hide, who is hiding, and who can back-stab.
Each group's `front_rank` says who can attack
that group in melee this round. Each of these matches a rejection that would refuse the whole
round, so if you read them, you offer only the declarations the session accepts. To check a
choice against the choices already made for the round, call
`preview_battle_round`.

EncumbranceMode.title: EncumbranceMode
EncumbranceMode.description:
Which system osrlib uses to track what the party carries, and how much it slows them down.

Set it on `Ruleset.encumbrance`. The weights and the
movement rates are in `osrlib.core.items`, and
`movement_rate_feet` reads this choice.

Saved games contain the lowercase values, and they stay fixed within a
`schema_version`, the version stamp that identifies a serialized model's format.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"end_encounter"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

outcome.title: Outcome
outcome.description:
How the encounter ended, as the `outcome` of the
`EncounterEndedEvent`. Use `"parley"` when the
party and the monsters came to terms, like a toll paid or a bluff believed. Use
`"departed"` when one side left the other, like a party that walks away from monsters
that let it go, or a pursuit that you call off.

resolve_area.title: Resolve Area
resolve_area.description:
Whether to mark the area the encounter came from as resolved, so its keyed monsters don't
appear when the party next walks in. With `false`, the default, the area stays unresolved,
and its monsters are back the next time the party enters it. A wandering or spawned
encounter didn't come from an area, so the flag does nothing for it.

EndEncounter.title: EndEncounter
EndEncounter.description:
Referee: close the open encounter when the party talks its way past or walks away.

Use it when the party pays a toll, bluffs the guards, or walks away from monsters that let
it go. The session closes the encounter the same way it does when the party wins or gets
away, and then switches to `exploring`:

- Monsters that were slain earlier in the encounter, or that fled, are still fleeing, or
  were turned, count as defeated and are worth experience. So does each afraid member of a
  group whose living members are all turned or afraid, because that group retreats as a whole.
  The session applies the same rule however the encounter ends.
- Slain monsters drop their treasure in a pile on the party's cell. Monsters that fled, were
  turned, or retreat with such a group take theirs with them.
- Monsters still standing aren't defeated and are worth no experience.
- Effects on the encounter's monsters end.
- The clock advances, so the encounter costs at least one turn.

In `battle`, the command closes the battle too, so `session.battle` is `null` afterward. It
emits no `BattleEndedEvent`, because the
`EncounterEndedEvent` closes both. To know the fight is over, check the session's mode.

The monsters keyed to an area of the adventure come back each time the party walks into
the area, until every one of them is slain or driven off. To stop them coming back, set
`resolve_area` to `true`, which marks the area resolved. The command is legal only while
an encounter is open, so you can't use it to resolve an area after its encounter has
closed.

Set `outcome` to `"parley"` when the two sides came to terms, or `"departed"` when one side
left the other. It has no default.

An adventure document can contain this command as an authored consequence, so a trigger
can close the encounter. For example, a trigger can close the encounter and resolve the
area when a flag records that the party paid the toll.

Modes:

`encounter`, `battle`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` or `encounter.none_active` - no encounter is open.

**Events:**

A `MonsterFledEvent` for each group of turned or
afraid members that breaks away from a group that still has a member who is neither, such
as one restored from an older save. Then a
`MonsterDefeatedEvent` for each monster
that counts as defeated, a `LootDroppedEvent`
when the slain leave anything on the floor, the events of effects ending on the
encounter's monsters, and the experience award when the ruleset awards it immediately.
Then the `EncounterEndedEvent` with the
command's `outcome`, and the events of the clock advance.

immunity.title: Immunity
immunity.description:
How much of this element the creature ignores.

`"all"` means no damage of this element hurts the creature, magical or not, as with a fire giant
and fire. `"nonmagical"` means only magical damage of this element hurts it. A red dragon takes
no damage from a dragon's fire breath or a flask of burning oil, and still takes damage from a
*fire ball*.

auto_save_magical.title: Auto Save Magical
auto_save_magical.description:
True when the creature passes every saving throw against a magical form of this element without rolling.

This is a dragon's automatic save against a spell of the element it resists, like a red dragon's save
against *fire ball*, so it takes half damage.

EnergyDefense.title: EnergyDefense
EnergyDefense.description:
How a monster resists one kind of energy.

Read them from `Defenses.energy`, keyed by
`Element`. Before rolling damage,
`check_immunity` looks up the element of the incoming
attack, and `saving_throw` reads `auto_save_magical`. Frozen.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"engage_battle"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

EngageBattle.title: EngageBattle
EngageBattle.description:
Start a battle with the monsters the party has met.

An encounter must be open. Attacks, spells, and an item's striking effects
happen only in battle, so this is how the party starts a fight.
`TurnUndead` is the one aggressive act the
party can take in an encounter without starting a battle first. When the monsters were
surprised at the start of the encounter, the party gets a free first round. During a
pursuit, the party turns and fights, and each group stands where the chase has left it, as
its `EncounterGroup.distance_feet` shows,
and no nearer than 5'. Once the battle has
started, send one `ResolveBattleRound` for
each round.

Modes:

`encounter`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - no encounter is open.
- `encounter.none_active` - a second check behind the mode gate, which normal
  play never reaches.

**Events:**

`BattleStartedEvent`. A monster group
whose morale score is 2 flees and gets away at once, with a
`MonsterFledEvent` followed right away by a
`MonsterEscapedEvent`. When every group
has got away, the battle ends at once, with a
`BattleEndedEvent` after the last
`MonsterEscapedEvent`, and the events of the encounter's end.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"enter_dungeon"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

dungeon_id.title: Dungeon Id
dungeon_id.description:
Which dungeon to set out for, by
`DungeonSpec.id` from the adventure's `dungeons`.
The party arrives at the entrance cell, on the first of that dungeon's levels that has
an entrance. The session refuses an id the adventure doesn't have, or a dungeon with no
entrance, with `session.command.unknown_location`.

EnterDungeon.title: EnterDungeon
EnterDungeon.description:
Travel from town to a dungeon's entrance and start exploring.

The party must be in town. The trip takes the number of turns in the town's `travel_turns`
for that dungeon, or no time when that dungeon has no entry there. On arrival the
party stands on the entrance cell facing north, and the session switches to
`exploring`. Leaving town also records what the party's treasure is worth. Under the
on-return XP timing, the treasure XP awarded back in town is the gain over that value.

Modes:

`town`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the party is not in town.
- `session.command.unknown_location` - `dungeon_id` matches no dungeon, or
  the dungeon has no level with an entrance.

**Events:**

First, the events of the travel time passing:
`EffectExpiredEvent` with a
`LightEvent` for a light burning out, and
`ProvisionsEvent` on a day boundary.
The engine makes no wandering-monster checks during travel, and travel doesn't count toward the party's rest,
so no `WanderingCheckEvent` or
`FatigueEvent` appears during travel.

Then `LocationEnteredEvent` for
the dungeon, `via` `"entrance"`, and the entrance cell's entry checks: a
`HoardGeneratedEvent` for area
treasure, a
`DetectionRolledEvent` and a
`TrapEvent` for a room trap with its
resolution, and the opening of an encounter with monsters keyed to that area in the adventure
(`SurpriseRolledEvent`s,
`EncounterStartedEvent`,
`ReactionRolledEvent`,
`StanceChangedEvent`, and
`BattleStartedEvent` when the monsters
attack).

id.title: Id
id.description: The area's authored id.

name.title: Name
name.description: The area's display name.

cells.title: Cells
cells.description: Only the area cells the party has walked, in authored order.

trap_state.title: Trap State
trap_state.description:
The room trap's state as the party knows it, with the values and meaning of
`MapFeatureView.trap_state`: `"found"` once a
`Search` has found it, and `"sprung"` once it has gone off. No
command removes a room trap, so a room never shows `"removed"`.

It's `null` while the party hasn't met the room's trap, and for a room with no trap, so a room
the players know nothing about looks the same whether or not it's trapped. The view lists an area
only once the party has entered it, so a trap found or sprung through a door of a room the party
hasn't entered shows here once the party walks in. Before then, the door shows it in
`EdgeView.trap_state`.

EnteredAreaView.title: EnteredAreaView
EnteredAreaView.description: An authored area after the party has entered at least one of its cells.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"equip_item"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member doing the equipping, by
`MemberView.id`. What they may wear and
wield depends on their class.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
What to equip, which has to be in this member's pack already. Name a magic item by its
per-instance id, because each one is a distinct object. Name a mundane item by its catalog
id, because mundane items stack and have no per-instance id. Both ids are in
`MemberView.inventory`.

EquipItem.title: EquipItem
EquipItem.description:
Equip an item from a member's pack: wear armour or a ring, or wield a weapon (takes no game time).

It's legal in town and while exploring. A weapon has to be equipped before a member can
attack with it in battle. The session checks the member's class rules for armour and
weapons before anything changes. Name a magic item by its instance id, and a mundane
item by its catalog id, because mundane items have no per-instance id. A mundane id is
either a built-in one from `load_equipment` (see the
[equipment id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/))
or one the adventure bundles, which isn't in that index.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - an encounter or battle is underway, or the
  session has ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `exploration.item.not_carried` - nothing by that id is in the member's pack.
- `items.equip.armour_forbidden`, `items.equip.armour_not_allowed`,
  `items.equip.shield_forbidden`, `items.equip.weapon_not_allowed`,
  `items.equip.weapon_forbidden` - the member's class may not use it.
- `items.equip.two_handed_with_shield` - the member would hold a two-handed
  weapon and a shield together.
- `items.equip.not_equippable` - potions, scrolls, ammunition, and gear with no
  combat use can't be equipped.
- `items.equip.not_usable` - the member's class can't use the magic item.
- `items.ring.hands_full` - the member already wears two rings.

**Events:**

Usually none. Equipping a magic item that works while it's worn can attach its
effects (`EffectAttachedEvent`). Putting
on a cursed ring identifies it and reveals its curse
(`ItemIdentifiedEvent`,
`CurseRevealedEvent`).

visibility.description: Player visibility: the players see what was lost.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

target_id.title: Target Id
target_id.description: The entity id of the victim.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
The names of the items that were destroyed, as the players know them: a mundane item's
`name`, like `"Torches (6)"`, an identified magic item's `name`, and an unidentified magic item's
masked name, like `"a sword with a faint aura"`, the `display` that
`MemberView.inventory` showed for it. The event has
player visibility, so it never names an unidentified item by its true name.

saved_items.title: Saved Items
saved_items.description:
The instance ids of the magic items that passed their save and still exist. Empty when none survived,
which is always so when the ruleset's `magic_item_death_save` flag is off.

saved_item_names.title: Saved Item Names
saved_item_names.description:
What to call one of each item in `saved_items`, keyed by the same id, such as
`{"magic-item-0003": "sword with a faint aura"}`. Each name is the name that
`PlayerView.item_names` has for that id, so an unidentified magic
item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never its true name. The save
identifies nothing. The destroyed items are in `item_names`, in a different form: an unidentified item has an
article there, and a mundane item has its printed name. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep
a view, can name the items from the event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the field
existed.

saved_item_names_plural.title: Saved Item Names Plural
saved_item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `saved_item_names`, with the same keys, such as
`{"magic-item-0003": "swords with a faint aura"}`, from
`PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of your
own.

EquipmentDestroyedEvent.title: EquipmentDestroyedEvent
EquipmentDestroyedEvent.description:
What a victim carried was destroyed with it, except any magic items that saved.

`destroy_equipment` reports this when a death destroys the victim and
what it carries, as a dragon's breath or *disintegrate* does. It reports no event for a victim that carried
nothing.

When the ruleset's `magic_item_death_save` flag is on, `destroy_equipment` rolls a save for each magic item, and
`saved_items` lists the ones that survive. `destroy_equipment` leaves them in the victim's inventory.

When the victim is a party member in a dungeon, a `GameSession` moves the
saved items to a drop pile on the party's cell, in the same command. The party picks them up with
`TakeTreasure` and the feature id `"pile"`.

EquipmentItem.title: EquipmentItem
EquipmentItem.description:
One equipment template: `WeaponTemplate`, `ArmourTemplate`, `GearTemplate`, or `AmmunitionTemplate`.

The `item_type` field identifies the template. The JSON is osrlib's model, unchanged.

id.title: Id
id.description:
Equipment identifier, such as `"sword"`. Pass to `GET /v1/rules/equipment/{item_id}`, in
`purchases` on `POST /v1/characters`, or in a session's `purchase_equipment` command.

name.title: Name
name.description: Display name of the item, such as `"Sword"`.

item_type.title: Item Type
item_type.description:
Equipment template category: `"weapon"`, `"armour"` (including shields), `"gear"`
(adventuring gear), or `"ammunition"`.

cost_gp.title: Cost Gp
cost_gp.description: Price in gold pieces for one purchase lot.

EquipmentSummary.title: EquipmentSummary
EquipmentSummary.description: Summary of a mundane equipment item from osrlib's equipment catalogs.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"evade"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

drop.title: Drop
drop.description:
What to scatter behind the party as it runs. `treasure` empties every living member's
purse onto the trail, where the coins are lost, and tempts intelligent monsters to stop
for them. `food` drops one ration from each living member who carries one, and tempts
unintelligent monsters. `none`, the default, drops nothing. The bait is dropped even when
the party gets away at once, but it has an effect only during a pursuit. When nobody has anything
of that kind to drop, the session refuses the command with
`encounter.evade.nothing_to_drop`, and the party doesn't run.

Evade.title: Evade
Evade.description:
Run from the encounter before a battle starts.

An encounter must be open. Monsters whose stance is `attacks` or `hostile` pursue the
party, if any of them can move. A group that is running itself, after a failed morale
check or because its living members are all turned or afraid, doesn't pursue. A group
that stops pursuing during the chase drops out of it, and when no group is left, the
party gets away at once. The party gets away at once when no monster pursues it,
or when it runs faster than the slowest monster that pursues it. Otherwise a pursuit
starts, and each `Wait` or
`DropItems` runs one round of it. `drop` scatters
bait as the party runs: coins tempt intelligent monsters, and food tempts unintelligent
ones. Once battle has started, the party can't evade. The OSE SRD allows evasion only
before combat. The members who can act carry a member who is asleep, paralysed, or turned
to stone at the party's usual rate. They can't carry a member out of a *web*, and a member
who carries more than the maximum load can't run. If nobody in the party can act during a
pursuit, or a member is caught in a *web*, the party stops running, and the pursuers close
the gap at their own rate.

Modes:

`encounter`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - no encounter is open.
- `encounter.none_active` - a second check behind the mode gate, which normal
  play never reaches.
- `encounter.evade.already_evading` - a pursuit is already running.
- `encounter.evade.nobody_able_to_act` - no living member can act, because each one
  is paralysed, petrified, or asleep. A party with nobody able to act can't run.
- `encounter.evade.cannot_move` - the party can't run. The `character` param names a
  living member caught in a *web*. The `reason` param `overloaded` means that a living
  member would still carry more than the maximum load once the drop is made. In
  practice only `treasure` can clear an overload, because it scatters every coin first.
- `encounter.evade.nothing_to_drop` - no living member has coins (for
  `treasure`) or rations (for `food`) to scatter.

`EncounterView.evade_rejections` in the
player view gives the rejections an `Evade` with each `drop` would get now, from the same
check the session makes. Read it to disable a drop the session would refuse.

**Events:**

An `ItemsDroppedEvent` for each member who
scatters bait. For `food`, its `item_ids` has the catalog id of the ration the member
dropped, `rations_standard` or `rations_iron`. Then an
`EvasionEvent` with code
`encounter.evasion.succeeded`, which ends the encounter, or
`encounter.evasion.pursuit`, which starts a pursuit, and the pursuit's first
`PursuitEvent` round. A pursuit ends when the
party escapes, when it exhausts the party at the round limit
(`ExhaustionEvent`, with an
`EffectAttachedEvent` and a
`ConditionGainedEvent` for the
exhaustion), or when the monsters catch the party and battle starts
(`BattleStartedEvent`).

When the encounter ends, the session emits an
`EncounterEndedEvent`, a
`MonsterDefeatedEvent` for each
monster killed or driven off, a
`LootDroppedEvent` when the slain leave
anything on the floor,
`EffectReleasedEvent`s for the
effects that end with it, and, under the immediate XP timing,
`XpAwardedEvent` and
`CharacterLeveledUpEvent`.
The clock then advances by the time the encounter took, with the usual
`LightEvent` and
`ProvisionsEvent` events for that time.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party knows whether it's being followed.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `evasion`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

EvasionEvent.title: EvasionEvent
EvasionEvent.description:
The party tried to get away, and either got away or is being chased.

Emitted by `Evade`. When the party gets clear at
once, the encounter ends in the same result. Otherwise a chase begins, and its
rounds arrive as `PursuitEvent`s, the first in
this same result.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Who may see the event. Filter on it before you show a log to a player.

Event.title: Event
Event.description:
The base class of every osrlib event: a frozen record of one thing the rules did.

Use it as the type you annotate with, as in `list[Event]`. The two fields declared here are the two you can
read on any event: `code`, which identifies what happened, and `visibility`, which is who may see it. The
other fields are on each subclass. Check `event_type` or use `isinstance` to find out which subclass you have.

Subclass it to add events of your own, for rules osrlib doesn't cover. Give the subclass structured fields
only, report each outcome as a code rather than a sentence, and give it an `event_type` that differs from every
osrlib event's. `parse_event` reads only osrlib's events and returns `null` for
yours, so read yours back with your class's `model_validate`. Defining a subclass that turns off `frozen`, or
sets `extra` to anything but `"ignore"`, raises `TypeError`. Either one would break two promises osrlib
makes about every event: the event never changes, and osrlib ignores its unknown fields.

Events never change once made, so you can keep a list of them as a log and read it at any time.

events.title: Events
events.description:
Events after the first `after` events of the requested `visibility`, oldest first. Events
written by a newer osrlib version without a local model class appear as raw JSON objects.

messages.title: Messages
messages.description:
Human-readable English line for each entry in `events` (or the event's `code` for unrecognized
event classes).

next_after.title: Next After
next_after.description:
Cursor value to pass as `after` on the next request to read subsequent events (`after` plus
`len(events)`).

total.title: Total
total.description: Total number of events of the requested `visibility` currently in the session log.

EventPage.title: EventPage
EventPage.description: Slice of a session's chronological event log for one visibility level.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the penalty is on the party's character sheets.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `exhaustion`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

ExhaustionEvent.title: ExhaustionEvent
ExhaustionEvent.description:
The party became exhausted from a long chase, or rested long enough to recover.

Running flat out for a long chase gives a party −2 to its attack and damage rolls
and makes it 2 easier to hit, until it rests. `encounter.exhaustion.gained` comes
from the `Evade`, `Wait`,
or `DropItems` whose round ends a chase that lasted
`PURSUIT_ROUND_CAP` rounds.
`encounter.exhaustion.recovered` comes from the
`Rest` that completes three turns of rest since the
chase.

odometer_thirds.title: Odometer Thirds
odometer_thirds.description:
How far the party has walked during the current turn, in thirds of a foot. When it reaches three
times the party's exploration rate, the clock advances one turn and this resets to zero.

turns_since_rest.title: Turns Since Rest
turns_since_rest.description:
Turns since the party last rested. The fatigue rule counts these, and a
`Rest` resets them.

wandering_counter.title: Wandering Counter
wandering_counter.description:
Turns since the last wandering-monster check. Reaching the level's interval fires the check and
resets this to zero.

noise_since_check.title: Noise Since Check
noise_since_check.description:
Whether the party has made noise since the last wandering check. Every attempt to force a door
makes noise, whether or not the door opens. Noise raises the next check's chance by 1 in 6, and
the check clears it.

sleep_count.title: Sleep Count
sleep_count.description:
How many nights or days the party has slept through. Preparing spells needs a sleep the caster
has not already prepared from.

last_prepared_sleep.title: Last Prepared Sleep
last_prepared_sleep.description:
The `sleep_count` at which each caster last prepared spells, keyed by character id. The session
uses it to allow one preparation per sleep.

alerted_areas.title: Alerted Areas
alerted_areas.description:
The keyed areas whose monsters have been alerted, as `"{dungeon}:{level}:{area}"` references.
Monsters that heard the party coming are not surprised when it walks in.

heard_areas.title: Heard Areas
heard_areas.description:
The keyed areas the party has heard something in, as `"{dungeon}:{level}:{area}"` references.
A party that knows what stands behind the door is not surprised by it.

provisions_day.title: Provisions Day
provisions_day.description:
How many whole game days of food and water the session has charged the party for, counting from
the start of the session. Each time the clock passes into a new day, the session charges the
party for the day and adds one to this.

ExplorationCounters.title: ExplorationCounters
ExplorationCounters.description:
The exploration counters a session keeps between commands: distance, rest, wandering, noise, sleep, food.

You get one from `RefereeView.exploration`. These
are the counters `GameSession` keeps as attributes, under the
same names, and a save contains them under its `exploration` key. They're for the referee, and none
of them reaches `PlayerView`, which reports the party's fatigue,
exhaustion, and deprivation as yes-or-no status instead.

dungeon_id.title: Dungeon Id
dungeon_id.description: The id of the dungeon this level belongs to.

cells.title: Cells
cells.description:
The known cells as `(x, y)` pairs: the cells the party has walked, then the cells
it remembers having seen, then the cells its light shows from where it stands right
now. When a member lights a torch, the next view includes the lit room, even if the party
hasn't moved.

edges.title: Edges
edges.description:
The edges around those cells, keyed by the canonical edge key that
`edge_key` returns, in the form `"{x},{y}:north"` or
`"{x},{y}:west"`. Each physical edge appears once, so a wall between two known cells
is one entry, not two.

areas.title: Areas
areas.description: The authored areas the party has entered, with only their walked cells.

features.title: Features
features.description: The features the party can currently see or has discovered.

transitions.title: Transitions
transitions.description: The transitions on known cells, without destinations or gates.

entrance.title: Entrance
entrance.description: The level's entrance when the party knows that cell, otherwise `null`.

ExploredLevelView.title: ExploredLevelView
ExploredLevelView.description:
One level's explored map: the cells the party knows, and the edges around them.

You get these from `PlayerView.explored`, one
for each level the party knows anything about. This is the map to draw. The party knows
nothing outside it.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"extinguish_source"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member whose light goes out, by
`MemberView.id`. Every torch and lantern this member has
burning goes out, and the remaining burn time is lost rather than saved for later.

ExtinguishSource.title: ExtinguishSource
ExtinguishSource.description:
Put out every torch and lantern one member has burning (takes no game time).

It's legal in town and while exploring. The remaining burn time is lost. A doused torch
is gone, and a doused lantern's oil is gone too, so lighting it again with
`LightSource` burns a new flask. A light from a
spell or a magic sword isn't affected.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - an encounter or battle is underway, or the
  session has ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `exploration.light.not_burning` - the member has no torch or lantern burning.

**Events:**

For each doused source, an
`EffectReleasedEvent` and a
`LightEvent` with code
`exploration.light.extinguished`.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party feels it, and the penalty is on their sheets.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `fatigue`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

FatigueEvent.title: FatigueEvent
FatigueEvent.description:
The party gained the penalty for going without rest, or recovered from it.

The B/X rules require a party to rest one turn in every six while it's in a dungeon. A
turn is 10 minutes of game time, or 60 rounds. A party that goes six turns without a rest
takes −1 to attack and damage rolls until it rests. These two codes mark when the penalty
starts and when it lifts.

`exploration.fatigue.gained` comes from any command that passes a turn while the session
is in `exploring` mode, once the party has gone six turns without a rest. Under the
`deprivation_penalties` ruleset flag, three turns are enough when a living member has gone
a full day without food or water. See
`check_fatigue`.

`exploration.fatigue.recovered` comes from a `Rest` once the
party has rested one full turn. One full turn of rest is enough, even if a wandering
monster interrupts the rest after that.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The feature's id. It has to be unique across the level, counting the features on the level
and on all its areas together. The id `"pile"` is reserved for the drop pile on a cell, and
`validate_adventure` reports a feature that
uses it.

The `feature_id` of `TakeTreasure`,
`InspectTreasure`, and
`RemoveTreasureTrap` takes either this id or the
opaque `feature:` handle in `MapFeatureView.id`, and
both forms stay supported. A player client sends the handle, because the player view lists
only handles. A referee tool can send this id. Both forms resolve against the same features,
the ones the party can reach where it stands, so this id reaches and reveals nothing that a
handle doesn't. A command that names a feature on another cell or level, or a construction
trick the party hasn't found, gets the same `exploration.feature.unknown` rejection as an id
that no feature has. A handle always names one feature. This id names two when a cache the
session generated on the same cell has the same id, like `"cache-0001"`, and the session
refuses it with that rejection too.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
What kind of feature this is. osrlib runs `"treasure_cache"` for the party. You decide what
`"construction_trick"` and `"custom"` do.

description.title: Description
description.description:
What the players read about the feature. The player view shows it as
`MapFeatureView.description` once the feature
comes into view. A feature without a `cell` comes into view when the party enters its area,
and a feature on a cell comes into view when that cell is on the party's map, because the party
has walked it, remembers seeing it, or lights it now. A construction trick also has to be found
first.

The players read a cache's description before anyone opens it, and they still read it after
the party empties it. So write what the party sees from outside, like "A banded chest under
the altar", and never what's inside or a trap the party hasn't found. Put the contents in the
cache's `item_ids`, `magic_item_ids`, `coins`, and `valuables`, the trap in `trap`, and
anything else meant for the referee alone in `referee_notes`.

Events contain the feature's id, not its text, so look the text up here.

referee_notes.title: Referee Notes
referee_notes.description:
What the referee reads about the feature, and the players never do: what a cache holds, how
its trap is hidden, or what a module's author tells the referee about it. Empty means you
wrote none.

osrlib never reads it, no event includes it, and no rule depends on it. It's in the adventure
document, so a save and the referee view's
`RefereeView.adventure` have it, and the player
view never does. Write what the players may read in `description`.

cell.title: Cell
cell.description:
The cell the feature is on. A feature listed on a level needs one. A feature listed on an area
can leave it `null`, and then the party can reach it from any cell of the area. When you set it
on an area's feature, it has to be one of the area's cells, and
`validate_adventure` reports one that isn't.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
Ordinary items in the cache, by template id, one item for each id. Use an id from
`load_equipment()`, listed in
[the equipment id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/),
or the id of an item in the adventure's `items`.

magic_item_ids.title: Magic Item Ids
magic_item_ids.description:
Magic items in the cache, by template id. Use an id from
`load_magic_items()`, listed in
[the magic item id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/magic-items/).
You can't bundle magic items in an adventure, so only built-in ids work here.

coins.description: Coins in the cache, by denomination.

valuables.title: Valuables
valuables.description:
Named gems and jewellery in the cache. See
`ValuableSpec`.

trap.description:
A trap guarding the cache, or `null`. It has to be a treasure trap, which can spring when the
party opens the cache. A thief finds it with
`InspectTreasure` and takes it out with
`RemoveTreasureTrap`. Each character gets one try at
each. A failed removal springs the trap, unless
`Ruleset.failed_trap_removal_springs` is off.

FeatureSpec.title: FeatureSpec
FeatureSpec.description:
A keyed thing in a room: a treasure cache, a construction trick, or custom content.

Put features on an `AreaSpec`, or on a
`LevelSpec` for one outside any room. A feature is something in
the dungeon that the party can find and act on. Stairs aren't features: they are
`TransitionSpec`s.

osrlib runs one kind of feature for you, the `treasure_cache`. The party empties it with
`TakeTreasure` and the feature's id, and the contents go to
the party. The session creates the magic items you list only when the party empties the cache.
It rolls their details then, like charges, quantities, or whether a sword is intelligent, on the
treasure stream, with `instantiate_magic_item`. A
`construction_trick` is one of the OSE SRD's odd architectural features, like a room that rotates
or a passage that is an illusion. The party finds one with a
`Search` for construction, and you describe what it does.
osrlib does nothing with a `custom` feature.

loc.title: Loc
loc.description:
Path to the invalid value: starts with `body`, `query`, `path`, or `header`, followed by field names and
0-based array indices. The server truncates each string segment to at most 128 characters.

msg.title: Msg
msg.description: Human-readable validation failure message, at most 128 characters.

type.title: Type
type.description:
Machine-readable validation error identifier, such as `missing`, `extra_forbidden`, or
`string_control_character`.

FieldError.title: FieldError
FieldError.description: One part of a request that failed validation.

condition_type.title: Condition Type
condition_type.description:
The discriminator value, `flag_equals`. It appears in every document that
includes this condition, and you never set it yourself.

key.title: Key
key.description: The name of the flag to read, as it appears in `session.flags`.

value.title: Value
value.description:
The value the flag has to have. Values of different types are never equal, so write
the same type that the `SetFlag` for this flag writes.

FlagEqualsCondition.title: FlagEqualsCondition
FlagEqualsCondition.description:
A condition that holds when a session flag equals `value`.

You write flags with `SetFlag`, and a trigger's
consequences can write them too. That's how a lever in one room opens a portcullis in
another: a trigger sets the flag, and a gate tests it. The comparison goes through
`flag_values_equal`, which is strict. A flag
that was never written equals nothing, not even `false`, and a stored `true` doesn't
match an authored `1`.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: flags are bookkeeping that the players don't see.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `flag_set`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

value.title: Value
value.description: What it was set to. Writing an existing key replaces its value.

FlagSetEvent.title: FlagSetEvent
FlagSetEvent.description:
A session flag was written.

Emitted by the referee's `SetFlag`. Flags are
where the session records state. An adventure's triggers and gates can depend on a flag
through a `FlagEqualsCondition`, and you can
store anything else you need there.

It has referee visibility, because flags record the game's state, not events in the
story the players see.

pattern_type.title: Pattern Type
pattern_type.description:
The discriminator value, `flag_set`. It appears in the document, and you
never set it yourself.

key.title: Key
key.description: The name of the flag to watch.

value.title: Value
value.description:
The written value to match, or `null` to match any write of the flag. A flag value is
a `str`, an `int`, or a `bool`, never `null`, so `null` can't be mistaken for a value.
The pattern compares values with
`flag_values_equal`, the same strict comparison
a `FlagEqualsCondition` uses, so a written
`true` doesn't match an authored `1`.

FlagSetPattern.title: FlagSetPattern
FlagSetPattern.description:
A pattern that matches a write to a session flag.

It matches the write, not the flag's state. When you execute
`SetFlag`, or the interpreter executes it for a trigger,
the session emits a `FlagSetEvent`, and a trigger with a
pattern for that flag fires. The pattern compares the value that was written, so writing a flag again with the
value it already has still matches. To test the value a flag has now, use a
`FlagEqualsCondition` instead.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"force_door"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

direction.description:
Which side of the party's cell the stuck door is on, from the `door` edges in
`ExploredLevelView.edges`. The session refuses a door
that isn't stuck with `exploration.door.not_stuck`. Open that one with
`OpenDoor`, which makes no noise.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who tries to force the door, by
`MemberView.id`. The member's STR sets the open-doors
chance, so send the strongest member. If the door gives way, a door trap the party hasn't
found springs on this member.

ForceDoor.title: ForceDoor
ForceDoor.description:
Force a stuck door open with one member's STR-based open-doors roll (takes no game time).

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`). Every attempt makes noise, so
the next wandering-monster check gets the noise bonus. A failed attempt also alerts the
area beyond the door, so its monsters can't be surprised when the party meets them
there. A door that gives way counts as opened: each room trap that triggers on `open`
in the area on either side gets its 2-in-6 chance to spring, unless the party has found
it. The trap springs on the member who forced the door, or on the next member standing
if an earlier spring killed them.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member cannot act.
- `exploration.door.no_door` - no known door on that side of the cell.
- `exploration.door.already_open` - the door already stands open.
- `exploration.door.locked` - the door is locked, and forcing doesn't open a
  lock. Pick it with `PickLock` first.
- `exploration.door.not_stuck` - the door isn't stuck. Open it with
  `OpenDoor`.
- `exploration.door.gate_refused` - the door has an authored
  condition (`GateSpec`) the party doesn't
  meet. The session checks the gate before the attempt, so a refused attempt
  makes no noise, alerts nobody, and costs no roll.

**Events:**

`ItemConsumedEvent` first when
the gate takes an item as a toll, then
`DoorEvent` with code
`exploration.door.forced` on success, which includes the gate's success text
when its author wrote one, or `exploration.door.stuck` on failure. A door that
gives way is followed by the trap events of each door trap's spring check, as
for `OpenDoor`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: it's the party's ending.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `game_over`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

reason.title: Reason
reason.description:
Why the session ended, as a short phrase. Every ending has the same reason, that the party
has fallen. What killed them is in the events just before it.

GameOverEvent.title: GameOverEvent
GameOverEvent.description:
No party member is left standing, and the session has ended.

A member stands while they are neither dead nor turned to stone. Emitted by the command
during which the last standing member died or was petrified, whatever felled them: a
lost battle, a trap, a fall down a chute, starvation, a poison that took effect
while the referee moved the clock, or a basilisk's gaze. It comes after that command's other
events, and the session mode becomes `game_over`.

The session refuses play commands from then on. Referee commands still work, and
`PlaceParty` takes the session out of
`game_over`. Placing the fallen party in town lets the temple raise the dead with
`PurchaseHealing`. The temple has no cure for
stone, so a statue needs *stone to flesh* from a magic-user, who can join the party in town
with `AddMember`.

condition.title: Condition
condition.description:
The condition the party has to meet. A gate has exactly one, and the engine evaluates
it against the session at the moment of each attempt. To require two things, put the
second condition on a trigger that sets a flag, and test that flag here with a
`FlagEqualsCondition`.

narrative.description:
The authored text for both outcomes. osrlib reads two fields of a gate's block,
`refusal` and `success`, and ignores the rest. With `null`, the gate has no text, and
the rejection has no `refusal` parameter.

GateSpec.title: GateSpec
GateSpec.description:
A condition the party has to meet to get through, with the authored text for both outcomes.

Put one in the `requires` field of a
`DoorSpec` or a
`TransitionSpec` when you build the dungeon.
The engine checks it every time the party tries that door, stair, or passage. When the
condition fails, the session rejects the attempt and puts the `refusal` text in the
rejection's `refusal` parameter. A refused attempt costs the party nothing: no dice, no
game time, no item, and no change to the door. On a successful attempt, the command's
event contains the `success` text in its `narrative`.

The engine checks a door's gate only when the party opens or forces the door. If you
open a gated door with `SetDoorState`, the party
walks through it freely until the door closes again.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The catalog id, for example `"torch"`. Get every id from `load_equipment`, or see
[the equipment id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/).

name.title: Name
name.description:
The display name as the price list prints it, which includes the lot size for gear sold in lots:
`"Torches (6)"`, `"Iron spikes (12)"`.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
What to call one unit of this gear in a sentence, like `"torch"` or `"vial of holy water"`.

It names one of the units that `ItemInstance.quantity`
counts, not a lot from the price list, so `"Torches (6)"` is `"torch"`, and a stack of six reads
"6 torches". Where the price list names a substance, it names the container or the measure the
session counts: `"vial of holy water"`, `"flask of oil"`, `"pint of wine"`. It's lowercase unless a
word is a proper noun or an abbreviation, and it has no article, so put a number or an article in
front of it. `PlayerView.item_names` gives it to the players' client.

A template you write that leaves it out gets its `name`.

display_name_plural.title: Display Name Plural
display_name_plural.description:
What to call two or more units, like `"torches"` or `"vials of holy water"`.

`PlayerView.item_names_plural` gives it to the players' client. A
template you write that leaves it out gets `display_name` with the regular English ending on the word that names the
item: the last word before the first `of`, `with`, or `vs`, a comma, a bonus like `+1`, a closing Roman numeral, or
an opening parenthesis, or the last word when the name has none of them. So `"Idol of the drowned saint"` becomes
`"Idols of the drowned saint"`, and `"Lantern (hooded)"` becomes `"Lanterns (hooded)"`. The ending is `s`, or `es`
after `s`, `x`, `z`, `ch`, or `sh`, or `ies` in place of a `y` that follows a consonant, and `staff` becomes
`staves` with its capital kept, so `"Staff of the Magi"` becomes `"Staves of the Magi"`. The connecting words count
in any case, so `"Staff Of Power"` becomes `"Staves Of Power"`, and any spaces after the word stay after the ending.
The compiled plural of every built-in template follows the same rule. Set it yourself when the name is already
plural, like `"Torches (6)"`, or when the plural is irregular.

cost_gp.title: Cost Gp
cost_gp.description: The listed price in gold pieces, for one lot.

lot_size.title: Lot Size
lot_size.description: How many units one purchase at `cost_gp` delivers. 1 for gear sold singly.

capacity_coins.title: Capacity Coins
capacity_coins.description:
How much fits in the container, in coins of weight, where the SRD gives a figure (backpack, small sack, large
sack). `null` for gear that contains nothing. osrlib doesn't enforce the figure, so if you want container
limits, enforce them yourself.

combat.description:
The combat statistics for the three items that are also weapons. See
`CombatFacet`. `null` for everything else.

params.title: Params
params.description:
The exploration mechanics the SRD's gear table prints, keyed by name: a torch's `burn_turns` and
`light_radius_feet`, the tinder box's `light_chance_in_six`, and so on. The dungeon-crawl procedures in
`osrlib.crawl.exploration` read these.

overrides_applied.title: Overrides Applied
overrides_applied.description:
Which fields were corrected when this row was compiled from the SRD text, as dotted paths. Empty when none were.
osrlib doesn't read it during play.

GearTemplate.title: GearTemplate
GearTemplate.description:
A piece of adventuring gear: a torch, a rope, a backpack, a flask of oil.

Every item on the equipment list that isn't a weapon, armour, or ammunition is gear. Get
one from `EquipmentCatalog.get` and buy it
with `purchase`. Gear sells in lots: one purchase at the
listed price delivers `lot_size` units, so buying torches once costs 1 gp and yields
six torches in one `ItemInstance`.

`equip` accepts only gear with a `combat` facet: the torch,
holy water, and burning oil. Gear has no per-item weight in the SRD, so detailed
encumbrance adds a flat
`MISC_GEAR_WEIGHT_COINS` once for carrying
any of it.

roll_min.title: Roll Min
roll_min.description: The lowest d20 result in this band.

roll_max.title: Roll Max
roll_max.description: The highest d20 result in this band.

value_gp.title: Value Gp
value_gp.description: What a gem rolled in this band is worth, in gold pieces.

GemValueBand.title: GemValueBand
GemValueBand.description:
One band of the gem value table, which gives what a gem is worth for a range of d20 rolls.

The bands are in `GemValueTable.bands`. Generation
reads them for you, and
`GemValueTable.value_for_roll` reads
them for a roll you made yourself. Read a band directly only to show the table.

bands.title: Bands
bands.description: The gem value bands, covering the whole d20. See `GemValueBand`.

jewellery_dice.title: Jewellery Dice
jewellery_dice.description: What one piece of jewellery is worth, as a dice expression.

manual_notes.title: Manual Notes
manual_notes.description:
The rules the referee applies by hand, as printed: that rough treatment can halve a piece of jewellery's value,
and that several gems may be combined into fewer, larger ones. osrlib does neither. If you use these rules, show
them to the referee.

GemValueTable.title: GemValueTable
GemValueTable.description:
The tables that give what a gem and a piece of jewellery are worth.

Generation rolls each gem's value on the d20 bands and each piece of jewellery's value on
`jewellery_dice`. It records the value on a
`ValuableInstance`, and the value never changes
after that. Roll a gem yourself with
`value_for_roll`.

name.title: Name
name.description: Character name, 1 to 100 characters, without control characters such as tabs or newlines.

class_id.title: Class Id
class_id.description:
Character class `id` from `GET /v1/rules/classes`, such as `fighter`. Must meet the class's
ability score requirements (`eligible_class_ids` on `POST /v1/ability-rolls`).

adjustment.description:
Optional point trade between ability scores before rolling hit points, as osrlib's
`AbilityAdjustment`. Map abilities to lower in `lowered` and abilities to raise in `raised`
using keys `str`, `int`, `wis`, `dex`, `con`, and `cha`. osrlib's descriptions of `lowered` and
`raised` name `ADJUSTMENT_FLOOR` and `MAX_SCORE`, which are osrlib's Python constants for the
lowest and the highest score a trade can leave. For the scores a trade can reach from a stored
ability roll with this class, and the reason for each limit, call
`GET /v1/ability-rolls/{roll_id}/adjustment-limits`. If osrlib refuses the trade, creation fails with 422
`character_invalid` and `rejections`. Omit or set to `null` to keep the rolled scores.

starting_spell_ids.title: Starting Spell Ids
starting_spell_ids.description:
First-level spell `id` values from `GET /v1/rules/spells` for an arcane caster's starting
spell book. A first-level `magic_user` or `elf` requires exactly one first-level `magic_user`
spell. Leave empty (`[]`) for every other class.

extra_languages.title: Extra Languages
extra_languages.description:
Extra language `id` values from `GET /v1/rules/languages` (entries with `choosable` set to
`true`), up to the bonus languages granted by the character's adjusted Intelligence score.

purchases.title: Purchases
purchases.description:
Starting equipment bought in list order from rolled starting gold (3d6 x 10 gp). To show the
player their gold before they shop, call `POST /v1/ability-rolls/{roll_id}/preview` with the
same roll, class, and `ruleset`, and read `rolls.gold_roll.total`. The purchases don't change
the gold roll.

equip_item_ids.title: Equip Item Ids
equip_item_ids.description:
Purchased item `id` values to wear or wield, applied in list order. Each entry equips one
purchased stack from `purchases` and must be permitted for `class_id`.

ruleset.description:
Optional rules for the creation rolls, as osrlib's `Ruleset`. Send the ruleset of the table
the character is for, the one you pass to `POST /v1/sessions`. Creation reads three of its
fields, and the others change nothing here:

- `ability_score_method`: `"3d6"` (the default) or `"4d6_drop_lowest"`. With an ability roll,
  it must be the method the roll was made with, or the request gets 409
  `ability_roll_ruleset_mismatch`.
- `hp_reroll_at_first_level`: reroll a first-level hit die that shows 1 or 2.
- `max_hp_at_first_level`: count the first-level hit die as its maximum.

Omit or set to `null` for the rules as written.

anyOf.description: Random number seed, an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991).

seed.title: Seed
seed.description:
Optional seed (0 to 2^53 - 1) for all creation rolls. Any caller may pass `seed` to reproduce
the character, or omit it to let the server draw one.

GenerateCharacterRequest.title: GenerateCharacterRequest
GenerateCharacterRequest.description: Choices and optional seed for rolling an unstored character via `POST /v1/generate/character`.

cell_ref.title: Cell Ref
cell_ref.description:
The cell the cache is on, as a `cell_ref` string. A lair
hoard is on the first cell in its area's `cells`. An area's rolled treasure is on the cell where
the party entered the area. The party has to stand on this cell to take the cache.

treasure_types.title: Treasure Types
treasure_types.description:
The tables the treasure was rolled on, for display and for a referee who wants to see them.
For treasure type letters, it contains the letters, like `("C",)`. For unguarded treasure, it is
`("unguarded",)`. For a lair hoard that is only a fixed number of gold pieces, it is empty.

coins.description: The coins in the cache, by denomination.

valuables.title: Valuables
valuables.description: The gems and jewellery in the cache, each with an id.

magic_items.title: Magic Items
magic_items.description: The magic items in the cache, each an instance with its charges or quantity already rolled.

origin.title: Origin
origin.description:
How the cache was created. New area treasure uses `"area"`, a keyed encounter's hoard uses
`"lair"`, and a cache loaded from an old save without provenance uses `"legacy"`.

lair_area_ref.title: Lair Area Ref
lair_area_ref.description:
The canonical area reference for a lair cache, or `null` for area treasure and legacy
caches.

GeneratedCache.title: GeneratedCache
GeneratedCache.description:
Treasure the session rolled and put down in the dungeon, recorded in the overlay.

A cache you write is a `FeatureSpec`, and it never changes.
This is the other kind: treasure the session rolled for a keyed encounter's lair hoard or for an
`AreaTreasureSpec`. The session puts it in
`DungeonState.generated_caches` under a new
internal id like `"cache-0001"`, and reports that id in a
`HoardGeneratedEvent`. When the party takes it with
`TakeTreasure`, the player view supplies an opaque
`MapFeatureView.id`. A current caller can still use an
unambiguous raw internal id for compatibility. The session removes a taken cache. Whatever the
party can't carry goes into a `DropPile` on the same cell.

The session never traps treasure it rolls, so the only trapped treasure is treasure you write.
That choice is one of the entries in
[the adaptations register](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/adaptations/), the page that
lists where osrlib picks one reading of an unclear rule or sets a default behind a
`Ruleset` option.

seed.title: Seed
seed.description: Random number seed, an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991).

derived.description: Combat, saving throw, modifier, and language values computed by osrlib from `character`.

rolls.description: Individual dice rolled for ability scores, hit points, and starting gold.

GeneratedCharacterResponse.title: GeneratedCharacterResponse
GeneratedCharacterResponse.description: Unstored first-level character, derived stats, creation dice, and seed.

magic_items.title: Magic Items
magic_items.description:
The magic items, already rolled up as instances.
See `MagicItemInstance`.

GeneratedTreasure.title: GeneratedTreasure
GeneratedTreasure.description:
Everything one roll of a treasure table produced.

`generate_treasure`,
`generate_unguarded_treasure`, and
`generate_treasure_entries` return
one. These functions don't place the treasure or give it to anyone. Put the coins in a purse, the valuables and
