magic items in an
`Inventory`, or keep the whole thing in a dungeon feature
until the party opens it. Any of the three fields can be empty, and an unlucky roll
leaves all three empty.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"give_items"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member handing the goods over, by
`MemberView.id`. The session refuses the recipient's id
here with `exploration.give.same_member`.

recipient_id.title: Recipient Id
recipient_id.description:
The member taking the goods, by
`MemberView.id`. Both members have to be alive and able
to act.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
What changes hands, one unit per entry, so repeat an id to give more than one. Name items
the same way as in `DropItems.item_ids`: a
catalog id for a mundane item, and a per-instance id for a magic item, a gem, or a piece
of jewellery. As there, the session refuses a per-instance id named twice with
`exploration.item.not_carried`. A magic item that was equipped releases its effects and
arrives unequipped in the recipient's pack.

coins.description:
Coins to hand over, by denomination. The default hands over none. Coins move from the
giver's purse to the recipient's, which is how a party evens out the weight after it takes
a lot of treasure.

GiveItems.title: GiveItems
GiveItems.description:
Hand items and coins from one party member to another.

Use it to spread the load across the party, or to put an item in the hands of the
member who can use it. `character_id` is the giver, and `recipient_id` is the member
who takes the goods. A magic item that was equipped releases its effects and arrives
unequipped in the recipient's pack. Both members must be alive and able to act.

It's legal in town, while exploring, and during an encounter. In town and while
exploring, it takes no game time. During an encounter, it uses up the encounter round,
and the monsters then act on their reaction to the party, as for a
`Wait`. While monsters pursue the party, that round is a
round of the pursuit. The party stands together outside a battle, so any member can
reach any other.

In a battle, a member hands over one item as their declaration for the round: a
`BattleDeclaration` with
`action="give_item"`. The session refuses this command in battle.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - a battle is underway, or the session has ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` or `recipient_id` matches
  no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the giver or the recipient can't
  act.
- `exploration.give.same_member` - the giver and the recipient are the same member.
- `items.curse.stuck` - a cursed item whose curse has been revealed can't be
  handed over.
- `exploration.item.not_carried` - the giver doesn't carry one of the items, or
  enough of the coins.

**Events:**

`EffectReleasedEvent`s for the effects of
an equipped magic item, then an
`ItemsGivenEvent` with what changed hands.
In an encounter, the encounter round's events follow. During a pursuit, a
`PursuitEvent` round follows instead.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"grant_coins"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member whose purse receives the coins, by
`MemberView.id`. A command you issue yourself has a
member id here, and the session refuses any other value with `session.command.unknown_member`.
A consequence or a reward in an adventure document has a party selector instead,
`"@party"` for every living member or `"@first"` for the first living member, because the
session assigns member ids when it starts. The trigger and quest interpreter replaces the selector
with member ids before it issues the command.

coins.description:
The coins to add to the member's purse, by denomination. The session doesn't check
weight, so a large grant can overload the member. An overloaded member slows the whole
party, or stops it moving, and then the session refuses
`MoveParty` with `exploration.move.cannot_move`.

GrantCoins.title: GrantCoins
GrantCoins.description:
Referee: put coins straight into a member's purse.

Use it to pay out a reward. This command is legal in every mode, `game_over` and
`victory` included.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`, `battle`, `game_over`, `victory`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.

**Events:**

`ItemAcquiredEvent` with the coins' value
and `origin` `"grant"`, so you can tell a granted reward from treasure the
party took.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"grant_item"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who receives the item, by
`MemberView.id`. A command you issue yourself has a
member id here, and the session refuses any other value with `session.command.unknown_member`.
A consequence or a reward in an adventure document has a party selector instead,
`"@party"` for every living member or `"@first"` for the first living member, because the
session assigns member ids when it starts. The trigger and quest interpreter replaces the selector
with member ids before it issues the command.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
Which item to create, by id. The session looks first in its
`effective_equipment` catalog. That
catalog has the built-in ids from `load_equipment` (see the
[equipment id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/))
and the ids the adventure bundles. Then it looks in the magic item catalog from
`load_magic_items` (see the
[magic item id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/magic-items/)).

quantity.title: Quantity
quantity.description:
How many to place, from 1 to 1,000, counted as single items rather than as purchase lots.
`quantity=6` grants six torches, the same number one lot of torches from
`PurchaseEquipment` delivers. For a magic
item, it's the number of separate magic items to create, each with its own instance id
and its own rolls. `quantity=2` of a bundle of arrows +1 grants two bundles. To grant more
than 1,000, send the command again.

GrantItem.title: GrantItem
GrantItem.description:
Referee: put an item straight into a member's pack.

Use it to hand out a reward, a found item, a starting kit, or a potion the party buys
from a shop your game runs. The command charges nothing. To charge a price, also send
`RemoveCoins`. This command is legal in every mode,
`game_over` and `victory` included.

The session creates a magic item the same way it creates treasure. The item arrives
unidentified.
`instantiate_magic_item` rolls whatever the
item's page leaves to chance, like a wand's charges, on
`TREASURE_STREAM`. A mundane grant makes no draws.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`, `battle`, `game_over`, `victory`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.unknown_item` - `item_id` matches no item in the session's
  `effective_equipment`
  catalog or the magic item catalog.

**Events:**

`ItemAcquiredEvent` with `origin`
`"grant"`. Its `item_ids` list a mundane item's catalog id once for each unit, and
each new magic item's instance id.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party watches them come on or draw off.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `group_moved`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

group_id.title: Group Id
group_id.description: Which group moved, as its encounter group id.

distance_feet.title: Distance Feet
distance_feet.description:
How far that group now is from the party line, in feet, after the move. A group that closes
in stops within `MELEE_RANGE_FEET` of the nearest
member it can see, where the two fight hand to hand.

GroupMovedEvent.title: GroupMovedEvent
GroupMovedEvent.description:
A monster group's distance from the party line changed.

The party line is where the party stood when the encounter opened. Each group's distance is
measured from it, and each party member stands at their own place on the same track, which
`MemberMovedEvent` reports. When every member the
monsters can see has fallen back behind the line, the line moves back to the foremost of them,
and every group's distance grows by the same amount with no event, because nobody moved toward
or away from anyone. `BattleState.advance_feet`
describes it.

Emitted by `ResolveBattleRound`
whenever a group's distance changes: monsters closing to strike, a broken group running
away, and the whole party backing away from every group in a formation move. A member who
closes on a group by themselves doesn't move the group, so that emits a `MemberMovedEvent`
and no `GroupMovedEvent`.

The event reports the group's distance right after its move. When the party line moves back
later in the round, the distance grows with no event, so use this event to narrate or animate
the move, not to draw where the group stands. A member's distance to this group is the group's
`distance_feet` minus the member's entry in
`EncounterView.advance_feet`, and
`EncounterGroupView.member_distance_feet`
lists it for you in the player view after the round.

condition_type.title: Condition Type
condition_type.description:
The discriminator value, `has_item`. It appears in every document that
includes this condition, and you never set it yourself.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
The catalog id to look for, from the equipment catalog (built-in items plus the
adventure's bundled ones) or the magic-item catalog.

consumes.title: Consumes
consumes.description:
Whether the session takes the item on a successful attempt. `true` makes the item a toll:
every time the gated command succeeds, the session takes one of the item from the first
member in marching order who carries it. A door that swings shut then needs another key to
open. Only a gate can charge a toll. In a trigger's or a quest's conditions, `true` fails
validation with a pydantic `ValidationError`, because a trigger or a quest reacts to
something that has already happened, and there's no attempt to charge.

HasItemCondition.title: HasItemCondition
HasItemCondition.description:
A condition that holds when the party carries an item with `item_id`, mundane or magic.

Put it in the `condition` of a `GateSpec` for a door
that opens only with a key. Put it in the `conditions` of a
`TriggerSpec` or a quest's
`TriggerClause` to make the trigger or clause
match only while someone carries the item. Any member's inventory satisfies it,
equipped items included. The party carries its dead and their packs, so a key in a
dead member's pack still counts.

`item_id` has to be in the equipment catalog, which is the built-in items plus the
adventure's bundled items, or in the magic-item catalog.
`GameSession.new` runs
`validate_adventure`, which raises
`ContentValidationError` for an id in neither
catalog.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description:
Player visibility: everyone sees a wound close. The hit points the creature now has are in the
`HitPointsReportedEvent` that follows, which only the referee
sees.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

target_id.title: Target Id
target_id.description: The entity id of the creature that was healed.

amount.title: Amount
amount.description: The hit points restored, after the maximum and any halving. 0 when the healing was blocked.

source.title: Source
source.description:
Where the healing came from: `magical` for a spell or potion, `natural` for rest, or `regeneration` for a
regenerating creature.

HealingAppliedEvent.title: HealingAppliedEvent
HealingAppliedEvent.description:
Hit points restored, or healing refused.

`apply_healing` reports this, and so does
`EffectsLedger.advance` each round a regeneration effect heals. Read
`amount`, not the amount you asked for: healing stops at the creature's maximum hit points, and a cursed creature
may have had it halved.

`apply_healing` can also refuse healing. Then the code is `combat.healing.blocked` and `amount` is 0. A diseased
creature gets no magical healing, and a weakened one gets no healing at all.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party bought it.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `healing_purchased`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member the service was cast on. Their purse is charged first, but the party covers
whatever is left, so read `payers` for who actually paid.

service.title: Service
service.description:
Which service was bought, as its key in
`HEALING_SERVICES`, like `"cure_light_wounds"`.

cost_gp.title: Cost Gp
cost_gp.description: What it cost, in gold pieces.

payers.title: Payers
payers.description:
The ids of the members whose purses paid, in the order they were charged: the treated
member first, then the rest of the party in marching order, dead members included. Each purse
pays as much of the fee still owed as its coins' value covers, in whole gold pieces, until the
fee is paid. A member whose purse paid nothing isn't listed. It's empty on an event loaded from
a save written before the field existed.

payments_gp.title: Payments Gp
payments_gp.description:
What each purse in `payers` paid, in gold pieces and in the same order. The entries sum to
`cost_gp`.

HealingPurchasedEvent.title: HealingPurchasedEvent
HealingPurchasedEvent.description:
The party paid for a temple service, and the temple cast it.

Emitted by `PurchaseHealing` in town,
followed by the kernel events of the spell the temple casts. The fee can come from
more than one member, so `payers` and `payments_gp` show which purses paid and how
much each one paid.

visibility.description:
Player visibility: the party sees its own member slip into the shadows, but not whether the
monsters noticed.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `hide_attempted`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who tried to hide, by party member id.

HideAttemptedEvent.title: HideAttemptedEvent
HideAttemptedEvent.description:
A party member tried to hide in shadows during a battle.

Emitted by `ResolveBattleRound` in the party's
movement step, after the members' moves, once for each member whose `hide` declaration
resolves, in marching order. The member is then hiding, as
`EncounterView.hiding` shows.

The event says only that the member tried. The session rolls the member's hide in shadows
skill in secret, as the OSE SRD's "the thief does not immediately know if the attempt was
successful" says, and reports the roll to the referee in a
`DetectionRolledEvent` of kind
`"hide_in_shadows"`. That event comes right after this one, so each member who hides adds
the two events in this order, before the next member's. The players learn how it went from the
`AttackRolledEvent.back_stab` of the
member's back-stab from hiding.

count.title: Count
count.description: The number of hit dice the class has at this level. At least 1.

die.title: Die
die.description:
The number of sides on each die, which is the class's hit die: 4 for the magic-user and thief, 6 for the cleric,
elf, and halfling, and 8 for the dwarf and fighter.

bonus.title: Bonus
bonus.description: The flat hit points added to the dice, which is how a character gains hit points past name level. At least 0.

con_applies.title: Con Applies
con_applies.description:
Whether the CON modifier applies to a die gained at this level.

It's False at the levels the SRD writes with an asterisk, as in `9d8+2*`. Whether a die is rolled at all is a
separate question, which depends on whether `count` rises from the level below.

HitDice.title: HitDice
HitDice.description:
A class's hit dice at one level: how many, of what size, and any flat bonus.

Read it off `ProgressionRow.hit_dice`.
`level_up` and
`drain_levels` compare the hit dice of two neighbouring
levels. When `count` rises from one level to the next, the level gained or lost is worth a
rolled die. When it doesn't, the level is worth the difference between the two `bonus` values.
Frozen.

A class stops gaining dice at name level, the level at which a character may build a
stronghold. After that it gains a flat number of hit points per level. The SRD writes those
levels with an asterisk, as in `9d8+2*`, to show that the CON modifier no longer applies.

rolls.title: Rolls
rolls.description:
Every die result, before the CON modifier, in the order thrown.

With the `hp_reroll_at_first_level` option of `Ruleset` on, the 1s and 2s that were
thrown again are here too, and the last entry is the die that counts. Otherwise there's one entry. The
`max_hp_at_first_level` option doesn't change what's thrown, so with both options on, the 1s and 2s set aside and
the last die are all here, and `maximized` says the hit points come from the die's size instead.

hit_points.title: Hit Points
hit_points.description:
The hit points the character starts with, and at least 1.

They're the last die plus the CON modifier, or with `maximized` true, the hit die's size plus the CON modifier.

maximized.title: Maximized
maximized.description:
Whether the hit die counted as its maximum, because `max_hp_at_first_level` was on in the ruleset.

When it's true, `hit_points` is the die's size plus the CON modifier, whatever the last entry of `rolls` shows, so
a client can say why. It's false for a roll that osrlib 2.8.0 or earlier recorded.

HitPointRoll.title: HitPointRoll
HitPointRoll.description:
A first-level hit point roll: every die thrown, and the hit points the character starts with.

`roll_hit_points` returns one, and
`create_character` includes one in its result. Use
`hit_points` as the new character's `max_hp` and `current_hp`. Frozen.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: in B/X, the players don't see monster hit points.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

target_id.title: Target Id
target_id.description: The entity id of the creature reported on.

current_hp.title: Current Hp
current_hp.description: The creature's hit points now, never below 0.

max_hp.title: Max Hp
max_hp.description: The creature's maximum hit points, which energy drain can lower.

HitPointsReportedEvent.title: HitPointsReportedEvent
HitPointsReportedEvent.description:
A creature's hit points after something changed them.

Every rules function that changes hit points reports one of these right after the change: the functions for
damage, healing, death, energy drain, and regeneration. Follow them and you know every creature's hit points without
reading the creatures.

This is the only event with a creature's current and maximum hit points. The others report only the change:
a `DamageDealtEvent` the damage, and a
`LevelDrainedEvent` the maximum hit points lost. Only the referee
sees this event, because in B/X the players don't see monster hit points. Show the players the events that
report the change.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: the party learns what the cache contains when it takes the treasure.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `hoard_generated`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

cache_ref.title: Cache Ref
cache_ref.description:
The id of the cache the treasure went into, like `"cache-0001"`. Pass it as `feature_id` to
`TakeTreasure` from the cache's cell.

treasure_types.title: Treasure Types
treasure_types.description:
The treasure-type letters that were rolled, one entry per roll, so a hoard rolled from two
letters lists both. Treasure rolled on the unguarded-treasure table has `("unguarded",)`.

coins_gp_value.title: Coins Gp Value
coins_gp_value.description: The coins in the hoard, as their value in gold pieces.

coins.description:
The same coins by denomination, so a client can show the exact amount, and every
coin of a small amount that `coins_gp_value` rounds down to zero.

valuable_ids.title: Valuable Ids
valuable_ids.description: The session-scoped instance ids of the gems and jewellery in the hoard.

magic_item_ids.title: Magic Item Ids
magic_item_ids.description: The session-scoped instance ids of the magic items in the hoard.

HoardGeneratedEvent.title: HoardGeneratedEvent
HoardGeneratedEvent.description:
The engine rolled treasure and put it in a cache, before the party has found it.

Emitted when the party first enters an area whose author declared treasure, on the
cell it enters, and when monsters the author placed in an area appear with their lair
hoard, on the area's first cell. The goods go into a cache on that cell, which the
party empties with `TakeTreasure`, passing the
cache's id as `feature_id` while standing on the cell.

It has referee visibility, and it lists everything: telling the players would be
telling them what is in the room. A referee front end, or an LLM running the game,
reads it to know what is there.

counters.title: Counters
counters.description:
How many ids have been handed out under each prefix, keyed by prefix.

`allocate` updates it. Don't set it yourself, or
the allocator can hand out an id it has already given.

IdAllocator.title: IdAllocator
IdAllocator.description:
Hands out entity ids, each one unique within a game.

Every creature, effect, and valuable in a game needs an id, and an allocator gives it one.
A `GameSession` has one allocator and uses it everywhere it
needs an id, so inside a session, pass the session's `allocator` rather than a new one. Outside
a session, construct one and pass the same one to every call that takes an allocator.

Ids count up per prefix and never repeat, so a save and its replay refer to the same creature by
the same id. The counters are a plain field, so you can save and load an allocator with
`model_dump` and `model_validate`, and it continues the count.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"identify_item"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member carrying the item, by
`MemberView.id`. A dead member's items can be
identified too.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
The magic item to identify, by its per-instance id. The id is in
`MemberView.inventory`, which shows the player
a masked name until the item is identified. The referee view has the true name. A mundane
item has nothing to identify, and the session refuses it with `session.command.unknown_item`.

IdentifyItem.title: IdentifyItem
IdentifyItem.description:
Referee: identify a magic item without the party having to use it.

Use it when you identify an item some other way, like a sage's fee or a
*detect magic* that osrlib doesn't resolve. Using an item with
`UseItem` identifies it as well. This command is
legal in every mode, `game_over` and `victory` included, and the session logs and replays it
like any other command.

Identifying an item tells the party what it is. After it, player-visible events can show the
item's name, not only its instance id. A cursed item also has its curse revealed, and the
bearer can't take it off until *remove curse*. An item that's already identified, with any
curse already revealed, emits no event, and the command still succeeds.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`, `battle`, `game_over`, `victory`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.unknown_item` - the member carries no magic item with
  that instance id.

**Events:**

`ItemIdentifiedEvent` the first time. For a
cursed item, a `CurseRevealedEvent` follows.
None for an item that's already identified and revealed.

key.title: Key
key.description:
Who rolled: a side's name under side initiative, or a combatant's entity id under individual
initiative.

rolls.title: Rolls
rolls.description:
Every d6 rolled for this side or combatant, in the order rolled. `roll_initiative` re-rolls a tie, so more
than one entry means there was a tie, and the later entries are the rolls that broke it. The last entry is the
one that counts.

modifier.title: Modifier
modifier.description:
The modifier added to the last roll. It's 0 under side initiative. Under individual initiative, a
character's comes from its DEX and class, through
`participant_modifier`, and a monster's is the one you chose.

total.title: Total
total.description: The last roll plus the modifier. `roll_initiative` sorts the acting order on this total.

InitiativeRoll.title: InitiativeRoll
InitiativeRoll.description:
One initiative roll on an `InitiativeRolledEvent`.

Read these from the event's `entries` to show what each side or combatant rolled. Check the event's
`mode` to know which: a side under side initiative, a combatant under individual initiative.

visibility.description: Player visibility: everyone at the table can see the order of play.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

mode.title: Mode
mode.description:
How initiative was rolled: `"side"` when each side rolled once for all its members, `"individual"` when
each combatant rolled for itself.

entries.title: Entries
entries.description:
One `InitiativeRoll` for each side, or for each combatant under
individual initiative. They're in the order `roll_initiative` received them, not the order they act.

order.title: Order
order.description: Every combatant's key, usually its entity id, in the order they act this round, first to last.

InitiativeRolledEvent.title: InitiativeRolledEvent
InitiativeRolledEvent.description:
Who acts first this round, and what everyone rolled to get there.

`roll_initiative` reports one of these each time it's called, which is
at the start of each combat round. Read `order` to know who acts next, and `entries` to show the dice.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"inspect_treasure"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The thief who inspects, by `MemberView.id`. Only a
member with thief skills can find a treasure trap, and each one gets a single attempt per
cache.

feature_id.title: Feature Id
feature_id.description:
Which cache to check for a trap: a `feature:` handle from
`MapFeatureView.id` in the current player view, or the
cache's raw id, an authored `FeatureSpec.id` or the id
of a cache the engine generated. Both forms stay supported. A player client sends the handle,
because the player view lists only handles. Both forms resolve against the same caches, the
available ones the party can reach where it stands, so a raw id reaches and reveals
nothing that a handle doesn't. A cache anywhere else gets the same
`exploration.feature.unknown` rejection as an id that no cache has.

InspectTreasure.title: InspectTreasure
InspectTreasure.description:
Have a thief check a treasure cache on the party's cell for a trap (one turn).

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`), and it needs light: infravision
isn't enough. Only a member with thief skills can find a treasure trap, and each member
gets one attempt at each cache. Remove a trap found here with
`RemoveTreasureTrap`. Until then, finding
the trap doesn't disarm it, and it still gets its chance to spring on every
`TakeTreasure`. Only an authored cache can be
trapped. Inspecting an available cache the engine generated always finds nothing. A
generated lair cache stays unknown until the party resolves the area's keyed encounter.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member cannot act.
- `exploration.trap.not_a_thief` - the member has no thief skills.
- `exploration.feature.unknown` - `feature_id` is malformed, stale, ambiguous,
  or matches no available treasure cache on this cell.
- `exploration.action.requires_light` - the party has no light. Infravision
  isn't enough to inspect a cache.
- `exploration.search.already_tried` - this member already inspected
  this cache.

**Events:**

`DetectionRolledEvent` with the
skill roll, then either a `TrapEvent` with code
`exploration.trap.found` or a
`SearchCompletedEvent`
reporting nothing. One turn passes, with the turn's usual events.

min_score.title: Min Score
min_score.description: The lowest score this row covers.

max_score.title: Max Score
max_score.description: The highest score this row covers. Equal to `min_score` on a one-score row.

additional_languages.title: Additional Languages
additional_languages.description: How many languages beyond the character's native ones they may choose at creation.

literacy.description: How well the character reads and writes. See `Literacy`.

broken_speech.title: Broken Speech
broken_speech.description: True only at intelligence 3, where the character speaks their native language brokenly.

IntelligenceRow.title: IntelligenceRow
IntelligenceRow.description:
One row of the intelligence table: a band of scores, with its languages and literacy.

Read the rows from `AbilityTables.intelligence` to
draw the table. To look up one score, call
`additional_languages` or
`literacy` instead.

code.title: Code
code.description:
Error code that `POST /v1/adventures` would return for the same document: `content_invalid`
when the envelope, schema, references, or adventure name fail validation, or
`version_unsupported` when `schema_version` exceeds the server's `schema_version`.

detail.title: Detail
detail.description: Human-readable validation error details, at most 1,000 characters.

InvalidAdventure.title: InvalidAdventure
InvalidAdventure.description: Validation result when `POST /v1/adventures/validate` refuses an adventure document.

items.title: Items
items.description:
What is carried but not in use, in the order it was acquired.
See `AnyInstance`.

worn_armour.title: Worn Armour
worn_armour.description: The suit of body armour being worn, or `null`.

wielded.title: Wielded
wielded.description:
Everything equipped that isn't armour, a shield, or a ring: weapons, a torch, a wand, and worn miscellaneous
magic items like gauntlets. A two-handed weapon here rules out a shield.

Inventory.title: Inventory
Inventory.description:
Everything one character carries, including items, coins, valuables, and what is in hand or worn.

Every `Character` has one. Build it up with
`purchase` and `equip`, search
it with `carried_item` and
`magic_item`, and weigh it with
`tracked_weight_coins` or
`movement_rate_feet`. In a running game the
commands do all of this and record it in the save.

To give a character treasure you generated outside a session, append each magic item to
`items` and each valuable to `valuables`, and add each denomination of the coins to the
matching field of `purse`.

An instance is in exactly one place: equipping moves it out of the item list and into
its slot, and unequipping moves it back. So iterate
`all_instances` rather than `items` when
you want everything a character has. The item list is in the order items were added,
and an unequipped item goes back on the end.

osrlib doesn't cap what a character can carry. Weight affects the movement rate instead.
Past the maximum load, the character can't move. The maximum load is
`MAX_LOAD_COINS`. Under detailed encumbrance, worn
gauntlets of ogre power raise it.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party knows what it picked up.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `item_acquired`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member whose pack the goods went into.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
What was acquired: a catalog id for mundane gear, and a session-scoped instance id for a
valuable or a magic item, so an unidentified item's true nature stays hidden.

coins_gp_value.title: Coins Gp Value
coins_gp_value.description:
The coins acquired, converted to their value in gold pieces, and zero when only items
changed hands.

coins.description:
The same coins by denomination, so a client can show the exact amount, and every
coin of a small amount that `coins_gp_value` rounds down to zero.

origin.title: Origin
origin.description:
Where the goods came from: `"treasure"` for a share of a haul taken with
`TakeTreasure`, `"purchase"` for gear bought with
`PurchaseEquipment`, and `"grant"` for a referee's
`GrantItem` or `GrantCoins`.
Every command that emits this event fills it, so it is `null` only on an event loaded from a save
written before the field existed.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call one of each item in `item_ids`, keyed by the same id, such as
`{"torch": "torch", "magic-item-0003": "potion", "valuable-0007": "gem"}`. Each name is the name that
`PlayerView.item_names` has for that id, so an unidentified magic
item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never its true name. The names
are the ones the party knew when the event happened. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep a
view, can name the items from the event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the field existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as
`{"torch": "torches", "magic-item-0003": "potions"}`, from
`PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of your
own.

ItemAcquiredEvent.title: ItemAcquiredEvent
ItemAcquiredEvent.description:
Items or coins arrived in a character's inventory.

Emitted by `TakeTreasure` once per carrier
who took a share, by
`PurchaseEquipment` in town, and by
the referee's `GrantItem` and
`GrantCoins`.

It reports what changed hands, not what the character now carries. Read the
inventory itself from `GameSession.view`
when you need the full sheet.

pattern_type.title: Pattern Type
pattern_type.description:
The discriminator value, `item_acquired`. It appears in the document, and you
never set it yourself.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
The catalog id of the item to watch for, from the equipment catalog or the
magic-item catalog. For a magic item, write its catalog id, not an instance id.

ItemAcquiredPattern.title: ItemAcquiredPattern
ItemAcquiredPattern.description:
A pattern that matches a party member acquiring an item with `item_id`.

It matches an `ItemAcquiredEvent`, so it
matches an item the party takes as treasure, buys in town, or gets from a referee's
`GrantItem`. An item one member hands to another
doesn't match, because `GiveItems` reports an
`ItemsGivenEvent` instead. It accepts the same ids as a
`HasItemCondition`: ids from the equipment
catalog, which is the built-in items plus the adventure's bundled items, or from the
magic-item catalog.

The event contains a mundane item's catalog id, or a magic item's instance id, which the
session assigns. To match a magic item, the interpreter looks up that instance
in the acquiring member's inventory and compares its catalog id.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party sees what it spent.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `item_consumed`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member whose pack the item came out of.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
What was consumed: the catalog id for mundane gear, and the session-scoped instance id for
a magic item, never its template id, so an unidentified item's identity never reaches a
player-visible event.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call the item in `item_id`, keyed by that id, such as `{"iron_spikes": "iron spike"}`. Each name is
the name that `PlayerView.item_names` has for that id, so an
unidentified magic item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never its
true name. The names are the ones the party knew when the event happened. The item may be the last unit the
member had, so the view built after the command may not name it. A client that replays an event log, or that
didn't keep a view, can name the items from the event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the
field existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as
`{"iron_spikes": "iron spikes"}`, from
`PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of your
own.

ItemConsumedEvent.title: ItemConsumedEvent
ItemConsumedEvent.description:
An item a member carried was used up, like a key a gate takes or an iron spike.

Emitted when the party passes a gate that requires an item and takes it, which can happen
on `OpenDoor`,
`ForceDoor`,
`UseStairs`, and a
`MoveParty` through a passage. A gate is a condition
the adventure's author puts on a door or a transition. Also emitted by
`WedgeDoor` for the iron spike it drives.

It reports that the item is gone. A potion drunk or a scroll read is an
`ItemUsedEvent` instead.

visibility.description: Player visibility: this is the moment the party learns what it has.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `item_identified`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

instance_id.title: Instance Id
instance_id.description: The session-scoped id of the item, the same id the earlier events contained.

template_id.title: Template Id
template_id.description: What it turned out to be, as its magic item catalog id.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
What to call the item now that the party knows it, the template's
`display_name`, like `"potion of healing"`.

It's here because the command that identifies an item can also use it up, like a potion drunk
before the party knew what it was. Then no view names it by its true name, because the view built
after the command no longer shows the item and the view from before showed it masked. When the
item is still carried, the view's
`PlayerView.item_names` has the same name under
`instance_id` and `template_id`.

display_name_plural.title: Display Name Plural
display_name_plural.description:
What to call two or more of the item, the template's
`display_name_plural`, like
`"potions of healing"`.

ItemIdentifiedEvent.title: ItemIdentifiedEvent
ItemIdentifiedEvent.description:
A magic item was identified, and the party now knows what it is.

Emitted the first time an item is used in a way that reveals it, which can happen
in `UseItem`,
`EquipItem`, and
`ResolveBattleRound`, and when the
referee identifies it with `IdentifyItem`.

Before this, player-visible events contain the item's `instance_id` and its masked name, such as
`"potion"`, in their `item_names`. After it, you can show the party the name of the item whose
catalog id is `template_id`, and the item events that follow name it by `display_name`.

template.title: Template
template.description:
The item itself, one of the four equipment templates. See `ItemTemplate`. The
whole template is embedded rather than referenced by id, so an instance of an item an adventure bundled stays
readable without that adventure.

A session gives an embedded template the display names of the template its catalog,
`GameSession.effective_equipment`, has under the same id.
It does this to every stack a party member or an NPC adventurer carries when the session starts, when
`load_game` restores it, and when `AddMember`
adds a member. Only `display_name` and `display_name_plural` change, with the entries of `overrides_applied` that
name those two fields, which record where the names came from. The rest of the template is rules data that travels
with the character. So a stack from a save or a party document that osrlib 2.7.0 wrote, whose
template has no display names, is named as the catalog names it, in the views and in the next save. A template
whose id the catalog doesn't have, like an item another adventure bundled, keeps the names it has.

quantity.title: Quantity
quantity.description:
How many units the stack contains, counting individual items rather than lots: buying one lot of torches gives
you one instance of quantity 6.

ItemInstance.title: ItemInstance
ItemInstance.description:
A stack of mundane items a character has.

`purchase` makes one. Construct one yourself to give a
character an item without charging for it, and add it to their
`Inventory`. Unlike a magic item, a mundane instance has
no instance id. Its template identifies it, so two stacks of the same item are
interchangeable.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party watched it happen.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `item_used`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who used the item. For a potion, that's the member who carried it, whoever drank it.

instance_id.title: Instance Id
instance_id.description:
The session-scoped id of the item used, never its catalog id, so an event about an item the
party hasn't identified doesn't reveal what the item is.

manual.title: Manual
manual.description:
The item's printed text, for an item whose effect the engine doesn't resolve, like a treasure
map, or the curse's text for a cursed scroll whose curse the engine doesn't apply. A use of the
staff of power or wizardry that strikes no group has the staff's text too, because the use is
one of the staff's other powers, like the cone of cold. Empty when the engine resolved the
effect itself, as it does a staff's strike. Show these lines to the players and rule on them
yourself.

target_id.title: Target Id
target_id.description:
The member who drank the potion, on `items.potion.drunk` and `items.potion.mixed`, when the
member in `character_id` gave it to another member to drink. The potion's effect, and the sickness
of mixed potions, land on this member.

It's `null` when the member who used the potion drank it, and on every other code. Name the drinker
in `UseItem.target_id`, or in the one id of a `use_item`
declaration's `targets`.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call the item in `instance_id`, keyed by that id, such as `{"magic-item-0003": "potion of healing"}`.
Each name is the name that `PlayerView.item_names` has for that id,
so an unidentified magic item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never
its true name. The first use of an item identifies it, and that use's
`ItemIdentifiedEvent` comes earlier in the same result, so the name
is always the item's true display name, the same as that event's `display_name`. A potion drunk or a scroll read
is used up, so no view built after the command names it. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep
a view, can name the items from the event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the field
existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as
`{"magic-item-0003": "potions of healing"}`, from
`PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of your
own.

ItemUsedEvent.title: ItemUsedEvent
ItemUsedEvent.description:
A magic item was used: a potion drunk, a scroll read, a device fired.

Emitted by `UseItem` outside battle and by
`ResolveBattleRound` for an item used
in a battle. Whatever the item does follows in the same result as kernel events. A member
can give a potion to another member to drink, and `target_id` is then the drinker's id.

Using an item for the first time identifies it, so an
`ItemIdentifiedEvent`, and a
`CurseRevealedEvent` for a cursed item,
come just before this one. Using a device that has no charges left emits no event:
the session refuses the command with `items.device.inert`, and the party loses
nothing. Charges never appear on any event, because only the referee knows how many
uses an item has left.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party knows what it let go of.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `items_dropped`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who dropped them.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
What was dropped, in the same id form the acquisition used: catalog ids for mundane gear,
instance ids for valuables and magic items.

coins_gp_value.title: Coins Gp Value
coins_gp_value.description: The coins dropped, as their value in gold pieces.

coins.description:
The same coins by denomination, so a client can show the exact amount, and every
coin of a small amount that `coins_gp_value` rounds down to zero.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call one of each item in `item_ids`, keyed by the same id, such as
`{"torch": "torch", "magic-item-0003": "potion"}`. Each name is the name that
`PlayerView.item_names` has for that id, so an unidentified magic
item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never its true name. The names
are the ones the party knew when the event happened. A drop made while fleeing leaves the goods on the trail, so
no view built after the command names them. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep a view, can
name the items from the event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the field existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as `{"torch": "torches"}`,
from `PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of
your own.

ItemsDroppedEvent.title: ItemsDroppedEvent
ItemsDroppedEvent.description:
Items or coins were dropped, onto the party's cell or behind it as bait.

Emitted by `DropItems`, and by
`Evade` when the party drops its coins or its food to
slow the monsters chasing it.

What is dropped goes into the drop pile on the party's cell, which
`TakeTreasure` with `feature_id="pile"` picks
back up. The exception is a drop made while fleeing: the drop of an `Evade`, or a
`DropItems` during a chase. Those goods are left on the trail and are gone.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party arranged the handover.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `items_given`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who handed the goods over.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
What was handed over, as catalog ids for mundane gear and instance ids for valuables and
magic items.

coins_gp_value.title: Coins Gp Value
coins_gp_value.description: The coins handed over, as their value in gold pieces.

coins.description:
The same coins by denomination, so a client can show the exact amount, and every
coin of a small amount that `coins_gp_value` rounds down to zero.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call one of each item in `item_ids`, keyed by the same id, such as
`{"torch": "torch", "magic-item-0003": "potion"}`. Each name is the name that
`PlayerView.item_names` has for that id, so an unidentified magic
item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never its true name. The names
are the ones the party knew when the event happened. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep a
view, can name the items from the event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the field existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as `{"torch": "torches"}`,
from `PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of
your own.

ItemsGivenEvent.title: ItemsGivenEvent
ItemsGivenEvent.description:
Items or coins passed from one party member to another.

Emitted by `GiveItems`, and by
`ResolveBattleRound` for a `give_item`
declaration, which hands over one item in the party's magic phase. Update both members'
inventories on screen when it arrives. Nothing enters or leaves the party, so
the party's total is unchanged.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party can see the pile it's walking away from.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `items_left_behind`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
What stayed behind, as catalog ids for mundane gear and instance ids for valuables and
magic items.

coins_gp_value.title: Coins Gp Value
coins_gp_value.description: The coins left behind, as their value in gold pieces.

coins.description:
The same coins by denomination, so a client can show the exact amount, and every
coin of a small amount that `coins_gp_value` rounds down to zero.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call one of each item in `item_ids`, keyed by the same id, such as
`{"torch": "torch", "valuable-0007": "gem"}`. Each name is the name that
`PlayerView.item_names` has for that id, so an unidentified magic
item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never its true name. The names
are the ones the party knew when the event happened. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep a
view, can name the items from the event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the field existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as `{"torch": "torches"}`,
from `PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of
your own.

ItemsLeftBehindEvent.title: ItemsLeftBehindEvent
ItemsLeftBehindEvent.description:
Treasure the party could not carry, left lying where it was found.

Emitted by `TakeTreasure` when the haul is
heavier than the carriers' remaining capacity.

Nothing is destroyed. The remainder goes into the drop pile on the party's cell,
and a party that has made room can get the rest with a `TakeTreasure` whose
`feature_id` is `"pile"`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party knows what it no longer has.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `items_removed`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who lost the items or coins.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
The ids of what was removed: a mundane item's catalog id once for each unit, and the instance
id of a magic item or a valuable. Empty for a removal of coins.

coins_gp_value.title: Coins Gp Value
coins_gp_value.description: The coins removed, as their value in gold pieces. 0 for a removal of items.

coins.description:
The same coins by denomination, so a client can show the exact amount, and every
coin of a small amount that `coins_gp_value` rounds down to zero.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call one of each item in `item_ids`, keyed by the same id, such as
`{"torch": "torch", "magic-item-0003": "potion"}`. Each name is the name that
`PlayerView.item_names` has for that id, so an unidentified magic
item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never its true name. The names
are the ones the party knew when the event happened. The items have left the party, so no view built after the
command names them. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep a view, can name the items from the
event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the field existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as `{"torch": "torches"}`,
from `PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of
your own.

ItemsRemovedEvent.title: ItemsRemovedEvent
ItemsRemovedEvent.description:
A referee took items or coins away from a party member.

Emitted by `RemoveItem` and
`RemoveCoins`. What was removed has left the
game, so update the member's inventory on screen. The event doesn't say why. The
command does: read the `source` of the `RemoveItem` or `RemoveCoins`, either the one you
executed or its entry in
`GameSession.command_log`. When a
trigger or a quest issued the command, `source` is its id.

text.title: Text
text.description:
The entry's text, from your code or from the adventure document. osrlib never writes it,
and it's never empty.

rounds.title: Rounds
rounds.description: Where the clock stood when the entry was appended, in rounds since the session began.

JournalEntry.title: JournalEntry
JournalEntry.description:
One entry in the party's journal: a line of the adventure's story, with the time it was written.

`AddJournalEntry` writes entries. So do the quest
commands, like `ActivateQuest`, which add the
adventure's text for each step of a quest. Read the journal from
`PlayerView.journal`, a tuple of these in the order
they were written.

Entries are appended and never changed. Each one records the clock at the moment it's written,
so you can show when it happened from the view alone, and a save made without its
event log still has the time of every entry.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the journal is written for the players.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `journal_entry_added`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

text.title: Text
text.description:
The line as it was written. It came from your code or from the adventure, not from the
engine.

rounds.title: Rounds
rounds.description:
Where the clock stood when the line was added, in rounds since the session began. The stored
journal entry has the same number.

JournalEntryAddedEvent.title: JournalEntryAddedEvent
JournalEntryAddedEvent.description:
A line of text was added to the session journal.

Emitted by `AddJournalEntry`. The
journal is the party's record of the adventure. Lines are added in order and never
changed, and the journal is part of what
`GameSession.view` shows a player.

Quest text also goes into the journal, but its quest event reports it, like
`QuestActivatedEvent`, with no
`JournalEntryAddedEvent`, so the players aren't shown the same line twice. Read the
whole journal from the view, and read these events to know when a line arrived.

JsonObject.description: A JSON object with string keys.

monsters.title: Monsters
monsters.description:
The monster lines in the encounter, at least one. See
`KeyedMonster`. The lines create at most 100 monsters
together, counting each line at its `count_fixed` or at the highest total its `count_dice` can
roll, so a line of 60 goblins and a line of `"2d20"` hobgoblins is legal, and 60 goblins with
`"1d6x7"` hobgoblins isn't.

alignment.description:
The alignment every spawned monster takes, for a template that allows more than one. With
`null`, the default, the session rolls it as usual. It has to be an alignment that each line's template allows, and
`validate_adventure` reports one that isn't.

aware.title: Aware
aware.description:
Whether the monsters expect the party. Aware monsters can't be surprised, so set it for a
lookout, or for an ambush that has heard the party coming.

stance.description:
The monsters' reaction, used instead of a reaction roll. Set it for monsters that always
attack on sight, or that are always friendly. Leave it `null`, the default, to roll the reaction
as usual.

hoard.title: Hoard
hoard.description:
Whether the monsters have their lair treasure. With the default, `true`, the session rolls the
treasure types in each monster's `treasure` the first time the monsters spawn. It puts the result
on the first cell of the area as a `GeneratedCache`. If the
party leaves and comes back before the area is clear, the monsters spawn again, but the session
doesn't roll the hoard again. Set it `false` for a monster room with no treasure. Stocking a
dungeon by the B/X rules often produces such a room, because only some monster rooms get treasure
on the stocking roll.

KeyedEncounter.title: KeyedEncounter
KeyedEncounter.description:
The monsters waiting in a keyed area, and what you decide about them in advance.

Put one on an `AreaSpec`. The monsters spawn when the party
enters any cell of the area, and the session opens an encounter. The session rolls surprise,
distance, and reaction, though you can set the reaction here, and stop the monsters from being
surprised. When the encounter ends with every monster slain or routed, the area is clear, and no
monsters spawn when the party enters it again.

template_id.title: Template Id
template_id.description:
The monster's template id. Use an id from `load_monsters()`,
listed in [the monster id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/monsters/),
or the id of a monster in the adventure's `monsters`.

count_dice.title: Count Dice
count_dice.description:
How many appear, as a dice expression like `"2d4"`. The session rolls it on the
`WANDERING_STREAM` when the monsters spawn, and a roll
below 1 counts as 1. Set this or `count_fixed`, not both. The model checks the expression when
you construct it, so a malformed one fails then, not during play, and so does an expression that
can roll more than 100, like `"1d100+1"` or `"11d10"`.

count_fixed.title: Count Fixed
count_fixed.description:
How many appear, as a fixed number from 1 to 100. Set this or `count_dice`, not both. A
printed adventure usually gives a fixed number, and so does
`stock_area` when it rolls a room for you.

KeyedMonster.title: KeyedMonster
KeyedMonster.description:
One line of a keyed encounter: which monster, and how many.

A `KeyedEncounter` has a tuple of these, so a room with
four orcs and their ogre bodyguard has two lines. Give each line either a fixed count or count
dice, not both. A line creates at most 100 monsters, the limit a
`SpawnMonsters` command has.

id.title: Id
id.description: The id to pass wherever a function takes a language id, like `"gnoll"` or `"common"`.

name.title: Name
name.description: The display name to show a player, like `"Gnoll"`.

choosable.title: Choosable
choosable.description:
Whether a character with a high enough INT may take this language as an extra.

True for the languages the SRD lists under Other Languages, which a high-INT character
chooses from. False for Common, which every character already speaks.

Language.title: Language
Language.description:
One spoken language from the language catalog.

You get one from `LanguageCatalog.get`, or from
`LanguageCatalog.languages` when you want to
offer a player the whole list. Pass its `id` in the `extra_languages` argument of
`create_character`, or in the `choices` argument
of `validate_extra_languages`.

The alignment languages aren't in the catalog. A character speaks the language of its
`Alignment` without choosing it.

The model is frozen: assigning to a field raises pydantic's `ValidationError`.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"learn_spell"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The arcane caster whose book gets the spell, by
`MemberView.id`. The session refuses a member whose class
isn't an arcane caster with `magic.book.not_arcane`.

spell_id.title: Spell Id
spell_id.description:
The spell to write into the book, by its id in
`GameSession.effective_spells`: a
built-in spell (see the
[spell id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/spells/)) or one
the adventure bundles. It has to be on the spell list of the caster's class. At each spell
level, no more spells fit in the book than the caster has slots at that level.
`MemberView.learnable_spells` lists each
spell that this caster may learn, so build a learn dialog from it.

LearnSpell.title: LearnSpell
LearnSpell.description:
Add a spell to an arcane caster's spell book, when they gain a level or a mentor teaches them.

It's legal in town and while exploring. At each spell level, no more spells fit in the book
than the caster has slots at that level. The book never shrinks, so a caster
who lost a level can have more spells in it than their slots, and can't learn more at
that level until they regain the slots. No game time passes. What the learning costs in
the story, like a mentor's week or the price of copying a scroll, is up to you.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - an encounter or battle is underway, or the
  session has ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `magic.book.not_arcane` - the member's class isn't an arcane caster.
- `magic.book.unknown_spell` - `spell_id`, or a spell already in the caster's
  book, matches no spell in the session's catalog.
- `magic.book.wrong_list` - the spell isn't on the caster's spell list.
- `magic.book.duplicate` - the book already contains the spell.
- `magic.book.capacity_exceeded` - the book is full at the spell's level.

**Events:**

`SpellBookUpdatedEvent` with
the added spell.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the players know when a level is lost.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

target_id.title: Target Id
target_id.description: The entity id of the victim.

levels_lost.title: Levels Lost
levels_lost.description: How many levels, or Hit Dice, the drain took.

new_level.title: New Level
new_level.description: The victim's level, or Hit Dice, after the drain. 0 when the drain killed it.

hp_lost.title: Hp Lost
hp_lost.description:
How far the drain lowered the victim's maximum hit points: the maximum before the drain less the maximum
after it.

While the victim has a level or a Hit Die left, maximum hit points don't drop below 1. So this can be less than
the hit points rolled for the lost levels. For example, a level-2 character with 3 maximum hit points who rolls a
7 for the lost level is left with 1, so `hp_lost` is 2. A drain that kills doesn't lower the maximum for the
level that kills, so `hp_lost` counts only the levels lost before that one.

xp_after.title: Xp After
xp_after.description:
The character's experience points after the drain. Depending on the draining monster, they're either
halfway between the old and new levels' thresholds, or at the new level's threshold. `null` for a monster, whose Hit
Dice are worth no experience points, and for a victim the drain killed.

spawn_consequence.title: Spawn Consequence
spawn_consequence.description:
What the rules say becomes of a character this undead creature kills, like rising as a wight in 1d4
days under the control of its killer. osrlib kills the victim, and playing out what it becomes is up to you.

It's set only on a `combat.drain.slain` event for a character, because it describes a victim the drain killed.
It's `null` on every `combat.drain.drained` event, for a monster victim, and when the undead creature's rules
say nothing about it.

LevelDrainedEvent.title: LevelDrainedEvent
LevelDrainedEvent.description:
An undead creature's touch has taken levels, or killed its victim.

`drain_levels` reports this for a character, and
`drain_monster_hd` for a monster, which loses Hit Dice instead of
levels.

When the victim has nothing left to lose, at level 1 or 1 Hit Die, the drain kills it instead. Then the code
is `combat.drain.slain`, and a `DeathEvent` follows. The killing level
counts as lost, so when a spectre, which drains two levels, kills a level-2 fighter, the event shows two levels
lost.

pattern_type.title: Pattern Type
pattern_type.description:
The discriminator value, `level_entered`. It appears in the document, and you
never set it yourself.

dungeon_id.title: Dungeon Id
dungeon_id.description: The id of the dungeon the level belongs to.

LevelEnteredPattern.title: LevelEnteredPattern
LevelEnteredPattern.description:
A pattern that matches the party arriving on a dungeon level.

It matches however the party got there, by a stair from another level or by entering
the dungeon from town. When one move enters both a dungeon and a level, the engine
reports only the dungeon entry, and this pattern matches that report too.

number.title: Number
number.description:
The level's number, 1 or more, where level 1 is the top. The session uses it to select the
built-in wandering-monster table and the row of the unguarded-treasure table. The numbers have to
be unique within a dungeon, and a `TransitionSpec` refers
to the level it leads to by its number.

width.title: Width
width.description: How many cells wide the grid is, west to east. `x` runs from `0` to `width - 1`.

height.title: Height
height.description: How many cells tall the grid is, north to south. `y` runs from `0` to `height - 1`.

edges.title: Edges
edges.description:
Every edge on the grid that isn't a wall, as an `Edge`. Write
each key with `edge_key`, like `"1,0:west"`, and only for an
edge between two cells on the grid. `validate_adventure`
reports a key that isn't the `edge_key` of a side of a cell on the grid, like `"0,0:east"` in place
of `"1,0:west"`. It accepts a key on the level's boundary, like `"0,0:west"`, but the session
treats that edge as a wall and doesn't read its entry. An edge with no entry is a wall, and so is
the level's boundary, so an empty map is a level of solid rock. Read an edge with
`edge` instead of indexing the map, because it works out
the key and returns a wall for an edge with no entry.

You pass a dict, and the level stores a read-only `FrozenMap` of
it, because every session started from the adventure reads the same level. To change an edge,
build a new level from a changed copy of the map:
`LevelSpec.model_validate({**level.model_dump(), "edges": edges})`, where `edges` is
`dict(level.edges)` with your changes.

areas.title: Areas
areas.description:
The level's keyed rooms and caves. Cells outside every area are corridor. Area ids have to be
unique within the level, and every cell an area lists has to be on the grid.

features.title: Features
features.description:
Features outside any room, like a cache in a corridor or a trick in a dead end. Each one needs
a `cell`, because there is no area to bind it to. Their ids have to be unique together with the
ids of the areas' features.

transitions.title: Transitions
transitions.description:
The stairs, trapdoors, chutes, and passages on this level, each on one cell. A transition
belongs to the level, not to an area, even when it stands inside a room.

wandering.description:
The level's wandering-monster check. The default is the B/X rule: a 1-in-6 chance every two
turns, on the built-in table for this level's number.

entrance.title: Entrance
entrance.description:
The cell the party arrives at from town, or `null` for a level with no way in from outside.
`EnterDungeon` puts the party here facing north, whatever
is around the cell. The session refuses `TravelToTown`
unless the party stands on its level's entrance. One level of every dungeon needs an entrance, and
`validate_adventure` reports a dungeon without
one.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.description:
Instructions for a narrator that uses a language model, while the party is on this level: the
mood of the place, what to say about it, and what never to say.

osrlib never reads it, no event includes it, and no rule depends on it. To use it, read it from
the adventure document. The player view doesn't include it, so treat it like an area's
description, and don't show it to a player as written.

LevelSpec.title: LevelSpec
LevelSpec.description:
One dungeon level: a grid of 10-foot cells with its edges, rooms, and stairs.

You give a level a size, declare the edges that aren't walls, key some of its cells as areas, and add features and
transitions. Then you put one or more levels in a `DungeonSpec`, and the dungeon
in an `Adventure`.

Its methods return what the session looks up about a level: whether a cell is on the grid, what
stands on one side of it, which area it belongs to, and whether a transition stands on it. Call
them to draw a map, or to check a level while you write it.

name.title: Name
name.description: License title, `"Open Game License 1.0a"`.

text.title: Text
text.description: Full license text in Markdown, including its Section 15 copyright notice.

License.title: License
License.description: Open Game License covering the rules catalogs.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description:
Player visibility: the party sees the light change. When a light burns out, the
`EffectExpiredEvent` for it has referee visibility, and
the session adds this event after it so the players learn of it.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `light`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member carrying the source, or `null` when the light belongs to no one in the party.

source.title: Source
source.description:
What is burning: `"torch"`, `"lantern"`, `"oil"` for a lit pool, `"sword"` for a blade that
glows, or the effect kind for a light cast as a spell.

LightEvent.title: LightEvent
LightEvent.description:
A light source was lit, went out, failed to catch, or burned away.

Emitted by `LightSource`,
`ExtinguishSource`, and
`UseItem` for an item that glows. The session
also emits the expiry form whenever a light runs out as time passes, which can happen
inside any command that passes time.

Without light, the session refuses several commands with
`exploration.action.requires_light`. Searching and listening at a door also work for
a character with infravision. Picking a lock, handling a treasure trap, and reading a
scroll need light. Read whether the party has light from
`GameSession.party_light` rather
than working it out from these events.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"light_source"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who strikes the light and then carries it, by
`MemberView.id`. The light goes with this member, so the
party loses it when this member dies.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
Which source to light: `torch`, `lantern`, or `oil_flask`. Lighting a torch uses it up,
and it burns for a torch's full duration. A lantern burns one oil flask from the member's
pack, and the member keeps the lantern. `oil_flask` sets fire to a flask already dropped on
the party's cell, not one in the pack, so drop it with
`DropItems` first. The session refuses any other id with
`exploration.light.not_a_source`.

LightSource.title: LightSource
LightSource.description:
Light a torch or a lantern, or set fire to a dropped flask of oil (one round).

It's legal in town and while exploring. When no living member already has a flame
burning, the member needs a tinder box, and each strike lights on a 2 in 6. Each
attempt takes a round, whether or not it lights, as the OSE SRD's tinder box entry says.
Lighting `oil_flask` sets fire to a flask already dropped on the party's cell, which
makes a pool of burning oil there.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - an encounter or battle is underway, or the
  session has ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `exploration.light.not_a_source` - `item_id` isn't `torch`, `lantern`,
  or `oil_flask`.
- `exploration.item.not_carried` - the member doesn't carry the torch or the
  lantern, or carries a lantern and no oil flask. For `oil_flask`, no dropped
  flask is on the cell, which is always so in town.
- `exploration.light.no_flame` - no flame is burning in the party, and the member
  has no tinder box.

**Events:**

An `EffectAttachedEvent` for the light's
burn time, then a `LightEvent` with code
`exploration.light.lit`. A strike that doesn't light produces only a `LightEvent` with
code `exploration.light.failed`. One round passes either way.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"listen_at_door"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

direction.description:
Which side of the party's cell the door is on, from the `door` edges in
`ExploredLevelView.edges`. Listening reaches
only the area directly beyond that door.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who listens, by `MemberView.id`. Each
member gets one attempt at each door for the rest of the game, so send the best listener
first. A thief hears on the hear-noise chance for their level. A dwarf, an elf, or a
halfling hears on 2 in 6, and every other class on 1 in 6.

ListenAtDoor.title: ListenAtDoor
ListenAtDoor.description:
Listen at a door for noise from the area beyond it (takes no game time).

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`). The listener needs light, or
infravision. Each member gets one attempt at each door for the rest of the game. A
listener who hears the monsters beyond the door keeps them from surprising the party
when it meets them there. Undead make no noise, so an area that contains only undead
always sounds silent.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member cannot act.
- `exploration.door.no_door` - no known door on that side of the cell.
- `exploration.action.requires_light` - the party is in the dark and the
  listener lacks infravision.
- `exploration.listen.already_tried` - this character has already listened
  at this door.

**Events:**

`DetectionRolledEvent` with the
roll, then `ListenedEvent` with code
`exploration.listen.heard` or `exploration.listen.silent`.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description:
Player visibility: what a character heard is theirs to know, while the die behind it is
not.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `listened`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who listened.

direction.title: Direction
