direction.description:
The side of the party's cell that was listened at, as a lowercase
`Direction` value.

ListenedEvent.title: ListenedEvent
ListenedEvent.description:
Someone listened at a door, and either heard something or heard nothing.

Emitted by `ListenAtDoor`, after the
referee-visibility `DetectionRolledEvent`
that reports the die.

`exploration.listen.heard` means the listener heard monsters in the area past the
door. When the party later meets those monsters, it can't be surprised.

`exploration.listen.silent` gives the party no information about what is there. Undead
make no noise, and the session rolls the die whether or not anything is on the other
side. Show it as "nothing heard", not as a sign that the way is clear.

Literacy.title: Literacy
Literacy.description:
How well a character reads and writes, which their intelligence score sets.

Read it off `AbilityTables.literacy`, passing the
character's intelligence score. osrlib's rules don't use it. You decide what a character who
can't read is unable to do, like reading a scroll, a map, or an inscription.

code.title: Code
code.description: The message code, always `exploration.location.entered`. The scale is in `location_kind`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: arriving somewhere is the first thing the players are told.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `location_entered`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

location_id.title: Location Id
location_id.description:
What was entered: the area id for an area entry, the dungeon id for a level or dungeon
entry, and `"town"` for the town.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
The authored name of the town or the dungeon, to show the player: the town's
`TownSpec.name` on a town entry, like `"Threshold"`, and
the dungeon's `DungeonSpec.name` on a level or dungeon
entry, like `"The Old Crypt"`, without the spaces at either end. The player view shows the same names, in
`PlayerView.town_name` and
`PlayerView.dungeons`. It's empty on an area entry, for
a dungeon whose author gave it no name, and on an event loaded from a save written before the field
existed.

level_number.title: Level Number
level_number.description: The level the party is on, for area, level, and dungeon entries, and `null` for town.

dungeon_id.title: Dungeon Id
dungeon_id.description:
The dungeon the area belongs to, filled on area entries only. On level and dungeon entries,
`location_id` is already the dungeon id.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description:
The success text the adventure's author wrote on the gate the party passed, or `null` when
there was no gate or no text. A gate is a condition the author puts on a door or a transition,
like a key the party must have. The author wrote this text, not the engine, and
`format_message` adds it after the line it builds from the
code. A transition to another cell of the same level enters no new level, so its gate's text is
on the `PartyMovedEvent` for the landing cell instead.

via.title: Via
via.description:
How the party got there, on level and dungeon entries: the kind of the transition it took
(`"stairs_down"`, `"stairs_up"`, `"trapdoor"`, or `"chute"`), `"passage"` for a passage it
walked through with `MoveParty`, `"trap"` for a trap that
moved the party, like a chute, `"entrance"` for
`EnterDungeon`, and `"placed"` for
`PlaceParty`. It is `null` on area and town entries, and on
an event loaded from a save written before the field existed.

transition_ref.title: Transition Ref
transition_ref.description:
The cell of the authored transition the party took, as
`cell_ref` gives it, so you can find the
`TransitionSpec` and the gate on it. Filled on a level or
dungeon entry made through `UseStairs` or through a passage,
`null` otherwise. For a passage crossing, it refers to the passage's cell. That cell can also have
stairs, and passages on its other sides, so find the passage with
`LevelSpec.passage_at` and the `direction` of the
`MoveParty` that crossed it.

LocationEnteredEvent.title: LocationEnteredEvent
LocationEnteredEvent.description:
The party crossed into a new area, level, dungeon, or town.

An area is a room or other region of a level that the adventure's author keyed with
content. The session emits the event whenever the party's location changes at one of
those four scales:

- `EnterDungeon` reports a dungeon entry.
- `UseStairs`, a passage crossed with
  `MoveParty`, and a trap that moves the party
  report a level entry when they change the level, or a dungeon entry when they change
  the dungeon.
- Each of those also reports an area entry when the cell the party arrives on is in
  an area, and so does a `MoveParty` step into a different area.
- `TravelToTown` reports a town entry.
- `PlaceParty`, when a referee puts the party
  somewhere, reports a dungeon entry or a town entry.

Which fields are filled depends on the scale, because an area id is unique only
within its level. An area entry has the area, its level number, and its dungeon. A
level or dungeon entry has the dungeon in `location_id` and the level number beside
it. A town entry has neither. A level or dungeon entry also records how the party got
there, in `via` and, for a transition it took, `transition_ref`, so you can tell from
the event alone whether the party climbed or descended. Use the event to
change the screen's header, and read the text the party can see from
`GameSession.view`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party sees what the fallen left on the floor.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `loot_dropped`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
What went into the pile, as a catalog id for each unit of mundane gear and an instance id for
each valuable and each magic item. An unidentified magic item has its instance id, so its true
nature stays hidden.

coins_gp_value.title: Coins Gp Value
coins_gp_value.description: The coins that went into the pile, as their value in gold pieces.

coins.description:
The same coins by denomination, so a client can show the exact amount, and every
coin of a small amount that `coins_gp_value` rounds down to zero.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call one of each item in `item_ids`, keyed by the same id, such as
`{"sword": "sword", "magic-item-0003": "potion", "valuable-0007": "gem"}`. Each name is the name that
`PlayerView.item_names` has for that id, so an unidentified magic
item has its masked name, such as `"potion"` or `"shield with a faint aura"`, and never its true name. The names
are the ones the party knew when the event happened. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep a
view, can name the items from the event. It's empty on an event from a log written before the field existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as `{"sword": "swords"}`,
from `PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of
your own.

LootDroppedEvent.title: LootDroppedEvent
LootDroppedEvent.description:
What the slain left behind went into the drop pile on the party's cell as the encounter ended.

Emitted by whatever ends the encounter, through
`end_encounter`: a won battle, an
`EndEncounter`, an evasion, an escape from a chase, or a
turning. It comes after the
`MonsterDefeatedEvent`s and before the
`EncounterEndedEvent`.

The loot is the treasure each slain monster carried, the shared treasure of a group whose
members were all slain, and everything a slain NPC adventurer had: gear, coins, valuables, and
magic items. Routed monsters take their treasure with them. An encounter where nothing drops
emits no `LootDroppedEvent`.

The goods join any pile already on the cell. Show the pile on screen when this event arrives.
`PlayerView.piles` has everything in it, and
`TakeTreasure` with `feature_id="pile"` picks it up.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: `"any"`, `"category"`, or `"pool"`.

categories.title: Categories
categories.description:
The types the clause specifies. See `MagicItemType`. Empty for `any`, one
for `category`, two or more for `pool`.

count.title: Count
count.description: A fixed number of items, or `null` when the count is rolled.

count_dice.title: Count Dice
count_dice.description: The number of items as a dice expression, or `null` when it's fixed.

exclude.title: Exclude
exclude.description: Types an `any` clause re-rolls. Empty on the other kinds, and never every type.

MagicAllotment.title: MagicAllotment
MagicAllotment.description:
One magic item clause of a treasure entry, giving how many items and which kinds.

Read `kind` to know what the clause means:

- `any`: roll the master *Magic Item Type* table for each item, re-rolling anything in
  `exclude`. This is how "any 3 magic items" and "any 1 magic item, no weapons" are
  stored.
- `category`: roll the one table named in `categories`, as in "1 potion".
- `pool`: choose evenly among the types in `categories`, then roll that type's table, as
  in "a magic sword, suit of armour, or weapon".

Exactly one of `count` and `count_dice` is set, and it gives the number of items. Only an `any` clause has
exclusions, because a clause that specifies its type has nothing to exclude. An `any` clause can't exclude every
type, because generation would then have no type to roll.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the players see the spell and what it ended.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

caster_id.title: Caster Id
caster_id.description: The entity id of the caster of *dispel magic*.

released_effect_ids.title: Released Effect Ids
released_effect_ids.description: The ids of the effects the spell ended.

surviving_effect_ids.title: Surviving Effect Ids
surviving_effect_ids.description: The ids of the dispellable effects that survived their roll.

MagicDispelledEvent.title: MagicDispelledEvent
MagicDispelledEvent.description:
A *dispel magic* ended the effects on its targets, except those that survived.

`cast_spell` reports this when *dispel magic* resolves. Only effects marked
dispellable can end: every effect a spell attaches is, and what a monster inflicts isn't. An effect cast by a
higher-level caster gets a roll to survive, with a better chance the
wider the gap in levels, so one dispel can end some effects and leave others. Each effect that ended also has
an `EffectReleasedEvent`, before this event.

MagicItemCategory.title: MagicItemCategory
MagicItemCategory.description:
What kind of magic item a template is, in the magic item catalog.

Every `MagicItemTemplate` has one. The category
governs how the item is handled: what `equip` does with it,
whether `treasure_weight_coins` weighs it as
treasure, and whether generation rolls sentience for it.

These are the categories of the catalog, not the types of the random-generation table.
The table's rod, staff, and wand row covers three categories here. See
`MagicItemType` for the table's types and
`MagicItemCatalog.sub_table` for how one
maps to the other.

The lowercase values appear in the compiled magic item data.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: Which behavior the engine runs for the item.

modifiers.title: Modifiers
modifiers.description: Stat modifiers the item grants. See `ModifierSpec`.

condition.title: Condition
condition.description: The condition the item inflicts, for the behaviors that inflict one.

damage_dice.title: Damage Dice
damage_dice.description: The damage it deals, as a dice expression.

heal_dice.title: Heal Dice
heal_dice.description: The hit points it restores, as a dice expression.

element.title: Element
element.description: The damage element, for example `"fire"`, for the target's immunity checks.

save_category.title: Save Category
save_category.description: Which saving throw column the target rolls against.

save_on.title: Save On
save_on.description: What a successful save does: `"negates"` the effect entirely, or `"half"` the damage.

shape.title: Shape
shape.description: What kind of area an area effect covers, like `"cone"` or `"sphere"`.

dimensions.title: Dimensions
dimensions.description: The area's measurements in feet, keyed by name.

duration_unit.title: Duration Unit
duration_unit.description: The unit the duration counts in, for example `"turns"` or `"rounds"`.

duration_dice.title: Duration Dice
duration_dice.description: A rolled duration, as a dice expression, in `duration_unit`s.

params.title: Params
params.description:
Per-item scalars the behavior reads, keyed by name. A `save_or_die` item kills by poison when `poison` is
the boolean `true`, as on the potion of poison, so *neutralize poison* can revive the character it kills. A
string such as `"true"` doesn't count.

MagicItemEffect.title: MagicItemEffect
MagicItemEffect.description:
The part of a magic item's behavior the engine resolves for you.

An item whose page describes something the engine can execute has one of these. The rest
have their page text in the template's `manual` field, for you to narrate and
adjudicate yourself. `kind` selects which behavior runs, and the behavior reads the fields
it needs, so most fields are empty on most items.

Read `kind` to find out which behavior the engine runs for an item. Read `modifiers` to
show what a worn item grants, since
`equipped_item_modifiers` returns exactly
those for every equipped always-active item.

The kinds the compiled catalog uses are `worn_modifiers`, `potion`, `damage_area`,
`condition_area`, `healing`, `save_or_die`, `on_hit_drain`, `striking`, `ward`,
`regeneration`, `light`, `giant_strength`, and `weakness`.

instance_type.title: Instance Type
instance_type.description:
Always `"magic_item"`. This field distinguishes it from a mundane
`ItemInstance` when both are stored in one list.

instance_id.title: Instance Id
instance_id.description:
The id of this copy, for example `"magic-item-0003"`, allocated by
`IdAllocator`. Commands that act on a magic item identify it by this, not by its
template id.

template_id.title: Template Id
template_id.description:
Which item it is. Get its template with
`magic_item_template`. Every id is in
`load_magic_items` and in [the magic item id
index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/magic-items/).

charges_remaining.title: Charges Remaining
charges_remaining.description:
How many charges are left in a rod, staff, or wand, or `null` for an item that has no charges. Keep this out of
the player's view: in the tabletop rules a charge count can't be discovered.

quantity.title: Quantity
quantity.description: How many the stack contains, for enchanted ammunition. A stack at 0 is spent and no longer counts as carried.

identified.title: Identified
identified.description:
True once the party knows what the item is. A player-facing view masks an unidentified item's name and
properties.

cursed_revealed.title: Cursed Revealed
cursed_revealed.description:
True once the engine has revealed the curse. From then on the item can't be unequipped or given away until the
*remove curse* spell lifts the curse, which sets this back to False.

base_item_id.title: Base Item Id
base_item_id.description:
The mundane item underneath an enchanted weapon, arrow, suit of armour, or staff. Look it up with
`load_equipment` (ids listed in [the equipment id
index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/)). For generic enchanted armour, this
is what the *Magic Armour Type* roll chose.

sentience.description:
The sword's mind, for a sentient sword. See `SwordSentience`. `null` on
everything else.

state.title: State
state.description:
State specific to this copy, keyed by name: the effects a worn item has attached, an energy-drain sword's
remaining drains, a ring of wishes' remaining wishes, the day a staff of healing last healed each target, the
spells left on a scroll.

MagicItemInstance.title: MagicItemInstance
MagicItemInstance.description:
One magic item a character has, with everything that differs from copy to copy.

Templates are shared and frozen. This is the copy in play, and it's mutable. Treasure
generation makes them
(`instantiate_magic_item` and
`generate_magic_item`), an
`Inventory` contains them, and
`magic_item_template` gets you back to the
template behind one.

An instance starts unidentified, and a player-facing view shows it as an unknown item
until it's identified. In a session, the engine identifies it the first time a character
uses it: drinks the potion, swings the sword, or puts on the ring. A referee can also
identify it with `IdentifyItem`. The engine reveals a
cursed item's curse at the same moment. From then on the bearer can't take it off until the *remove curse* spell
lifts the curse, and `unequip` raises a `ValueError` whose
message includes `items.curse.stuck`.

id.title: Id
id.description:
Magic item identifier, such as `"potion_of_healing"`. Pass to
`GET /v1/rules/magic-items/{item_id}`.

name.title: Name
name.description: True display name of the magic item.

MagicItemSummary.title: MagicItemSummary
MagicItemSummary.description: Summary of a magic item from osrlib's `MagicItemTemplate`.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The catalog id, for example `"potion_of_healing"`. Get every id from
`load_magic_items`, or see [the magic item id
index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/magic-items/).

name.title: Name
name.description: The display name. Show this only once the instance is identified.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
What to call one of these items in a sentence once the party knows what it is, like
`"potion of healing"` or `"sword +1"`.

It's lowercase unless a word is a proper noun or an abbreviation, like the `ESP` of
`"potion of ESP"`, and it has no article, so put a number or an article in front of it. For
enchanted ammunition it names one of the units that
`MagicItemInstance.quantity` counts, so
`"Arrows +1 (3d10 arrows)"` is `"arrow +1"`. Footwear and gloves are named as a pair, like
`"pair of boots of speed"`, so a count reads "2 pairs of boots of speed".

Like `name`, show it only once the instance is identified. Until then,
`PlayerView.item_names` names the item by its masked name.

A template you construct yourself that leaves it out gets its `name`.

display_name_plural.title: Display Name Plural
display_name_plural.description:
What to call two or more of these items, like `"potions of healing"` or `"swords +1"`.

`PlayerView.item_names_plural` gives it to the players' client. A
template you construct yourself that leaves it out gets `display_name` with the regular English ending on the word
that names the item: the last word before the first `of`, `with`, or `vs`, a comma, a bonus like `+1`, a closing
Roman numeral, or an opening parenthesis, or the last word when the name has none of them. So `"Idol of the drowned
saint"` becomes `"Idols of the drowned saint"`, and `"Lantern (hooded)"` becomes `"Lanterns (hooded)"`. The ending
is `s`, or `es` after `s`, `x`, `z`, `ch`, or `sh`, or `ies` in place of a `y` that follows a consonant, and `staff`
becomes `staves` with its capital kept, so `"Staff of the Magi"` becomes `"Staves of the Magi"`. The connecting
words count in any case, so `"Staff Of Power"` becomes `"Staves Of Power"`, and any spaces after the word stay after
the ending. The compiled plural of every built-in template follows the same rule. Set it yourself when the name is
already plural, like `"Torches (6)"`, or when the plural is irregular.

category.description: What kind of item it is. See `MagicItemCategory`.

base_item_id.title: Base Item Id
base_item_id.description:
The mundane equipment id the enchantment overlays, for an enchanted sword, weapon, ammunition, or shield, and
`"staff"` for every magic staff. Look it up with `load_equipment` (ids listed in [the
equipment id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/)). `null` for everything
else, including generic enchanted armour, whose base is rolled for each copy on the *Magic Armour Type* table and
recorded on the instance's `base_item_id`.

attack_bonus.title: Attack Bonus
attack_bonus.description: What the item adds to an attack roll. Negative when cursed. The staves of wizardry and snakes add 1.

damage_bonus.title: Damage Bonus
damage_bonus.description: What it adds to damage. Negative when cursed.

ac_bonus.title: Ac Bonus
ac_bonus.description: What it adds to the wearer's armour class. Negative when cursed.

ac_set.title: Ac Set
ac_set.description:
The armour class the item forces, on the descending scale, for the cursed armour and shield whose pages print
`AC 9 [10]`. `null` on every other item.

ac_set_ascending.title: Ac Set Ascending
ac_set_ascending.description: The same forced armour class on the ascending scale.

cursed.title: Cursed
cursed.description:
True when the item is cursed. In a session, the engine reveals the curse the first time a character uses
the item. From then on the bearer can't take it off until the *remove curse* spell lifts the curse.

charges_dice.title: Charges Dice
charges_dice.description:
How many charges are in a new copy, as a dice expression, for a rod, staff, or wand. `null` for an item with no
charges, like the staves of healing and snakes, whose pages say "Does not use charges".

quantity_dice.title: Quantity Dice
quantity_dice.description: How many arrive at once, as a dice expression, for enchanted ammunition.

always_active.title: Always Active
always_active.description: True when the item works while it's worn or wielded, with nothing to invoke.

effect.description:
What the engine resolves for the item. See `MagicItemEffect`. `null` for an
item whose behavior is left to you, which has `manual` prose instead.

params.title: Params
params.description:
Per-item scalars, keyed by name, for behaviors that read them. On a staff, `melee_class_ids` lists the classes
that may wield it whatever their weapon policy says: the magic-user, on the staves of power, striking, and wizardry.
`manual_powers` is true on a staff that strikes and has other powers, which the session leaves to the referee in
`manual`: the staves of power and wizardry. A use of such a staff that strikes no group is one of those powers.

manual.title: Manual
manual.description: The item's page text, for the parts you adjudicate yourself. Show these lines to the referee.

weight_coins.title: Weight Coins
weight_coins.description:
The weight of one item in coins, for the potions, scrolls, rods, staves, and wands that weigh as treasure. The
figure comes from the `TreasureWeight` rows. 0 on every other item: an
enchanted weapon or suit of armour weighs as its mundane base item (see
`equipment_weight_coins`), and the SRD gives rings and miscellaneous
items no weight.

hoard_recipe.title: Hoard Recipe
hoard_recipe.description:
The treasure a map leads to, as printed treasure entries. See
`TreasureEntry`. Empty on everything but a treasure map. Generate the hoard
with `generate_treasure_entries`.

curses.title: Curses
curses.description:
The cursed scroll's example curses. See `ScrollCurse`. Empty on every other
item.

overrides_applied.title: Overrides Applied
overrides_applied.description:
Which fields were corrected when this item was compiled from the SRD text, as dotted paths. Empty when none were.
osrlib doesn't read it during play.

MagicItemTemplate.title: MagicItemTemplate
MagicItemTemplate.description:
A magic item, compiled from the generation tables and the per-item pages.

Get one from `MagicItemCatalog.get`, or from
`magic_item_template` when what you have is an
instance. Templates are frozen and shared. In play, each
copy is a `MagicItemInstance`, which
`instantiate_magic_item` creates from a template.
That function rolls the details that differ from copy to copy.

A cursed item's penalty is a negative bonus, so the arithmetic is the same as for a good
item. The cursed armour and cursed shield that set armour class to a fixed value use
`ac_set` instead.

MagicItemType.title: MagicItemType
MagicItemType.description:
The types of the master *Magic Item Type* table, which is the first roll in generating a magic item.

Roll the master table to get one of these, then roll that type's table for the item:
`generate_magic_item` does both. A magic
allotment for one kind of item gives its type as one of these values.

These are the table's types, not the catalog's categories. Rods, staves, and wands share
a single printed row and a single table, while the catalog has a separate category for each. See
`MagicItemCategory`.

The lowercase values appear in the compiled treasure data.

category.description: The type this row selects. See `MagicItemType`.

basic_min.title: Basic Min
basic_min.description: The lowest d% roll that selects it in the B column.

basic_max.title: Basic Max
basic_max.description: The highest d% roll that selects it in the B column.

expert_min.title: Expert Min
expert_min.description: The lowest d% roll that selects it in the X column.

expert_max.title: Expert Max
expert_max.description: The highest d% roll that selects it in the X column.

MagicItemTypeRow.title: MagicItemTypeRow
MagicItemTypeRow.description:
One row of the master *Magic Item Type* table, with the d% rolls that select its type in each column.

The rules print two columns, B for Basic play and X for Expert play, and some types have
different odds in each. Scrolls are likelier in Expert play, and potions and other
weapons less likely. A printed `00` is read as 100, so both columns end at 100.

rows.title: Rows
rows.description:
The rows, in printed order, each column covering the whole d%. See
`MagicItemTypeRow`.

MagicItemTypeTable.title: MagicItemTypeTable
MagicItemTypeTable.description:
The master *Magic Item Type* table, which gives the kind of magic item a d% roll produces.

It's the first of the two rolls that generate a magic item. Roll it with
`category_for_roll`, then
roll the type's table, which
`MagicItemCatalog.sub_table` returns. Or
let `generate_magic_item` do both and
instantiate the item.

id.title: Id
id.description:
An opaque `feature:` handle. Pass this value in a feature command's `feature_id`
instead of an internal authored or generated cache id.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: The feature's public kind. Generated caches use `"generated_cache"`.

description.title: Description
description.description:
The feature's authored `FeatureSpec.description`,
or an empty string for a generated cache. It's written for the players to read. The view shows
it from the moment the feature comes into view, and for a cache, before anyone opens it and
after the party empties it. The feature's
`FeatureSpec.referee_notes` never appear in
the player view.

cell.title: Cell
cell.description: The feature's cell, or `null` when an area feature applies to the whole entered area.

area_id.title: Area Id
area_id.description:
The id of the area the feature is in, once the party has entered that area, otherwise `null`.
For an authored feature, it's the area that lists the feature. For a generated cache, it's the
area that owns the cache's cell, the area that
`LevelSpec.area_at` returns. It never names an area
the party hasn't entered.

trap_state.title: Trap State
trap_state.description: The party's known trap state, or `null` when the party knows no trap state.

emptied.title: Emptied
emptied.description:
True for an authored treasure cache the party has emptied with
`TakeTreasure`.

The cache stays in the list under the same `id` and description, so you can draw it opened.
Don't offer it to `TakeTreasure`, which refuses it with `exploration.feature.emptied`. It's
false for every other feature, and for a cache the party hasn't emptied, however little it
holds. A generated cache is never marked emptied, because the session removes it when the
party takes it, so it leaves the list.

MapFeatureView.title: MapFeatureView
MapFeatureView.description: One known actionable or descriptive feature on the player map.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"mark_trigger_fired"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

trigger_id.title: Trigger Id
trigger_id.description:
Which trigger fired. Any non-empty id is accepted, so you can mark firings from your
systems with ids you choose. The session's state records each id once, which is what
the interpreter checks for a trigger that fires once, and the command log records every mark.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description:
The referee's text about this firing, included on the
`TriggerFiredEvent`, which has referee
visibility. Players don't see it. To give the players a line about what happened, issue
an `AddJournalEntry`. Leave it `null` when there's
nothing to say. An empty string fails validation.

MarkTriggerFired.title: MarkTriggerFired
MarkTriggerFired.description:
Referee: record that a trigger has fired.

A trigger is an authored rule for commands to issue when something happens in play.
The trigger and quest interpreter
(`Interpreter`) issues this command for each
trigger it fires, and a listener you write or an LLM referee can issue it too. The
interpreter marks a trigger before it issues the trigger's consequences, so it reads the
mark and doesn't fire a once-only trigger again. The mark survives save,
load, and replay like the rest of the session's state. This command is legal in
every mode, `game_over` and `victory` included.

Marking a trigger that's already marked is accepted and changes no state, but it's
still logged. The session's state records whether a trigger has fired, and the command
log records each firing.

Any `trigger_id` is accepted, because a mark needs no authored trigger behind it, so you
can mark ids from any of your game's systems. The quest commands are different:
`ActivateQuest` and the other quest commands
accept only the ids of quests the adventure defines.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`, `battle`, `game_over`, `victory`

**Rejections:**

None.

**Events:**

A `TriggerFiredEvent` with the
trigger id and the `narrative` text, for every mark. The event has referee
visibility.

Material.title: Material
Material.description:
What a weapon or piece of ammunition is made of, where the rules care.

Some monsters are hurt only by silver or magical weapons. The `material` field of
`WeaponTemplate` and
`AmmunitionTemplate` marks a mundane weapon as
silver, and the damage pipeline in `osrlib.core.combat` reads it
when it checks a target's immunities. The field defaults to `STANDARD`. The compiled
catalog uses `SILVER` for the silver dagger and silver-tipped arrows.

The values `"standard"` and `"silver"` appear in the compiled equipment data.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the players see who joins them.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `member_added`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The id the session gave the new member, like `"character-0005"`. Later commands and
events refer to the member by this id.

name.title: Name
name.description: The new member's name, so you can show the event without looking up the party.

class_id.title: Class Id
class_id.description: The new member's class id, like `"fighter"`.

level.title: Level
level.description: The new member's experience level when they joined.

MemberAddedEvent.title: MemberAddedEvent
MemberAddedEvent.description:
A new member joined the party during play.

Emitted by `AddMember`. The member is already in the
party, at the back of the marching order, so add them to the party on screen. Their full
sheet is in the views, under `character_id`. The event doesn't say why they joined. The
command does: read the `source` of the `AddMember`, either the one you executed or its
entry in `GameSession.command_log`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The id of the member the effect is attached to, matching a
`MemberView.id`.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
The effect kind, like `"light"` or `"fatigue"`. It's the same string an
`EffectActiveCondition` checks for. A spell's effect
has the spell's id as its kind unless the spell's data gives it a kind of its own, and
`PlayerView.spell_names` contains the name for a kind
that is a spell id.

remaining_rounds.title: Remaining Rounds
remaining_rounds.description:
Rounds left before the effect expires, never below zero. `null` when the effect has no
expiry, and for any effect a potion gave, because by the rules the referee tracks a potion's
duration and never tells the players.

MemberEffectView.title: MemberEffectView
MemberEffectView.description:
One active effect on a party member, like a burning torch or a running spell.

You get these from `PlayerView.effects`. Only
effects on a party member appear. An effect attached to a dungeon cell, like a pool of
burning oil, is for the referee and doesn't appear.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party sees its own members move.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `member_moved`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who moved, by party member id.

move.title: Move
move.description:
The move the member made: `"close"`, `"fighting_withdrawal"`, or `"retreat"`, as they
declared it in `BattleDeclaration.move`.

advance_feet.title: Advance Feet
advance_feet.description:
The member's advance right after the move, in feet forward of the party line. Zero is the line,
and a negative value is behind it. When the party line moves back at the end of the movement step,
every member's advance grows by the same amount, and this value isn't updated. Read
`EncounterView.advance_feet` after the round for
where the member stands.

group_id.title: Group Id
group_id.description:
The group `distance_feet` is measured to. For a `close`, it's the group the member closed
on. For a `fighting_withdrawal` or a `retreat`, it's the group nearest the member after the
move, among the groups that haven't fled and still have a living member. When two are equally
near, it's the one that comes first in
`EncounterView.groups`.

distance_feet.title: Distance Feet
distance_feet.description:
The member's distance to the group in `group_id` after the move, in feet. It's that group's
distance from the party line minus `advance_feet`. At 5' or less, the member and the group can
reach each other in melee.

MemberMovedEvent.title: MemberMovedEvent
MemberMovedEvent.description:
A party member moved by themselves on the range track, closing on a group or falling back.

The range track is how a battle measures distance. Each group stands at a distance from the
party line, the place where the party stood when the encounter opened. Each member stands at
an advance, in feet, forward of that line toward the monsters. Every member starts the battle
on the line, at an advance of zero.

Emitted by `ResolveBattleRound` in the party's
movement step, once for each member whose advance changes:

- A member who declares `move="close"`, with a `move` action or with an `attack`, moves at
  their own encounter movement rate toward the group they named. They stop 5' from that group,
  and they never come closer than 5' to another group that's still in the fight.
- A member who makes a `fighting_withdrawal` or a `retreat` that not every declarer makes moves
  back alone, at half their encounter rate or their full rate. Their advance goes down, and it
  can go below zero, behind the line.

When the moves leave every member the monsters can see behind the line, the line moves back to
the foremost of them at the end of the movement step, as
`BattleState.advance_feet` describes. The session
emits no event for that, and no distance between a member and a group changes.

The events come in two runs, each in marching order: the members who fall back first, then
the members who close. A member who closes while already within 5' of the group doesn't move,
and the session emits nothing for them. A formation move, a defensive move that every declarer
makes, moves the groups instead of the members, so it emits
`GroupMovedEvent`s and none of these.

The event reports the member's advance right after their move, before the party line moves back,
so it isn't always where the member stands once the round is over. Use it to narrate or animate
the move. To draw where each member stands, read
`EncounterView.advance_feet` and
`EncounterGroupView.member_distance_feet`
from the player view after the round.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the players see who leaves them.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `member_removed`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The id the member had, like `"character-0002"`. The session never gives it to another
member, so earlier events that name it still mean this character.

name.title: Name
name.description: The member's name, so you can show the event without the member at hand.

given_to.title: Given To
given_to.description:
The id of the member who took everything the leaving member carried, or `null` when it
all left the game with them.

MemberRemovedEvent.title: MemberRemovedEvent
MemberRemovedEvent.description:
A member left the party during play.

Emitted by `RemoveMember`. The member is already gone
from the party and from the views, so take them off the party on screen. When `given_to` is
set, the `ItemsGivenEvent` just before this event
lists what that member took. The event doesn't say why the member left. The command does:
read the `source` of the `RemoveMember`, either the one you executed or its entry in
`GameSession.command_log`.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The member's character id, like `"character-0001"`. It's the id you put in the
`character_id` of a command like `GrantItem` or a battle
declaration, so a remote client can issue commands without having the session.

name.title: Name
name.description: The character's name, as the player wrote it.

class_id.title: Class Id
class_id.description:
The character class id, like `"fighter"`, as in
`Character.class_id`. For a class your game wrote, it's
the id of the character's `custom_class`. To show
the class, use `class_name`.

class_name.title: Class Name
class_name.description:
The character class's name, like `"Fighter"`, read from
`Character.definition`, so it's right for a custom
class too.

current_hp.title: Current Hp
current_hp.description:
Current hit points. Zero or less means the member is down, and `conditions` shows
what took them out.

max_hp.title: Max Hp
max_hp.description: Maximum hit points at the current level.

conditions.title: Conditions
conditions.description:
The conditions on the member right now, as
`Condition` serialized values like `"dead"` or
`"asleep"`, in the order the member gained them.

inventory.title: Inventory
inventory.description:
The member's pack, as a JSON-ready dict with the keys `items`, `purse`, `valuables`,
`worn_armour`, `shield`, `wielded`, and `rings`. Mundane items appear as the inventory
serializes them.

A magic item is masked until it's identified. An unidentified one has a `display` name in place of its true
name, like `"a potion"`, or `"a dagger with a faint aura"` for a magic weapon. An enchanted weapon, suit of
armour, or shield is named after one unit of the mundane item underneath it, its
`display_name` with an article, so enchanted arrows display as
`"an arrow with a faint aura"` and enchanted chainmail as `"a suit of chainmail with a faint aura"`. A suit of
enchanted armour with no mundane item recorded displays as `"a suit of armour with a faint aura"`. When the
display name refers to a weapon, the entry also has the `qualities` of that plain weapon, as an identified one
does, so you can tell a melee attack from a missile attack without revealing the weapon's bonus or curse. It has
a `missile_ranges` key only when the rules give the weapon ranges, so on a sword the key is absent rather than
empty. Every magic staff displays as `"a staff"` and has the staff's `qualities`. Any other item whose display
name comes from its category, like `"a wand"`, has neither key, because its display name doesn't refer to a
weapon. An identified item shows its `name`, its `template_id`, and whether a curse has been revealed. Charges
never appear.

An identified spell scroll also has a `spells` key, the ids of the spells left on it, in the order that
`UseItem` reads them, so the first is the one that a `UseItem` with `spell_id`
unset reads. A spell appears once for each time it's on the scroll. Send one of them as `UseItem.spell_id` to
read it, and look its name and usages up in `PlayerView.spell_names`
and `PlayerView.spell_modes`. Reading the scroll identifies it, and
so does a referee's `IdentifyItem`. An unidentified scroll has no `spells`
key, and neither has a scroll with no spells on it, such as a cursed scroll, a scroll of protection, or a
treasure map.

To name an item in a sentence, look up the id it has here in
`PlayerView.item_names`: a mundane item's
`template.id`, and a magic item's or a valuable's `instance_id`.

memorized_spells.title: Memorized Spells
memorized_spells.description:
The prepared spells, one dumped
`MemorizedSpell` per copy, in memorization
order. Empty for a class that casts nothing. To show a copy's name, look its `spell_id` up in
`PlayerView.spell_names`, or in
`PlayerView.reversed_spell_names` for a copy
whose `reversed` is true.

encounter_rate_feet.title: Encounter Rate Feet
encounter_rate_feet.description:
How far the member can move in one round of a battle or an encounter, in feet.

It's a third of the member's movement rate after encumbrance, doubled while *haste* is on them.
In a battle, a member who declares `move="close"` moves up to this far toward the group, and
stops 5' from it. So a member can close on a group and attack it in the same round when their
distance to it, in
`EncounterGroupView.member_distance_feet`,
is at most this rate plus 5'. Use it to offer "close in and attack" only to the members who can
reach.

It doesn't account for conditions. A member who can't move this round, like one held by a web,
still has a rate here, and
`EncounterView.immobile` lists them.

race.title: Race
race.description:
The character's race id, like `"human"` or `"dwarf"`, as in
`Character.race`.

alignment.title: Alignment
alignment.description:
The character's alignment, as an `Alignment` serialized
value: `"lawful"`, `"neutral"`, or `"chaotic"`.

title.title: Title
title.description:
The level title, like `"Veteran"` for a 1st-level fighter, as
`level_title` returns it. `null` past the last title the
class has, so show the class name instead.

xp.title: Xp
xp.description: The experience points the character has.

xp_next_level.title: Xp Next Level
xp_next_level.description:
The experience points the next level needs, or `null` when the character has reached the
highest level of the class.

scores.title: Scores
scores.description:
The six ability scores, keyed by `AbilityScore`
serialized value: `"str"`, `"int"`, `"wis"`, `"dex"`, `"con"`, and `"cha"`.

They're the scores the character rolled, as in
`Character.scores`. A STR that an item sets, like
the 18 of gauntlets of ogre power, changes `effective_strength` but not `"str"`.

effective_strength.title: Effective Strength
effective_strength.description:
The STR score the rules use during play, as
`Character.effective_strength` gives it.
`melee_modifier` and `open_doors_chance` come from it.

It's `scores["str"]` unless an item sets the member's STR. So a fighter who rolled STR 11 and
wears gauntlets of ogre power has 18 here and 11 in `scores`. To show a player what the item
did, show both numbers. Like the armour class, it counts the gauntlets before the party
identifies them, while `inventory` still shows them as `"a curious device"`.

melee_modifier.title: Melee Modifier
melee_modifier.description:
The Strength modifier to melee attack rolls and melee damage, as
`Character.melee_modifier`. It's the
modifier combat adds.

It comes from `effective_strength`, not from `scores["str"]`. So a fighter with STR 11 who
wears gauntlets of ogre power has +3 here.

missile_modifier.title: Missile Modifier
missile_modifier.description:
The Dexterity modifier to missile attack rolls, as
`Character.missile_modifier`.

initiative_modifier.title: Initiative Modifier
initiative_modifier.description:
The Dexterity modifier to the member's initiative roll, as
`Character.initiative_modifier`. The
session uses it only under individual initiative.

hit_point_modifier.title: Hit Point Modifier
hit_point_modifier.description:
The Constitution modifier to each Hit Die rolled, as
`Character.hit_point_modifier`.

magic_save_modifier.title: Magic Save Modifier
magic_save_modifier.description:
The Wisdom modifier to saving throws against magic, as
`Character.magic_save_modifier`.

npc_reaction_modifier.title: Npc Reaction Modifier
npc_reaction_modifier.description:
The Charisma modifier to reaction rolls, as
`Character.npc_reaction_modifier`.

open_doors_chance.title: Open Doors Chance
open_doors_chance.description:
The chance in 6 of forcing a stuck door open, as
`Character.open_doors_chance`. It's the
chance the session rolls against for a `ForceDoor`, and it
comes from `effective_strength`.

thac0.title: Thac0
thac0.description:
The d20 roll the member needs to hit armour class 0, as
`Character.thac0`. Show it when your game uses
descending armour class.

attack_bonus.title: Attack Bonus
attack_bonus.description:
The bonus the member adds to an attack roll against ascending armour class, as
`Character.attack_bonus`.

armour_class.title: Armour Class
armour_class.description:
The member's descending armour class, where lower is better, as the players know it.

It counts everything the member wears, unidentified magic items included, because a magic item
works when it's worn. So it can show that a shield is better than a plain one while `inventory`
still calls it `"a shield with a faint aura"`. It's the number in
`Character.armour_class`, the one the monsters
roll against, with one exception.

The exception is a worn cursed shield or suit of armour that the party hasn't identified. The
OSE SRD says every test shows such an item as enchanted with a +1 bonus, so until the curse is
revealed, this number counts it as its base item with a +1 enchantment, and as setting no armour
class of its own. An unarmoured fighter with AC 9 reads 7 with an unidentified cursed shield -2,
as with a shield +1, while the monsters roll against the real 10. In cursed chainmail -2 the same
fighter reads 4, as in chainmail +1, while the real armour class is 7. Everything else the member
wears, and the DEX modifier, count as usual.

The session reveals the curse and identifies the item at the same moment: the first time the
member is attacked in a battle, or when a referee sends
`IdentifyItem`. From then on this is the real number. It
stays the real number after *remove curse* frees the member, because the item stays
identified.

armour_class_ascending.title: Armour Class Ascending
armour_class_ascending.description:
The member's ascending armour class, where higher is better, as the players know it. It
describes the same defense as `armour_class` and counts the same items the same way, so it's
`Character.armour_class_ascending`
except while the member wears a cursed shield or suit of armour that the party hasn't
identified. Then it counts that item as its base item with a +1 enchantment, so the fighter
with AC 9 [10] and an unidentified cursed shield -2 reads 12 here while the monsters roll
against the real 9.

saves.title: Saves
saves.description:
The five saving throws, keyed by the field names of
`SavingThrows`: `"death"`, `"wands"`, `"paralysis"`, `"breath"`,
and `"spells"`. Each value is the d20 roll the member needs, as
`Character.saves` gives it.

movement_rate_feet.title: Movement Rate Feet
movement_rate_feet.description:
How far the member moves in one exploration turn, in feet, as
`Character.movement_rate` returns it under the
session's ruleset. The party moves at the rate of its slowest living member.

languages.title: Languages
languages.description:
The ids of the languages the member speaks, as
`Character.languages` lists them.

spell_book.title: Spell Book
spell_book.description:
The ids of the spells in the member's spell book, as in
`Character.spell_book`, in the order they were
written in. Empty for a class that has no spell book. An arcane caster prepares only from the
book, and `preparable_spells` lists the spells in it that the member has a slot for. To show a
spell's name, look its id up in
`PlayerView.spell_names`.

spell_slots.title: Spell Slots
spell_slots.description:
How many spells the member can memorize at each spell level, lowest level first, as in the
`spell_slots` of the class's progression row
for the member's level. Entry `i` is the slot count at spell level `i + 1`. It comes from
`Character.definition`, so it's right for a custom
class too.

A `PrepareSpells` fits these counts: at each spell level,
select no more copies than the count there, and group `preparable_spells` by
`PlayerView.spell_levels` to fill them. An arcane
caster's book has room at a spell level for this count less the spells the book already has
there. A 1st-level cleric has a count of 0 at every level, and a class that casts nothing has no
counts.

preparable_spells.title: Preparable Spells
preparable_spells.description:
The ids of the spells the member may select in a
`PrepareSpells`, in the order of the session's catalog,
`GameSession.effective_spells`. Build a
prepare dialog from it.

For an arcane caster, they're the spells in `spell_book` at the spell levels where the member has
a slot, so a spell that a lost level left in the book without a slot isn't here. For a divine
caster, they're the spells on the class's spell list at every spell level where the member has a
slot, and the spells the adventure bundles for that list are among them. A cleric has no slot
until 2nd level, so the list is empty for a 1st-level cleric. It's empty for a class that casts
nothing.

A spell id is here exactly when a `PrepareSpells` that selects one copy of it in its normal form
is refused with none of these codes, which belong to the spell and the member:
`magic.memorize.not_a_caster`, `magic.memorize.unknown_spell`, `magic.memorize.wrong_list`,
`magic.memorize.not_in_book`, and `magic.memorize.slots_exceeded`. The list doesn't depend on
the moment, so it's the same before the party has slept (`magic.memorize.needs_sleep`), during an
encounter or a battle (`session.command.wrong_mode`), and while the member can't act
(`session.command.member_incapacitated`). The selections as a whole still have to fit
`spell_slots` at each spell level.

The form of a copy is up to the caster's kind. An arcane caster may select the reversed form of a
spell that has an entry in
`PlayerView.reversed_spell_names`, and the
session refuses the reversed form of any other spell with `magic.memorize.not_reversible`. A
divine caster selects the normal form and chooses the form when casting, and the session refuses a
reversed selection with `magic.memorize.divine_reverses_at_cast`. To show a spell's name, look its
id up in `PlayerView.spell_names`.

learnable_spells.title: Learnable Spells
learnable_spells.description:
The ids of the spells the member may write into their spell book with
`LearnSpell`, in the order of the session's catalog,
`GameSession.effective_spells`. Build a learn
dialog from it.

They're the spells on the class's spell list that aren't in `spell_book`, at each spell level
where the book has room. The room at a spell level is the member's count there in `spell_slots`,
less the spells the book already has at that level. The spells the adventure bundles for that list
are among them. The list is empty for a divine caster and for a class that casts nothing,
because neither keeps a spell book. It's also empty while the book has a spell that the session's
catalog doesn't have, because the session can't tell that spell's level, and so can't tell how
much room the book has left.

A spell id is here exactly when a `LearnSpell` for it is refused with none of these codes, which
belong to the spell and the member: `magic.book.not_arcane`, `magic.book.unknown_spell`,
`magic.book.wrong_list`, `magic.book.duplicate`, and `magic.book.capacity_exceeded`. The list
doesn't depend on the moment, so it's the same during an encounter or a battle
(`session.command.wrong_mode`) and while the member can't act
(`session.command.member_incapacitated`). Learning one spell can fill the book at that spell's
level, so read the view again after each `LearnSpell`. To show a spell's name, look its id up in
`PlayerView.spell_names`.

missile_counts.title: Missile Counts
missile_counts.description:
How many missiles the member's cast of a spell shoots, keyed by spell id, for each spell in `spell_book`,
`memorized_spells`, `preparable_spells`, or `learnable_spells` whose normal form has a usage that takes one
target per missile, such as `{"magic_missile": 3}` for a 6th-level magic-user. A cast of that usage takes
exactly this many targets, and the session refuses any other number with `magic.cast.target_count`. Name a
creature more than once to send it more missiles.

The number grows with the member's level, as the OSE SRD's *magic missile* gives "2 more missiles for every 5
experience levels", so read the view again after the member levels up or is drained. A usage takes one target per
missile when its `SpellModeView.one_target_per_missile`
is true. A reading from a scroll takes the scroll's number instead, in
`SpellModeView.scroll_missile_count`. A `MemberView`
that osrlib 2.11.0 or earlier built validates with this map empty.

reversed_missile_counts.title: Reversed Missile Counts
reversed_missile_counts.description:
How many missiles the member's cast of a spell's reverse shoots, keyed by spell id, for the spells in the same
lists as `missile_counts` whose reverse has a usage that takes one target per missile. No built-in spell's
reverse has one, but a spell that an adventure bundles can. A `MemberView` that osrlib 2.11.0 or earlier built
validates with this map empty.

reverses_at.title: Reverses At
reverses_at.description:
When the member chooses the form of a spell that reverses: `"memorize"`, `"cast"`, or `null` for a
class that casts nothing.

It comes from the kind of caster the class is, as
`caster_profile` reads it from
`Character.definition`, so it's right for a custom class
too, whatever its spell list and whether or not the member has a spell book. The OSE SRD says of arcane
casters that "The normal or reversed form of a spell must be selected when the spell is memorized", and
of divine casters that they "can cast the reversed version of a spell by speaking the words and
performing the gestures backwards when it is cast."

- `"memorize"`, for an arcane caster: a `PrepareSpells` may
  select the reversed form of a spell that has an entry in
  `PlayerView.reversed_spell_names`, and each
  memorized copy is cast in the form its `reversed` in `memorized_spells` gives.
- `"cast"`, for a divine caster: the session refuses a reversed selection with
  `magic.memorize.divine_reverses_at_cast`, and every memorized copy of a spell that reverses can be cast
  in either form, with the `reversed` of `CastSpell` or of a `cast`
  `BattleDeclaration`.

So offer a reversed copy in a prepare dialog only when it's `"memorize"`, and offer both forms of a
memorized copy in a cast dialog only when it's `"cast"`.

can_prepare_now.title: Can Prepare Now
can_prepare_now.description:
Whether the session accepts a `PrepareSpells` from the member
now, with selections that fit `preparable_spells` and `spell_slots`. Read it to offer or withhold a
prepare dialog.

It's false exactly when one of the refusals that belong to the moment applies to the member:

- `session.command.wrong_mode`: the session isn't in town or exploring.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated`: the member can't act.
- `magic.memorize.needs_sleep`: the party hasn't slept since the member last prepared, which
  `needs_sleep_to_prepare` gives by itself.

It's also false for a class that casts nothing, which the session refuses with
`magic.memorize.not_a_caster`. It doesn't depend on the slots, so it's true for a 1st-level cleric who
has slept, whose `preparable_spells` is empty and who can prepare only an empty selection.

The session reads the moment from its own state, never from the event log, so the field is right in a
session restored from a save. A `Rest`, a `PrepareSpells`, an encounter,
or a condition can change it, so read the view again after each command.

needs_sleep_to_prepare.title: Needs Sleep To Prepare
needs_sleep_to_prepare.description:
Whether the member has to sleep before they can prepare spells again. Read it to tell the table which
casters need a night's rest.

It's true exactly when the party hasn't slept since the member last prepared, the rule by which the
session refuses a `PrepareSpells` with
`magic.memorize.needs_sleep`. So it's true for every caster in a new session, before the party's first
sleep, and for a caster who has prepared, until the party sleeps again. A `night` or `day`
`Rest` that a wandering encounter doesn't interrupt is sleep. The OSE SRD
says "A spell caster can memorize new spells once a day, after an uninterrupted night’s sleep."

It reads the party's sleeps and the member's last preparation alone. During an encounter or a battle,
and while the member can't act, the session refuses the command with `session.command.wrong_mode` or
`session.command.member_incapacitated` before it checks the sleep, and this field still says whether the
member will need to sleep. It's false for a class that casts nothing, which the session refuses with
`magic.memorize.not_a_caster` whether or not the party has slept.

thief_skills.title: Thief Skills
thief_skills.description:
The member's chance at each thief skill at their level, keyed by the skill field names of
`ThiefSkillRow`, like `"open_locks"` and `"move_silently"`.
`"hear_noise"` is a chance in 6, and every other skill is a percentage. Empty for a class that has no
thief skills.

MemberView.title: MemberView
MemberView.description:
One party member's character sheet, as the players see it.

You get these from `PlayerView.party`, in marching
order, and every party member has one, living or dead. The players know everything about
their characters, so the view has every number on a B/X character sheet, and a client can draw
the sheet from it alone. What the view keeps back is what the party hasn't learned about a magic
item yet: an unidentified item's name, its bonus, and its curse.

The numbers are the member's current ones, read from the live
`Character`. They count what the member wears right now, like
armour, a shield, or a ring of protection, whether or not the party has identified it, because a
B/X magic item works when it's worn. So an unidentified item can change a number while
`inventory` still masks its name. They don't count a timed effect from a spell or a potion, like
the *shield* spell. `PlayerView.effects` lists the timed
effects on each member.

Cursed armour and shields are the one exception, because the OSE SRD says "All types of tests
indicate that a cursed shield or suit of armour is enchanted with a +1 bonus. It is only when the
armour is used in deadly combat that the curse is revealed." Until the session reveals the curse,
`armour_class` and `armour_class_ascending` count a worn cursed shield or suit of armour as the +1
item it tests as, while the monsters roll against the real armour class. `armour_class` says
when the real number appears.

A STR that an item sets counts too. A member who wears gauntlets of ogre power has the numbers
for STR 18. Six rounds after a member puts on a ring of weakness, the ring's curse takes hold,
and the member has the numbers for STR 3. Either way, `effective_strength`, `melee_modifier`,
and `open_doors_chance` change, and `scores` still shows the rolled STR.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party sees its own marching order change.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `member_withdrew`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who fell back, by party member id. They now have the replacement's place in the
marching order.

replacement_id.title: Replacement Id
replacement_id.description:
The member they named, by party member id. They now have the withdrawing member's place in
the marching order.

MemberWithdrewEvent.title: MemberWithdrewEvent
MemberWithdrewEvent.description:
A member who fell back alone traded places in the marching order with the member they named.

Emitted by `ResolveBattleRound` in the party's
movement step, right after the withdrawing member's
`MemberMovedEvent`.

A member who makes a fighting withdrawal or a retreat alone can name another member in
`replacement_id`. The two then
trade places in the marching order, and the session emits this event. The trade moves
nobody on the range track. It decides who stands in front among members at the same
distance from a group who got there in the same round, and it's the marching order the
party keeps after the battle.

The trade happens only when the withdrawing member's move happens, and only while both
members are alive. A member who can no longer move when the movement step comes doesn't
fall back, so they don't trade places either, and the session emits neither event.

Redraw a battle screen's marching order from this event, or read it again from
`PlayerView.party`.

spell_id.title: Spell Id
spell_id.description:
The spell's id, like `"magic_missile"`.

For the built-in ids, iterate `load_spells().spells` or see
[the spell id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/spells/).

reversed.title: Reversed
reversed.description:
True when this copy is prepared as the spell's reversed form.

Only an arcane caster sets it, because in the SRD an arcane caster chooses the form when the
spell is memorized. A divine caster memorizes the normal form and chooses the form when casting,
so a divine caster's copies are always False, and
`memorize_spells` rejects a copy marked True.

MemorizedSpell.title: MemorizedSpell
MemorizedSpell.description:
One spell a caster has ready to cast: which spell, and in which form.

Construct one for each slot you want filled, and pass them to
`memorize_spells` or to the
`PrepareSpells` command. Read them back from a
character's `memorized_spells`, in the order they were prepared. Which copy goes depends on
the order: casting spends the first copy that matches, and
`forget_excess_memorized`, which
`drain_levels` calls, removes the last ones first.

A copy has only a spell id and a form. What the spell can do comes from the template you get
with `SpellCatalog.get`.

api_version.title: Api Version
api_version.description: Installed bxapi version string, such as `"0.1.0"`.

engine_version.title: Engine Version
engine_version.description: Installed osrlib rules engine version string, such as `"2.9.0"`.

schema_version.title: Schema Version
schema_version.description:
osrlib document format version. The server refuses adventure, character, party, and save
documents stamped with a higher `schema_version` with 409 `version_unsupported`.

auth_enabled.title: Auth Enabled
auth_enabled.description: Whether the server requires a bearer API key under `/v1`.

client.title: Client
client.description: Client application name bound to your API key, or `"local"` when `auth_enabled` is `false`.

role.description: Role granted to your API key (`"player"` or `"referee"`).

storage.description: Current document storage usage and quota for `client`.

Meta.title: Meta
Meta.description: Server versions, authentication mode, caller identity, and client storage usage.

short.description: The nearest band, worth +1 to hit.

medium.description: The middle band, with no attack modifier.

long.description: The farthest band, worth −1 to hit, and the limit of the weapon's range.

MissileRanges.title: MissileRanges
MissileRanges.description:
A missile weapon's three range bands, near to far.

Attack resolution measures the distance to the target, finds the band it falls in, and
applies that band's modifier: +1 at short range, nothing at medium, −1 at long. Beyond
the long band the shot is out of range. A
`WeaponTemplate` or a
`CombatFacet` has one of these exactly when it has the
`MISSILE` quality of `WeaponQuality`. Building either
with one and not the other raises a pydantic `ValidationError`. The compiled combat facets
of holy water and burning oil have ranges and the missile quality. The torch's has neither.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
Which statistic the modifier adjusts, one of `MODIFIER_KINDS`. Any
other value raises pydantic's `ValidationError`.

value.title: Value
value.description:
The signed adjustment, like +1 for *bless*'s attack bonus or -1 for *protection from evil*'s penalty on
attackers. For `ac_set` and `ac_set_vs_missile` it's the armour class to set, and for `strength_set` the
strength score. Leave it at 0 for a kind that uses `dice` or acts as a flag.

dice.title: Dice
dice.description:
A dice expression rolled instead of adding `value`, for a kind that grants dice, like *striking*'s `"1d6"`
of extra weapon damage. osrlib checks it with `parse`, so a malformed
expression raises `ContentValidationError` when you build the
`ModifierSpec`, not when the combat code rolls it.

element.title: Element
element.description:
Narrows the modifier to one damage or save element, like `"fire"` for *resist fire*. The modifier counts
only for a roll with that same element. `null` means every element.

versus_other_alignment.title: Versus Other Alignment
versus_other_alignment.description:
True narrows the modifier to rolls against creatures of a different alignment, which is how *protection
from evil* works. The modifier then counts only when the call that reads it passes `versus_differs=True`.

save_categories.title: Save Categories
save_categories.description:
Narrows a save bonus to the named saving throw categories. A Displacer Cloak, for example, covers
`"paralysis"`, `"wands"`, and `"spells"` but not the others. Empty means every category.

melee_only.title: Melee Only
melee_only.description:
True narrows the modifier to melee attacks. That's how the Displacer Cloak's -2 on attackers leaves
missile attacks alone. The modifier then counts only when the call that reads it passes `melee=True`.

from_item.title: From Item
from_item.description:
True marks the modifier as coming from a magic item rather than a spell. Such a modifier is exempt from
the rule that only the largest spell bonus and the largest spell penalty count:
`modifier_total` adds every item modifier to the capped spell total.
Set it on the effects of potions and scrolls as well as worn items, because the rule covers magic items in
general.

ModifierSpec.title: ModifierSpec
ModifierSpec.description:
One adjustment to a combat statistic, granted by an effect or by an equipped magic item.

You write these when you author a spell, a magic item, or an effect of your own. Put them in an
`EffectDefinition`'s `modifiers`. Attaching that definition turns
each spec into an `ActiveModifier` in the creature's `stat_modifiers`,
and the combat functions read them back through `modifier_total` and the
other modifier functions. A magic item template lists specs too. The combat functions read an equipped item's
specs through
`equipped_item_modifiers` instead, and they never appear in
`stat_modifiers`. A spec is frozen, so the same one can be in several definitions.

The scope fields, `element`, `versus_other_alignment`, `save_categories`, and `melee_only`, narrow when the
modifier counts. Leave them at their defaults and the modifier applies to every roll of its kind.

tag.title: Tag
tag.description:
The ability's identifier, a lowercase name like `"regeneration"`.

The combat functions read four tags: `"regeneration"`, `"energy_drain"`, `"breath_weapon"`, and
`"uses_fire"`. A battle in a `GameSession` also reads these:

- `"paralysis"`, `"poison"`, `"disease"`, `"petrification"`, and `"blindness"`, when a
  monster's attack hits.
- `"averting_eyes"`, for the bonus a gazer gets against a creature that averts its eyes.
- `"surprise"`, when its `params` have `meets_gaze`. Every character the monster surprises
  is then affected by its gaze, as with a basilisk.
- `attacks_others` in the `params` of a `"paralysis"` ability, as the ghoul's and the thoul's
  have. The default action policy then has the monster pass over every paralysed member,
  whoever paralysed them, while a target that's neither paralysed nor turned to stone is in
  reach.

name.title: Name
name.description: The ability's name as the SRD prints it, for display.

prose.title: Prose
prose.description: The SRD's description, to show a player or referee.

manual.title: Manual
manual.description: True when osrlib doesn't act on this ability, so the referee applies it from the description.

params.title: Params
params.description:
The numbers and options the SRD gives for the ability, keyed by name.

A troll's regeneration has `delay_rounds` 3 and `per_round` 3, and a wight's energy drain has
`levels` 1. The keys differ by tag. Empty when the SRD gives no numbers.

A `regeneration` ability's params become an effect when an encounter starts, through
`regeneration_definition`. Constructing the ability raises
`pydantic.ValidationError` when the params can't build that effect, such as a `per_round` of `"three"` or a
`revive` of `"lots"`, which isn't a dice expression.

MonsterAbility.title: MonsterAbility
MonsterAbility.description:
One thing a monster can do, as a tag plus the SRD text it came from.

Read them from `MonsterTemplate.abilities`, or
look one up by tag with `MonsterTemplate.ability`.
The combat functions find an ability by its tag and read the numbers in `params`, so a monster's
special powers are data rather than code. Frozen.

An ability marked `manual` is text for a referee to read and act on, and osrlib doesn't use it.

count.title: Count
count.description: How many of this attack the monster makes in a round.

name.title: Name
name.description: The attack's name as the SRD prints it, like `"talon"`, `"bite"`, or `"weapon"`.

damage.title: Damage
damage.description:
The damage as a dice expression, like `"1d6"`, which `roll` evaluates.

`null` when the damage is fixed, and when the attack has no damage dice, like a
dragon's breath, whose damage comes from its `breath_weapon` ability.

fixed_damage.title: Fixed Damage
fixed_damage.description: Damage that is a flat number rather than a roll. `null` when `damage` is set.

fixed_damage_options.title: Fixed Damage Options
fixed_damage_options.description:
The alternative damage values the SRD prints when the referee decides between them.

An insect swarm does 2 or 4 damage depending on the target's armour, and the referee picks one.
Empty for every other attack.

by_weapon.title: By Weapon
by_weapon.description:
True when the monster attacks with whatever weapon it has, so `damage` is the SRD's typical value rather than
a fixed property of the creature.

by_weapon_modifier.title: By Weapon Modifier
by_weapon_modifier.description: The bonus or penalty the SRD prints with a by-weapon attack, like a bugbear's +1 to damage.

effects.title: Effects
effects.description:
What a hit does beyond damage, as tags like `"poison"`, `"paralysis"`, or `"energy_drain"`.

For the numbers behind a tag, call `MonsterTemplate.ability`
with the same tag. It returns `null` when the template has no ability with that tag.

MonsterAttack.title: MonsterAttack
MonsterAttack.description:
One attack a monster makes: its name, how often it's made, how much it hurts, and what else it does.

Read them from `AttackRoutine.attacks`, and pass
one to `resolve_attack` as the attack. A troll's routine
is two talon attacks and a bite, so it has two of these, and the talon's `count` is 2.

Constructing one raises `pydantic.ValidationError` when `damage` is not a valid dice
expression. Frozen.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party sees them fall or flee.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `monster_defeated`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

monster_id.title: Monster Id
monster_id.description: The session id of the creature that was defeated.

template_id.title: Template Id
template_id.description: What it was: a monster catalog id, or `"npc:<class id>"` for a defeated NPC adventurer.

outcome.title: Outcome
outcome.description: How it was defeated: `"slain"`, or `"routed"` when it ran away or was turned.

xp.title: Xp
xp.description:
What it's worth: the monster catalog's printed award, or the level-based award for an NPC
adventurer.

MonsterDefeatedEvent.title: MonsterDefeatedEvent
MonsterDefeatedEvent.description:
One monster was defeated, with the experience it's worth.

Emitted when the encounter ends, once for each creature that was slain, ran away, or
was turned, before the `EncounterEndedEvent`.
A creature the party got away from without defeating has no event.

The session adds up their `xp` for the experience award. Under the default ruleset the
award arrives as an `AdventureXpAwardEvent`
when the party travels back to town. When
`Ruleset.xp_award_timing` is set to award
experience immediately, each survivor's
`XpAwardedEvent` arrives at the end of the
encounter instead, before the `EncounterEndedEvent`.

pattern_type.title: Pattern Type
pattern_type.description:
The discriminator value, `monster_defeated`. It appears in the document, and you
never set it yourself.

template_id.title: Template Id
template_id.description:
The id of the monster to watch for, from the monster catalog, which is the built-in
monsters plus the adventure's bundled monsters. It's the catalog id, not an instance id,
so every monster of that kind matches.

MonsterDefeatedPattern.title: MonsterDefeatedPattern
MonsterDefeatedPattern.description:
A pattern that matches a monster of `template_id` being slain or routed.

Slain and routed both count as defeated, and the pattern matches either one. The engine
reports each defeat with a
`MonsterDefeatedEvent` when the encounter
closes, not when the monster falls. A trigger on a boss therefore fires after the
fighting stops, never in the middle of a round. No pattern matches the moment of a
kill.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
Always `"monster"`. Check it to tell this entry from an
`NpcPartyEncounterEntry` when you read a row.

monster_ids.title: Monster Ids
monster_ids.description:
The ids of the monster templates this row can give, at least one.

Each id refers to a monster template: one that comes with osrlib, from
`load_monsters` and listed in
[the monster id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/monsters/), or one an adventure
includes.

Usually there's one id. Several ids mean the printed row covers several forms of one
monster, like a veteran at three different levels. Unless `variant_dice` is set, osrlib
chooses the form of each individual separately. The tabletop rules leave that choice to the
referee. osrlib rolls it instead, so the same seed gives the same encounter.

variant_dice.title: Variant Dice
variant_dice.description:
A dice expression rolled once to choose one form for the whole group, or `null` when osrlib chooses each
individual's form separately.

The hydra's row has one. Its Hit Dice are rolled once, and every hydra in the group has that many heads. The
expression's lowest total gives the first id, the next total the second, and so on.

MonsterEncounterEntry.title: MonsterEncounterEntry
MonsterEncounterEntry.description:
The entry of an encounter table row for monsters: which monsters can appear.

Pass it with the number that appear to
`select_encounter_individuals`, which
returns one monster id for each. Then create each monster with
`spawn_monster`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party sees the group get away.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `monster_escaped`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

group_id.title: Group Id
group_id.description: Which group got away, as its encounter group id.

MonsterEscapedEvent.title: MonsterEscapedEvent
MonsterEscapedEvent.description:
A monster group got away and left the battle.

A group that's running leaves the battle once it stands farther than
`FLEE_EXIT_FEET` from every living party member. A group
runs when it fails its morale check, or when its living members are all turned or afraid. The
session emits this event in the round the group's move takes it that far, right after that
group's `GroupMovedEvent`. That's a round that
`ResolveBattleRound` resolves, or the monsters'
free first round, which the command that opens the battle resolves.

A group whose morale score is 2 never fights, so it gets away as it enters the battle, either
when the battle opens or when a `SpawnMonsters` adds it
to a battle that's already running. The command that brings the group into the battle then
emits this event right after that group's
`MonsterFledEvent`.

A group whose living members are all turned or afraid can also end up farther than
`FLEE_EXIT_FEET` from every living member without a move of its own: a group turned where it
stands 130' away, or a group the party leaves behind by falling back before the group's next
move. Such a group counts as gone, so once no other group is left fighting, the battle ends.
The session then marks each such group fled and emits this event for it right before the
`BattleEndedEvent`.

The session emits one of these events for a group in the same command result in which
`EncounterGroupView.fled` becomes true, and
never in any other result, so you can tell that the group got away from the event stream
alone. When the escape leaves no group fighting, the battle ends in the same result, and the
`BattleEndedEvent` comes after this event.

The group stays in `EncounterView.groups` with
`fled` true, and the session refuses every declaration aimed at it with
`battle.declaration.unknown_group`. When the encounter ends, its living members count as
defeated for the experience award, as `routed` in their
`MonsterDefeatedEvent`s.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
