the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party sees them break.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `monster_fled`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

group_id.title: Group Id
group_id.description: Which group broke, as its encounter group id.

MonsterFledEvent.title: MonsterFledEvent
MonsterFledEvent.description:
A monster group broke and ran.

Emitted by `ResolveBattleRound` when
a group fails its morale check and flees. When a battle opens, or when a
`SpawnMonsters` adds a group to a running battle, it's
also emitted for a group whose morale is so low that it never fights at all. That group leaves
the battle at once, and a `MonsterEscapedEvent` for
it comes right after this event.

When a cleric turns only some of a group, or a fear effect such as a wand of fear or *cause
fear* frightens only some of it, the turned and afraid members leave the group and flee as a
new group, and `group_id` is the new group's id. A fear effect used outside a battle, during an
encounter or a pursuit, splits the group the same way, and the event comes in the result of the
`UseItem` that frightened them.

A group that fails its morale check is still in the battle when this event comes, and
`EncounterGroupView.fleeing` is true from
then on. It moves away each round, and it has left the battle once it's more than
`FLEE_EXIT_FEET` from the party, when
`EncounterGroupView.fled` becomes true. That
happens in the round its move takes it that far. A group that breaks far enough away gets away
in the round it breaks, and any other group in a later round. The result of the round in which
it gets away contains a `MonsterEscapedEvent` for the group right after the group's
`GroupMovedEvent`. Its members still count as defeated
for the experience award.

count.title: Count
count.description: How many dice are rolled. 0 for a creature whose hit points are fixed.

die.title: Die
die.description: The size of each die: 8, or 4 for a creature with half a Hit Die, which rolls 1d4.

modifier.title: Modifier
modifier.description:
Hit points added to the rolled total, or taken from it when negative. The SRD's `1-1` is a modifier of −1.

A positive modifier also makes the creature attack as though it had one more Hit Die, and moves
it to the higher `+` row of its experience band. A negative modifier drops it a row.

asterisks.title: Asterisks
asterisks.description:
How many asterisks the SRD prints after the Hit Dice, one per special ability. Each one raises the experience
award.

average_hp.title: Average Hp
average_hp.description:
The average hit points the SRD prints, for a referee who would rather not roll. `spawn_monster` ignores it and
rolls.

fixed_hp.title: Fixed Hp
fixed_hp.description: Hit points that are not rolled, like a normal bat's 1 or a hydra's 8 per head. `null` when they're rolled.

MonsterHitDice.title: MonsterHitDice
MonsterHitDice.description:
A monster's Hit Dice, as the stat block prints them.

Read it as `MonsterTemplate.hit_dice`.
`spawn_monster` rolls hit points from it, and
`osrlib.core.tables` uses it to place the monster on the attack matrix
and in an experience band. The SRD's `6+3*` is a `count` of 6, a `modifier` of 3, and one
asterisk.

Constructing one raises `pydantic.ValidationError` when `die` is not 8 or 4, or when `count` is
0 and `fixed_hp` is `null`. Frozen.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The entity id, usually from `IdAllocator.allocate`. Events refer
to the creature by it.

template.description: The stat block this creature was spawned from. Read anything the creature shares with its kind from here.

max_hp.title: Max Hp
max_hp.description: The hit points it was spawned with, 1 or more.

current_hp.title: Current Hp
current_hp.description:
The hit points it has left, from 0 up to `max_hp`.

`deal_damage` stops it at 0 and applies the `dead` condition
through `kill`. Healing stops it at `max_hp`.

conditions.title: Conditions
conditions.description: The conditions on it. Apply and clear them through `osrlib.core.effects`.

stat_modifiers.title: Stat Modifiers
stat_modifiers.description: Timed bonuses and penalties on it, from spells and effects.

alignment.description:
The alignment this creature has, set when it was spawned.

`null` when the template offered several alignments with no usual one, and you passed none to
`spawn_monster`. A ward that depends on alignment treats
such a creature as being of a different alignment, so the ward protects the party.

nonregen_damage.title: Nonregen Damage
nonregen_damage.description:
Damage a regenerating creature can never heal, up to `max_hp`.

Damage of an element in the `blocked_by` param of the template's `regeneration` ability counts
here, which is fire and acid for a troll. A troll stays dead only once this damage alone reaches
its maximum hit points.

last_damaged_round.title: Last Damaged Round
last_damaged_round.description:
The combat round in which it was last hurt, from which the regeneration delay is counted. `null` before anything
has hurt it.

breath_uses_today.title: Breath Uses Today
breath_uses_today.description:
How many times it has used its breath weapon today.

`resolve_breath` adds 1 each time when the breath has a
daily limit. The limit is the `uses_per_day` param of the template's `breath_weapon` ability,
which is 3 for a dragon. A breath weapon with no `uses_per_day` has no daily limit.

drained_hd.title: Drained Hd
drained_hd.description:
How many Hit Dice have been drained from it, which `drain_monster_hd`
adds to. Its THAC0, attack bonus, and saving throws follow the Hit Dice it has left.

When it's above 0, it's less than the template's Hit Dice count, because a drain that would take the last Hit
Die kills the creature instead. Setting a value at or above that count raises `pydantic.ValidationError`.

MonsterInstance.title: MonsterInstance
MonsterInstance.description:
One creature in play, spawned from a frozen `MonsterTemplate`.

Get one from `spawn_monster`. An instance is what takes
damage, gains conditions, and dies. The template it came from never changes, and what happens to
one instance doesn't affect the other creatures spawned from the same template.

An instance has the same rules attributes as a `Character`:
THAC0, attack bonus, both armour classes, saving throws, conditions, and stat modifiers. The
functions in `osrlib.core.combat` and
`osrlib.core.effects` therefore accept either one, through the protocols
in `osrlib.core.creature`.

The instance doesn't copy what the template defines. Read that through `template`. For the
values a drain changes, read the instance's properties, like
`thac0` and
`saves`, rather than the template's fields.

An instance isn't frozen. Each assignment to a field is validated. A value that breaks a rule, like
a negative `current_hp` or a `current_hp` above `max_hp`, raises `pydantic.ValidationError`, and
every field still has the value it had before the assignment.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the players see the monster get back up.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

target_id.title: Target Id
target_id.description: The entity id of the monster that came back.

MonsterRevivedEvent.title: MonsterRevivedEvent
MonsterRevivedEvent.description:
A monster the party thought dead has got back up.

`EffectsLedger.advance` reports this for a regeneration effect
when the monster's countdown runs out,
which for a troll is 2d6 rounds after it was killed. The monster comes back with 1 hit point, and loses the
`dead` condition at the same time. A monster stops getting back up once the damage it can't regenerate, fire
and acid for a troll, adds up to its maximum hit points.

label.title: Label
label.description:
The band as the SRD prints it: `"NH"` for a normal human, then `"1–3"` and so on up to `"22 or more"`.

The ranges use an en dash.

min_hd.title: Min Hd
min_hd.description: The lowest Hit Dice count in the band, or `null` on the `"NH"` band, which is below 1 Hit Die.

max_hd.title: Max Hd
max_hd.description: The highest Hit Dice count in the band, or `null` on the `"22 or more"` band, which has no upper limit.

saves.description: The saving throw targets for a monster in this band.

MonsterSaveBand.title: MonsterSaveBand
MonsterSaveBand.description:
One band of the monster saving throw table: the saving throws for a range of Hit Dice.

Find the band for a monster with
`monster_save_band_label` and
`CombatTables.save_band`. A monster that
comes with osrlib already has its saving throws, so you need this to write a monster or
to check one.

values.description: The five saving throw targets. See `SavingThrows`.

save_as.title: Save As
save_as.description:
The stat block's save-as entry, like `"2"` for a 2nd-level fighter, `"NH"` for a normal human, or `"Cleric 1"`.

Show it, or use it to check `values` against the SRD's tables. osrlib uses only `values`.

MonsterSaves.title: MonsterSaves
MonsterSaves.description:
A monster's saving throws, and the stat block's entry for which class and level it saves as.

Read it as `MonsterTemplate.saves`. To get the
values adjusted for a creature that has been drained of Hit Dice, read
`MonsterInstance.saves` instead. Frozen.

id.title: Id
id.description:
Monster template identifier, such as `"goblin"`. Pass to `GET /v1/rules/monsters/{monster_id}`
or `POST /v1/generate/monsters`.

name.title: Name
name.description:
Index name as printed in the rulebook, such as `"Goblin"` or `"Centipede, Giant"`. For prose
names, read `display_name` and `display_name_plural` on `GET /v1/rules/monsters/{monster_id}`.

ac.title: Ac
ac.description:
Descending armour class (lower is harder to hit), or `null` when attacks hit automatically
(`attack_roll_required` is `false`).

ac_ascending.title: Ac Ascending
ac_ascending.description: Ascending armour class (higher is harder to hit), or `null` when `ac` is `null`.

xp.title: Xp
xp.description:
Experience point value for defeating one monster, as printed in the Old-School Essentials
System Reference Document (SRD).

alignment.description: Permitted alignments (`options`) and typical alignment (`usual`), when specified.

MonsterSummary.title: MonsterSummary
MonsterSummary.description: Summary statistics of a monster from osrlib's `MonsterTemplate`.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The monster id, like `"troll"`.

Pass it to `MonsterCatalog.get` to look the template up.

name.title: Name
name.description:
The creature's name as the SRD prints it, like `"Centipede, Giant"` or `"Veteran (2)"`.

Many of the SRD's names are written for a rulebook's index. To name the creature to the players, use
`display_name`.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
What to call one of these creatures in a sentence, like `"giant centipede"`.

It's lowercase unless a word is a proper noun, so capitalize the first letter where it starts a line. It
leaves out what the players can't see. `"Veteran (2)"`, a 2nd-level veteran, is `"veteran"`, and
`"Hellhound (5)"`, a hellhound with 5 Hit Dice, is `"hellhound"`. The session gives a group of these
creatures this name as its `label`.

A template you write that leaves it out gets its `name`. When `name` is empty or only spaces too, it gets the
words of its `id`, so `cave_goblin` is called `"cave goblin"`.

display_name_plural.title: Display Name Plural
display_name_plural.description:
What to call two or more of these creatures, like `"giant centipedes"` or `"wolves"`.

A template you write that leaves it out gets `display_name` with the regular English ending: `s`, or `es`
after `s`, `x`, `z`, `ch`, or `sh`, or `ies` in place of a `y` that follows a consonant. Set it yourself
when the plural is irregular.

family_id.title: Family Id
family_id.description:
The id this template shares with the other forms of the same creature, like `"hellhound"`.

The SRD gives some creatures several stat blocks, and each one is a template. A veteran of each level is a
template, `veteran_1` to `veteran_3`, and the family of all three is `"veteran"`. The players see a
veteran and can't see its level, so the player view reports a group's family and not its template, in
`EncounterGroupView.family_id`. Pass a family id to
`MonsterCatalog.family` to get every form.

A creature with one form is a family of one, and its family id is its `id`. A template you write that
leaves this out gets its `id` too. The player view shows the family id to the players, so a template
that disguises one creature as another, like a doppelganger the players see as a goblin, sets this to
the family the players should see, `"goblin"`. The players also see the template's `display_name`
and its `categories`.

page.title: Page
page.description:
The file name of the SRD page this template was compiled from, like `"Hydra.md"`.

Templates with the same page describe related creatures, like the sizes of hydra or the colours of
dragon. The sizes of hydra are forms of one creature and the colours of dragon aren't, so to find the
forms of one creature, use `family_id`.

intro.title: Intro
intro.description: The SRD's description of the creature, for a referee or a narrator to read out.

ac.title: Ac
ac.description:
Armour class in the descending presentation, where lower is better.

`null` for a creature that every attack hits without a roll, when `attack_roll_required` is False.

ac_ascending.title: Ac Ascending
ac_ascending.description: The same armour class in the ascending presentation, where higher is better. `null` when `ac` is.

ac_alternates.title: Ac Alternates
ac_alternates.description:
Armour classes that apply only in particular circumstances. See
`AcAlternate`.

attack_roll_required.title: Attack Roll Required
attack_roll_required.description:
False for a creature that every attack hits without a roll, like a green slime. Both armour class fields are
`null` then.

hit_dice.description: The dice its hit points are rolled on. See `MonsterHitDice`.

attacks.title: Attacks
attacks.description:
The sets of attacks it can make, one set per round.
See `AttackRoutine`.

thac0.title: Thac0
thac0.description:
Its THAC0 ("to hit armour class 0"): the d20 roll it needs to hit armour class 0 under descending armour class.

To read the value for a creature that has been drained of Hit Dice, use
`MonsterInstance.thac0`.

attack_bonus.title: Attack Bonus
attack_bonus.description: The bonus it adds to a d20 attack roll under ascending armour class. It is the same attack skill as `thac0`.

movement.title: Movement
movement.description:
How it gets around and how fast, ordinary movement first. See
`MovementMode`.

morale.title: Morale
morale.description:
How willing it is to keep fighting, from 2 to 12. A morale check is a 2d6 roll, and the creature holds on a
result at or under the score. Pass it to `check_morale`. `null` when the stat
block prints no morale score.

morale_alternates.title: Morale Alternates
morale_alternates.description:
Morale scores that apply only in particular circumstances. See
`MoraleAlternate`.

alignment.description: Which alignments it may have. See `AlignmentSpec`.

xp.title: Xp
xp.description: The experience for defeating one, as the SRD prints it.

xp_notes.title: Xp Notes
xp_notes.description:
What a leader or other special member of a group is worth instead of `xp`. See
`XpNote`.

number_appearing.description:
How many appear, which depends on where they are met. See
`NumberAppearing`.

abilities.title: Abilities
abilities.description: What it can do beyond its attacks. See `MonsterAbility`.

defenses.description: What it resists, in the form the damage rules check. See `Defenses`.

categories.title: Categories
categories.description:
What kind of creature it is, as tags like `"undead"`, `"person"`, and `"enchanted"`.

Spells and turning check these. *Hold person* affects a monster only when it has `"person"`, and
turning affects only `"undead"`.

The player view shows them to the players, in
`EncounterGroupView.categories`.

intelligent.title: Intelligent
intelligent.description:
Whether the creature is intelligent, as its SRD page states, or `null` when the page doesn't say.

The session reads it when monsters pursue a fleeing party. Intelligent pursuers may stop for dropped
treasure, and unintelligent ones for dropped food. For a template that leaves it `null`, the session
judges the monster by its treasure type instead: a monster whose `treasure` lists letters counts as
intelligent, and any other monster counts as unintelligent.

The built-in templates set it only where the SRD page says so in its prose, such as the invisible stalker's
"Highly intelligent" (`true`) or the basilisk's "Unintelligent" (`false`). A page that calls its creature
semi-intelligent or of low intelligence leaves it `null`. Set it on a template you write to say which
bait tempts the creature.

overrides_applied.title: Overrides Applied
overrides_applied.description:
The field paths, like `"categories"`, that a correction changed when this template was compiled from the SRD.

Empty when the SRD page compiled without corrections. Read it when you check osrlib's data
against the SRD. osrlib doesn't read it during play.

MonsterTemplate.title: MonsterTemplate
MonsterTemplate.description:
A monster's stat block: everything true of every creature of that kind.

Get one from `load_monsters().get(monster_id)`.
[The monster id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/monsters/) lists the ids. Then
call `spawn_monster` to put a creature into play.
To write a monster of your own, construct one, and pass it to `spawn_monster` the same way.

A template is frozen, and play never changes it. Every creature of its kind shares it. The hit
points one creature has left, the wounds it has taken, and the conditions on it are on the
`MonsterInstance` spawned from it, so a wounded troll
doesn't weaken every other troll in the dungeon.

Constructing one raises `pydantic.ValidationError` when `attack_roll_required` is True and
either armour class is `null`, or when it is False and either armour class is set.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party can see who was abandoned.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `monsters_left_behind`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

group_id.title: Group Id
group_id.description: The new group the helpless members were put into.

source_group_id.title: Source Group Id
source_group_id.description: The group that ran off without them.

MonstersLeftBehindEvent.title: MonstersLeftBehindEvent
MonstersLeftBehindEvent.description:
A group that ran left its helpless members lying where they were.

Emitted by `ResolveBattleRound` when
a broken group has members who can't move, like those asleep, paralysed, or held.

The runners stay in the original group and go on fleeing. The ones left behind become
a new group at the distance where the side broke, so the party can finish them,
take what they carry, or walk past.

count.title: Count
count.description: Number of monster instances to spawn, from 1 to 100. Defaults to 1.

anyOf.description: Random number seed, an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991).

seed.title: Seed
seed.description:
Optional seed (0 to 2^53 - 1). Pass the `seed` from an earlier response with the same body to reproduce the
hit points, or omit it to let the server draw a random seed.

MonstersRequest.title: MonstersRequest
MonstersRequest.description: Monster template id, count, and optional seed for spawning monsters with rolled hit points.

seed.title: Seed
seed.description: Random number seed, an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991).

monsters.title: Monsters
monsters.description: Monster instances in spawn order (`monster-0001` onward), each with `template`, `max_hp`, and `current_hp`.

MonstersResponse.title: MonstersResponse
MonstersResponse.description: Spawned monster instances and the seed that produced them.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: this is bookkeeping, not a moment in the fiction.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `monsters_spawned`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

template_id.title: Template Id
template_id.description: What was spawned, as a monster catalog id.

monster_ids.title: Monster Ids
monster_ids.description:
The session ids of the new instances, in spawn order. Every later event about
those creatures refers to them by these ids.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
The template's `display_name`, like
`"giant centipede"` for `centipede_giant`, for a line about one monster. An event loaded from a
save written before the field existed has an empty string, and
`format_message` names the monsters by `template_id`.

display_name_plural.title: Display Name Plural
display_name_plural.description:
The template's `display_name_plural`,
like `"giant centipedes"`, for a line about more than one. It's empty on an event loaded from a
save written before the field existed.

MonstersSpawnedEvent.title: MonstersSpawnedEvent
MonstersSpawnedEvent.description:
Monsters were put into the session by the referee.

Emitted by `SpawnMonsters`, first in its
result. When no encounter is open, the events of the encounter's opening follow. When
one is open, the monsters join it as a new group.

It has referee visibility. It names the monsters by catalog id and by the template's display
name, and lists the session ids of the new instances. The party learns which monsters arrived from
`EncounterStartedEvent` when the
encounter opens, or from
`EncounterGroupJoinedEvent` when the
monsters join an open one.

score.title: Score
score.description:
The morale score in this situation, from 2 to 12. A morale check is a 2d6 roll, and the creature holds on a
result at or under the score.

condition.title: Condition
condition.description: When it applies, in the SRD's words, like `"in melee"` or `"fear of fire"`.

MoraleAlternate.title: MoraleAlternate
MoraleAlternate.description:
A morale score that applies only in a particular situation.

Read them from `MonsterTemplate.morale_alternates`. A
creature that fights bravely except when fire is involved has its usual score in the template's
`morale` and the exception here.

The functions in `osrlib.core` never apply these, because deciding whether the situation holds
is the referee's call. In a game session's battle, the `osrlib.crawl` package
uses an alternate whose `condition` mentions fire once the group has taken fire damage. Frozen.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: the players learn that a side has broken by watching it run.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

subject.title: Subject
subject.description: The key of the side whose morale was checked, as you passed it.

score.title: Score
score.description:
The side's morale score. A side with a score from 3 to 11 rolls. A side with 2 or less doesn't roll and has
broken, and a side with 12 or more doesn't roll and holds.

roll.title: Roll
roll.description: The 2d6 total, before the modifier. `null` when the side didn't roll.

modifier.title: Modifier
modifier.description: The adjustment applied, after it was limited to the range −2 to +2.

held.title: Held
held.description:
Whether the side keeps fighting.

`check_morale` sets it on every event, whatever the code. After a roll, it's
the outcome of the roll. It's `true` for a score of 12 or more, and `false` for a score of 2 or less. Show the
outcome from this field, not from the code and the score. It's `null` on an event loaded from a save written
before the field existed, because osrlib doesn't fill it in when it loads such a save.

MoraleCheckedEvent.title: MoraleCheckedEvent
MoraleCheckedEvent.description:
A side's morale check, and whether the side held.

`check_morale` reports one of these each time a side checks morale. A side
that breaks flees or surrenders, and making it do so is up to you.

At some morale scores, a side never rolls. A side with a score of 2 or less never fights, and a side with 12 or
more never checks. `check_morale` reports both with `combat.morale.exempt` and no roll. Read `held` to tell them
apart, as for any other code: at 2 or less the side has broken, and at 12 or more it holds.

passed.title: Passed
passed.description:
How many checks each side has held, by the side's key as you pass it to `check`.

The tracker never checks a side at 2 again.

MoraleTracker.title: MoraleTracker
MoraleTracker.description:
Counts morale checks through one encounter, so a side that holds twice stops checking.

Build one for each encounter and check morale through it instead of calling
`check_morale` directly. It applies the rule "If a
monster passes two morale checks in an encounter, it will fight until killed, with no
further checks."

A tracker can be changed, unlike the result models in this module, because it keeps a
count through the encounter. Build a new one for the next encounter, which starts the
count again. A session's battle keeps one for you.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"move_party"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

direction.description:
Which way to step. The party turns to face that way as it goes, so a move is also a turn.
To change facing without moving, use `TurnParty`. A
direction with a wall, a closed door, an undiscovered secret door, or the edge of the map
on that side of the party's cell gets the refusal `exploration.move.blocked`, unless a
passage stands on that side. Read
`ExploredLevelView.edges` to find which sides
of the cell the party can leave by.

MoveParty.title: MoveParty
MoveParty.description:
Move the party one cell, turning to face the way it goes.

The party must already be in a dungeon. A new session starts in town, and
`EnterDungeon` places the party at the entrance
and switches the session to `exploring`. A step onto a cell the party hasn't explored
uses 10 feet of the party's movement, and a step onto an explored cell uses a third of
that. Each time the movement adds up to the party's exploration rate, one turn passes on
the game clock.

A passage is a `TransitionSpec` whose `kind` is
`"passage"`, standing on one side of a cell. A move toward that side crosses the passage
instead of stopping at the wall there. The party arrives at the passage's destination,
facing its `to_facing`, and the move costs what a step onto that destination cell costs.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `exploration.move.cannot_move` - the party cannot move: it is overloaded,
  or a living member is unable to walk.
- `exploration.move.blocked` - a wall, a closed door, an undiscovered secret
  door, or the edge of the map is on that side, and no passage stands there.
- `exploration.transition.gate_refused` - the move would cross a passage
  whose authored condition (`GateSpec`) the
  party doesn't meet. The rejection includes the gate's authored refusal text.
  Like every refusal, it costs no movement, no time, and no toll.

**Events:**

`PartyMovedEvent` with the new position
and facing. Arriving in the new cell can set off more, each with a
separate event. A `LocationEnteredEvent`
follows when the party crosses into a new area, level, or dungeon. A
`DoorEvent` follows for each unwedged door the party
opened that swings shut behind it. The area's treasure roll arrives as a
`HoardGeneratedEvent`. A room
trap's spring check produces a
`DetectionRolledEvent` and a
`TrapEvent`, and a trap that springs
resolves at once.

A pool of burning oil or a *web* on the cell affects the party as it arrives
(`DamageDealtEvent`,
`HitPointsReportedEvent`,
`DeathEvent`,
`EffectAttachedEvent`,
`ConditionGainedEvent`). Monsters keyed to
the area in the adventure (a keyed encounter) meet the party the first time it enters,
with `SurpriseRolledEvent`s,
`EncounterStartedEvent`,
`ReactionRolledEvent`, and
`StanceChangedEvent`. When their reaction is
to attack, battle opens at once
(`BattleStartedEvent`).

A move through a passage reports the crossing before the step, as
`UseStairs` does. An
`ItemConsumedEvent` comes first when
the passage's gate takes an item as a toll. A `LocationEnteredEvent` follows when the
level or dungeon changes, with `via` set to `"passage"` and `transition_ref`
set to the passage's cell. Then come the `DoorEvent`s for the doors that swing shut
on the level the party left, the `PartyMovedEvent` for the landing cell, and the
landing cell's events.

When the step's movement completes a turn on the game clock, the events of that turn
follow:
`EffectExpiredEvent` with a
`LightEvent` for a light burning out,
`FatigueEvent` when the fatigue penalty starts or ends,
`ProvisionsEvent` on a day boundary,
and `WanderingCheckEvent` when a
wandering-monster check is due.

rate_feet.title: Rate Feet
rate_feet.description: Feet covered in one exploration turn of 10 minutes, the rate used while mapping and searching.

encounter_rate_feet.title: Encounter Rate Feet
encounter_rate_feet.description: Feet covered in one combat round, a third of `rate_feet`, rounded down.

descriptor.title: Descriptor
descriptor.description: How the creature is moving, in the SRD's word: `"flying"`, `"swimming"`, `"in webs"`. `null` for walking.

MovementMode.title: MovementMode
MovementMode.description:
One way a monster moves, and how fast.

Read them from `MonsterTemplate.movement`. The
first is the rate the stat block prints first, which is the creature's main way of moving.
Later ones are its other ways of moving, and you pick the one the situation calls for. Frozen.

refusal.title: Refusal
refusal.description:
A gate's refusal line. When the session refuses an attempt because the gate's condition isn't
met, the rejection includes this line as its `refusal` parameter. Leave it empty and the
rejection has no `refusal` parameter.

success.title: Success
success.description:
A gate's success line. It goes in the `narrative` of the event for the successful attempt: a
`DoorEvent` for a door, a
`LocationEnteredEvent` for a transition to another
level, or a `PartyMovedEvent` for a transition to another
cell of the same level.

fired.title: Fired
fired.description:
A trigger's firing line, for the referee. It goes in the `narrative` of the
`TriggerFiredEvent`, which players never see.

offer.title: Offer
offer.description:
A quest's activation line, or an objective's reveal line. It goes in the event's `narrative`
and into the journal.

progress.title: Progress
progress.description:
An objective's completion line. It goes in the event's `narrative` and into the journal.
osrlib doesn't read it on a quest.

completion.title: Completion
completion.description:
A quest's completion line. It goes in the event's `narrative` and into the journal. osrlib
doesn't read it on an objective.

journal.title: Journal
journal.description:
A trigger's journal line, for the players. When the trigger fires, the
`Interpreter` adds it to the journal with
`AddJournalEntry`. osrlib doesn't read it on a quest,
because for a quest the session writes the line it showed to the journal.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.description:
Instructions for a narrator that uses a language model, while the object is in play. It isn't
text to show a player as written.

osrlib never reads it, no event includes it, and no rule depends on it. Read it from the
adventure document when your narrator writes its text. The adventure document is referee-only
content, so don't show the field to a player. `LevelSpec.guidance`
does the same job for a whole level.

speaker.title: Speaker
speaker.description:
An attribution, like "the bronze sentinel", that you can show in front of a beat.
osrlib reads it only on a quest, and passes it to the player view as
`QuestView.speaker`.

NarrativeBlock.title: NarrativeBlock
NarrativeBlock.description:
The authored beats for one gate, trigger, quest, or objective.

Construct one and pass it as the `narrative` of the object it belongs to. Every field is free
text. The empty string, the default, means the beat isn't written, so a block with only a
refusal is normal. Which beats osrlib reads depends on the object the block belongs to:

- For a gate (`GateSpec`), osrlib reads `refusal` and `success`. When the
  session refuses an attempt, its rejection includes `refusal`. When an attempt succeeds, its event
  includes `success`.
- For a trigger (`TriggerSpec`), osrlib reads `fired` and
  `journal` when its consequences run. `fired` goes on a referee-only event, so it's the referee's line
  about what happened. `journal` is the players' line about the same moment.
- For a quest (`QuestSpec`), osrlib reads `offer` when the quest
  activates and `completion` when it completes.
- For an objective (`ObjectiveSpec`), osrlib reads `offer`
  when the objective is revealed and `progress` when it completes. If an objective completes before
  it's revealed, the session uses only its `progress`.

osrlib ignores the beats it doesn't read for an object, like `progress` on a quest, `completion` on an
objective, `fired` on a gate, or `offer` on a trigger. A block that sets them still parses.

Two fields apply to every object. `guidance` is instructions for a narrator that uses a language
model, and osrlib never reads it. `speaker` is an attribution, like "the bronze sentinel" or
"Sister Halda", that you can show in front of a beat.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: a note is for the person running the game.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `note_recorded`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

text.title: Text
text.description: The note as it was written.

NoteRecordedEvent.title: NoteRecordedEvent
NoteRecordedEvent.description:
A referee note was recorded, and no game state changed.

Emitted by `RecordNote`. The
`Interpreter` uses it to leave a
machine-written note in the log when a consequence can't be applied, and referees
use it for their margin notes.

roll_min.title: Roll Min
roll_min.description: The lowest d6 result in this band.

roll_max.title: Roll Max
roll_max.description: The highest d6 result in this band.

alignment.title: Alignment
alignment.description:
The alignment this band gives, as the value of an
`Alignment`, like `"lawful"`. Pass it to `Alignment` to get
the enum member: `Alignment("lawful")`.

NpcAlignmentBand.title: NpcAlignmentBand
NpcAlignmentBand.description:
One band of the d6 table that gives an NPC adventuring party its alignment.

The bands are in
`EncounterTables.npc_alignment`. Roll
a d6 and take the band whose range from `roll_min` to `roll_max` includes the result.
The whole party has that alignment.
`generate_npc_party` rolls this for you, so read the
bands only to display the table or to generate a party some other way.

roll.title: Roll
roll.description: The d8 result this row is for. Two results give a fighter, with different level dice for an expert party.

class_id.title: Class Id
class_id.description:
The id of the class this result gives, like `"cleric"` or `"fighter"`.

Look the class up with `load_classes().get(class_id)`, or see
[the class id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/classes/).

basic_dice.title: Basic Dice
basic_dice.description: The dice to roll for the NPC's level in a basic party. It's `"1d3"` on every row.

expert_dice.title: Expert Dice
expert_dice.description: The dice to roll for the NPC's level in an expert party, like `"1d6+3"`. It depends on the row.

NpcClassLevelRow.title: NpcClassLevelRow
NpcClassLevelRow.description:
One d8 result on the table that gives an NPC adventurer a class and a level.

`generate_npc_party` rolls on this table for each
member, so read the rows only to display the table or to generate a party some other
way.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
`"basic"` for a party of low-level adventurers, or `"expert"` for a higher-level one.

The dice rolled for each member's level, the armour the members wear, and whether they roll for magic items all
depend on it.

alignment.description:
The alignment every member shares, from one roll for the whole party. A spell that works differently against
another alignment, like *protection from evil*, treats every member the same way.

members.title: Members
members.description:
The adventurers, as `Character` models.

Each member's `id` comes from the allocator you passed, like `"npc-0001"`. Each member's `name` is the class name
and the member's position, like `"Thief adventurer 2"`. Every function that takes a character takes these.

treasure.description:
The coins, valuables, and magic items the party carries, rolled once for the whole party.

In a session, the treasure drops where the players' party stands once every member is slain. If any member fled
or routed, the party takes the treasure away with it.

NpcParty.title: NpcParty
NpcParty.description:
A party of NPC adventurers, with the alignment they share and the treasure they carry.

`generate_npc_party` returns one. Run the members as an
encounter: roll the monster reaction with `roll_reaction`,
fight them with the functions in `osrlib.core.combat`, and, if the
players win, award `npc_defeat_xp` for each member defeated.
In a session, execute a `SpawnNpcParty` command
instead. The engine generates the party and opens the encounter for you.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: The kind of party, `"basic"` or `"expert"`.

count_dice.title: Count Dice
count_dice.description: The dice to roll for the party's size: `"1d4+4"` for a basic party, and `"1d6+3"` for an expert party.

NpcPartyComposition.title: NpcPartyComposition
NpcPartyComposition.description:
The dice that give the number of adventurers in an NPC party of one kind.

Use it when you place an NPC party yourself, rather than from an encounter table row. Find
the entry for the kind of party in
`EncounterTables.npc_compositions`,
roll its `count_dice` with `roll`, and pass the total as `count`
to `generate_npc_party`.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
Always `"npc_party"`. Check it to tell this entry from a
`MonsterEncounterEntry` when you read a row.

party_kind.title: Party Kind
party_kind.description: The kind of party to generate: `"basic"` for low-level adventurers, or `"expert"` for higher-level ones.

NpcPartyEncounterEntry.title: NpcPartyEncounterEntry
NpcPartyEncounterEntry.description:
The entry of an encounter table row for a party of NPC adventurers instead of monsters.

Roll the party's size from the row's `count_dice`, which are the same dice as the
matching entry in
`EncounterTables.npc_compositions`.
Then pass `party_kind` and the size to
`generate_npc_party`, which rolls each member's
class, level, scores, and gear. In a session, the engine does both steps when it resolves a
`SpawnNpcParty` command.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: Party table: `"basic"` for levels 1 to 3, or `"expert"` for higher-level adventurers.

count.title: Count
count.description: Number of NPC adventurers to generate, from 1 to 100.

anyOf.description: Random number seed, an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991).

seed.title: Seed
seed.description:
Optional seed (0 to 2^53 - 1). Pass the `seed` from an earlier response with the same body to reproduce the
party, or omit it to let the server draw a random seed.

NpcPartyRequest.title: NpcPartyRequest
NpcPartyRequest.description: Party tier, member count, and optional seed for generating an NPC adventuring party.

seed.title: Seed
seed.description: Random number seed, an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991).

party.description: Generated adventurers (`members`), their shared `alignment`, and party `treasure`.

NpcPartyResponse.title: NpcPartyResponse
NpcPartyResponse.description: Generated NPC adventuring party and the seed that produced it.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: the players see only the label and the count on the encounter event.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `npc_party_spawned`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

party_kind.title: Party Kind
party_kind.description: Which table the party was rolled from: `"basic"` or `"expert"`.

npc_ids.title: Npc Ids
npc_ids.description:
The session ids of its members, in roster order. The other three tuples line up with this
one.

class_ids.title: Class Ids
class_ids.description: Each member's class, as a class catalog id.

alignment.title: Alignment
alignment.description: The party's alignment, as a lowercase `Alignment` value.

NpcPartySpawnedEvent.title: NpcPartySpawnedEvent
NpcPartySpawnedEvent.description:
The engine generated an NPC adventuring party and added it to the session.

Emitted by the referee's
`SpawnNpcParty` and by a wandering roll
that comes up adventurers, before the encounter opens.

It has referee visibility and contains the whole roster. What the party sees is the
`EncounterStartedEvent`, which labels
them as adventurers and contains a count. The party learns their classes and levels by
talking or by fighting.

dungeon.description: How many appear when they are met wandering in a dungeon.

lair.description: How many appear in their lair or in the wilderness, where they are usually found in larger numbers.

NumberAppearing.title: NumberAppearing
NumberAppearing.description:
How many of a creature appear, which depends on where they are met.

Read it as
`MonsterTemplate.number_appearing`, and
roll the value that matches the encounter. Frozen.

dice.title: Dice
dice.description: The dice to roll, like `"1d8"`. `null` when the count is fixed or given in prose.

fixed.title: Fixed
fixed.description: A flat count. `null` when the count is rolled or given in prose.

see_below.title: See Below
see_below.description:
True when the SRD gives no number here and the creature's description gives it instead. `dice` and `fixed`
are both `null` then.

NumberAppearingValue.title: NumberAppearingValue
NumberAppearingValue.description:
How many of a creature appear, as either dice to roll or a flat number.

Read it from `NumberAppearing.dungeon` or
`NumberAppearing.lair`. Exactly one of the three
fields applies. When `dice` is set, roll it with `roll`. When `fixed`
is set, use it. When `see_below` is True, read the number from the creature's description.

Constructing one raises `pydantic.ValidationError` when `dice` is not a valid dice expression,
or when the fields don't set exactly one of the three. Frozen.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party sees its progress.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `objective_completed`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

quest_id.title: Quest Id
quest_id.description: The quest the objective belongs to.

quest_name.title: Quest Name
quest_name.description:
The quest's display name. The engine always fills it. It's empty only on an event loaded from
a save written before the field existed.

name.title: Name
name.description:
The objective's display label: the name its author wrote, or its id when the author wrote
none.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description: The progress text the author wrote, or `null`. The journal has the same line.

ObjectiveCompletedEvent.title: ObjectiveCompletedEvent
ObjectiveCompletedEvent.description:
One objective of a quest is done.

Emitted by `CompleteObjective`.
Completing a hidden objective also reveals it, with no
`ObjectiveRevealedEvent`, so the
players may learn of an objective first from this event.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party is being told what to do.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `objective_revealed`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

quest_id.title: Quest Id
quest_id.description: The quest the objective belongs to.

quest_name.title: Quest Name
quest_name.description:
The quest's display name, so you don't need the adventure to look it up. The engine
always fills it. It's empty only on an event loaded from a save written before the field
existed.

objective_id.title: Objective Id
objective_id.description: Which objective, as the id the adventure gave it.

name.title: Name
name.description:
The objective's display label: the name its author wrote, or its id when the author wrote
none. Like `quest_name`, it's empty only on an event loaded from a save written before the field
existed.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description:
The offer text the author wrote for this objective, or `null`. The journal has the same
line.

ObjectiveRevealedEvent.title: ObjectiveRevealedEvent
ObjectiveRevealedEvent.description:
A hidden objective was revealed, so the party can now be told what it's asked to do.

Emitted by `RevealObjective`. An
objective the author didn't mark hidden is visible from the start and never
gets this event.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The objective's id. It has to be unique within its quest, and another quest can use
the same id. The objective's state and view use it as their key, and it's shown in
place of `name` when `name` is empty.

name.title: Name
name.description:
The objective's display name, the words a quest log shows beside its checkbox. When
it's empty, the view, the quest events, and the default message text use the id
instead.

when.description:
The clause that completes the objective. Completing an objective also reveals it,
so a hidden objective needs no reveal clause to appear once it's done.

hidden.title: Hidden
hidden.description:
Whether the objective starts hidden from the party. A hidden objective has no view
until it's revealed.

reveal_when.description:
The clause that reveals a hidden objective before it completes. On an objective that
starts visible, it fails validation with a pydantic `ValidationError`.

narrative.description:
The objective's text. osrlib reads two fields of the block: `offer`, the line shown
and added to the journal when the objective is revealed, and `progress`, the line shown
and added to the journal when it completes.

ObjectiveSpec.title: ObjectiveSpec
ObjectiveSpec.description:
One objective: what it is called, how it completes, whether it starts hidden, and its text.

Put your objectives in the `objectives` tuple of a
`QuestSpec`, in the order the quest log should show
them. The session tracks each objective in play as an
`ObjectiveState`, and you get the revealed ones
as `ObjectiveView`s.

An objective's state changes in one direction only. A hidden objective becomes
revealed, an incomplete one becomes complete, and neither change is undone. There's no
way to write an objective that repeats.

A hidden objective with no `reveal_when` is normal. It appears in the quest log when it
completes, because completing an objective reveals it. `reveal_when` on an objective
that starts visible fails validation with a pydantic `ValidationError`, because the
interpreter would never read it.

revealed.title: Revealed
revealed.description:
Whether the party may be shown this objective. It starts true unless the objective's
`ObjectiveSpec.hidden` is true, and
`RevealObjective` turns it on.

complete.title: Complete
complete.description:
Whether the objective is done. `CompleteObjective`
turns it on, and turns `revealed` on with it.

ObjectiveState.title: ObjectiveState
ObjectiveState.description:
One objective's state in play: whether the party may see it, and whether it's done.

The session creates one for each objective in the adventure and stores them in
`QuestState.objectives`. A player view includes
the revealed objectives of active quests, and the referee view includes them all.

Both flags change only from false to true, because no quest command turns either one off.
Completing an objective reveals it too, so the players see an objective they finished
before anyone told them about it.

id.title: Id
id.description: The objective's id, unique within its quest.

name.title: Name
name.description:
The objective's display name: its `name` in the adventure, or its id when the adventure
gives it no name. It's never empty.

ObjectiveView.title: ObjectiveView
ObjectiveView.description:
One revealed objective as the players know it: what it's called, and whether it's done.

You get these from `QuestView.objectives`. An
objective the players haven't been told about is absent from the list, not listed as
unknown, so `state` has only the two values a revealed objective can have. The adventure
defines the objective in an `ObjectiveSpec`, and the
session tracks it in an `ObjectiveState`. A remote
client has neither.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"open_door"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

direction.description:
Which side of the party's cell the door is on. Read the cell's sides from
`ExploredLevelView.edges`: you can name any
side whose edge has kind `door`. An undiscovered secret door shows as a wall until a
`secret_doors` `Search` finds it.

OpenDoor.title: OpenDoor
OpenDoor.description:
Open an unstuck, unlocked door on one side of the party's cell (takes no game time).

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`). A closed door blocks
`MoveParty`, so open it first and then step
through. The session refuses a command at an undiscovered secret door exactly as it
refuses one at a blank wall, so a refusal never reveals a hidden door. To open a stuck
door, use `ForceDoor`. To open a locked one, use
`PickLock` first.

A room trap that triggers on `open` belongs to the area on either side of the door.
Opening the door gives each such trap a 2-in-6 chance to spring on the first living
member in marching order, unless the party has already found the trap.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `exploration.door.no_door` - no known door on that side of the cell
  (undiscovered secret doors included).
- `exploration.door.already_open` - the door already stands open.
- `exploration.door.locked` - the door is still locked. Pick the lock with
  `PickLock` first.
- `exploration.door.stuck` - the door is stuck. Force it with
  `ForceDoor`.
- `exploration.door.gate_refused` - the door has an authored
  condition (`GateSpec`) the party doesn't
  meet. The rejection includes the gate's authored refusal text. The session checks
  the gate after every other check, so this code means the gate is the only obstacle.

**Events:**

`ItemConsumedEvent` first when
the gate takes an item as a toll, then
`DoorEvent` with code
`exploration.door.opened`, which includes the gate's success text when its author
wrote one. A door trap's spring check then produces a
`DetectionRolledEvent` and a
`TrapEvent`, and a trap that springs
resolves at once: a
`SavingThrowRolledEvent` when
it allows a save,
`DamageDealtEvent` and
`HitPointsReportedEvent` for
damage, `EffectAttachedEvent` and
`ConditionGainedEvent` for a
condition it inflicts, and
`DeathEvent` when it kills outright.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"parley"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who does the talking, by
`MemberView.id`. The member's CHA modifier applies to
the new reaction roll, so send the member with the best CHA.

Parley.title: Parley
Parley.description:
Talk to the monsters: roll their reaction again, with the speaker's CHA modifier.

An encounter must be open. An encounter opens when a wandering-monster check turns up
monsters, when the party enters an area with monsters keyed to it in the adventure, or when
the referee spawns them. The monsters' reaction to the party is their stance:
`attacks`, `hostile`, `uncertain`, `indifferent`, or `friendly`. The party can parley
any number of times. A result of `attacks` opens battle at once, and a `hostile` result
can open battle when the round ends.

Modes:

`encounter`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - no encounter is open.
- `encounter.none_active` - a second check behind the mode gate, which normal
  play never reaches.
- `encounter.parley.mid_pursuit` - the monsters are pursuing the party, and
  nobody can talk during a pursuit.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the speaker can't act.

**Events:**

`ReactionRolledEvent`, and a
`StanceChangedEvent` when the
stance changes. A result of `attacks` opens battle at once
(`BattleStartedEvent` and what
follows). Otherwise the encounter round ends, and the monsters act on their
stance, as for `Wait`.

members.title: Members
members.description:
The party's characters, in marching order: index 0 walks in front and meets whatever the party
walks into first. At least one member is required.
`GameSession.new` assigns ids when the party joins a
session, so a member you just built has `null` as its `id` until then.

Don't change this list directly. Use a command, so the change is logged and a replay
reproduces it:

- To add a member during play, execute `AddMember`. It
  assigns the new member's id and puts them at the back.
- To take a member out of play, execute
  `RemoveMember`.
- To change the order outside a fight, execute
  `ReorderParty`.
- In a battle, a member who withdraws alone names the member to trade places with in
  `BattleDeclaration.replacement_id`.

Party.title: Party
Party.description:
The adventuring party, in marching order.

Construct one with at least one member and pass it to
`GameSession.new`, which assigns each member an id and
keeps the party for the life of the session. To add a member during play, execute
`AddMember`. The methods return facts about the group as a
whole: who is still alive, how fast the group walks, and who stands where in a fight.

A party is mutable. The session heals, wounds, and re-equips its members in place, and assigning
a new list to `members` validates it. The list is never empty: when the last member dies, the
session ends in `game_over` and the dead stay in the list.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
`"town"` when the party is in the base town, or `"dungeon"` when it stands on a dungeon cell.
A new session starts in town.

dungeon_id.title: Dungeon Id
dungeon_id.description: The id of the dungeon the party is in, and `null` in town.

level_number.title: Level Number
level_number.description: The number of the level the party is on, and `null` in town.

position.title: Position
position.description: The cell the party stands on, and `null` in town.

facing.description:
The direction the party faces, and `null` in town. Draw the party's view facing this way.
`MoveParty` includes a direction, so the party can
step any way, whichever way it faces, and the step turns it to face the way it moved.

PartyLocation.title: PartyLocation
PartyLocation.description:
Where the party is: in the base town, or on a dungeon cell facing a direction.

The session keeps one in `DungeonState.location`
and replaces it as the party moves. Read it to draw the map and to know whether the party is in
town or in a dungeon. Don't change it yourself: to move the party by the referee's decision,
execute `PlaceParty`, which takes one of these.

A town location has none of the dungeon fields, and a dungeon location has all four.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party knows where it stands.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `party_moved`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

x.title: X
x.description: The column the party is in after the step or turn, counting from zero at the level's west edge.

y.title: Y
y.description: The row the party is in after the step or turn, counting from zero at the level's north edge.

facing.title: Facing
facing.description:
The direction the party now faces, as the lowercase value of a
`Direction` (`"north"`, `"east"`, `"south"`, `"west"`). After
a step, the party faces the way it went, so this changes on a step as well as on a turn. After
a step through a passage, the party faces the way the adventure's author set for the passage's
far side.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description:
The success text the adventure's author wrote on the gate of a transition that took the party to
another cell of the same level, or `null`.

For a transition to another level, the text is on the
`LocationEnteredEvent` instead.
`format_message` adds it after the line it builds from the
code.

PartyMovedEvent.title: PartyMovedEvent
PartyMovedEvent.description:
The party moved a cell or turned in place, with its new cell and facing.

Emitted by `MoveParty` with the cell it
stepped into, and by `TurnParty` with the
unchanged cell and the new facing. Redraw a first-person view from this event.

Two moves that leave the party's cell work differently:

- A `MoveParty` through a passage, a `TransitionSpec`
  that the party walks through, emits it with the cell the party arrives on. When the
  passage leads to another level, this event comes after that level's
  `LocationEnteredEvent`.
- A `UseStairs` to another cell of the same level
  emits it only when the gate on the stairs has success text. The event is for the
  landing cell, and its `narrative` contains the text.

A step that a wall, a closed door, or the edge of the map blocks emits no event. The
session refuses the command with the rejection code `exploration.move.blocked`, and
nothing in the game changes.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the players chose the order.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `party_reordered`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

order.title: Order
order.description:
Every member's id in the new marching order, front first, the same list the command
gave.

PartyReorderedEvent.title: PartyReorderedEvent
PartyReorderedEvent.description:
The party has a new marching order.

Emitted by `ReorderParty`. Marching order is the order
the members walk in, front first, so redraw the party on screen in this order when the event
arrives. A member who withdraws or retreats in a battle also changes the order, and that change
arrives as a `MemberWithdrewEvent` instead.

min_level.title: Min Level
min_level.description: The lowest character level the adventure is written for, 1 or more.

max_level.title: Max Level
max_level.description:
The highest character level the adventure is written for, `min_level` or more. Equal to
`min_level` for an adventure written for one level.

min_size.title: Min Size
min_size.description: The fewest characters the adventure is written for, or `null` when it gives no number.

max_size.title: Max Size
max_size.description:
The most characters the adventure is written for, or `null` when it gives no number. When
`min_size` is also given, it's `min_size` or more.

PartySpec.title: PartySpec
PartySpec.description:
The party an adventure is written for: the character levels, and how many characters.

A published adventure states this on its cover or in its introduction, like "for 6 to 8
characters of levels 1 to 3". osrlib never reads it. It's there so you can pick a party that
suits the adventure, in a front end, a converter, or a playtest.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"pick_lock"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

direction.description:
Which side of the party's cell the locked door is on, from the `door` edges in
`ExploredLevelView.edges`. The session refuses a door
that isn't locked with `exploration.lock.not_locked`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The thief who picks, by `MemberView.id`. The member
needs thief skills and thieves' tools in their pack. A member who fails can't try that lock
again until they gain a level, so send the best lock picker first.

PickLock.title: PickLock
PickLock.description:
Pick the lock of a locked door with a thief's skill and thieves' tools (one turn).

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`). Only a member with thief
skills can pick a lock. That member needs thieves' tools in their pack and light,
and infravision isn't enough. A member who fails can't try that lock again until they
gain a level. A picked door is unlocked but still closed, so follow with
`OpenDoor`.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member cannot act.
- `exploration.lock.not_a_thief` - the member has no thief skills.
- `exploration.lock.no_tools` - the member carries no thieves' tools.
- `exploration.door.no_door` - no known door on that side of the cell.
- `exploration.lock.not_locked` - the door has no lock left to pick.
- `exploration.action.requires_light` - the party has no light. Infravision
  isn't enough to pick a lock.
- `exploration.lock.locked_out` - this member already failed at this lock at
  their current level.

**Events:**

`DetectionRolledEvent` with the
skill roll and, on success, a `DoorEvent`
with code `exploration.door.unlocked`. The attempt costs one turn, and the events of
that turn follow: light burning down, the fatigue rule, and the wandering-monster
check, each with its usual events.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
The catalog id of a mundane stack, like `"holy_water"`, or the instance id of a magic item,
like `"magic-item-0003"`, or of a gem or piece of jewellery, like `"valuable-0007"`. It's the form
of id that `ItemsDroppedEvent.item_ids` and the
other item events use, and an unidentified magic item's template id never appears here.

quantity.title: Quantity
quantity.description:
How many units: the size of a mundane stack, the
`quantity` of a magic item, which is more than 1
only for enchanted ammunition, and always 1 for a gem or piece of jewellery.

PileItemView.title: PileItemView
PileItemView.description:
One thing in a dropped pile, by the id the events name it by, with its count.

You get these from `PileView.contents`. Look `item_id` up
in `PlayerView.item_names` and
`PlayerView.item_names_plural` to name it. A gem or
piece of jewellery that has a name of its own has it in
`PlayerView.valuable_names` too, which you show as
written in a list, and a phrase in
`PlayerView.valuable_phrases`, which you use as
written in a sentence.

items.title: Items
items.description:
One display string per thing in the pile, in the order mundane items, magic items,
then valuables. A mundane entry has the form `"{item_id}×{quantity}"`. A magic item shows its
name once identified and its masked display name before that. A valuable shows its
name, without any spaces around it, or its kind when its name is empty or only whitespace.

coins_gp_value.title: Coins Gp Value
coins_gp_value.description: The pile's coins, as their value in whole gold pieces, rounded down.

coins.description: The pile's coins by denomination, so a pile of copper alone isn't mistaken for an empty one.

contents.title: Contents
contents.description:
One entry per thing in the pile, in the order of `items`, each with the id the events name
it by and its count.

A mundane stack has its catalog id, so a client reads `"holy_water"` and 2 here where `items` has
the string `"holy_water×2"`. A magic item and a valuable have their instance ids. Name each entry
from `PlayerView.item_names`, which has a key for
every id here.

PileView.title: PileView
PileView.description:
A known dropped pile in explored space.

You get these from `PlayerView.piles`, keyed by
cell reference. A pile in a cell the party has not walked is left out, so the view never
shows the players loot they haven't found.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"place_party"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

location.description:
Where the party ends up. A `PartyLocation` with
`kind="town"` has no other fields. One with `kind="dungeon"` needs the dungeon id, the
level number, the cell, and the facing, all four together, or constructing it fails
validation. The session refuses a position off the level's grid with
`session.command.out_of_bounds`.

PlaceParty.title: PlaceParty
PlaceParty.description:
Referee: move the party straight to a dungeon cell or to town.

Use it for an authored teleport, a trapdoor you handle yourself, or a rescue. The
party can't be moved out of an open encounter or battle, so the command isn't legal in
`encounter` or `battle`. To move the party away from monsters, close the encounter first
with `EndEncounter`. Placing the party in a dungeon
marks the cell explored and switches the session to `exploring`. Placing it in town
switches the session to `town`. The party arrives without the entry checks of a step, so
no treasure roll, room trap, or encounter happens on the destination cell, and no game
time passes.

Because the switch restarts play, the command isn't legal in `victory`. It's legal in
`game_over`, where it's the only way out: placing the dead party in town lets you buy
*raise dead* with `PurchaseHealing`.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `game_over`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - an encounter or a battle is open, or the session
  is in `victory`.
- `session.command.unknown_location` - the location matches no dungeon, or no
  level in it.
- `session.command.out_of_bounds` - the position is off the level's grid.

**Events:**

`LocationEnteredEvent` for the
destination. A dungeon destination has `via` set to `"placed"`, so the log
shows that the referee moved the party rather than that it took the stairs.

adventure_description.title: Adventure Description
adventure_description.description: The adventure's description, for a title screen.

town_services.title: Town Services
town_services.description: The services the town offers, as text from the adventure for you to list.

town_healing_prices.title: Town Healing Prices
town_healing_prices.description:
What the town's temple charges for each of its services, in gold pieces, keyed by the
`HealingService` name, like `"raise_dead"`. Every
service is listed. A price comes from
`TownSpec.healing_prices` where the adventure
sets one, and from the standard prices in
`HEALING_SERVICES` otherwise. Read it to show the
temple's price list, and to check the party's gold against a price before you send a
`PurchaseHealing`.

town_healing_rejections.title: Town Healing Rejections
town_healing_rejections.description:
Why the temple would refuse each of its services for each party member now, keyed by
`MemberView.id` and then by the
`HealingService` name, like `"raise_dead"`.

Read it to disable a temple service that a member can't use, and to show the reason. Each value is a tuple of
`Rejection` models with the `code` and `params` that a
`PurchaseHealing` for that member and service gets with `spell_mode`
unset, which is the spell's first usage. For a service the temple sells in more than one usage, such as *cure light
wounds*, which also cures paralysis, read
`town_healing_mode_rejections` for each usage.
An empty tuple means that some temple cleric can perform the service for the member, and
`town_healing_caster_levels` gives the level to send.
A tuple that isn't empty means that no temple cleric, of any level, can, and it contains the rejections that a
purchase with `caster_level` unset gets.

Turn a rejection into text by its code, as you do for a refused command. The code you'll meet is
`town.healing.no_effect`, for a service that would do nothing for the member, and its `reason` param says why:

- `dead`: *cure light wounds* or *cure serious wounds* for a dead member.
- `weakened` or `diseased`: a cure for a member whose condition stops them from healing by magic.
- `full_hit_points`: a cure for a member at their maximum hit points.
- `not_diseased`: *cure disease* for a member who isn't diseased.
- `not_poisoned`: *neutralize poison* for a member who isn't poisoned and didn't die of poison in the last 10
  rounds.
- `not_cursed`: *remove curse* for a member with no curse that the spell lifts.
- `not_dead`: *raise dead* for a living member.
- `dead_too_long`: *raise dead* for a member who has been dead longer than the highest-level temple cleric
  reaches.
- `no_death_record`: *raise dead* for a dead member whose death the session didn't record, so it can't tell how
  long ago the member died.

A purchase whose `caster_level` is too low to raise a member whom a higher cleric could raise gets one more
*raise dead* reason, `caster_level_too_low`. This map never shows it, because a higher level works for that
member, and the map shows an empty tuple and the level instead.

The fee isn't part of the answer, so a service the party can't afford is listed as one the temple can perform.
Compare the price in `town_healing_prices` with
`town_healing_funds_gp`, because the session refuses a
purchase the party can't pay for with `items.purchase.insufficient_funds` before it makes these checks.

The map has an entry for every party member, the dead included, and every service, while the session is in the
`"town"` mode. The town's `town_services` don't change it, because the temple serves the party in any town. In
any other mode the map is empty, because the session refuses every `PurchaseHealing` there with
`session.command.wrong_mode`. A `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.10.0 built, such as a stored feed entry, has no
`town_healing_rejections`, and it validates with this map empty.

town_healing_caster_levels.title: Town Healing Caster Levels
town_healing_caster_levels.description:
The lowest temple cleric level that can perform each service for each party member, keyed like
`town_healing_rejections`.

Send the number as `PurchaseHealing.caster_level`, and a
party that can pay gets the service. A service that no temple cleric can perform for the member has no entry, and
its rejections are in `town_healing_rejections`. For every service except *raise dead*, the level is the lowest
that can cast the service, so leaving `caster_level` unset gives the same result. For *raise dead* it's the lowest
level whose reach covers how long the member has been dead: 7 for a member who died less than a day ago, and 8
for one dead 3 days.

The price is the same at every level, and a higher level changes nothing but how far back *raise dead* reaches
and the caster level recorded on the weakness that *raise dead* leaves, which *dispel magic* rolls against. So
the level here gives the same result as any higher level, except that a *dispel magic* that a party cleric casts
on that weakness succeeds at least as often. If your game limits its temple to clerics of some level, compare
that limit with this number, as you compare a price with the party's funds.

The map is empty outside the `"town"` mode, and a `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.10.0 built validates with it
empty.

town_healing_mode_rejections.title: Town Healing Mode Rejections
town_healing_mode_rejections.description:
Why the temple would refuse each usage of a service for each party member now, for the services it sells in
more than one usage. The map is keyed by `MemberView.id`, then by the
`HealingService` name, and then by the usage's
`SpellMode.key`, which is what you send as
`PurchaseHealing.spell_mode`.

Read it to offer a usage beside the service's first one, such as "cure paralysis" beside *cure light wounds*'s
healing. Each value means what a value of
`town_healing_rejections` means, for a purchase that
names that usage: an empty tuple means that some temple cleric can perform it for the member, and a tuple that
isn't empty contains the rejections that a purchase with `caster_level` unset gets. The usages come in the order
the spell lists them, so the first is the one that `town_healing_rejections` answers for, with the same tuple.
The session makes the same check for the view and the command, so they can't disagree. Look a usage's display
name up in `town_healing_mode_names`.

The temple sells *cure light wounds* in its `heal` and `cure_paralysis` usages, and every other service in its
first usage alone, so *cure light wounds* is the only service in this map. A refusal of `cure_paralysis` is
`town.healing.no_effect` with the `reason` param `dead` for a dead member or `not_paralysed` for a member who
isn't paralysed. The cleric level doesn't change the answer for either usage of cure light wounds, so leave
`caster_level` unset, which uses the service's lowest level.

The map has an entry for every party member, the dead included, while the session is in the `"town"` mode, and
it's empty in any other mode. A `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.11.0 or earlier built validates with it empty.

town_healing_mode_names.title: Town Healing Mode Names
town_healing_mode_names.description:
The display name of each usage of a service, for the services the temple sells in more than one usage, keyed
by the `HealingService` name and then by the usage's
`SpellMode.key`, such as `{"cure_light_wounds": {"heal": "Heal a living subject",
"cure_paralysis": "Cure paralysis"}}`.

Each name is the usage's `SpellMode.display_name` in the session's spell catalog,
so a remote client can label each usage in
`town_healing_mode_rejections` without the
catalog. The services and usages are the same as there, in the same order. The session fills it in every mode,
like `town_healing_prices`, and a `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.11.0 or earlier built validates with it empty.

town_healing_funds_gp.title: Town Healing Funds Gp
town_healing_funds_gp.description:
The whole gold pieces that the party's purses can pay toward a temple fee now.

The temple sells a service the party can pay for when the service's price in
`town_healing_prices` is at most this number, and it refuses
one that costs more with `items.purchase.insufficient_funds`. The session computes this number with the function
its funds check uses, so the two can't disagree. Each purse pays in whole gold pieces of its total value, across
every coin type, and any value below a gold piece stays in the purse, so this is the sum over the party, dead
members included, of each purse's value rounded down to a gold piece. For example, two members who each have 12
gp and 5 sp give 24, not 25. Whoever is treated, the total is the same, because the patient's purse only pays
first.

The session fills it in every mode, like `town_healing_prices`. A `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.10.0 built has no
`town_healing_funds_gp`, and it validates with `null`, which means the view doesn't state the funds, not that
the party has none.

party.title: Party
party.description: The party's character sheets, in marching order, the dead included.

location.description: Where the party is: the town, or a dungeon cell with its facing.

clock_rounds.title: Clock Rounds
clock_rounds.description: How much game time has passed since the session began, in rounds.

mode.title: Mode
mode.description:
The session mode as a `SessionMode` serialized
value: `"town"`, `"exploring"`, `"encounter"`, `"battle"`, `"game_over"`, or
`"victory"`. Read it to decide which commands to offer, because each mode
accepts different commands.

explored.title: Explored
explored.description: The party's map, one entry per level it knows anything about.

dungeons.title: Dungeons
dungeons.description: The dungeons the party has entered, in adventure order.

can_travel_to_town.title: Can Travel To Town
can_travel_to_town.description:
Whether the exploring party can use
`TravelToTown` from its current position.

features_here.title: Features Here
features_here.description:
The handles that the feature commands accept in `feature_id` from where the party stands, in
the order the current level's `features` lists
them. The commands are `TakeTreasure`,
`InspectTreasure`, and
`RemoveTreasureTrap`.

Each entry is the `MapFeatureView.id` of a treasure cache
the party can reach: an authored or generated cache on the party's cell, or an authored cache
that belongs to the whole of the area the party stands in. The session resolves a command's
`feature_id` against the same caches, so a cache that isn't listed here is refused with
`exploration.feature.unknown`. It's empty unless the session is exploring, because the commands
are legal only then. A custom feature or a construction trick is never listed, because no
command acts on one.

A command can still refuse a listed cache for another reason. `TakeTreasure` refuses an emptied
cache with `exploration.feature.emptied`, which
`MapFeatureView.emptied` tells you beforehand.
`RemoveTreasureTrap` accepts only a cache whose
`trap_state` is `"found"`. To take the goods
dropped on the party's cell, send `"pile"`, when `piles`
has an entry for the cell.

piles.title: Piles
piles.description:
The dropped piles the party knows about, keyed by the cell reference
`cell_ref` returns. A pile in a cell the party has
