not walked is left out.

emptied_caches.title: Emptied Caches
emptied_caches.description:
The authored treasure caches the party has emptied, as `"{dungeon}:{level}:{id}"` feature
references, in the order the party emptied them.

To draw an emptied cache, read
`MapFeatureView.emptied` instead, which marks the
cache in `features` under its handle. Command targets come from
`MapFeatureView.id`.

effects.title: Effects
effects.description: The active effects on party members, in ledger order.

spell_names.title: Spell Names
spell_names.description:
The name of each spell whose id the view shows, keyed by spell id, like
`{"magic_missile": "Magic Missile"}`. Show these names, not the ids.

A spell id appears in six places in the view: in a member's
`spell_book`,
`preparable_spells`, and
`learnable_spells`, as the `spell_id` of a copy in
a member's `memorized_spells`, in the `spells` of an
identified spell scroll in a member's `inventory`, and as the
`kind` of an effect in `effects`, because a spell's
effect has the spell's id as its kind unless the spell's data gives it a kind of its own. Every one
of those ids that the session's catalog,
`GameSession.effective_spells`, has is a key
here, with the spell's `name`. A spell the adventure
bundles has its name here too, which `load_spells` doesn't have. An
effect kind that isn't a spell id, like a torch's `"light"`, has no entry.

It names no spell whose id the view doesn't show. So a spell the adventure bundles for a list that
no member casts from stays hidden, and so does a spell at a level where no member could prepare or
learn it, unless a member carries an identified scroll with the spell on it. A spell on an
unidentified scroll is named only when the view shows its id in another place. A spell
id on a member that the session's catalog doesn't have, like one from a party made for another
adventure, has no entry either, and the session refuses to prepare or cast that spell. The name here
is always the spell's normal form. For a copy prepared reversed, show its name from
`reversed_spell_names`.

reversed_spell_names.title: Reversed Spell Names
reversed_spell_names.description:
The name of each spell's reverse, keyed by spell id, like `{"light_mu": "Darkness"}`, for every
spell in `spell_names` that has one.

Each value is the `name` of the spell's
`reversed_form`, read from the same catalog as
`spell_names`, so a spell the adventure bundles has the name its author gave the reverse. A spell
that doesn't reverse has no entry.

Show this name for an arcane caster's copy whose `reversed` is true in
`memorized_spells`. A divine caster prepares the
normal form and chooses the form when casting, so every memorized copy of a reversible spell can be
cast either way. To offer that choice, show both names.

spell_levels.title: Spell Levels
spell_levels.description:
The level of each spell in `spell_names`, keyed by spell id, like
`{"magic_missile": 1, "web": 2}`. Group a prepare or learn dialog by it, because a member's slots
are counted per spell level, in
`MemberView.spell_slots`.

Each value is the spell's `level`, read from the same
catalog as `spell_names`, so a spell the adventure bundles has the level its author gave it. A
spell id belongs to exactly one spell list, like `light_mu` to the magic-user's and `light_c` to
the cleric's, so each id has one level for every class that casts from its list, like the elf,
who casts from the magic-user's list.

spell_ranges.title: Spell Ranges
spell_ranges.description:
How far each spell in `spell_names` reaches in its normal form, keyed by spell id, as the
`RangeSpec` that
`SpellTemplate.range_spec_for` returns, such as `kind` `"feet"`
and `feet` 150 for `"magic_missile"`. Use it to offer only the targets a cast can reach.

The session checks the range in a battle, where it measures the distance from the caster to the target's group,
the caster's entry in that group's
`member_distance_feet`, or to a targeted party
member where that member will stand once the round's moves are made. It refuses a target beyond the range with
`magic.cast.out_of_range`. Outside a battle it checks no distance. The reach of each kind:

- `feet` and `yards`: `feet`, with yards already converted.
- `per_level`: `feet`, or 0 when it's `null`, plus `per_level_feet` times the caster's level, which is
  `MemberView.level`. A spell read from a scroll uses the lowest level
  that could cast it instead, whatever the reader's level.
- `touch`: 5', the reach of a melee attack. In a battle, the session also refuses a touch spell on a monster with
  `battle.declaration.not_in_front_rank` when the caster isn't in the party's front rank toward the monster's
  group, and with `combat.attack.out_of_reach` when the monster isn't in its group's front rank.
- `caster` and `special`: no distance that the session checks.

It's read from the same catalog as `spell_names`, and every spell there has an entry. A `PlayerView` that
osrlib 2.11.0 or earlier built validates with this map empty.

reversed_spell_ranges.title: Reversed Spell Ranges
reversed_spell_ranges.description:
How far each spell's reverse reaches, keyed by spell id, for every spell in `reversed_spell_names`, read the
way `spell_ranges` is. A reverse can reach a different distance from the normal form: `spell_ranges["remove_fear"]`
is touch, and `reversed_spell_ranges["remove_fear"]`, for *cause fear*, is 120 feet. A `PlayerView` that osrlib
2.11.0 or earlier built validates with this map empty.

spell_range_texts.title: Spell Range Texts
spell_range_texts.description:
The range of each spell in `spell_names` as its page prints it, keyed by spell id, such as
`{"remove_fear": "The caster or a creature touched"}`. Show it to the player beside the spell's name. It's the
`range` that `spell_ranges` is parsed from, and for a range that osrlib
can't parse, whose `kind` in `spell_ranges` is `"special"`, such as *create food*'s `"Appears in the caster’s
presence"`, it's the only statement of the range. It's read from the same catalog as `spell_names`, and every spell
there has an entry. A `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.11.0 or earlier built validates with this map empty.

reversed_spell_range_texts.title: Reversed Spell Range Texts
reversed_spell_range_texts.description:
The range of each spell's reverse as its page prints it, keyed by spell id, for every spell in
`reversed_spell_names`. It's the reverse's own `range` when the reverse
has one, such as `"120’"` for *cause fear*, and the spell's `range` otherwise. A `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.11.0 or
earlier built validates with this map empty.

spell_modes.title: Spell Modes
spell_modes.description:
The usages of each spell in `spell_names`, in its normal form, keyed by spell id, as
`SpellModeView` models in the order the form lists them. Build a cast dialog
from them: each one has the key to send as the cast's mode, a label to show, and what the session checks of the
cast's targets. For example, `spell_modes["light_mu"]` has the usages `illuminate`, `blind`, and `cancel`, labelled
`"Conjure light"`, `"Blind a creature"`, and `"Cancel darkness"`.

Each usage is read from the same catalog as `spell_names`,
`GameSession.effective_spells`, so a spell the adventure
bundles has the usages its author wrote. Every spell in `spell_names` has an entry, and no other spell does. A
`PlayerView` that osrlib 2.11.0 or earlier built validates with this map empty.

reversed_spell_modes.title: Reversed Spell Modes
reversed_spell_modes.description:
The usages of each spell's reverse, keyed by spell id, for every spell in `reversed_spell_names`, as
`SpellModeView` models in the order the reverse lists them. The reverse's keys
can differ from the normal form's: `spell_modes["cure_light_wounds"]` has `heal` and `cure_paralysis`, and
`reversed_spell_modes["cure_light_wounds"]` has `harm`. Send a key from here with `reversed` set.

It's read from the same catalog as `spell_modes`. A spell that doesn't reverse has no entry, and a `PlayerView`
that osrlib 2.11.0 or earlier built validates with this map empty.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call one of each item whose id the view shows, keyed by that id, like
`{"torch": "torch", "holy_water": "vial of holy water", "magic-item-0003": "potion"}`. Show these
names, not the ids, and put a number or an article in front of one: "a torch". To word a count,
like "6 torches", use `item_names_plural`.

An item id appears in the view in four forms, and each is a key here:

- The catalog id of a mundane stack, like `"holy_water"`, in a member's
  `inventory` and in a pile's
  `contents`. For a stack a member carries, its name is
  the `display_name` of the template the stack
  embeds, which the session gives the display names of the template its catalog,
  `GameSession.effective_equipment`, has
  under that id, as `ItemInstance.template` says. So a
  stack from a save or a party document that osrlib 2.7.0 wrote is named as the catalog names it,
  and the name here matches the stack's template in `inventory`. A bundled id can't shadow a
  built-in one, because a session refuses an adventure whose bundled id collides with a built-in
  id. A carried stack whose id the catalog doesn't have, like an item another adventure bundled,
  keeps the names its template has. For a pile, the name comes from the catalog, and a pile's
  catalog id that the catalog doesn't have has no entry.
- The instance id of a magic item, like `"magic-item-0003"`, in an inventory and in a pile.
  Until the party identifies the item, its name is the masked name the inventory shows, without
  the article: `"potion"`, `"curious device"`, or `"shield with a faint aura"`. So a cursed item
  and the item it passes for have the same name, and the name tells nothing the inventory
  doesn't. Once the item is identified, its name is the
  `display_name` of its template in the magic
  item catalog, like `"potion of healing"`.
- The template id of an identified magic item, like `"potion_of_healing"`, which the inventory
  shows once the item is identified, with the same name. A pile shows a magic item by its
  instance id alone, identified or not, so an identified item's template id is a key only while
  a member carries it. An unidentified item's template id is never a key.
- The instance id of a gem or a piece of jewellery, like `"valuable-0007"`. Its name is its kind,
  `"gem"` or `"piece of jewellery"`. The players see everything else about it from the moment
  they take it, its own name and its value in gold pieces included, in the inventory's
  `valuables`. A piece that has a name of its own, like `"Prior's chain of office"`, has it in
  `valuable_names` under the same id, and what to call it in a sentence, like
  `"the Prior's chain of office"`, in `valuable_phrases`. Show the name in place of the kind in
  a list, and the phrase in place of the kind in a sentence.

It names no item whose id the view doesn't show. The player-visible item events, like
`ItemAcquiredEvent`, list items by the same ids, and
each has its own `item_names` and `item_names_plural` for the ids it lists. An event's names come
from the same function as these, so an event names an id as a view built when the event happened
would. Read the event's names for an item the command used up, sold, or left behind on a trail,
because the view you build after the command doesn't name it.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, like
`{"torch": "torches", "holy_water": "vials of holy water", "magic-item-0003": "potions"}`.

Each value is the plural of the name in `item_names`: the template's
`display_name_plural`, the plural of a
masked name, like `"shields with a faint aura"`, or `"gems"` or `"pieces of jewellery"`. Use it
with a count from a pile's `contents` or an inventory
entry's `quantity`: "2 vials of holy water".

valuable_names.title: Valuable Names
valuable_names.description:
The own name of each gem and piece of jewellery that has one, keyed by its instance id, like
`{"valuable-0007": "Prior's chain of office"}`. Show it as written in a list, such as an inventory
row. To put the piece in a sentence, use its phrase in
`valuable_phrases`, which has the article and
the case: "Sam takes the Prior's chain of office." For an id that isn't a key, use the kind in
`item_names`, with an article: "Sam takes a gem."

A piece has a name of its own when its `name` is neither empty, nor only whitespace, nor the
plain name that treasure generation gives its kind, `"Gem"` for a gem or `"Jewellery"` for a piece
of jewellery. Spaces around the name don't count. So a piece an
adventure places in a cache with a named `ValuableSpec` is a
key, and neither a piece the session rolls on the treasure tables nor a placed piece whose `name`
is empty is a key.

The keys are the instance ids of those pieces in the members'
`inventory` `valuables` and in the
`contents` of the known piles. Each value is the name that
the inventory's `valuables` give the piece, without any spaces around it, and the string at the
same place in the pile's `items`. A piece in a pile the party
doesn't know, or in a cache the party hasn't emptied, isn't a key, as it isn't one in `item_names`.
Every key here is also a key in `item_names`.

valuable_phrases.title: Valuable Phrases
valuable_phrases.description:
What to call each piece in `valuable_names` in the middle of a sentence, with its article and its case, keyed
by the same instance id, like `{"valuable-0007": "the abbot's seal ring", "valuable-0008": "a silver altar
candlestick", "valuable-0009": "Ossor's Eye"}`. Use it as written in a sentence: "Wren takes a silver altar
candlestick." Use `valuable_names` in a list, such as an inventory row.

The keys are exactly the keys of `valuable_names`, for a piece in a member's
`inventory` and for a piece in a known pile alike. Each value is the
piece's `phrase` when it has one. Otherwise osrlib makes the phrase
from the name. A name whose first word is "the", "a", or "an", in any case, keeps its words with that first word in
lowercase, so `"The abbot's seal ring"` becomes `"the abbot's seal ring"`. Any other name has its first character in
lowercase and the indefinite article in front, "an" before `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, or `u`, with or without an accent,
and "a" otherwise, so `"Silver altar candlestick"` becomes `"a silver altar candlestick"` and `"Eye of Ossor"`
becomes `"an eye of Ossor"`. Only that first character changes case. A phrase that's only whitespace counts as no
phrase, and no value here has spaces around it.

A piece from a save that osrlib 2.9.0 wrote has no phrase, so the view makes its phrase from its name, and every
key of `valuable_names` is a key here. A `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.9.0 built, such as a stored feed entry, has no
`valuable_phrases`, and it validates with this map empty. For such a view, word each name in `valuable_names`
yourself.

deprivation.title: Deprivation
deprivation.description:
Food and water deprivation, keyed by character id, each value containing
`food_days` and `water_days`. A member with no deprivation on either track is left
out, so an empty dict means the party has been eating and drinking.

journal.title: Journal
journal.description:
The session journal, the players' record of the adventure, in the order the entries were
written. Each entry has the clock time when it was written. The record of which triggers
fired, and the referee's notes, stay out.

quests.title: Quests
quests.description:
The active quests, in the order the adventure lists them. A quest the party hasn't
taken on yet is left out. A finished quest leaves the list, and the journal still contains
every entry it added.

encounter.description:
The current encounter or battle's public state, or `null` when the party is not in
one.

supplies.description:
How long the party's light and food will last, as a
`SuppliesView`. The session always fills it in.

A `PlayerView` that osrlib 2.10.0 built, such as a stored feed entry, has no `supplies`, and it validates with
`supplies` set to `null`, so such a view has no supplies summary to show.

PlayerView.title: PlayerView
PlayerView.description:
What a player may see of a session: a fixed list of fields, every one safe to show.

Get one from `GameSession.view` with
`Visibility.PLAYER`, or from `build_player_view`.
In a networked game, send this object to a player's client. Every field is safe to show at
the table, and it contains only what the party has learned. Get a new one after every
command, because a view is a frozen snapshot that doesn't change.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"prepare_spells"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The caster, by `MemberView.id`. The party has to
have slept since this caster's last preparation, so send a `night` or `day`
`Rest` first.

selections.title: Selections
selections.description:
The spells to memorize. They replace the caster's current list rather than adding to it.
Each `MemorizedSpell` has a spell id and, for an
arcane caster, whether the copy is the reversed form of a reversible spell. Repeat a spell
to memorize more than one copy of it. The number at each spell level has to fit the
caster's slots at that level, and an empty tuple clears the list. The caster's current
list is in
`MemberView.memorized_spells`.

Choose the spells from
`MemberView.preparable_spells`, which lists
each spell that this caster may select in its normal form. An arcane caster may also select the
reversed form of a listed spell that has an entry in
`PlayerView.reversed_spell_names`. Group
the list by `PlayerView.spell_levels`, and at each
spell level select no more copies than the count there in
`MemberView.spell_slots`.

PrepareSpells.title: PrepareSpells
PrepareSpells.description:
Choose the spells a caster memorizes, replacing what they had memorized (six turns).

It's legal in town and while exploring. The caster must have slept since their last
preparation: a `night` or `day` `Rest` that a
wandering encounter didn't interrupt. In a new session the party hasn't slept yet, so a
caster's first preparation comes after a rest. The selections replace the memorized list rather
than adding to it. Cast what the caster memorized with
`CastSpell` outside battle, or with a `cast`
`BattleDeclaration` in one.
The `CastSpell` example shows a caster resting, preparing, and casting.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - an encounter or battle is underway, or the
  session has ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `magic.memorize.not_a_caster` - the member's class casts no spells.
- `magic.memorize.needs_sleep` - the party hasn't slept since this caster's last
  preparation.
- `magic.memorize.unknown_spell` - a selection matches no spell in the session's
  catalog.
- `magic.memorize.wrong_list` - a selection isn't on the caster's spell list.
- `magic.memorize.divine_reverses_at_cast` - a selection for a divine caster is
  reversed. A divine caster chooses the reversed form when casting instead.
- `magic.memorize.not_in_book` - an arcane caster's selection isn't in their
  spell book.
- `magic.memorize.not_reversible` - a reversed selection has no reversed
  form.
- `magic.memorize.slots_exceeded` - the selections at some spell level outnumber
  the caster's slots at that level.

**Events:**

`SpellsMemorizedEvent` with the
memorized list. Six turns pass, with each turn's usual events.

reversed.title: Reversed
reversed.description:
True when the copy was prepared in the spell's reversed form, as *cause light wounds* is the reverse of
*cure light wounds*.

PreparedSpell.title: PreparedSpell
PreparedSpell.description:
One spell a caster has in memory, as a memorization event lists it.

Read these from the `prepared` field of a `SpellsMemorizedEvent`.

A caster who prepares a reversible spell chooses its form when preparing it, not when casting it, so each
prepared copy records its form.

min_score.title: Min Score
min_score.description: The lowest score this row covers.

max_score.title: Max Score
max_score.description: The highest score this row covers. Equal to `min_score` on a one-score row.

xp_modifier_pct.title: Xp Modifier Pct
xp_modifier_pct.description: The percentage added to or taken off experience earned, from −20 at a score of 3 to +10 at 16 or above.

PrimeRequisiteRow.title: PrimeRequisiteRow
PrimeRequisiteRow.description:
One row of the prime requisite table, which sets how fast a character earns experience.

A prime requisite is the ability a class is built around: wisdom for a cleric,
strength for a fighter. This table applies to a class with a single prime requisite. A
class with more than one has separate tiers in its class definition, and
`xp_modifier_pct` reads the right one for any
class.

title.title: Title
title.description: Standard HTTP status phrase, such as `"Not Found"`.

status.title: Status
status.description: HTTP status code, matching the response status.

detail.title: Detail
detail.description: Human-readable explanation of what went wrong, at most 1,000 characters.

code.title: Code
code.description: Stable snake_case error identifier, such as `"not_found"`, for programmatic branching.

request_id.title: Request Id
request_id.description:
Request identifier matching the `X-Request-Id` response header, logged by the server.
Include it when reporting an error to the server's operator.

errors.title: Errors
errors.description: Present on `validation_error`: the first 20 validation failures in the request.

error_count.title: Error Count
error_count.description:
Present on `validation_error`: total number of validation failures, including any omitted
from `errors`.

resource.title: Resource
resource.description: Present on `not_found`: kind of resource requested, such as `"session"` or `"character"`.

id.title: Id
id.description:
On `not_found`, the requested id (truncated to 128 characters with `...`). On
`character_invalid` without `rejections`, the offending id value, such as an unknown item id.

revision.title: Revision
revision.description: Present on `revision_conflict` and `session_busy`: the session's current revision.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Present on `referee_command`: the `command_type` of the referee command a player sent.

field.title: Field
field.description:
Present on `character_invalid` when osrlib reports no `rejections`: the offending request
field, such as `"class_id"`, `"purchases"`, or `"equip_item_ids"`.

index.title: Index
index.description:
Present on `character_invalid` when `field` is a list: 0-based index of the offending
entry.

used_bytes.title: Used Bytes
used_bytes.description: Present on `storage_full`: bytes of documents currently stored for your client.

max_bytes.title: Max Bytes
max_bytes.description: Present on `storage_full`: maximum bytes of documents the server stores for one client.

rejections.title: Rejections
rejections.description:
Present on `character_invalid` when osrlib reports rule violations: osrlib `Rejection`
entries, each with `code` and `params`.

Problem.title: Problem
Problem.description:
RFC 9457 problem document returned in every 4xx and 5xx error response.

Every problem document includes `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `code`, and `request_id`.
The server omits the other members unless the specific `code` adds them:

- `validation_error` adds `errors` and `error_count`.
- `not_found` adds `resource` and `id`.
- `revision_conflict` and `session_busy` add `revision`.
- `referee_command` adds `command_type`.
- `character_invalid` adds `rejections` when osrlib reports them. Otherwise it adds `field`
  and `id`, plus `index` when `field` is a list.
- `storage_full` adds `used_bytes` and `max_bytes`.

Later releases may add members, so ignore any member your client doesn't recognize.

level.title: Level
level.description: The level this row describes, from 1.

xp.title: Xp
xp.description: The total experience points a character needs to reach this level. It's 0 at level 1, and rises each level.

hit_dice.description: The class's hit dice at this level. See `HitDice`.

thac0.title: Thac0
thac0.description: The d20 roll needed to hit armour class 0, for descending armour class.

attack_bonus.title: Attack Bonus
attack_bonus.description: The bonus added to an attack roll, for ascending armour class. It describes the same attack as `thac0`.

saves.description: The saving throw targets at this level. See `SavingThrows`.

spell_slots.title: Spell Slots
spell_slots.description:
How many spells of each spell level the class can memorize at this level.

The first entry is for first-level spells, the second for second-level spells, and so on. An entry is 0 when the
class can't yet memorize spells of that level, as with a first-level cleric. Empty for a class that casts no spells.

ProgressionRow.title: ProgressionRow
ProgressionRow.description:
A class's values at one level: the experience a character needs to reach the level, and what the level grants.

Get one from `ClassDefinition.row`. A character's
THAC0, attack bonus, saving throws, and spell slots come from the row for their current level,
read each time rather than stored. That's why `level_up` and
`drain_levels` need to change only the level. Frozen.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party knows whether it ate and drank.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `provisions`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member whose rations or water this was.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
Which supply the event is about: `"food"` or `"water"`. Each member gets one of each per
day.

ProvisionsEvent.title: ProvisionsEvent
ProvisionsEvent.description:
A day passed, and a character either ate and drank or went without.

Emitted once per living member per kind whenever a day boundary passes, which can
happen inside any command that passes time, and most often inside a
`Rest`.

Going short adds a day to a count the session keeps for that member (see
`consume_provisions`). Whether the
count brings a penalty depends on
`Ruleset.deprivation_penalties`,
which is off by default. [The adaptations
register](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/adaptations/), the page that lists
where osrlib settles an ambiguous rule or supplies a default, describes the
penalties. In town nobody runs short.

quantity.title: Quantity
quantity.description:
Number of purchase lots to buy, from 1 to 10,000 (defaults to 1). Weapons and armour sell
one item per lot, whereas adventuring gear and ammunition sell in bundles (for example, one lot
of `torch` is six torches).

Purchase.title: Purchase
Purchase.description: One equipment purchase paid from the character's starting gold.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"purchase_equipment"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The buyer, by `MemberView.id`. This member's purse
pays for every entry, and the goods go into this member's pack.

item_ids.title: Item Ids
item_ids.description:
What to buy, one purchase lot per entry, so repeat an id to buy more lots. A purchase lot
is what one purchase at the item's listed price delivers: a lot of torches costs 1 gp and
arrives as six torches, while a weapon or a suit of armour is a single item. The ids come
from `load_equipment` (see the
[equipment id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/)).
The session refuses an id the adventure bundles with `items.purchase.not_stocked`, because
it isn't for sale.
An empty tuple fails validation when the command is constructed.

PurchaseEquipment.title: PurchaseEquipment
PurchaseEquipment.description:
Buy equipment in town for one member, one purchase lot for each `item_ids` entry (takes no game time).

The party must be in town. The session adds up the price of every entry first, and if
the member can't afford the total, nothing is bought. The shop stocks only the built-in
equipment from `load_equipment` (see the
[equipment id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/)).
An item the adventure bundles isn't for sale, even when the party has seen its id, and
the session refuses it as not stocked rather than as unknown.

Modes:

`town`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the party is not in town.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `session.command.unknown_item` - an entry matches no equipment item.
- `items.purchase.not_stocked` - an entry is an item the adventure
  bundles, which the shop doesn't sell.
- `items.purchase.insufficient_funds` - the member's purse can't cover the total.

**Events:**

`ItemAcquiredEvent` listing the
purchases, `origin` `"purchase"`.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"purchase_healing"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
Who is treated, by `MemberView.id`. This member's
purse pays first, and the rest of the party pays whatever is left. The member can be dead.
`raise_dead` is the service for a dead member, and the session refuses it for a living
one.

service.title: Service
service.description:
Which service to buy. Each works as the matching spell, cast by the temple cleric.
`remove_curse` also frees the member from cursed items whose curse has been revealed, so they
can take them off.

caster_level.title: Caster Level
caster_level.description:
The level of the temple cleric who casts the service, or `null` for the lowest level that
can cast it, like level 2 for `cure_light_wounds` and level 7 for `raise_dead`.

The level decides how long dead a member `raise_dead` can bring back: 4 days for each level
above 7th. A level 7 cleric raises only a member who died less than a day ago, and a level 9
cleric raises a member dead up to 8 days. The session refuses a level below the lowest that can
cast the service, or above 14, the highest level a cleric can reach. The price is the same at
every level. For each member and service,
`PlayerView.town_healing_caster_levels`
gives the lowest level that works.

spell_mode.title: Spell Mode
spell_mode.description:
Which usage of the service's spell the temple cleric casts, by that usage's
`SpellMode.key`, or `null` for the spell's first usage.

The temple sells *cure light wounds* in two usages: `heal`, the first, which restores 1d6+1
hit points, and `cure_paralysis`, which ends the member's paralysis. Every other service has
one usage the temple sells, which is the spell's first. The temple doesn't sell a manual usage,
such as *cure disease*'s `kill_green_slime` or *neutralize poison*'s `items`, because the session
resolves nothing for one, or *raise dead*'s `destroy_undead`, which works only on undead. It
refuses those with `town.healing.mode_not_offered`, and a key the spell doesn't have with
`magic.cast.unknown_mode`. The price is the same for every usage of a service. For each member
and each service the temple sells in more than one usage,
`PlayerView.town_healing_mode_rejections`
gives the answer for each usage, and
`PlayerView.town_healing_mode_names`
gives each usage's display name.

PurchaseHealing.title: PurchaseHealing
PurchaseHealing.description:
Buy a temple healing service in town (takes no game time).

The party must be in town. Name the patient in `character_id` and the service in `service`.
Each service works as the matching spell, cast on the member by a temple cleric. The cleric is
of the lowest level that can cast the service unless you choose a level in `caster_level`.
The cleric casts the spell's first usage unless you choose another in `spell_mode`, such as
*cure light wounds*'s `cure_paralysis`.

The town's `TownSpec.healing_prices` sets
what each service costs, and a service the town doesn't list costs the standard price from
`HEALING_SERVICES`. The OSE SRD describes the base
town in prose and lists no temple prices, so osrlib sets the standard prices, by `service`
value: `cure_light_wounds` 25 gp, `cure_serious_wounds` 100 gp, `cure_disease` 150 gp,
`neutralize_poison` 150 gp, `remove_curse` 200 gp, and `raise_dead` 1,500 gp. The price is the
same at every cleric level. To show what the party's town charges, read
`PlayerView.town_healing_prices`.

The whole party pays the fee, not only the patient. The temple takes it from the patient's
purse first, then from the other members' purses in marching order, dead members included,
until the fee is paid. A service the town sets at 0 gp takes nothing from any purse.

Each purse pays only in whole gold pieces, and any value below a gold piece stays in the
purse. For example, two members who each have 12 gp and
5 sp are worth 25 gp together. Each purse can pay only 12 gp, so together they can pay 24
gp, and the session refuses a 25 gp service.

Because the party pays, a dead member can be raised even when that member's purse is
empty, and the party doesn't have to move coins between purses first.

To learn before you send the command which services the temple can perform for each
member, read
`PlayerView.town_healing_rejections`,
which contains the rejections that follow the funds check, and
`PlayerView.town_healing_caster_levels`,
which gives the `caster_level` to send. Both answer for each service's first usage. For a
service the temple sells in more than one usage, read
`PlayerView.town_healing_mode_rejections`
for the answer for each usage. To learn whether the party can pay, compare the
price with
`PlayerView.town_healing_funds_gp`.

Modes:

`town`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the party is not in town.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `magic.cast.unknown_mode` - `spell_mode` matches no usage of the service's spell.
- `town.healing.mode_not_offered` - `spell_mode` names a usage the temple doesn't sell:
  a manual usage, which the session can't resolve, or one that works only on undead.
- `town.healing.caster_level_out_of_range` - `caster_level` is below the lowest level
  that can cast the service, or above the highest level a cleric can reach. The
  rejection's `minimum` and `maximum` params give the lowest and highest levels the
  temple accepts for the service.
- `items.purchase.insufficient_funds` - the whole gold pieces in the party's
  purses add up to less than the town's price for the service.
- `town.healing.no_effect` - the usage would do nothing for the member. The
  rejection's `reason` param says why. For the healing usage of `cure_light_wounds` and
  `cure_serious_wounds` it's `dead`, `weakened`, `diseased`, or `full_hit_points`,
  checked in that order, because neither condition lets a member heal by magic. For
  `cure_light_wounds`'s `cure_paralysis` usage it's `dead` or `not_paralysed`, checked
  in that order. For
  `cure_disease` it's `not_diseased`. For `neutralize_poison` it's `not_poisoned`, for
  a member who isn't poisoned and didn't die of poison in the last 10 rounds. For
  `remove_curse` it's `not_cursed`, for a member who carries no item whose curse has
  been revealed and has no item curse's effect. For `raise_dead` it's `not_dead` for a
  living member, `no_death_record` for a dead member whose death the session didn't
  record, `caster_level_too_low` for a member a higher-level cleric could raise, and
  `dead_too_long` for a member no temple cleric can raise, checked in that order. The
  session checks the party's funds first, so a party that can't pay gets
  `items.purchase.insufficient_funds` instead.

**Events:**

A `HealingPurchasedEvent` listing
which purses paid and how much each one paid, then the events of the service's
spell, like healing, the end of a poison or a disease, or the result of a *raise dead*.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party can see how close the chase is.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `pursuit`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

round.title: Round
round.description: Which round of the chase this is, counting from one.

gap_feet.title: Gap Feet
gap_feet.description:
How far ahead of its nearest pursuer the party is, in feet, at the end of this round. It never
goes below zero, and at five feet or less the pursuers have caught up.

PursuitEvent.title: PursuitEvent
PursuitEvent.description:
One round of a chase: the gap, a distraction taken, an escape, or a capture.

Emitted by `Evade` for the first round of the chase.
Each further round comes from `Wait`, to keep running,
or `DropItems`, to drop something behind the party
as it runs.

A capture opens battle at once. An escape or a distraction ends the encounter. A
chase that lasts `PURSUIT_ROUND_CAP` rounds
ends in an escape and tires the party out, which arrives as
`ExhaustionEvent`.

round.title: Round
round.description:
The number of chase rounds run so far. The first round sets it to 1. The party escapes when it
reaches `PURSUIT_ROUND_CAP`.

gap_feet.title: Gap Feet
gap_feet.description:
The distance between the party and its nearest pursuer, in feet. It starts at the distance of the
nearest pursuing group. When the pursuit follows a retreat from a battle, it starts at the smallest
distance from any living member to any group that can follow, after the retreat's move, because
members can stand at different places on the battle's range track. That retreat also sets each
group's `distance_feet` to its distance from
the nearest standing member, because the party runs as one body from then on.

Each round, every pursuing group's `distance_feet` grows by the party's running rate and shrinks by
the running rate of the slowest pursuing group, and this field becomes the smallest of them. A group
that stops pursuing stays where it is, and the gap is measured to the pursuers that remain. At 5 feet
or less, the pursuers catch the party, and a battle starts. The groups that reached the party stand
at 5 feet, and every other group stays as far behind as the chase left it. When the nearest pursuer
stops pursuing and the next one is farther back, the gap grows to that group's distance.

pursuer_ids.title: Pursuer Ids
pursuer_ids.description:
The ids of the groups that pursued the party in the last round, or at the start of the chase
before its first round. A group that has stopped pursuing joins the chase again only while it
stands within `FLEE_EXIT_FEET` of the party, so the session
reads this to tell a pursuer from a group that has dropped out.

It's None in a chase saved by an engine that didn't record it. That engine kept the gap here and
left each group at the encounter's starting distance, so
`load_game` moves every group that hasn't fled to `gap_feet`, and
the next round counts every group able and willing to pursue as a pursuer.

PursuitState.title: PursuitState
PursuitState.description:
A chase in progress: the gap between the running party and its pursuers, updated each round.

Read it from `session.encounter.pursuit`. It's None until a chase starts. A chase starts when the
party evades with `Evade` and an attacking or hostile group runs
at least as fast as the party. It also starts when the whole party retreats from a battle and a
monster group is still able and willing to follow. During a chase, the session
rejects `Parley` and
`TurnUndead`, and `Wait` runs
one round of the chase. `EngageBattle` turns the party to
fight, and each group stands where the chase has left it.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party is being given the job.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `quest_activated`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

quest_id.title: Quest Id
quest_id.description: Which quest, as the id the adventure gave it.

name.title: Name
name.description: The quest's display name, so you don't need the adventure to show it.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description:
The offer text the author wrote, or `null` when there's none. The session adds the same line
to the journal with no separate journal event, so the players see it once.

QuestActivatedEvent.title: QuestActivatedEvent
QuestActivatedEvent.description:
A quest became active.

Emitted by `ActivateQuest`. A quest whose
`activate_when` is `null` is active from the start of the session, with no command
and no event.

It has player visibility, because the party knows the job it has taken on. The
trigger that activated the quest stays hidden, like the trigger and flag events.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party learns the quest is done.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `quest_completed`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

name.title: Name
name.description: The quest's display name.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description: The completion text the author wrote, or `null`. The journal has the same line.

QuestCompletedEvent.title: QuestCompletedEvent
QuestCompletedEvent.description:
A quest is finished.

Emitted by `CompleteQuest`. Whether the
quest is done is the referee's ruling: the engine checks that the quest is
active, not that every objective was completed.

A quest's rewards arrive after this event, as the events of the commands that pay
them. When the quest concludes the adventure, an
`AdventureCompletedEvent` follows
in the same result.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The quest's id, unique across the adventure. `session.quests` uses it as the key, and
every command the interpreter runs for the quest has `source` set to `quest:{id}`.

name.title: Name
name.description:
The quest's display name. The quest events and the quest's view include it, so you
can show it without the adventure document.

activation.description:
The clause that starts the quest. With `null`, the quest is active from the start of
the session. No command starts it, so the session emits no
`QuestActivatedEvent` for it, but its
`QuestView` still includes the `offer` text. With a clause,
the quest starts when an event matches the clause.

objectives.title: Objectives
objectives.description:
What the quest asks for, in the order a quest log should show the objectives. At least
one is required, because a quest with no objectives under the `"all"` rule would be
complete from the start.

rewards.title: Rewards
rewards.description:
The referee commands the interpreter runs after the quest completes, in the order you
write them. The interpreter replaces
`PARTY_SELECTOR`,
`FIRST_LIVING_SELECTOR`, and
`CARRIER_SELECTOR` with the members they select.
When the session rejects one reward, the interpreter drops it, records a note, and runs the
rest. A reward with `source` set fails validation with a pydantic `ValidationError`, because
the interpreter sets `source` itself.

completion.title: Completion
completion.description:
The rule for completing the quest. With `"all"`, the quest completes when every
objective is complete. With `"any"`, it completes when the first objective completes.

Once the quest is complete, its other objectives never change. Under `"any"`, an
objective that wasn't complete stays incomplete, even when the same event matched its
clause.

concludes_adventure.title: Concludes Adventure
concludes_adventure.description:
Whether completing this quest ends the adventure. The session moves to `victory`
mode and emits an
`AdventureCompletedEvent` before the
interpreter runs the first reward. A reward that `victory` mode doesn't allow, like
`SpawnMonsters` or
`PlaceParty`, is rejected, and the interpreter drops
it and records a note. Grants and experience awards still apply.

narrative.description:
The quest's text. osrlib reads two fields of the block: `offer`, the line shown and
added to the journal when the quest starts, and `completion`, the line shown and added
to the journal when it completes. Each objective's text is in its
`ObjectiveSpec.narrative`.

QuestSpec.title: QuestSpec
QuestSpec.description:
One authored quest: when it starts, what it asks for, and what it pays.

Put your quests in the `quests` tuple of an
`Adventure`, and register an
`Interpreter` on the session to run them. The
interpreter is the only part of osrlib that reads a quest, so without it the quest
doesn't advance. The session tracks each quest in play as a
`QuestState` in `session.quests`, and you get each
active quest as a `QuestView`.

The interpreter runs the rewards after the quest completes, in the order you write
them, and only when the interpreter completed the quest. A quest you complete
with `CompleteQuest` pays no rewards.

status.title: Status
status.description:
Where the quest stands. It moves from `inactive` to `active` to `completed` and never
goes back.

objectives.title: Objectives
objectives.description:
The state of each objective, keyed by objective id, in the order the adventure lists them
in `QuestSpec.objectives`.

QuestState.title: QuestState
QuestState.description:
One quest's state in play: where it stands, and where each of its objectives stands.

The session creates one for each quest in the adventure and stores them in
`GameSession.quests`, keyed by quest id. Only the
quest commands change them: `ActivateQuest`,
`RevealObjective`,
`CompleteObjective`, and
`CompleteQuest`. So a replay of the command log
rebuilds them exactly.

A quest with no activation clause, meaning its
`QuestSpec.activation` is `null`, starts `active`,
because the party has it from the start. The rest start `inactive` and wait for
`ActivateQuest`.

id.title: Id
id.description: The quest's id in the adventure.

name.title: Name
name.description: The quest's display name.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description:
The adventure's text for offering the quest, its narrative's `offer`, or the empty
string when it has none. The view includes the text because a remote client has no
adventure document to look it up in.

speaker.title: Speaker
speaker.description:
Who speaks the offer, like `"Sister Halda"`, or the empty string when the adventure gives
no speaker.

objectives.title: Objectives
objectives.description: The revealed objectives, in the order the quest lists them.

QuestView.title: QuestView
QuestView.description:
One active quest as the players know it: the task, who gave it, and where it stands.

You get these from `PlayerView.quests`. The rules
that start a quest, complete it, and reward it never appear, because they're hidden from
the players the same way a trigger's rules are. When you have the session, read the quest's
definition from `QuestSpec` and its state from
`QuestState`.

min_feet.title: Min Feet
min_feet.description: The band's nearest distance in feet, inclusive.

max_feet.title: Max Feet
max_feet.description:
The band's farthest distance in feet, inclusive. Never less than `min_feet`: building a band with a reversed pair
raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

RangeBand.title: RangeBand
RangeBand.description:
One missile range band in feet, as the SRD prints it (`5'–80'`).

Three of these make up a weapon's `MissileRanges`,
and the band a shot falls into sets its attack modifier. Bands come from the
compiled equipment data (`load_equipment`). Construct one
yourself only when you build a missile weapon template to bundle with an adventure.
Both bounds are inclusive. The engine rejects an attack at a distance past the long
band's maximum with `combat.attack.out_of_range`.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
Which kind of range this is.

- `caster`: the spell affects only the caster.
- `touch`: the spell affects a creature the caster touches, which can be the caster. It reaches 5', as far
  as a melee attack (`MELEE_REACH_FEET`), so `validate_cast` refuses
  a touch spell at a `distance_feet` beyond that with `magic.cast.out_of_range`.
- `feet` and `yards`: a fixed distance, in `feet`.
- `per_level`: a distance that grows with caster level.
- `special`: the printed line has no structure osrlib can read.

feet.title: Feet
feet.description:
The distance in feet, for the `feet`, `yards`, and `per_level` kinds. `null` on the other kinds.

Yards are converted, so a range printed as 240 yards is 720 here. On a `per_level` range this is
the distance before the per-level bonus, and it is `null` when the printed range is only a
distance per level, like `10’ per level`.

per_level_feet.title: Per Level Feet
per_level_feet.description:
Extra feet of reach per caster level on a `per_level` range. `null` on the other kinds.

A range printed `60’ +10’ per level` is `feet` 60 and `per_level_feet` 10, so a 5th-level caster
reaches 110 feet.

RangeSpec.title: RangeSpec
RangeSpec.description:
How far a spell reaches, parsed out of the printed range line.

Read one from `SpellTemplate.range_spec`.
`validate_cast` reads it for you, but only when you pass
the distance to the target in
`CastContext.distance_feet`. osrlib has no map,
so with no distance there's no range check. Read this model yourself when you draw a range
indicator, filter spells by reach, or decide which targets to offer.

The printed line is the template's `range`, and that's what you show a player. A printed range
with no structure osrlib can read, like `"Appears in the caster’s presence"`, is stored as
`kind="special"` with no distance.

label.title: Label
label.description: The range as the SRD prints it, like `"2 or less"`, `"3–5"`, or `"12 or more"`. The ranges use an en dash.

text.title: Text
text.description:
The SRD's English text for the band, like `"Hostile, may attack"`.

Show it to a referee. For text that players see, write your own wording for each
`result` value.

min_total.title: Min Total
min_total.description:
The lowest 2d6 total in the band, or `null` on the lowest band, which has no lower limit.

A CHA modifier can take a total below 2, and that total falls in the lowest band.

max_total.title: Max Total
max_total.description: The highest 2d6 total in the band, or `null` on the highest band, which has no upper limit.

result.description: The reaction for a total in this band. Act on this value.

ReactionBand.title: ReactionBand
ReactionBand.description:
One band of the monster reaction table: a range of 2d6 totals and the reaction it gives.

Read the bands to display the table. To look up a total, call
`reaction_result`.

ReactionResult.title: ReactionResult
ReactionResult.description:
How monsters respond to the party when they meet, from the SRD's monster reaction table.

`reaction_result` returns one from a 2d6 total.
What the party does next, like fighting, talking, or fleeing, is up to the players.

The values are lowercase strings, like `"hostile"`. They appear in events and saved
games, so you can store them and compare with them.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: the players learn a monster's mood from what it does, not from the dice.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

modifier.title: Modifier
modifier.description: The CHA modifier to reactions of the character who spoke to the monsters, or 0 when no one did.

total.title: Total
total.description:
The roll plus the modifier, which is the number osrlib looks up on the reaction table. osrlib reads a total
outside 2 to 12 as the nearest end of the table.

result.title: Result
result.description:
How the monsters react, as a `ReactionResult` value: `attacks`,
`hostile`, `uncertain`, `indifferent`, or `friendly`.

ReactionRolledEvent.title: ReactionRolledEvent
ReactionRolledEvent.description:
How monsters react to meeting the party.

`roll_reaction` reports one of these each time it's called, which is when
the party meets monsters that aren't already fighting. Use the result to decide how the monsters act.

bands.title: Bands
bands.description: The bands, from the most hostile reaction to the most friendly. Together they cover every total, with no gaps.

ReactionTable.title: ReactionTable
ReactionTable.description:
The monster reaction table, which turns a 2d6 total into how monsters respond to the party.

Get it from `CombatTables.reaction` and pass
it to `reaction_result` with a rolled total.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"record_note"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

text.title: Text
text.description:
The note to record. It goes into the log as an event at referee visibility and changes no
state. To give the players a line to read, issue an
`AddJournalEntry` instead.

RecordNote.title: RecordNote
RecordNote.description:
Referee: write a note into the logs, with no effect on the game.

The note becomes an event at referee visibility and changes nothing else. Use it for a
record from your code, like an authored consequence that was dropped, or for a
referee's notes. The trigger and quest interpreter issues it to record what it dropped
and why. This command is legal in every mode, `game_over` and `victory` included.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`, `battle`, `game_over`, `victory`

**Rejections:**

None.

**Events:**

`NoteRecordedEvent` with the text.

ruleset.description:
The options this session plays under, as a `Ruleset`, whose
flags turn the optional rules on and off.

party.description:
The party, as a `Party` of full
`Character` sheets in marching order, the dead included. Every
number is here, the spell book and the true names of magic items among them, so render a player's
sheet from `PlayerView.party` instead, which masks what
the party has not identified.

adventure.description:
The whole adventure document, as an `Adventure`: the town, the
dungeons with their complete geometry and keyed areas, the triggers, and the quests. It is the map
with nothing hidden, so draw the party's map from
`PlayerView.explored` instead. The document is frozen and
the view copies it even so, because the tree under it contains dicts you can edit in place, the
town's travel turns and each level's edges among them.

mode.description:
The `SessionMode` the session is in. The mode sets which
commands the session accepts right now.

clock_rounds.title: Clock Rounds
clock_rounds.description: How much game time has passed since the session began, in rounds.

allocator.description:
The source of session ids, as an `IdAllocator`. It hands out
each `<kind>-NNNN` id by counting up, so two runs of the same commands assign the same ids.

ledger.description:
The active effects, as an `EffectsLedger`: spells running,
conditions, a torch burning down, each with the round it expires at. It includes the effects
attached to dungeon cells as well as the ones on members, and the true duration of a potion's
effect, which the players aren't allowed to know.

dungeon_state.description:
What the session has recorded on top of the adventure's map during play, as a
`DungeonState`: where the party stands, the cells it has walked
and seen, door state, found and sprung traps, drop piles, and generated caches.

monsters.title: Monsters
monsters.description:
Every monster spawned this session, as
`MonsterInstance` values in the order they were spawned,
the defeated ones included, so a later event can still refer to them. Their hit points and other
statistics are here. The players see monsters only as
`EncounterGroupView` values.

npcs.title: Npcs
npcs.description:
The NPC adventurers in play, as `Character` sheets in the order
they joined. They are characters rather than monsters, and they fight by the same rules as the party.

flags.title: Flags
flags.description:
The session flags: the key-value store that `SetFlag` writes and
an adventure's triggers, quests, and door and exit conditions read. Flags are part of the
adventure's hidden rules, so no flag ever reaches a player view.

fired_triggers.title: Fired Triggers
fired_triggers.description:
The ids of the triggers that have fired, in the order they first fired. Use it to check whether a
trigger has fired before. It's for the referee only. The players learn what a trigger did from the
journal entry it added, if any.

journal.title: Journal
journal.description:
The journal, as `JournalEntry` values in the order they were
written. The players see the same list, and you read it for them from
`PlayerView.journal`.

quests.title: Quests
quests.description:
The state of every quest in the adventure, as `QuestState`
values keyed by quest id, in the order the adventure lists them. It includes the inactive and
completed quests as well as the active ones, and every objective, revealed or hidden. The players'
version is `PlayerView.quests`.

listener_state.title: Listener State
listener_state.description:
Each registered listener's state, keyed by the listener's `key`, as that listener's `handle`
returned it. The session stores it and never reads it, so the listener decides what it means.

death_records.title: Death Records
death_records.description:
When and how each dead party member died, as `DeathRecord`
values keyed by character id. When the engine resolves *raise dead*, it reads the day count from
here, and for *neutralize poison*, the round window.

defeated_monsters.title: Defeated Monsters
defeated_monsters.description:
The creatures defeated since the last experience award, as
`DefeatedMonsterRecord` values in the order they fell.
`GameSession.award_adventure_xp` adds up their
`xp` and clears the list.

deprivation.title: Deprivation
deprivation.description:
The food and water counts, as `DeprivationState` values
keyed by character id. There's one for each member the session has charged for food and water at
the start of a new day, including members whose counts are zero.
`PlayerView.deprivation` reports the same counts, but
only for members whose counts aren't zero.

treasure_snapshot_cp.title: Treasure Snapshot Cp
treasure_snapshot_cp.description:
What the party's treasure was worth in copper pieces when it left town, or `null` when no delve
is under way. The adventure award pays for the difference between this and what comes back.

exploration.description:
The exploration counters, as `ExplorationCounters`:
distance walked, turns since a rest, turns since a wandering check, noise, sleep, and food.

encounter.description:
The encounter under way, as an `EncounterState`, or
`null` when nothing is happening. It contains each group's monster ids, its distance, the stance the
reaction roll settled, and any chase in progress. The players' reading of the same encounter is
`PlayerView.encounter`.

battle.description:
The battle under way, as a `BattleState`, or `null` outside
one. It contains the round number and the state that persists from round to round,
including who fired a weapon that needs reloading last round.

command_log.title: Command Log
command_log.description:
Every accepted command, in order, each one the `Command`
subclass it was issued as, so its fields are there to read. Refused commands are absent, because
they changed nothing, and `replay_game` re-executes this list from
the master seed to rebuild the session.

event_log.title: Event Log
event_log.description:
Everything that has happened, in order, each entry the `Event`
subclass that was emitted, including the referee-visibility events a player never sees. An entry
restored from a save whose event type this library has no class for stays the raw mapping it
arrived as, so check for a `dict` before reading an entry's attributes.

feature_handles.title: Feature Handles
feature_handles.description:
The player handle of every feature in the session, keyed by the reference the save uses for
the feature. An authored feature's key is `"{dungeon}:{level}:{feature id}"`, the form in
`DungeonState.emptied_caches` and
`DungeonState.found_traps`, and every feature the
adventure authors has one, on a level or in an area, found or not. A generated cache's key is its
id in `DungeonState.generated_caches`, like
`"cache-0001"`. Every cache that the session rolled or that `load_game`
restored has one, including a lair cache the players can't see yet. A cache you write into
`DungeonState.generated_caches` yourself on a cell that doesn't exist has none.

Each value is the `MapFeatureView.id` that the player view
shows for the feature once the party knows it. Use it to show a referee the feature the players
see, and to send the same `feature_id` they do. This is the one field the save doesn't contain:
the session derives each handle from the player-handle key, and neither view contains the key.
The session removes a generated cache when the party takes it, and its entry leaves with it.

RefereeView.title: RefereeView
RefereeView.description:
The referee state in a save, except seeds, random streams, and the player-handle key.

Get one from `GameSession.view` with
`Visibility.REFEREE`, or from `build_referee_view`. Use
it where players can't see it: as the context an LLM referee reasons over, in a debugging panel,
or in a test that checks state a player may not see. Never send it to a player's client, and draw
nothing a player sees from it. `PlayerView` is for that.

Each field is the session's model rather than a dict, so you read
`view.monsters[0].current_hp` and `view.flags["key"]` with the types this reference documents, and
each field's docstring links the model to read next. The fields are the groups
`session_state` writes, minus the master seed, the RNG stream
positions, and the player-handle key, so `view.model_dump(mode="json")` is that save payload
without those keys, plus one field the save doesn't contain,
`feature_handles`. The seed and stream
positions let a player predict every roll to come. The key lets someone reproduce and control the
session's opaque feature handles, so the view gives you the handles themselves instead.

The view is a snapshot of the moment it was built. The session's mutable state is copied into it,
so later play leaves the view as it was, and editing what you find on a view changes nothing on
the session. Being frozen fixes the view's fields rather than their contents, so
rebinding `view.flags` raises while `view.flags["key"] = 1` and `view.monsters[0].current_hp = 0`
edit the view's copies and are allowed. Build a fresh view after each command rather than
editing one. The command log, the event log, and the journal are shared with the session instead of
copied, because a command, an event, and a journal entry are frozen records of something that has
already happened.

code.title: Code
code.description:
Which refusal this is, as a dotted message code like `items.equip.armour_forbidden`.

Match on this value to choose what to show the player. A code is two or more
snake_case segments joined by dots, and the first segment is the subsystem that
refused. Building a rejection with any other format raises a pydantic
`ValidationError`.

params.title: Params
params.description:
The facts behind the refusal, like the ability that was too low or the class that may not wear the armour.

Values are integers, strings, or tuples of either. Which keys appear depends on the
code, so read the keys of the codes you handle and skip any you don't recognize. A
string is an id or a value name, except where an adventure's author wrote the text,
like a gate's refusal line in the `refusal` key.

Rejection.title: Rejection
Rejection.description:
One reason a validator refused an input, as a code plus the facts behind it.

A validator returns these. Match on `code` to decide what to tell the player, and read
`params` for the numbers and names to put in the sentence. osrlib writes no English
into a rejection, so write your own wording for the codes you expect, and show the
code itself for the rest.
[The rejection code reference](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/rejection-codes/)
lists every code osrlib returns, with what it means.

Build one yourself only when you write your own validator, for a house rule or a
custom item, and want it to report a refusal the same way osrlib does.

The model is frozen, so you can keep a rejection around and compare rejections for
equality.

label.title: Label
label.description:
New label, 1 to 200 characters without control characters such as tabs or newlines, or `null` to
remove the existing label.

RelabelSaveRequest.title: RelabelSaveRequest
RelabelSaveRequest.description: New label (or `null` to clear it) for `PATCH /v1/saves/{save_id}`.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"remove_coins"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member whose purse pays, by
`MemberView.id`. A command you issue yourself has a
member id here, and the session refuses any other value with `session.command.unknown_member`.
A consequence or a reward in an adventure document has a party selector instead,
`"@party"` for every living member or `"@first"` for the first living member, because the
session assigns member ids when it starts. The trigger and quest interpreter replaces the selector
with member ids before it issues the command.

coins.description:
The coins to take, by denomination. The purse must have at least this many coins of each
denomination.

RemoveCoins.title: RemoveCoins
RemoveCoins.description:
Referee: take coins out of a member's purse, the inverse of `GrantCoins`.

Use it to charge a price or a toll. The session takes exactly the coins you name. It
doesn't make change between denominations, so a member who has gold but no silver can't
pay a toll in silver. Convert the price to coins the member has before you send the
command. This command is legal in every mode, `game_over` and `victory` included. It makes no draws
and takes no time.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`, `battle`, `game_over`, `victory`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `items.coins.insufficient` - the purse has fewer coins of some denomination than
  `coins` asks for.

**Events:**

`ItemsRemovedEvent` with the coins' value.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"remove_item"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who loses the item, by
`MemberView.id`. A command you issue yourself has a
member id here, and the session refuses any other value with `session.command.unknown_member`.
A consequence or a reward in an adventure document has a selector instead, because the
session assigns member ids when it starts. `"@party"` takes the item from every living
member, `"@first"` from the first living member, and `"@carrier"` from the first living
member in marching order who carries it. The trigger and quest interpreter replaces the
selector with member ids before it issues the command.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
Which item to take. A mundane item's catalog id, like `"torch"`, takes units from the
member's pack first and then from what the member has equipped. A magic item's or a
valuable's instance id, like `"magic-item-0003"` or `"valuable-0002"`, takes that one
item. The session refuses a magic item's catalog id with `items.remove.not_carried`,
because two copies of a magic item can differ. Read instance ids from the member's
inventory in the referee view.

quantity.title: Quantity
quantity.description: How many units of a mundane item to take. It has to be 1 for an instance id.

RemoveItem.title: RemoveItem
RemoveItem.description:
Referee: take an item away from a member, the inverse of `GrantItem`.

Use it when your game takes something the party has: armour a shop buys back, a quest
item used up when the quest completes, or an offering left on an altar. The item is
destroyed, not dropped, so the party can't pick it back up. When your game pays for the
item, also send `GrantCoins`. This command is legal in
every mode, `game_over` and `victory` included.

Name the item in `item_id`, by one of two kinds of id. A mundane item, like a torch, has a
catalog id, and a member can carry several units of it. Set `quantity` to the number of units
to take. A magic item or a valuable has an instance id, which names one item, so `quantity`
stays 1.

The session takes an equipped item off before it removes it. Any effect the item attached
ends, as it would with `UnequipItem`. A revealed
curse doesn't stop the removal, because a curse stops only the bearer from taking the item
off. The command makes no draws and takes no time.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`, `battle`, `game_over`, `victory`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `items.remove.not_carried` - the member doesn't carry `quantity` units of
  `item_id`, or `item_id` is an instance id and `quantity` isn't 1.

**Events:**

`ItemsRemovedEvent` with the removed
items. When an equipped magic item's effects end, their events come first.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"remove_member"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who leaves, by `MemberView.id`. They can
be alive, dead, asleep, or turned to stone.

give_to.title: Give To
give_to.description:
The member who takes everything the leaving member carries, by
`MemberView.id`. Leave it `null` to let it all leave the
game with the member. The session refuses `null` when the member carries an item the
adventure depends on. The member named here has to be able to act.

RemoveMember.title: RemoveMember
RemoveMember.description:
Referee: take a member out of the party for good.

Use it when a character leaves play: one who died too long ago for *raise dead*, a hireling
who quits, or a character the player retires. To bring in a replacement, send
`AddMember` as well. The member can be in any state:
alive, dead, turned to stone, or asleep. The other members keep their marching order.

Name another member in `give_to` to keep what the leaving member carries in the party.
Every item and all the coins go to that member: mundane gear, magic items, gems, and
jewellery. Equipped items arrive unequipped in their pack, and an equipped magic item's
effects end, as with `GiveItems`. A cursed item moves
too, even when its curse is revealed, because the curse holds only its wearer, and the wearer
has left. It arrives with its curse hidden again, as *remove curse* leaves an item, so the
new owner can drop it or give it away. If they put it on, the curse is revealed again.
Without `give_to`, everything the member carries leaves the game with them.

Without `give_to`, the session refuses to remove a member who carries an item the adventure
depends on, because the party might then never open a door or finish a quest. The adventure
depends on an item when its catalog id appears in a
`HasItemCondition` or an
`ItemAcquiredPattern` anywhere in the adventure.
That means the gate of a door, a stair, or a passage, a trigger, or any clause of a quest. The
session matches ids the way a `HasItemCondition` does. Mundane items, magic items, and the
adventure's own items all count, equipped or not. An item counts even when another member
carries the same item too. When the session refuses, send the command again and name a
member in `give_to` to take everything, the item included.

Some parts of an adventure can't matter again, and they stop protecting their items. A quest
that `GameSession.quests` shows as `completed`
protects nothing. A trigger protects nothing once it has fired, which means its id is in
`GameSession.fired_triggers`, unless it's `repeatable`. A quest that is still open protects
the items in all its clauses, even an objective that is already complete. A gate always
protects its item, because the party can come back to it.

The session also drops what it tracks about the member. The effects on them end without
events, and their death record, their food and water counts, and the record of when they
last prepared spells are deleted. An effect the member cast on another member lasts its full
duration. A light the member carried goes out with them. A burning torch leaves with its
bearer, and a lantern given to `give_to` arrives unlit. Read
`GameSession.party_light` afterwards to find
out whether the party still has light.

The member's id is retired. The session never gives it to another member, so an old event
that names it can't be mistaken for a new member. A replacement that joins with `AddMember`
gets a new id. The session refuses the old id in later commands with
`session.command.unknown_member`.

In a dungeon, the coins and valuables that leave with the member come off
`treasure_snapshot_cp`, so the
departure doesn't change the experience the party earns for treasure when it comes back to
town. With `give_to`, nothing leaves the party, and the snapshot stays as it was.

Removing a member makes no draws and takes no time. The command is legal only in `town` and
`exploring`, like `AddMember`. The session never removes the last member who stands, which
means one who is neither dead nor turned to stone, because a party with nobody standing has
lost the game. To replace a player's last standing character, add the new character with
`AddMember` first, and then remove the old one.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - an encounter or a battle is open, or the session
  has ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` or `give_to` matches no party
  member.
- `party.remove.same_member` - `give_to` names the member who leaves.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the `give_to` member can't act, because
  they're dead, asleep, paralysed, or turned to stone.
- `party.remove.last_standing` - no member would be left standing. That includes
  removing the only member.
- `party.remove.carries_quest_item` - `give_to` is `null`, and the member carries an
  item the adventure depends on. The rejection includes the member's id as `character`
  and the item's catalog id as `item`. When the member carries more than one such item,
  it names the first in the order that
  `Inventory.all_instances` lists them.

The session checks in this order and reports the first that fails.

**Events:**

With `give_to`, an `EffectReleasedEvent`
for each effect of an equipped magic item, then an
`ItemsGivenEvent` with what moved, when
anything did. Then a `MemberRemovedEvent`
with the member's id and name.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"remove_treasure_trap"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The thief who works on the trap, by
`MemberView.id`. A failed attempt springs the trap on
this member.

feature_id.title: Feature Id
feature_id.description:
Which trapped cache to disarm: a `feature:` handle from
`MapFeatureView.id` in the current player view, or the
cache's raw `FeatureSpec.id`, since only an authored
cache can be trapped. Both forms stay supported. A player client sends the handle, because the
player view lists only handles. Both forms resolve against the same caches, the available
ones the party can reach where it stands, so a raw id reaches and reveals nothing that a
handle doesn't. A cache anywhere else, a cache with no trap, and a cache whose trap nobody has
found all get the same `exploration.feature.unknown` rejection as an id that no cache has.

RemoveTreasureTrap.title: RemoveTreasureTrap
RemoveTreasureTrap.description:
Have a thief disarm a treasure trap the party has already found (one turn).

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`), and it needs light: infravision
isn't enough. A member must already have found the trap with
`InspectTreasure`. Only a member with thief
