  dies. Any of the checks can cause a fizzle, and `reason` has the rejection code of the one that failed.

Either way, nothing happened and the memorized copy is gone, as if the spell had been cast. Tell the player
the spell failed and the copy is used up. A spell read from a scroll that fizzles uses up the scroll's spell
the same way, and the caster loses no memorized copy.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: What casting does, one of `EFFECT_KINDS`.

condition.description:
The `Condition` a `condition` effect puts on each target, like `blind` or
`charmed`. `null` on every other kind.

cures_conditions.title: Cures Conditions
cures_conditions.description:
The conditions a `cure` effect lifts. *Cure light wounds*' `cure_paralysis` mode lifts `paralysed`.

Casting releases each effect in the target's `EffectsLedger` that puts one
of these conditions on it. Paralysis, disease, and poison come off however they were put on. Casting also removes
a `paralysed`, `diseased`, or `poisoned` condition in this tuple that has no ledger effect behind it, like one
granted with `grant_condition`. The other conditions come off only with the
ledger effect that granted them.

cures_effect_kinds.title: Cures Effect Kinds
cures_effect_kinds.description:
The kinds of ledger effect a `cure` effect releases, by name.

This is for spells that cancel a named magic rather than a condition. *Light*'s `cancel` mode
releases `"darkness"`.

modifiers.title: Modifiers
modifiers.description:
The bonuses and penalties a `modifiers` effect gives, as `ModifierSpec`
models.

A bonus to armour class or to saves, for example. They belong to the attached effect and end
when it ends.

params.title: Params
params.description:
The numbers and options for this spell that casting reads for `kind`, keyed by name.

They include damage dice, per-level scaling, which creatures are eligible, how long after death
a spell can revive, and area sizes. The keys differ by spell and by kind, so read them for the
mode you have rather than expecting a fixed set.

SpellEffect.title: SpellEffect
SpellEffect.description:
What one castable usage of a spell does to its targets.

Read one from `SpellMode.effect`. Casting runs it for
you. You need this model to describe a spell in an interface, to decide whether a spell is worth
casting on a given target, or to write a spell of your own.

A mode marked `manual` in the built-in catalog has no
effect: its `effect` is `null`, and casting it spends the copy, returns the cast event, and
leaves the outcome to you. Every other mode has an effect.

Constructing one raises `pydantic.ValidationError` when `kind` isn't one of
`EFFECT_KINDS`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the caster's memory is the player's to track.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

caster_id.title: Caster Id
caster_id.description: The entity id of the caster.

reversed.title: Reversed
reversed.description: True when the forgotten copy was the spell's reversed form.

SpellForgottenEvent.title: SpellForgottenEvent
SpellForgottenEvent.description:
A caster forgot a memorized spell, because the caster no longer has room for it.

`forget_excess_memorized` reports one of these for each copy the
caster forgets. That happens when energy drain takes a caster's levels, and the caster has fewer spell slots
than spells in memory. A caster who forgot two copies gets two events.

key.title: Key
key.description:
The mode's name, like `"heal"`. No two modes of the same form have the same key.

Pass it as `mode` to `cast_spell` and
`validate_cast`. A spell with a single usage still has a
mode, like *fire ball*'s `"damage"`. To show a mode to a player, use `display_name`.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
A short label for the mode, like `"Blind a creature"`. Show it where a player chooses one of a form's modes.

The label says what the caster does, as an instruction in sentence case with no closing punctuation:
`"Conjure light"`, `"Cancel darkness"`, and `"Hold a group"`. In the built-in catalog, no two modes of one
form have the same label, in the normal form or in the reverse, so a cast dialog can list a form's
modes by label alone. A built-in label comes from the lead-in that the OSE SRD prints before the
usage, like "Blinding a creature:". A mode whose page prints no lead-in, or a lead-in that names a
situation rather than an action, like *bless*'s "Battle:", has a label written for it from the
page's words, like `"Bless allies in battle"` and the reverse of *light*'s `"Conjure darkness"`.

When you write a mode and leave the label out, or give one that is empty or only spaces, the
mode gets a label made from its key: each run of underscores becomes one space, the spaces at
either end are dropped, and the first letter becomes a capital, so `"darken"` is labelled
`"Darken"` and `"kill_green_slime"` is labelled `"Kill green slime"`. A key made only of
underscores is its own label, so a label is never empty. A spell you wrote for an earlier osrlib
loads this way, with a label on every mode. A spell with a single mode has nothing to choose
between, so the built-in catalog gives that mode the label from its key too, like *fire ball*'s
`"Damage"`. For a form with one mode, show the spell's name and not the mode's label.

The cast event includes the label of the mode that was cast, in
`SpellCastEvent.mode_display_name`.

targeting.description:
Who the mode can affect and how many, as a `TargetingSpec`.

`null` only on a manual mode.

save.description:
The saving throw the targets get, as a `SaveSpec`. `null` when the mode allows
no save.

effect.description:
What the mode does, as a `SpellEffect`.

`null` only on a manual mode.

manual.title: Manual
manual.description: True when casting spends the copy and returns the event, and you decide the outcome.

prose.title: Prose
prose.description:
The SRD text for this usage.

Show it to the player. For a manual mode, it's all the information osrlib has about the result.

In the built-in catalog, the value is line-oriented text, and lines are separated by a single newline. Each
line is one paragraph, list item, heading, table row, or stat line of the page, and no line is empty. The
lines have no inline markup: the page's bold and italic markers and its link targets are removed, and an
asterisk that remains, such as the one in a stat line's `HD 12*`, is part of the data. A run of consecutive
lines that start with `|` is a table. Its first line is the header row, its second is the delimiter row,
such as `| --- | --- |`, and every row of the run has the same number of cells. The text as a whole is not
Markdown, so lay it out line by line rather than passing it to a Markdown renderer. A heading is a line like
any paragraph, such as `"Tornado"` on the *control weather* page, and nothing in the value marks it as a
heading.

A mode that covers one numbered usage has that usage's line, followed by the text the page prints after its
usages that applies to the mode. Both modes of *hold person* and of *hold monster* end with the
**Restrictions** line. The `hd_budget` mode of *sleep* has the rules for creatures of 4 HD or less, and both
of its modes have the **Killing** and **Awakening** rules. The `restore_life` mode of *raise dead* has the
stipulations for restoring life. Every other built-in mode has the whole text of its form, except where the
page describes several usages in one passage, as the next paragraph says. Each line of a spell page's text
is in the prose of at least one mode, in the reverse's prose, or in the template's `intro`.

In the built-in catalog, no two modes of one form have the same prose. Where the page describes several
usages in one passage, like the reverse of *light*, each mode's prose is the part of the passage that covers
that usage, and the whole passage is the form's own prose, such as
`ReversedForm.prose`.

SpellMode.title: SpellMode
SpellMode.description:
One castable usage of a spell: what it targets, what it allows, and what it does.

Many SRD spell pages print more than one numbered usage. *Cure light wounds* heals or lifts
paralysis, and *light* lights an area, blinds a creature, or cancels darkness. Each usage is a
mode, and you choose one by its `key`, which is the `mode` argument of
`cast_spell`. Get a spell's modes from
`SpellTemplate.modes`, or one mode by key from
`SpellTemplate.mode`.

A mode is either automated or manual, and the difference changes what casting does for you. An
automated mode has both `targeting` and `effect`, and osrlib resolves it: it picks the targets,
rolls the saves and the dice, applies the outcome, and attaches any lasting effect. A manual
mode has `manual=True`, and in the built-in catalog it has no targeting and no effect, because
the SRD page gives osrlib nothing to resolve. Casting a manual mode still spends the memorized
copy and returns a `CastResult` with `manual` set and the
mode's `prose`, and you decide what happens. Check `manual` before you
promise a player an outcome.

Constructing one raises `pydantic.ValidationError` when `manual` is False and `targeting` or
`effect` is `null`. It raises the same error for an automated `up_to_n` mode that can't size its
group: its targeting has neither `count` nor `count_dice`, and its effect has no
`missiles_base` param, which *magic missile* uses to count its missiles.

key.title: Key
key.description: The usage's `SpellMode.key`, such as `"blind"`, which is what you send.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
The usage's `SpellMode.display_name`, such as `"Blind a creature"`. Show it where
a player chooses one of a form's usages. For a form with one usage, show the spell's name instead.

manual.title: Manual
manual.description:
True when osrlib doesn't resolve the usage's outcome, as for
`SpellMode.manual`. Casting spends the copy and leaves the result to the referee,
so tell the player that before they cast it.

targeting.description:
How the usage picks who it affects, the `TargetingMode` of its
`SpellMode.targeting`, such as `"single"` or `"area"`. `null` for a usage with no
targeting, which is a manual usage in the built-in catalog, and the session then checks no number of targets.

min_targets.title: Min Targets
min_targets.description:
The fewest ids that `targets` may hold: 1 for a `single` or `hd_budget` usage and for an `up_to_n` usage that
osrlib resolves, and 0 for every other usage, such as a `self` or `area` usage. The session refuses fewer with
`magic.cast.target_count`.

A battle declaration of an `area` usage names a group in
`target_group_id` instead, and so can one of an
`hd_budget` usage, as `target_group` states. A usage whose `one_target_per_missile` is true takes an exact
number of targets instead, which depends on the caster.

max_targets.title: Max Targets
max_targets.description:
The most ids that `targets` may hold: 0 for a `self` usage, 1 for a `single` usage, and `null` for every other
usage, which the session doesn't limit. The session refuses more with `magic.cast.target_count`.

For an `up_to_n` or `hd_budget` usage, send every creature that the player wants the spell to reach, in the order
the player prefers. The spell affects at most the number of creatures that its targeting allows, and the session
picks them from the ones you send. An `up_to_n` usage affects the first ones in your order, up to the fixed
`count` or a roll of
`count_dice` made when the spell is cast, such as *hold person*'s
1d4. An `hd_budget` usage affects the weakest first, until a roll of
`hd_budget_dice`, such as *sleep*'s 2d8 Hit Dice, runs out.
The others are unaffected, and the cast is still accepted. A usage whose `one_target_per_missile` is true takes
an exact number of targets instead.

one_target_per_missile.title: One Target Per Missile
one_target_per_missile.description:
True for a usage that shoots missiles and takes one target for each, such as *magic missile*'s. Name a
creature more than once to send it more missiles. The number of targets has to equal the number of missiles,
which grows with the caster's level, and the session refuses any other number with `magic.cast.target_count`.
Read the caster's number in `MemberView.missile_counts`, or
`scroll_missile_count` for a reading from a scroll.

scroll_missile_count.title: Scroll Missile Count
scroll_missile_count.description:
How many targets a reading of the spell from a scroll takes, for a usage whose `one_target_per_missile` is
true. A scroll's spell resolves at the lowest level that could cast it, whatever the reader's level, so every
reader sends this many. `null` for every other usage, and for a spell on a list that no built-in class casts
from.

accepts_cells.title: Accepts Cells
accepts_cells.description:
Whether a target may be a cell reference in the `cell:{dungeon}:{level}:{x},{y}` form that
`cell_ref` builds, for a usage that affects a place, such as *light*'s
`illuminate` or *web*. A usage that works only on creatures, such as one that allows a saving throw or deals
damage, has `false`, and the session refuses a cell reference for it with `magic.cast.target_must_be_creature`.

target_group.title: Target Group
target_group.description:
Whether a battle `cast` declaration of the usage names a group in
`target_group_id`.

- `required`: an `area` usage, such as *fire ball*'s. The session takes the group's living members that the
  area covers, ignores `targets`, and refuses a declaration with no group or a group that has fled with
  `battle.declaration.unknown_group`.
- `optional`: an `hd_budget` usage, such as *sleep*'s. A declaration with a group and no `targets` takes the
  group's living members, and one with `targets` takes those.
- `none`: every other usage, whose declaration names its targets in `targets`.

Outside a battle, `CastSpell` names targets alone, because the party can act
on no monster there.

SpellModeView.title: SpellModeView
SpellModeView.description:
One usage of a spell's form, with what a cast dialog needs to label it and to collect its targets.

You get these from `PlayerView.spell_modes` and
`PlayerView.reversed_spell_modes`, one per
`SpellMode` of the form, in the order the form lists them. Send `key` as
`CastSpell.mode`, as a battle `cast` declaration's
`spell_mode`, or as
`UseItem.mode` for a scroll.

The target fields describe the checks that the session makes of a cast's targets for this usage, the same checks
whichever command casts it: how many targets it takes, whether a cell reference may be one, and whether a battle
declaration names a group. A cast that passes them can still be refused for something the targets are, such as
`magic.cast.unknown_target` for an id that names nobody the party can act on, or for the range, such as
`magic.cast.out_of_range`. The range belongs to the whole form, in
`PlayerView.spell_ranges` and
`PlayerView.reversed_spell_ranges`.

Every field comes from the session's spell catalog alone, so a usage reads the same in every view of a session.

id.title: Id
id.description:
Spell identifier, such as `"magic_missile"`. Pass to `GET /v1/rules/spells/{spell_id}` or in
`starting_spell_ids` on `POST /v1/characters`.

name.title: Name
name.description: Display name of the spell, such as `"Magic Missile"`.

spell_list.title: Spell List
spell_list.description:
Spell list identifier (`"cleric"` or `"magic_user"`). Clerics cast from `"cleric"`, while
magic-users and elves cast from `"magic_user"`.

range.title: Range
range.description: Printed range line, such as `"150'"` or `"The caster"`.

duration.title: Duration
duration.description: Printed duration line, such as `"1 turn"` or `"Instant"`.

SpellSummary.title: SpellSummary
SpellSummary.description: Summary of a spell from osrlib's `SpellTemplate`.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The id you look the spell up by, made from its name in lowercase with underscores, like `"fire_ball"`.

A few spells appear in the SRD as a cleric page and a magic-user page with different rules.
Each such pair is two entries: the cleric one has the suffix `_c` and the magic-user one `_mu`,
like `"light_c"` and `"light_mu"`. For the built-in ids, iterate
`load_spells().spells` or see [the spell id
index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/spells/).

name.title: Name
name.description: The spell's printed name, like `"Cure Light Wounds"`. Show this, not the id.

spell_list.title: Spell List
spell_list.description:
Which class's spell list the spell belongs to, in lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

The built-in catalog has `"cleric"` and `"magic_user"`. A spell you write can use another list,
for a class you write. It must match the
`CasterProfile.spell_list` of any caster who
memorizes or learns the spell.

level.title: Level
level.description:
The spell's level, 1 to 6.

A caster's slots are counted by spell level, not by the caster's level.

duration.title: Duration
duration.description: The duration line as printed. Show this to a player.

duration_spec.description:
The structured form of `duration`, as a `DurationSpec`.

Casting reads it to set how long an attached effect lasts.

range.title: Range
range.description: The range line as printed. Show this to a player.

range_spec.description:
The structured form of `range`, as a `RangeSpec`.

It's the normal form's range. A reverse can state a range of its own, in
`ReversedForm.range_spec`, so read the range of a
cast from `range_spec_for`.

reversed_form.description:
The spell's reverse, as a `ReversedForm`.

`null` when the spell doesn't reverse.

modes.title: Modes
modes.description:
One `SpellMode` per numbered usage on the page, in the page's order.

There's at least one. Their keys are the values casting accepts as its `mode` argument.

intro.title: Intro
intro.description:
The page's opening text, above the numbered usages.

On a page with several usages, it's the lead-in, like `"This spell has two usages:"`. On a
page with one usage, it's the opening of the spell's description, and that mode's `prose` is
the full text. In the built-in catalog, it's the first line of the page's text, in the format of
`SpellMode.prose`: one line with no inline markup, never a
table row. It's not Markdown.

conjured_monsters.title: Conjured Monsters
conjured_monsters.description:
Monster stat blocks printed on the spell's page rather than in the monster catalog.

The *sticks to snakes* page, for example, prints the snake's stat block. Spawn them with
`spawn_monster` when you resolve the spell. Casting
doesn't spawn them.

conjured_monster_ids.title: Conjured Monster Ids
conjured_monster_ids.description:
Ids of monsters the spell summons that are in the monster catalog.

Look them up with `load_monsters().get(monster_id)`. *Conjure
elemental* lists its four elementals this way. Casting doesn't spawn them.

overrides_applied.title: Overrides Applied
overrides_applied.description:
The field paths that a correction changed when this template was compiled from the SRD page.

Empty when the page compiled without corrections. It lists where the data departs from the
SRD, for anyone checking it, and osrlib never reads it during play.

SpellTemplate.title: SpellTemplate
SpellTemplate.description:
One spell, compiled from its SRD page: the data that casting it uses.

Get one by id from `SpellCatalog.get`, or a class's
whole list from `SpellCatalog.by_list`. The catalog
comes from `load_spells`. Pass the template to
`validate_cast`,
`cast_spell`, or
`cast_from_scroll`, and read its `modes` for the mode
keys those calls accept.

A template is frozen and shared, and it doesn't change during play. What changes during play are the
`MemorizedSpell` copies a caster has prepared and the
effects a cast leaves on the ledger. Both refer to the template by id.

Constructing one raises `pydantic.ValidationError` when two modes of the same form have the
same key.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the player may see what their caster has memorized.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

caster_id.title: Caster Id
caster_id.description: The entity id of the caster.

prepared.title: Prepared
prepared.description:
Every copy now in the caster's memory, as `PreparedSpell` entries. A
spell prepared twice appears twice.

SpellsMemorizedEvent.title: SpellsMemorizedEvent
SpellsMemorizedEvent.description:
A caster has finished preparing spells for the day.

`memorize_spells` reports one of these each time it prepares a caster's
spells. Preparing replaces everything the caster had in memory, so `prepared` lists all of the caster's
memory now, not only what was added.

visibility.description: Player visibility: behavior is visible even when the roll behind it isn't.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `stance_changed`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

stance.title: Stance
stance.description:
How the monsters are acting now, as a
`ReactionResult` value: `"attacks"`, `"hostile"`,
`"uncertain"`, `"indifferent"`, or `"friendly"`. An attacking stance opens battle in the same
result.

StanceChangedEvent.title: StanceChangedEvent
StanceChangedEvent.description:
The monsters' attitude toward the party changed.

Emitted when an encounter opens, with the first stance. Also emitted when
`Parley` changes the monsters' mood, when an
uncertain stance is rolled again on a later encounter round and changes, and when
undead that `TurnUndead` failed to turn attack.

The 2d6 reaction roll behind a stance is a kernel event at referee visibility. An
encounter whose stance the adventure's author fixed has no roll. What reaches the
party is how the creatures are acting.

contents.title: Contents
contents.description:
What the room-contents d6 rolled: `"empty"`, `"monster"`, `"special"`, or `"trap"`. A special
is a magical or unusual feature, and a trap is a room trap. B/X describes both with example lists
for the referee, so neither comes with a model.

treasure_present.title: Treasure Present
treasure_present.description:
Whether the treasure d6 rolled within the row's chance of treasure. It's always `false` when
the row gives no chance, as for a special room, and then `stock_area` rolls no die. On a
monster room it's the same value as the encounter's `hoard` flag.

encounter.description:
The monsters in the room, on a monster room, and `null` otherwise. Each line has a fixed count
that is already rolled. The encounter's `hoard` is the same as `treasure_present`. It's also
`null` on a monster room whose encounter roll produced an NPC party.

npc_party.description:
The NPC party the encounter roll produced, or `null`. It's set only on a monster room, and
never together with `encounter`. See `StockedNpcParty`.

treasure.description:
Unguarded treasure for an empty or trap room that rolled some, and `null` otherwise. It's
always the unguarded form, never treasure type letters, because a treasure type is a monster's
hoard and no monster lives here. The session rolls the treasure the first time the party
enters the area.

StockedArea.title: StockedArea
StockedArea.description:
The content the stocking rolls produced for one keyed room, for you to place on an area.

`stock_area` returns one. Read `contents` to find out what
kind of room you rolled, then copy the payload that came with it onto the
`AreaSpec` you're building for that room.

There is at most one payload:

- `encounter` on a monster room.
- `npc_party` on a monster room whose encounter roll produced an NPC party.
- `treasure` on an empty or trap room that rolled treasure.

A monster room's treasure is its encounter's `hoard` flag, so `treasure` is always `null` on a
monster room. A trap or a special room has no payload, because B/X leaves those to the referee.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
Which NPC party table the encounter row selected: `"basic"` for a party of low-level
adventurers, or `"expert"` for a higher-level one.

count.title: Count
count.description: How many adventurers are in the party, from the row's count. A count below 1 counts as 1.

StockedNpcParty.title: StockedNpcParty
StockedNpcParty.description:
The kind and size of NPC party that a monster room's encounter roll produced.

An NPC party is a band of adventurers the referee runs. No content model describes one, because
the session builds the party during play from character classes and gear, not from monster
templates and treasure letters. So `stock_area` has no model
to hand back. It reports the kind and the count the roll gave instead.

You get one in `StockedArea.npc_party`, only on a
room whose `contents` is `"monster"`. To put a party in play, execute
`SpawnNpcParty` with this `kind` as its `party_kind`, from
your own code or as a trigger's consequence.

roll_min.title: Roll Min
roll_min.description: The lowest d6 result in this row.

roll_max.title: Roll Max
roll_max.description: The highest d6 result in this row.

contents.title: Contents
contents.description: What is in the room: `"empty"`, `"monster"`, `"special"`, or `"trap"`.

treasure_chance_in_six.title: Treasure Chance In Six
treasure_chance_in_six.description:
How many faces of a d6 mean treasure as well, for example 3 for a 3-in-6 chance. 0 where the table prints no
chance, and no die is rolled then.

StockingRow.title: StockingRow
StockingRow.description:
One row of the room stocking table, giving what is in a room and how likely treasure is with it.

`roll_room_contents` rolls the d6, selects the
row, and rolls its treasure chance, and returns the row in
`RoomContentsResult.row`. Read `contents` to
decide what to place: a monster, a trap, something special, or nothing.

rows.title: Rows
rows.description: The rows, covering the whole d6. See `StockingRow`.

StockingTable.title: StockingTable
StockingTable.description:
The *Random Dungeon Room Contents* table, which lists what to put in a room when you stock a dungeon.

Rolling it takes two steps, so call
`roll_room_contents` unless you're rolling by
hand. It rolls the contents, then the treasure chance that goes with them, and returns
both.

You use this table to fill a dungeon level before anyone explores it. The session never rolls on it during play.

used_bytes.title: Used Bytes
used_bytes.description:
Bytes currently stored for your client. Deleting sessions, saves, adventures, or characters
reduces this count.

max_bytes.title: Max Bytes
max_bytes.description:
Maximum bytes the server stores for one client (`BXAPI_MAX_CLIENT_BYTES`, 1,073,741,824 by
default), or `null` when storage quotas are disabled. When `used_bytes` reaches `max_bytes`,
requests that store new documents fail with 507 `storage_full`.

Storage.title: Storage
Storage.description:
Stored document byte usage and quota for your client application.

Counts the stored JSON bytes of your client's ability rolls, characters, adventures, sessions,
saves, and 24-hour idempotency replay responses.

id.title: Id
id.description:
Character identifier (`chr_` followed by 22 characters). Pass in `character_ids` to
`POST /v1/sessions`.

name.title: Name
name.description: Character name.

level.title: Level
level.description: Character experience level (1 for newly created characters, or higher when imported).

created_at.title: Created At
created_at.description:
UTC timestamp when the server stored the character, in RFC 3339 format such as
`"2026-11-20T22:01:05Z"`.

character.description: Full osrlib `Character` model: ability scores, hit points, inventory, spells, and conditions.

derived.description: Combat, saving throw, modifier, and language values computed by osrlib from `character`.

StoredCharacter.title: StoredCharacter
StoredCharacter.description: Stored character record with osrlib's `Character` model and computed stats.

min_score.title: Min Score
min_score.description: The lowest score this row covers.

max_score.title: Max Score
max_score.description: The highest score this row covers. Equal to `min_score` on a one-score row.

melee.title: Melee
melee.description: What to add to a melee attack roll and to melee damage. Negative at a low score.

open_doors.title: Open Doors
open_doors.description:
The chance in 6 of forcing a stuck door open.

Pass it to `open_doors_check`, which rolls
the die against it.

StrengthRow.title: StrengthRow
StrengthRow.description:
One row of the strength table: a band of scores, with its melee modifier and open-doors chance.

Read the rows from `AbilityTables.strength` to draw
the table. To look up one score, call
`melee_modifier` or
`open_doors_chance` instead.

light_burning_rounds.title: Light Burning Rounds
light_burning_rounds.description:
The rounds left on the timed light that will burn longest, among the lights burning now, and 0 when no
timed light burns.

Lights burn at the same time, so this is the longest time left, not a sum: two torches burning at once, with 40
and 300 rounds left, give 300. It counts every light effect on a living member, which is a lit torch or lantern,
the *light* spell, and any effect whose kind is in
`LIGHT_EFFECT_KINDS`. Each light's own time left is its entry's
`remaining_rounds` in `PlayerView.effects`. A light from a potion has
no `remaining_rounds` there, because the referee keeps a potion's duration secret, so it doesn't count here or
in `light_permanent`.

A *darkness* effect puts the party's light out while it lasts without ending the lights, so it doesn't change
this number. To learn whether the party has light right now, look for a `darkness` or `continual_darkness`
effect in `effects`.

light_permanent.title: Light Permanent
light_permanent.description:
Whether a light with no duration is burning on a living member, such as *continual light* or a sword that
sheds light. Such a light adds nothing to `light_burning_rounds`, and while it burns the party doesn't run out
of light.

light_reserve_rounds.title: Light Reserve Rounds
light_reserve_rounds.description:
How many rounds of light the party carries and hasn't lit yet.

It's the living members' unlit torches times the rounds one torch burns, plus their oil flasks times the
rounds one flask burns in a lantern. A lit torch is used up when it's lit, so `torches` counts only unlit ones
and nothing is counted twice. Oil counts only when a living member carries a lantern, and then every living
member's flasks count, because members can pass items to each other. So the reserve can include oil that stays
unusable until a flask or the lantern changes hands. Read `light_reserve_usable` to learn whether the
party holds what it needs to light something.

light_reserve_usable.title: Light Reserve Usable
light_reserve_usable.description:
Whether the party has what `LightSource` needs to light a carried torch
or lantern now.

It's true when a living member who can act carries a torch, or carries a lantern and an oil flask, and either
carries a tinder box or stands in a party where a living member already has a flame burning. `LightSource`
uses the same carrying check. So while the session is in a mode that accepts
`LightSource`, `"town"` or `"exploring"`, some `LightSource` that names a torch or a lantern is accepted when
this is true, and every one is refused when it's false. The flag doesn't depend on the mode. In an encounter or
a battle, the session refuses `LightSource` with `session.command.wrong_mode` whatever this flag says, so read
`PlayerView.mode` to learn whether the party can light anything this
moment. When the reserve isn't zero and this is false, the likely cause is that no member who carries a torch
or a lantern has a tinder box, that the oil and the lantern are in different packs, or that the carriers can't
act.

An accepted command strikes the tinder box when the party has no flame, and the strike can fail, so an
accepted command doesn't always light the source. Setting fire to a flask dropped on the
floor doesn't count, because a pool of burning oil on the floor isn't a light that the party carries.

torches.title: Torches
torches.description: The unlit torches the living members carry.

oil_flasks.title: Oil Flasks
oil_flasks.description: The oil flasks the living members carry.

lanterns.title: Lanterns
lanterns.description: The lanterns the living members carry, lit or not.

rations.title: Rations
rations.description: The rations the living members carry, standard and iron together.

rations_standard.title: Rations Standard
rations_standard.description: The standard rations the living members carry.

rations_iron.title: Rations Iron
rations_iron.description: The iron rations the living members carry.

food_days.title: Food Days
food_days.description:
How many days the party eats before the first living member goes short, as the packs are now.

Each member eats from their own pack, one ration a day, so it's the fewest rations any living member carries.
The session feeds every living member at the start of each new day. The party eats for `food_days` days, and
at the feeding after those, the members in `food_short_first_ids` go short. In town nobody goes short,
because a member with no rations is fed anyway, but this is still the number of days a member's own pack
lasts. It's 0 when every member is dead.

food_days_shared.title: Food Days Shared
food_days_shared.description:
How many days the party could eat if its rations were shared out evenly: the living members' rations
divided by the number of living members, rounded down. When it's larger than `food_days`, passing rations
between members with `GiveItems` feeds the party longer. It's 0 when every
member is dead.

food_short_first_ids.title: Food Short First Ids
food_short_first_ids.description:
The ids of the living members who carry the fewest rations, the count that sets `food_days`, in marching
order. They go short first. It's empty when every member is dead.

SuppliesView.title: SuppliesView
SuppliesView.description:
How long the party's light and food will last, counted from what the living members carry.

You get this from `PlayerView.supplies`. osrlib computes each number
by the rules the session applies, so you can show "light left" and "food left" without knowing the burn time of
a torch or how the party eats. Every time is in rounds, as
`MemberEffectView.remaining_rounds` is, and a turn is
`ROUNDS_PER_TURN` rounds.

Only the items that living members carry count, because a dead member's torch or ration is of use only after a
living member takes it.
Items in a dropped pile don't count either. In town the summary reports the same numbers as in a dungeon, and
you decide from `PlayerView.location` whether to show them. When
every member is dead, every count is 0, every flag is false, and `food_short_first_ids` is empty.

visibility.description:
Referee visibility: the die is the referee's, and the result reaches the players through the
encounter event.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `surprise_rolled`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

threshold.title: Threshold
threshold.description:
The number on a d6 at or under which that side is surprised. It's 2, except for a party
without light that has a living member without infravision, where it's 3.

roll.title: Roll
roll.description: The d6 that came up, or `null` when this side never had to roll.

SurpriseRolledEvent.title: SurpriseRolledEvent
SurpriseRolledEvent.description:
One side's surprise die, rolled in secret.

Emitted twice when an encounter opens, once for each side, before
`EncounterStartedEvent` reports the
outcomes to the players.

A side that can't be surprised doesn't roll, and its event has `roll` set to `null`.
The party doesn't roll when it already heard the monsters through the door. The
monsters don't roll when they know the party is coming, when they can see its light,
or when they're wandering monsters, which know the dungeon. An NPC party met on a
wandering check still rolls.

intelligence.title: Intelligence
intelligence.description: The sword's intelligence, 7 to 12. It sets how the sword communicates and how many powers it has.

ego.title: Ego
ego.description:
The sword's ego, 1 to 12, or 12 for a sword of special purpose. In a contest of wills, the sword's total starts
from its intelligence plus its ego.

communication.title: Communication
communication.description: How it makes itself understood: `"empathy"` or `"speech"`.

reading.title: Reading
reading.description: True when the sword can read.

alignment.title: Alignment
alignment.description:
The sword's alignment, as a lowercase name. A bearer of a different alignment takes damage for holding it, which
the rules leave to the referee to apply.

languages.title: Languages
languages.description: How many languages a speaking sword knows. 0 for an empathic sword.

sensory_powers.title: Sensory Powers
sensory_powers.description:
The ids of its sensory powers, the ones that detect things. Look them up with
`SentientSwordTables.power`.

extraordinary_powers.title: Extraordinary Powers
extraordinary_powers.description: The ids of its extraordinary powers, the ones that do things. Look them up the same way.

special_purpose.title: Special Purpose
special_purpose.description:
What the sword was made to do, for example `"chaotic_creatures"`, or `null` for a sword with no special
purpose.

SwordSentience.title: SwordSentience
SwordSentience.description:
A sentient sword's mind, alignment, and powers.

`instantiate_magic_item` rolls it once when it creates the
sword, and it doesn't change after that. It's the `sentience` field of the sword's
`MagicItemInstance`. Most swords have none, and
the field is `null` for those. Pass the sword to
`sword_control_check` to find out whether it
takes charge of its wielder.

TableSet.title: TableSet
TableSet.description:
One set of printed tables, as osrlib's model for the table name.

`abilities` is osrlib's `AbilityTables`, `combat` is `CombatTables`, `encounters` is
`EncounterTables`, and `treasure` is `TreasureTables`. The JSON is osrlib's model, unchanged.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"take_treasure"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

feature_id.title: Feature Id
feature_id.description:
What to empty: a `feature:` handle from
`MapFeatureView.id` in the current player view, or the
cache's raw id, an authored `FeatureSpec.id` or the id
of a cache the engine generated. Both forms stay supported. A player client sends the handle,
because the player view lists only handles. Both forms resolve against the same caches, the
available ones the party can reach where it stands, so a raw id reaches and reveals
nothing that a handle doesn't. A cache anywhere else gets the same
`exploration.feature.unknown` rejection as an id that no cache has. The literal `"pile"` means
the goods dropped on the party's cell, which
`PlayerView.piles` lists by cell reference. The session
refuses a cache that's already emptied with `exploration.feature.emptied`.

recipient_id.title: Recipient Id
recipient_id.description:
One member to take all the goods, by
`MemberView.id`, or `null` to spread it across the
living members. The named member fills their pack up to their maximum load, and the rest
stays on the cell. Name a recipient to keep a specific item with a specific member. The
named member is also the one who reaches into the cache, so a trap that hasn't been
removed springs on them. If that trap leaves them unable to act, the goods spread across
the living members instead.

TakeTreasure.title: TakeTreasure
TakeTreasure.description:
Empty a treasure cache or a pile of dropped goods into the party's packs (one turn).

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`). `feature_id` is the id
of an authored cache or a cache the engine generated, or the literal `"pile"` for goods
dropped on the party's cell.

By default the goods spread across the living members:

- Each item goes to a member whose class can use it, so the fighter takes the plate mail
  and the magic-user takes the arcane scroll.
- Gems and jewellery divide by worth.
- Coins divide evenly, one denomination at a time.

A member who carries more than their maximum load can't move, and then the party can't
move either. So the session never gives a member more than their maximum load. The maximum
load is a weight of 1,600 coins. Under detailed encumbrance, a member who wears gauntlets of
ogre power can carry 2,600. The party moves at its slowest member's rate, so a heavy load on
one member slows everyone.

Name `recipient_id` to have one member take all the goods instead, up to their maximum
load. Whatever the carriers can't carry stays in the pile on the cell. The party can
lighten its load and come back for it. To change who carries what afterwards, use
`GiveItems`.

Under the immediate XP timing, the treasure's XP divides evenly among the living
members, however the goods end up split, as the OSE SRD's rule for treasure XP says.

The named recipient, or the first living member in marching order when nobody is named,
reaches into the cache. A cache whose trap hasn't been removed gets its chance to spring
on that member first.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `session.command.no_living_members` - nobody is left alive to carry anything.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `recipient_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the recipient can't act.
- `exploration.feature.unknown` - `feature_id` is malformed, stale, or
  ambiguous, no available cache by that id is on this cell, or there's no
  pile on it.
- `exploration.feature.emptied` - the cache has already been emptied.

**Events:**

When the cache has a trap that hasn't been removed or sprung, its spring check comes
first: a `DetectionRolledEvent`, a
`TrapEvent`, and the trap's resolution
when it springs. Then comes one
`ItemAcquiredEvent` for each member
who took something, in marching order, listing their goods and coin value with
`origin` `"treasure"`. An
`ItemsLeftBehindEvent` follows
when the party couldn't carry it all. Under the immediate XP timing, an
`XpAwardedEvent` follows for each living member.
One turn passes. A trap that kills the whole party leaves the cache full, and only
the turn passes.

TargetingMode.title: TargetingMode
TargetingMode.description:
The ways `select_targets` chooses targets from a list of candidates.

Pass one to `select_targets` with the candidates it chooses from. A spell that targets
creatures targets with one of these modes, and so does a breath weapon. `osrlib.core`
doesn't work out who is in range, so you supply the candidates. Inside a session,
`osrlib.crawl.battle` supplies them from the distances it
tracks.

The values appear in events and stay fixed within a `schema_version`, the version stamp
of the saved format.

mode.description:
Which targeting mode the spell's mode uses, and so how many targets you pass.

- `self`: no targets. The spell affects the caster.
- `single`: exactly one target.
- `up_to_n`: a group, sized by `count` or `count_dice`. *Magic missile* is the exception: it
  takes exactly one target per missile, and the same target can appear more than once.
- `hd_budget`: as many creatures as a rolled pool of Hit Dice pays for.
- `area`: every candidate you pass, which should be the creatures inside the area.
- `gaze`: every candidate you pass, for a gaze that reaches everyone engaged with the gazer.

count.title: Count
count.description: The fixed size of an `up_to_n` group, when the page prints a number rather than dice. At least 1.

count_dice.title: Count Dice
count_dice.description:
The dice rolled when the spell is cast to size an `up_to_n` group, on the magic stream.

*Hold person*'s group mode is `"1d4"` and *charm monster*'s is `"3d6"`. In the `up_to_n` mode, the
lowest total the dice can roll is at least 1.

hd_budget_dice.title: Hd Budget Dice
hd_budget_dice.description:
The dice rolled to size an `hd_budget` pool, like `"2d8"` for *sleep*. The `hd_budget` mode needs them, and the
lowest total they can roll is at least 1.

The spell affects creatures in order of Hit Dice, fewest first, until the pool can't pay for
the next one. The rest of the pool is lost rather than spent on anyone else.

hd_cap.title: Hd Cap
hd_cap.description:
The most Hit Dice a creature may have and still be eligible.

*Sleep*'s `hd_budget` mode sets 4, and *charm monster*'s group mode sets 3.

hd_min.title: Hd Min
hd_min.description:
The fewest Hit Dice a creature must have to be eligible.

*Charm monster*'s single-target mode sets 4, for the page's "more than 3 Hit Dice".

shape.title: Shape
shape.description: The name of the area an `area` mode covers, like `"sphere"`. `null` on every other mode.

dimensions.title: Dimensions
dimensions.description:
The area's measurements in feet, keyed by name. *Fire ball*'s sphere is `{"radius_feet": 20}`.

osrlib doesn't work out which creatures are inside the area. You decide who is caught and pass
them as candidates.

creatures_only.title: Creatures Only
creatures_only.description:
True when every target has to be a creature, not a location string.

`validate_cast` refuses a location string as a target of a mode that sets
it, with `magic.cast.target_must_be_creature`. Set it on a mode whose effect does something only on a creature,
when neither the mode's save nor its effect already requires a creature. An effect with no condition and no
modifiers, like *light*'s, would otherwise take a location. In the built-in catalog, *fly*, *infravision*, *water
breathing*, and *haste* set it, because their pages name a creature as the subject. `false`, the default, leaves
the decision to the mode's save and effect.

TargetingSpec.title: TargetingSpec
TargetingSpec.description:
Who one castable usage of a spell can hit, and how many of them.

Read one from `SpellMode.targeting` to find out how
many targets to collect before you call `cast_spell`. `mode` is
the `TargetingMode` that
`select_targets` also uses, and the other fields are the
numbers that size and limit it for this spell.

The targets you pass to casting are candidates, not the final list. Casting drops the ones the
mode can't affect and then applies `mode` to the rest, so an ineligible creature in the list
uses up no Hit Dice and no place in a group. An ineligible target is therefore an outcome of the
cast rather than a reason to refuse it. If no candidate is eligible, casting returns a
`CastResult` with `no_effect` set, and the memorized copy is
still spent.

Constructing one raises `pydantic.ValidationError` when `count_dice` or `hd_budget_dice` isn't
a valid dice expression, and when the targeting could pick nobody:

- `count` is below 1.
- The mode is `up_to_n`, and `count_dice` can roll a total below 1.
- The mode is `hd_budget`, and `hd_budget_dice` is `null` or can roll a total below 1.

`up_to_n` targeting with neither `count` nor `count_dice` builds, because *magic missile*'s
targeting has neither: the caster's level sets how many missiles it shoots.
`SpellMode` refuses that targeting in an automated mode whose
effect has no `missiles_base` param.

visibility.description:
Referee visibility: this is a record for the referee. What happens to the targets comes as separate
events.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

mode.title: Mode
mode.description:
How the targets were chosen, as a `TargetingMode` value: `self`,
`single`, `up_to_n`, `hd_budget`, `area`, or `gaze`.

target_ids.title: Target Ids
target_ids.description: The entity ids of the selected creatures, in the order they were chosen.

TargetsSelectedEvent.title: TargetsSelectedEvent
TargetsSelectedEvent.description:
Which of the candidates a spell reached.

`select_targets` reports this before the spell's other events, so a log
shows which creatures a spell like *sleep* or *hold person* reached, not only the creatures it was aimed
at.

level.title: Level
level.description: The thief level this row describes.

climb_sheer_surfaces.title: Climb Sheer Surfaces
climb_sheer_surfaces.description: The percent chance to climb a sheer surface. It's 87 at first level.

find_remove_treasure_traps.title: Find Remove Treasure Traps
find_remove_treasure_traps.description:
The percent chance to find or remove a trap on a treasure container, like a chest.

Spotting a trap in a room is a different check, made with
`detection_chance`.

hear_noise.title: Hear Noise
hear_noise.description: The chance in 6 of hearing noise through a door, rolled on 1d6.

hide_in_shadows.title: Hide In Shadows
hide_in_shadows.description: The percent chance to stay unseen while keeping still in shadow.

move_silently.title: Move Silently
move_silently.description: The percent chance to move without being heard.

open_locks.title: Open Locks
open_locks.description:
The percent chance to pick a lock. In a session, the engine rejects a
`PickLock` command unless the thief carries thieves' tools.

pick_pockets.title: Pick Pockets
pick_pockets.description: The percent chance to steal something a person is carrying.

ThiefSkillRow.title: ThiefSkillRow
ThiefSkillRow.description:
A thief's skill chances at one level.

Read the row for a thief's level from
`ClassDefinition.thief_skills`, or let
`thief_skill_check` find it and roll for you. Frozen.

Every skill except `hear_noise` is a percentage, rolled on d%, and succeeds on a roll equal to
or under the chance. `hear_noise` is a chance in 6, rolled on 1d6, so osrlib stores the SRD's
"1-2" as 2. `pick_pockets` is above 100 at high levels. `thief_skill_check` lowers the chance
to 99, so a theft can always fail.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: the players see what the time passing does, not the command that passed it.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `time_advanced`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

n.title: N
n.description: How many units were asked for.

unit.title: Unit
unit.description:
Which unit, as a lowercase `TimeUnit` value: `"round"`,
`"turn"`, or `"day"`.

rounds_total.title: Rounds Total
rounds_total.description:
Where the clock now stands, in rounds since the session began. It's the same number as
`GameSession.clock.rounds`.

TimeAdvancedEvent.title: TimeAdvancedEvent
TimeAdvancedEvent.description:
The referee moved the clock.

Emitted by `AdvanceTime`, after the events of the
time that passed. Effects run out, lights burn out, and the session uses up provisions
for each day crossed, and those events arrive in the same result. No wandering-monster
check and no fatigue check runs: a referee moving the clock decides what happens.

TimeUnit.title: TimeUnit
TimeUnit.description:
The unit an amount of game time is counted in.

Pass one to `advance` to say what your number
means, and read one off a `BoundaryCrossing` to
see which kind of boundary you crossed. The rounds each unit is worth are
`ROUNDS_PER_TURN` and
`ROUNDS_PER_DAY`.

pattern_type.title: Pattern Type
pattern_type.description:
The discriminator value, `town_entered`. It appears in the document, and you
never set it yourself.

TownEnteredPattern.title: TownEnteredPattern
TownEnteredPattern.description:
A pattern that matches the party arriving in the adventure's town, however it got there.

An adventure has one town, so the pattern has no fields. It matches when the party
travels back to town and when a referee command places the party there. Pair it with a
`HasItemCondition` for an errand that is done only
when the party comes home carrying an item.

name.title: Name
name.description: Town display name.

description.title: Description
description.description: Player-facing town description written by the adventure's author, or `""` when none is set.

TownInfo.title: TownInfo
TownInfo.description: Player-visible summary of an adventure's base town.

name.title: Name
name.description: The town's name, to show the player, like `"Threshold"`.

description.title: Description
description.description: Text to show the player while the party is in town.

services.title: Services
services.description:
The services the town offers, as free-form strings like `("temple", "smith")`. osrlib doesn't
read them: the shop and temple commands work in any town. The session passes them to the player view as
`PlayerView.town_services`, so you can list them on
a town screen.

travel_turns.title: Travel Turns
travel_turns.description:
How long the trip from town to each dungeon's entrance takes, in exploration turns, keyed by
dungeon id. `EnterDungeon` and
`TravelToTown` each advance the clock by this many turns,
so on the way to a distant dungeon and back, light sources burn down and the session uses up the
party's rations at each day boundary. A trip to a dungeon with no entry here, or with 0, takes no
time. Each value is 0 or more, and the model raises `ValueError` when you construct it with a
negative one. Every key has to be the id of a dungeon in this adventure, and
`validate_adventure` reports one that isn't.

You pass a dict, and the town stores a read-only `FrozenMap` of
it, as it does for `healing_prices`, because every session started from the adventure reads the
same town.

healing_prices.title: Healing Prices
healing_prices.description:
What this town's temple charges for a service, in gold pieces, keyed by the service's name, like
`{"raise_dead": 1000}`. `PurchaseHealing` charges this
price, and a service you don't list costs the standard price from
`HEALING_SERVICES`. Each price is 0 or more, and a
price of 0 makes the service free. The model raises `ValueError` when you construct it with a
negative price or with a key that isn't a `HealingService`.

The prices are part of the adventure, so a save contains them and a replayed purchase charges
what it charged the first time. The session passes what the town charges for every service to
the player view as
`PlayerView.town_healing_prices`.

TownSpec.title: TownSpec
TownSpec.description:
The base town: where the party is safe, buys gear, and comes back to.

Every adventure has exactly one town, and a session starts there. The town is not a map: it has
no grid, no rooms, and nothing to explore. It is where the rules that need a safe place apply.
In town the party can rest, buy equipment, sell treasure, and pay a temple for healing. Under
the default ruleset, the party earns the experience for a delve only once it is back in town.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
What the party sees and uses: `"stairs_up"`, `"stairs_down"`, `"trapdoor"`, `"chute"`, or
`"passage"`. The first four kinds all work the same way: the party takes them with
`UseStairs`, the destination fields set where it goes, and the
session reports the kind on the arrival event, so you can describe it. The party crosses a
`"passage"` by walking across its `side` instead.

position.title: Position
position.description:
The cell on this level where the transition stands. The party has to stand here to use it
with `UseStairs` or to cross it as a passage. In a trap's
`TrapEffect.transition`, the session doesn't read
it, because the trap moves the party from the cell where it springs.

side.description:
The side of `position` that a passage stands on, and `null` for every other kind. A
`MoveParty` from `position` in this direction crosses the
passage. A passage without a side raises `ValueError` when you construct it, and so does a
transition of any other kind with one.

to_dungeon_id.title: To Dungeon Id
to_dungeon_id.description:
The id of the dungeon the party arrives in. It is usually the dungeon this level is in. Set
it to another dungeon of the adventure to join the two.

to_level_number.title: To Level Number
to_level_number.description: The number of the level the party arrives on, 1 or more.

to_position.title: To Position
to_position.description: The cell the party arrives at, on the destination level's grid.

to_facing.description: The direction the party faces on arrival. Draw the party's view facing this way.

requires.description:
A gate on taking the transition, or `null` for one with no gate.

`UseStairs`, or `MoveParty`
for a passage, checks the gate after the command's other checks and before the party moves. A
gate that takes an item takes it then, as the party crosses. When the party changes level or
dungeon, the gate's `success` text goes on the arrival's
`LocationEnteredEvent`. For a transition to another
cell of the same level, it goes on the `PartyMovedEvent`
for the landing cell.

A transition in a `TrapEffect` can't have a gate, because a
trap moves the party by force and the party attempts nothing. `TrapEffect` raises `ValueError`
for one that does.

TransitionSpec.title: TransitionSpec
TransitionSpec.description:
A way from one cell to another: stairs, a trapdoor, a chute, or a passage.

Transitions belong to a level, in
`LevelSpec.transitions`, not to an area. They join
the levels of a dungeon, and they join two dungeons when one points at the other's id. Each
transition stands on a cell and moves the party to `to_position`, facing `to_facing`.
`validate_adventure` checks that the cell it stands on
and the cell it leads to are both on their levels' grids.

The party takes stairs, a trapdoor, or a chute with
`UseStairs`. The party walks through a passage instead. A
passage stands on one `side` of its cell, and a `MoveParty`
from that cell in that direction moves the party to the passage's destination. That side of the
cell is a wall in the level's `edges`. The cell one step across the wall is the passage's *far
cell*, which has walls on every side and belongs to no area. Use a passage where a map shows two
cells side by side that the adventure can't put side by side, like the floors of two levels that
meet, or two halves of one map that you lay out apart.

A transition leads one way only, and osrlib doesn't add the way back. Stairs the party can climb
back up are two transitions, one on each level, each pointing at the other. Leave out the second
one and you have a chute: the session refuses `UseStairs`
at the bottom, because no transition stands on the arrival cell. A passage's way back is a second
passage. It stands on the first passage's destination cell, on the side opposite the first
passage's `to_facing`. Its destination is the first passage's cell, and its `to_facing` is
opposite the first passage's `side`.

position.title: Position
position.description: The cell where the transition stands.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: The visible transition kind.

side.description: The passage side, or `null` for every transition the party uses at the cell.

TransitionView.title: TransitionView
TransitionView.description: A known level transition without its destination or gate.

damage_dice.title: Damage Dice
damage_dice.description:
The damage the trap deals, as a dice expression like `"1d6"`, or `null` for a trap that deals
none. With `volley_dice` set, it is the damage of each projectile. The model checks the
expression when you construct it, so a malformed one fails then, not when the trap springs.

volley_dice.title: Volley Dice
volley_dice.description:
How many projectiles the trap fires, as a dice expression, or `null` for a trap that fires one
or none. Use it for a dart trap: `volley_dice="1d6"` with `damage_dice="1d4"` fires 1d6 darts
and rolls 1d4 damage for each. There's no dice expression for "roll this many times that much",
so a volley uses two fields. Set it only with `damage_dice`.

save.description:
The saving throw the victim rolls, or `null` for a trap that allows none. Its `category` is the
saving throw to roll, and its `on_save` sets what a passed save does to the damage:
`"negates"` spares the victim from all of it, and `"half"` halves both the `damage_dice` damage
and the falling damage, rounding down. A passed save always spares the victim from `kills` and
`condition`.

kills.title: Kills
kills.description:
Whether the trap kills a victim who fails the save, like a poison gas trap. A victim who
passes the save survives, whatever `on_save` is. With no `save`, the trap kills every victim.
Set `poison` as well when the trap kills by poison.

poison.title: Poison
poison.description:
Whether the trap's kill is a death by poison, such as the OSE SRD's poison gas and poisoned
needle, or `false` for any other kill, such as a death ray. The save versus death covers both, so
the save's category doesn't say which. *Neutralize poison* revives a character who died of
poison within ten rounds and no one else, so set this for every trap that kills with poison.
The victim's `DeathEvent` reports it in its `poison` field,
which the players see. Set it only with `kills`: damage from a trap is a death by damage.

condition.description:
A condition the trap gives a victim who fails the save, like blindness, or `null`. A victim who
passes the save doesn't get it. With no `save`, every victim gets it.

condition_duration_dice.title: Condition Duration Dice
condition_duration_dice.description:
The condition's duration as a dice expression, for a duration that varies. Set this or
`condition_duration_amount`, not both, together with `condition_duration_unit` and a `condition`.
The session rolls it on the effects stream when the condition takes hold.

condition_duration_amount.title: Condition Duration Amount
condition_duration_amount.description:
The condition's duration as a fixed number, for a duration that doesn't vary. Set this or
`condition_duration_dice`, not both, together with `condition_duration_unit` and a
`condition`.

condition_duration_unit.description:
The unit the duration counts in: rounds, turns, or days. Set it together with
`condition_duration_dice` or `condition_duration_amount`. Leave the three duration fields unset
for a condition that lasts until something removes it. The model raises `ValueError` when you
construct it with a unit and no length, or a length and no unit.

fall_feet.title: Fall Feet
fall_feet.description:
How far the victim falls, in feet, or `null` for a trap with no fall, like a pit's depth. The
fall deals 1d6 damage for each full 10 feet, the OSE SRD's falling rule, as
`falling_damage` rolls it. That damage is separate from
`damage_dice`, and a `"half"` save halves it too.

transition.description:
Where the trap moves the party, or `null` for a trap that moves no one. Use it for a chute
that slides the party to another cell or level. The party has one location, so the trap moves
the whole party or no one. With a `save`, it moves the party when at least one victim fails
the save, and leaves the party on the trapped cell when every victim passes. With no `save`,
it always moves the party. The transition can't have a `requires` gate, because the party
doesn't choose to take it. The session moves the party to `to_position` from the cell where the
trap springs, so it doesn't read the transition's `position`. Set `position` to a cell the trap
covers. `validate_adventure`
checks it as it checks a level's transitions: it has to stand on the grid of the trap's level and
lead to a cell on the grid of a level that exists. It also reports a transition whose `kind` is
`"passage"`.

manual.title: Manual
manual.description:
A description of a trap your own code resolves, or `null`. osrlib never reads it. Use it for a
trap whose effect is the referee's call rather than a die roll.

TrapEffect.title: TrapEffect
TrapEffect.description:
What a trap does when it springs.

Put one in the `effect` of a `TrapSpec`, which sets when the
trap springs and whom it hits. The fields combine: a dart trap deals damage, a pit deals falling
damage and can add a condition, and a poison gas trap calls for a saving throw and kills by poison on a
failure.
For a trap that your own code resolves, leave the other fields unset and describe the trap in
`manual`.

The session rolls a trap's damage, saves, and falls on its exploration stream. It makes no attack
roll for a trap, so the damage always applies unless a save reduces it.

A passed save always spares the victim from `kills` and from `condition`, whatever the save's
`on_save` is, because B/X has no half death or half blindness. `on_save` affects only
the damage: `"negates"` spares the victim from all of it, and `"half"` halves it.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party feels the trap go off, or sees the one it found.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `trap`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

trap_ref.title: Trap Ref
trap_ref.description:
Which trap this is, as `"<dungeon id>:<level number>:<area or feature id>"`. The session
stores the same reference in its lists of found, sprung, and removed traps, so a trap that has
sprung or been removed stays that way.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member the event is about. For `exploration.trap.sprung` and `exploration.trap.safe`,
it's the member who set the trap off: the one who forced the door, reached into the cache, or
tried to remove the trap. For a trap that springs when the party enters its area or opens its
door with `OpenDoor`, it's the first living member in
marching order. It's set even when the trap hits the whole party. For
`exploration.trap.removed` and `exploration.trap.removal_failed`, and for a treasure trap
found with `InspectTreasure`, it's the thief who
tried. For a room trap found with `Search`, it's the member
who searched.

direction.title: Direction
direction.description:
The direction of the door a room trap was found through, from the searched cell, as a
`Direction` value. Set for that find alone: it is `null` on a
room trap found inside the searched area, on a treasure trap found on a cache, and on every code but
`exploration.trap.found`.

feature_id.title: Feature Id
feature_id.description:
The `feature:` handle of the treasure cache whose trap this is, the
`MapFeatureView.id` under which the player view lists the
cache, so you can tell which listed cache the event is about without reading the authored id in
`trap_ref`. It's set on every code for a treasure trap, and `null` for a room trap. The cache's
commands act only on a cache where the party stands, which the player view lists, so the handle
here is always one the view already shows.

TrapEvent.title: TrapEvent
TrapEvent.description:
A trap sprang, was found, was removed, resisted removal, or was known and didn't spring.

Emitted by the commands that can set a trap off or look for one:
`MoveParty`,
`UseStairs` and
`EnterDungeon`, which run the arrival cell's
entry checks the same way a step does,
`OpenDoor` and
`ForceDoor`,
`Search`,
`TakeTreasure`,
`InspectTreasure`, and
`RemoveTreasureTrap`. A trap that
fires resolves at once, so its saves and damage follow in the same result as
kernel events.

A trap the party doesn't know about that fails to fire emits no `TrapEvent`. Its die
goes only into the referee-visibility
`DetectionRolledEvent`, so to the players
an uneventful step looks like a step on safe ground.

What finding a trap does depends on the kind of trap. A found room trap never springs,
whether the party enters its area or opens one of its doors: the party walks around
the known pit and stands clear of the known blade, so the engine rolls no die for it
and emits nothing more. A found treasure trap still gets its 2-in-6 roll when the
party takes the treasure with `TakeTreasure`,
unless a thief has removed it with
`RemoveTreasureTrap`, because finding a
treasure trap doesn't disarm it. That is why `exploration.trap.safe`, a known trap
getting its chance and not springing, appears only for a treasure cache.

A thief who fails to remove a treasure trap springs it, unless
`Ruleset.failed_trap_removal_springs`
is off. With the flag off, the failure emits `exploration.trap.removal_failed` and the trap
stays armed and found.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
`"room"` for a trap over an area, or `"treasure"` for a trap on a cache.
`AreaSpec` accepts only room traps, and
`FeatureSpec` accepts only treasure traps.

trigger.title: Trigger
trigger.description:
The action that springs the trap.

- `"enter"`: the party moves into a cell of the trapped area. The session rolls for the trap on
  every move into one of its cells, including moves within the area, until it springs or the
  party finds it.
- `"open"` on a room trap: the party opens or forces a door on an edge of one of the area's
  cells, from either side, like a blade that drops when the door swings.
- `"open"` on a treasure trap: the party opens the cache with
  `TakeTreasure`.

A treasure trap has to use `"open"`, because there is nothing to walk into on a cache.

effect.description: What the trap does once it springs. See `TrapEffect`.

affects.title: Affects
affects.description:
Whom the effect hits. `"party"` hits every living member, like poison gas filling a room.
`"triggerer"`, the default, hits one character: the member named in the
`ForceDoor` or `TakeTreasure`
that sprang it, the thief whose `RemoveTreasureTrap`
failed, or otherwise the first living member in marching order.

TrapSpec.title: TrapSpec
TrapSpec.description:
A trap: when it springs, what it does, and whom it hits.

A trap can be in two places, and its `kind` sets which. A room trap goes on an
`AreaSpec` and covers the whole area. A treasure trap goes on a
`FeatureSpec` and guards that one cache. Each of the two
models accepts only one kind of trap.

A trap doesn't always spring. Each time the party does the thing that springs it, the session
rolls a d6, and the trap springs on a 1 or 2, the OSE SRD's 2-in-6 rule. A trap that has sprung
never springs again. The party can find a trap before it springs: a room trap with a
`Search` for room traps, and a treasure trap with a thief's
`InspectTreasure`. A room trap that the party has found
no longer springs, so the party walks around it. For a treasure trap that the party has found,
the session still rolls when the party opens the cache, until a thief takes it out with
`RemoveTreasureTrap`. There is no way to disarm a room
trap.

The traps you write are the only traps in the game. Treasure the session rolls is never trapped.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"travel_to_town"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

TravelToTown.title: TravelToTown
TravelToTown.description:
Travel from a dungeon's entrance back to town.

The party must be exploring and standing on the entrance cell it arrived on. The trip
takes as many turns as the trip out, with no wandering-monster checks. The unwedged
doors the party opened on the level swing shut behind it. Under the on-return XP
timing, the session awards the party's XP for the trip when it arrives in town.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `exploration.travel.not_at_entrance` - the party is not on the entrance
  cell.

**Events:**

`DoorEvent`s for the doors swinging shut, the
events of the travel time passing, then
`LocationEnteredEvent` for
town. Under the on-return XP timing, an
`AdventureXpAwardEvent` and an
`XpAwardedEvent` for each living member follow,
with a `CharacterLeveledUpEvent` for
each member who gains a level.

coins.description: The coins, by denomination. A new bundle has none.

valuables.title: Valuables
valuables.description: The gems and jewellery, each an instance with an id and a value.

magic_items.title: Magic Items
magic_items.description: The magic items, each an instance with its charges or quantity already rolled.

TreasureBundle.title: TreasureBundle
TreasureBundle.description:
Rolled treasure grouped as one lot: coins, valuables, and magic items.

When the session spawns monsters, it rolls the treasure they carry into bundles. You find them
on an `EncounterGroup`: `member_treasure` contains what
each monster carries, and `group_treasure` contains what the group shares. When the encounter ends,
the bundles of slain monsters drop onto the party's cell as a
`DropPile`. The descriptions of those two fields give the rules
for which bundles drop. The session also uses a bundle while it rolls a hoard, then moves the
contents into a `GeneratedCache`.

Unlike the authored models in this module, a bundle is mutable, because the session adds to it
one entry at a time as it rolls treasure.

chance_pct.title: Chance Pct
chance_pct.description:
The percentage chance the entry is present at all. 0 means it always is, which is how the entries printed without
a chance are stored.

coins.description: The coins this entry yields, or `null`. See `CoinQuantity`.

gems_dice.title: Gems Dice
gems_dice.description: How many gems, as a dice expression, or `null`. Each gem's value is rolled separately on the gem table.

jewellery_dice.title: Jewellery Dice
jewellery_dice.description: How many pieces of jewellery, as a dice expression, or `null`. Each piece's value is rolled separately.

magic.title: Magic
magic.description: The magic item clauses, or empty. See `MagicAllotment`.

TreasureEntry.title: TreasureEntry
TreasureEntry.description:
One printed line of a treasure type, which is one thing that might be in the hoard.

A treasure type is a list of these, and generation goes through them in order. Each has exactly
one payload, so an entry is coins, or gems, or jewellery, or magic items, never a
mixture. Generate a list of them with
`generate_treasure_entries`, which is
also how you generate the hoard a treasure map leads to.

letters.title: Letters
letters.description:
The treasure type letters, like `("D",)`.

When there is more than one, each of them is generated.
`plan_treasure_ref` sorts them by section, so each
letter goes to the lair, to each creature, or to the group, according to its table.

parenthetical.title: Parenthetical
parenthetical.description:
The letters the SRD prints in brackets.

`plan_treasure_ref` adds them to the lair treasure,
whatever section their tables are in, so a bandit's `U (A)` puts U on the group and A in the
lair.

extra_gp.title: Extra Gp
extra_gp.description: Gold pieces added to the lair hoard on top of the rolled treasure, like a cloud giant's 5,000.

multiplier.title: Multiplier
multiplier.description:
How many times to generate every listed letter, as with a noble's `V × 3`.

1 unless the SRD prints a multiplier.

special.title: Special
special.description:
Valuables that are not treasure types, like an elephant's tusks or a killer bee's honey.

osrlib doesn't generate these, so show them to the referee.

see_below.title: See Below
see_below.description: True when the creature's description, not its treasure line, gives what it has.

TreasureRef.title: TreasureRef
TreasureRef.description:
What treasure a monster has, as the stat block prints it.

Read it as `MonsterTemplate.treasure`, then
pass it to `plan_treasure_ref`. That function sorts
the letters into lair, per-creature, and per-group treasure, and returns `extra_gp` and
`multiplier` with them. Generate each letter in the plan with
`generate_treasure`. Each letter is the `letter` of
one table in `load_treasure_tables().treasure_types`, and
[the treasure type index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/treasure-types/) lists them.

Use the plan rather than passing each of `letters` to `generate_treasure` yourself. A loop over
`letters` drops the bracketed letters, the extra gold, and the multiplier, and it treats a
per-creature letter as a lair hoard.

A creature with no treasure has an empty reference. Frozen.

treasure_type.title: Treasure Type
treasure_type.description: Uppercase B/X treasure type letter from `"A"` to `"V"`, as listed in `GET /v1/rules/tables/treasure`.

tier.title: Tier
tier.description:
Magic item table column: `"basic"` for parties of levels 1 to 3, or `"expert"` for parties of level 4 and
higher.

anyOf.description: Random number seed, an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991).

seed.title: Seed
seed.description:
Optional seed (0 to 2^53 - 1). Pass the `seed` from an earlier response with the same body to reproduce the
hoard, or omit it to let the server draw a random seed.

TreasureRequest.title: TreasureRequest
TreasureRequest.description: Treasure type, magic item tier, and optional seed for rolling a treasure hoard.

seed.title: Seed
seed.description: Random number seed, an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991).

treasure.description: Coins, gems, jewellery, and magic items rolled by osrlib.

TreasureResponse.title: TreasureResponse
TreasureResponse.description: Rolled treasure hoard and the seed that produced it.

TreasureSection.title: TreasureSection
TreasureSection.description:
Which section of the treasure tables a letter belongs to, which sets when you generate it.

A monster's stat block lists treasure types by letter, and when you generate a letter
depends on its section: once for the lair, once per monster, or once for the whole
group.
`plan_treasure_ref` sorts a stat block's
letters into those three groups for you.

The lowercase values appear in the compiled treasure data.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the party made the sale.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `treasure_sold`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who sold them and now has the coins.

instance_ids.title: Instance Ids
instance_ids.description: The session-scoped ids of the valuables that were sold.

gp_value.title: Gp Value
gp_value.description: What they fetched, in gold pieces.

item_names.title: Item Names
item_names.description:
What to call one of each item in `instance_ids`, keyed by the same id, such as
`{"valuable-0007": "gem", "valuable-0008": "piece of jewellery"}`. Each name is the name that
`PlayerView.item_names` has for that id. The names are the ones the
party knew when the event happened. The items have left the party, so no view built after the command names
them. A client that replays an event log, or that didn't keep a view, can name the items from the event. It's
empty on an event from a log written before the field existed.

item_names_plural.title: Item Names Plural
item_names_plural.description:
What to call two or more of each item in `item_names`, with the same keys, such as
`{"valuable-0007": "gems"}`, from
`PlayerView.item_names_plural`. Use it with a count of your
own.

TreasureSoldEvent.title: TreasureSoldEvent
TreasureSoldEvent.description:
Valuables were sold in town, and the coins are in the purse.

Emitted by `SellTreasure`, one event for each
