member whose valuables were sold. Gems and jewellery sell for their full listed
value, so selling them neither adds to nor takes from the treasure the experience
award counts.

treasure_types.title: Treasure Types
treasure_types.description:
Every treasure type, A through V. See `TreasureTypeTable`. Reach one by
letter with `treasure_type`.

gems.description: What gems and jewellery are worth. See `GemValueTable`.

magic_item_types.description: Which kind of magic item a roll produces. See `MagicItemTypeTable`.

stocking.description: What is in a room when you stock a dungeon. See `StockingTable`.

unguarded.description:
What an unguarded cache contains, by level. See
`UnguardedTreasureTable`.

TreasureTables.title: TreasureTables
TreasureTables.description:
Every treasure table, loaded and ready to generate from.

Call `load_treasure_tables` to get the built-in set.
It's frozen, and every call returns the same cached object. The generation functions load it themselves, so you
need this only to read a table: to show a referee what a letter can produce, or to roll
a table by hand.

letter.title: Letter
letter.description:
The type letter, for example `"A"`. Every letter is in the `treasure_types` of the tables that
`load_treasure_tables` returns, and listed in
[the treasure type index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/treasure-types/).

kind.description:
Whether the letter is lair treasure, carried by one monster, or carried by a group. See
`TreasureSection`.

average_gp.title: Average Gp
average_gp.description:
The average value of a hoard of this type in gold pieces, as the rules print it. Use it to plan an
adventure. Generation doesn't adjust a hoard toward it, so a single hoard can be worth far more or less.

entries.title: Entries
entries.description: The printed lines, in order. See `TreasureEntry`.

TreasureTypeTable.title: TreasureTypeTable
TreasureTypeTable.description:
One treasure type, A through V, with everything a hoard of that letter can contain.

Get one with
`TreasureTables.treasure_type`, or
skip straight to the result with
`generate_treasure`. Read the entries when you
want to show a referee what a letter can produce before rolling it.

pattern.title: Pattern
pattern.description:
The event the clause matches, as one member of
`TriggerPattern`. The field is named `pattern`,
not `when`, so an objective's completion pattern is `objective.when.pattern`.

conditions.title: Conditions
conditions.description:
Extra tests, every one of which has to hold when an event matches `pattern`. There's
no way to write "or". The interpreter evaluates each condition against the session at
that moment with `condition_holds`. A condition
with `consumes=True` fails validation with a pydantic `ValidationError`.

TriggerClause.title: TriggerClause
TriggerClause.description:
A pattern to match, and the conditions that must hold when an event matches it.

A quest has clauses in three places, and they work the same way in all three: the
`activation` of a `QuestSpec`, and the `when` and
`reveal_when` of an `ObjectiveSpec`. The
`Interpreter` matches a clause the same way it
matches a `TriggerSpec`, so an event that matches a
trigger's pattern and conditions also matches a clause with that pattern and those
conditions.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: which triggers an adventure has is hidden from the players.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `trigger_fired`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

trigger_id.title: Trigger Id
trigger_id.description: Which trigger fired, as the id the adventure gave it.

narrative.title: Narrative
narrative.description:
The text the author wrote for this firing, or `null`. The author wrote it, not the engine,
and `format_message` adds it after the line it builds from the
code. This event has referee visibility, so the players don't see this text. Text meant for
them belongs in the journal.

TriggerFiredEvent.title: TriggerFiredEvent
TriggerFiredEvent.description:
A trigger the adventure's author wrote fired.

A trigger is a rule the adventure's author wrote: when a given event happens, run
given commands. Emitted by `MarkTriggerFired`
every time it runs, including for a trigger that has fired before. The session keeps
only whether a trigger has fired, and these events are the record of each firing.

It has referee visibility, because which trigger fired is part of how the adventure
works, not part of the story the players see. Text the author wrote for the players
goes in the journal and arrives as a
`JournalEntryAddedEvent` or as one of
the quest events.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The trigger's id, unique across the adventure. `session.fired_triggers` records it, and
every command the interpreter runs for the trigger has `source` set to `trigger:{id}`.

when.title: When
when.description:
The pattern of the event that fires the trigger, as one member of
`TriggerPattern`.

conditions.title: Conditions
conditions.description:
Extra tests, every one of which has to hold when an event matches `when`. There's no
way to write "or". The interpreter evaluates each condition against the session at
that moment with `condition_holds`. A condition
with `consumes=True` fails validation with a pydantic `ValidationError`.

repeatable.title: Repeatable
repeatable.description:
Whether the trigger fires every time its pattern matches. With `false`, the default,
it fires once per session.

consequences.title: Consequences
consequences.description:
The referee commands the interpreter runs when the trigger fires, in the order you write
them. The interpreter replaces `PARTY_SELECTOR`,
`FIRST_LIVING_SELECTOR`, and
`CARRIER_SELECTOR` with the members they select.
When the session rejects one command, the interpreter drops it, records a note, and runs the
rest. The tuple can be empty, for a trigger that only adds a journal entry. A command with
`source` set fails validation with a pydantic `ValidationError`, because the interpreter sets
`source` itself.

narrative.description:
The trigger's authored text. osrlib reads two fields of the block. `fired` goes on the
`TriggerFiredEvent`, which only the referee
sees. `journal` becomes a journal entry that the players see.

TriggerSpec.title: TriggerSpec
TriggerSpec.description:
One authored trigger: what it reacts to, what has to hold, and what happens.

Put your triggers in the `triggers` tuple of an
`Adventure`, and register an
`Interpreter` on the session to run them. The
interpreter is the only part of osrlib that reads a trigger, so without it the
trigger does nothing.

By default a trigger fires once per session. When it fires, the interpreter executes
`MarkTriggerFired`, which adds the trigger's
id to `session.fired_triggers`. That record is part of the session, so a trigger that
has fired stays fired after a save, a load, or a replay. Set `repeatable=True` for a
trigger that fires every time its pattern matches.

For a trigger in a session from start to finish, see the
`Interpreter` example.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"turn_party"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

facing.description:
The direction the party ends up facing. Its position doesn't change and no game time
passes. The new facing is on the
`PartyMovedEvent`, so you can redraw a first-person
view from that event.

TurnParty.title: TurnParty
TurnParty.description:
Turn the party in place to a new facing (takes no game time).

The party must already be in a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`). A turn never fails once the
session is `exploring`.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.

**Events:**

`PartyMovedEvent` with the unchanged
position and the new facing.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"turn_undead"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member who presents the holy symbol, usually a cleric, by
`MemberView.id`. The session refuses a member whose
class can't turn undead with `magic.turning.not_a_turner`.

TurnUndead.title: TurnUndead
TurnUndead.description:
Present a holy symbol to turn undead monsters before a battle starts (one round).

An encounter must be open, because outside one there are no monsters to turn. In
battle, declare a `turn_undead`
`BattleDeclaration` instead.

The turning reaches every living monster in the encounter's groups that haven't fled. It
skips a monster that died earlier in the encounter, from a wand for example.

A turned monster gains the `turned` condition. It flees from the cleric and attacks no one.
A destroyed monster dies. The
`UndeadTurnedEvent` reports the outcome, and a
separate condition or death event follows for each monster it affects.

Presenting the symbol is an aggressive act. If any monster is left neither turned nor
destroyed, the monsters that weren't turned attack at once, and battle starts. In a group
that was only partly turned, the turned monsters, and any afraid ones, split off as a new
group and flee.

Modes:

`encounter`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` or `encounter.none_active` - no encounter is open.
- `encounter.turning.mid_pursuit` - the monsters are pursuing the party, and
  nobody can turn undead during a pursuit.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `magic.turning.not_a_turner` - the member's class can't turn undead.
- `magic.turning.caster_incapacitated` - a condition on the member prevents
  the attempt.

**Events:**

`UndeadTurnedEvent` with the roll
and the affected monsters, with each condition it causes as a separate event.
One round passes. When every monster is turned or destroyed, the encounter ends
(`EncounterEndedEvent`), after a
`LootDroppedEvent` when the destroyed
undead leave anything on the floor. Otherwise a
`StanceChangedEvent` to `attacks`
comes before the round, and battle starts after it
(`BattleStartedEvent`). A
`MonsterFledEvent` follows for each new group
of turned and afraid members.

label.title: Label
label.description: The cleric level the row is for: `"1"` to `"10"`, or `"11+"` for level 11 and higher.

cells.title: Cells
cells.description:
The row's cells, keyed by the column labels in `TURNING_COLUMNS`.

Each value is what the SRD prints: an em dash (`"—"`) when the cleric can't turn the
undead, a number for the 2d6 total needed, `"T"` when the undead are turned with no
roll, or `"D"` when they're destroyed with no roll.

TurningRow.title: TurningRow
TurningRow.description:
One cleric level's row of the table for turning undead, as printed.

Read the rows to display the table. To look up an attempt, call
`TurningTable.result`, which reads the cell
and returns a `TurningResult`.

rows.title: Rows
rows.description: One row for each cleric level from 1 to 10, then the `"11+"` row.

TurningTable.title: TurningTable
TurningTable.description:
The table for turning undead: what a cleric of each level can do to undead of each Hit Dice.

Turning undead is a cleric's power to drive undead away or destroy them. Get the table from
`CombatTables.turning` and call
`result`.

template_id.title: Template Id
template_id.description: The monster template's content id, like `"skeleton"`.

column.title: Column
column.description:
The turning table column this kind is read in, which depends on its Hit Dice. `null` when the kind is too
strong to have a column, or isn't undead.

outcome.title: Outcome
outcome.description:
The result for this kind, as one of four strings.

`turn` means the roll reached the threshold, or the table's entry is an automatic turn. `fail` means the roll
fell short, the table's entry gives the cleric no chance, or the kind has no column. `destroy` means the
table's entry at the cleric's level is an automatic destroy. `unaffected` means the monster isn't undead.

threshold.title: Threshold
threshold.description:
The 2d6 total the cleric needed for this kind. `null` when the table has an automatic result instead of
a number.

TurningTypeOutcome.title: TurningTypeOutcome
TurningTypeOutcome.description:
How one kind of monster fared against a cleric's attempt to turn undead.

`turn_undead` reads the turning table once for each kind of monster present, not once for each monster, and
each of these is one reading. Read them from the `types` field of an
`UndeadTurnedEvent`.

code.title: Code
code.description:
What happened, like `combat.attack.hit`: two or more lowercase parts separated by dots. The first part is
the area of the rules the event comes from, like `combat` or `magic`.

Branch on it, and pass the event to `format_message` to turn it into English.
Building an event with a code in any other format raises a pydantic `ValidationError`.

visibility.description: Player visibility: the player rolls the turning dice.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The fixed string that identifies this event class in a serialized event.

caster_id.title: Caster Id
caster_id.description: The entity id of the cleric who tried to turn undead.

roll.title: Roll
roll.description: The first 2d6, read on the turning table.

hd_pool.title: Hd Pool
hd_pool.description:
The second 2d6: how many Hit Dice of undead the turning affects. `null` when no kind was turned or
destroyed, so no second roll was made.

`turn_undead` takes the weakest undead first. When the next one has more Hit Dice than are left, the rest go
unused, and it takes no other monster in its place.

types.title: Types
types.description:
One `TurningTypeOutcome` for each kind of monster present, in the
order you listed the monsters.

affected_ids.title: Affected Ids
affected_ids.description:
The entity ids of the monsters the second roll reached. When any kind was turned or destroyed, at least one
monster is affected, even when the second roll was too low for it.

UndeadTurnedEvent.title: UndeadTurnedEvent
UndeadTurnedEvent.description:
A cleric tried to turn undead, and this is what happened.

`turn_undead` reports one of these for each attempt. Turning takes two
rolls. `turn_undead` reads the first on the turning table once for each kind of undead present. When any kind is
turned or destroyed, a second roll sets how many Hit Dice of those kinds are affected. What then happens to each
monster comes as separate events: a condition gained, or a death.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"unequip_item"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member doing the unequipping, by
`MemberView.id`.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
What to take off or put away. Name it the same way as in
`EquipItem.item_id`. The item has to be equipped
now, not in the pack. A cursed item whose curse has been revealed stays equipped until a
*remove curse* lifts the curse.

UnequipItem.title: UnequipItem
UnequipItem.description:
Take off or put away an equipped item, returning it to the member's pack (takes no game time).

It's legal in town and while exploring. A cursed item whose curse has been revealed
can't be taken off until a *remove curse* lifts the curse, from a caster or from the
temple's `PurchaseHealing`.

Modes:

`town`, `exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - an encounter or battle is underway, or the
  session has ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `exploration.item.not_equipped` - the member has nothing by that id equipped.
- `items.curse.stuck` - a cursed item whose curse has been revealed can't be
  taken off.

**Events:**

Usually none. Taking off a magic item that works while it's worn releases its effects
(`EffectReleasedEvent`).

label.title: Label
label.description: The band as the table prints it, for example `"Level 2–3"`.

min_level.title: Min Level
min_level.description: The shallowest dungeon level in the band.

max_level.title: Max Level
max_level.description: The deepest dungeon level in the band.

entries.title: Entries
entries.description: The printed lines, in order. See `TreasureEntry`.

UnguardedTreasureBand.title: UnguardedTreasureBand
UnguardedTreasureBand.description:
One dungeon-level band of the unguarded treasure table.

Deeper levels have more treasure, so the table is divided into bands of levels. Each band's
entries have the same structure as a treasure type's. Get the band for a level with
`UnguardedTreasureTable.band_for_level`.

bands.title: Bands
bands.description:
The bands, in level order and contiguous from level 1. See
`UnguardedTreasureBand`.

UnguardedTreasureTable.title: UnguardedTreasureTable
UnguardedTreasureTable.description:
The unguarded treasure table, which lists what an unguarded cache contains at each dungeon level.

Use it through
`generate_unguarded_treasure`, which
picks the band and generates from it. The deepest printed band covers levels 8 and 9, and
every deeper level uses it too, so a level 12 cache is no richer than a level 9 one.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
`"all"` for anything a character can use, `"classes"` to restrict to named classes, `"caster"` to restrict to
spell casters of a kind.

class_ids.title: Class Ids
class_ids.description:
The classes that may use it, when `kind` is `"classes"`, as ids from `load_classes`.
They're listed in [the class id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/classes/). Empty
otherwise.

caster.title: Caster
caster.description:
Which kind of caster may use it, when `kind` is `"caster"`: `"arcane"` (magic-users and elves), `"divine"`
(clerics), or `"any"`. `null` otherwise. Wands are arcane-only. Each staff follows the rule on its page.

UsableBy.title: UsableBy
UsableBy.description:
Which characters a magic item works for.

`usable_by_class` checks a class against this
model, and `validate_equip` applies it to rods, wands,
and miscellaneous items, rejecting with `items.equip.not_usable`.

Enchanted swords, weapons, and armour stay at the default `all`: their pages print "per
normal class restrictions", and those restrictions are the class's armour and weapon
policies, applied to the mundane item underneath rather than here. A magic staff's
usability decides who can use its powers. Who can wield it follows the class's weapon
policy for the mundane staff, as `validate_equip` says.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"use_item"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description:
The member using the item, by `MemberView.id`. The
member has to carry the item, and for a wand, staff, or rod, the member's class has to be
able to use it.

item_id.title: Item Id
item_id.description:
The magic item to use, by its per-instance id from
`MemberView.inventory`. Only magic items can be
used with this command, so the session refuses a mundane item's id with
`exploration.item.not_carried`.

target_id.title: Target Id
target_id.description:
Who the item is used on, for a potion or a device: a wand, a staff, or a rod.

For a potion, pass the id of the party member who drinks it. The member in `character_id`
gives it to them, and the potion's effect lands on them. Leave it `null`, or pass
`character_id`, and the member who uses the potion drinks it. The session refuses an id that
isn't a party member's with `items.use.target_not_allowed`, and a member who is dead or turned
to stone with `items.use.target_cannot_drink`.

For a device, pass a creature's id for a device that heals by touch, or an encounter group's
`EncounterGroupView.id` for a device that covers
an area. A healing device with `null` heals the member using it. It can touch a party member
or a creature in a group of the open encounter that hasn't fled, and the session refuses any
other id with `items.use.unknown_target`, a creature of an encounter that has ended included.
The session refuses a healing device on a creature that's dead or turned to stone with
`items.use.target_cannot_be_healed`. Then it refuses an invisible monster or NPC adventurer of
the open encounter with `items.use.invisible_target`, while an invisible member is still a
target. It refuses a healing device on a creature it already healed today with
`items.use.target_healed_today`.

spell_id.title: Spell Id
spell_id.description:
Which spell to read off a scroll that has more than one, by its id (see the
[spell id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/spells/)).
`null` reads the first spell left on the scroll. Once the party has identified the scroll, its entry in
`MemberView.inventory` lists the spells left, in the order a read
takes them. Leave it `null` for anything that isn't a scroll.

mode.title: Mode
mode.description:
Which of the read spell's usages to cast, by that usage's
`SpellMode.key`. `null` casts the spell's first usage,
which is right for a spell with one usage.

targets.title: Targets
targets.description:
The read spell's targets, named as in
`CastSpell.targets`. During an encounter, a target
can also be a living creature in a group that hasn't fled, by its
`EncounterMemberView.id`. When it's empty,
`target_id` is the single target, so a scroll spell with one target needs only `target_id`.

UseItem.title: UseItem
UseItem.description:
Use a magic item: drink a potion, read a scroll, or activate a wand, staff, or rod (one round).

It's legal while exploring and during an encounter. In battle, use an item with a
`use_item` `BattleDeclaration` instead. Name the
member in `character_id` and the item in `item_id`. Using an item identifies it and reveals
any curse. A magic sword that can light up when its wielder says so turns its light on or off.

A device is a wand, a staff, or a rod. `target_id` is the id of whoever the item is used on:
the party member who drinks a potion, a creature for a staff of healing's touch, or an
encounter group for a device that covers an area. When the member reads a scroll with several
spells on it, choose the spell and its targets with `spell_id`, `mode`, and `targets`. They
work like the same fields of `CastSpell`.

A scroll or a staff of healing names as a target only a creature the party can act on now: a
party member, in any state, or a creature in a group of the open encounter that hasn't fled,
which the player view lists in
`EncounterGroupView.members`. A scroll's
spell can't name a dead creature of the encounter, as a battle's `cast` can't. The session
refuses any other id with the code it gives an id that matches nothing, so a creature of an
encounter that has ended gets the same answer as an id that never existed.

A device whose powers the session doesn't resolve, like a staff of commanding, spends a charge,
and its `ItemUsedEvent` has the device's text in `manual`
for the referee to rule on. The staves of power and wizardry strike only in a battle, so here
a use of either one is one of their other powers, like the cone of cold, the same way. The
staff of striking has no other power, so the session refuses it with `items.use.battle_only`.

A member can give a potion they carry to another member to drink. The use is the carrier's,
and so is the round it takes. The potion's effect lands on the drinker. Outside a battle the
party stands together, so any member can reach any other.

A scroll casts its spell at the lowest level that can cast it, whatever the reader's level.
The session checks the read at that level. For example, a *magic missile* scroll fires one
missile, so it takes one target, even when a 6th-level magic-user reads it. The session
refuses a read before it uses up the scroll.

Modes:

`exploring`, `encounter`

**Rejections:**

Any item:

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is in town or in battle, or has
  ended.
- `session.command.unknown_member` - `character_id` matches no party member.
- `session.command.member_incapacitated` - the member can't act.
- `exploration.item.not_carried` - the member carries no magic item with
  that instance id.
- `items.use.not_usable` - the item has no use, or the member's class can't
  use the device.

By kind of item:

- Potions: `items.use.target_not_allowed` when `target_id` isn't a party member's
  id, and `items.use.target_cannot_drink` when it's the id of a member who is dead or
  turned to stone. A member who is asleep or paralysed can be given a potion to drink.
- Scrolls: `exploration.action.requires_light` (reading needs light, and
  infravision isn't enough), `items.scroll.spent`, `items.scroll.wrong_caster`, and
  `items.scroll.no_such_spell`, in that order, so a member who can't read the scroll
  gets `items.scroll.wrong_caster` whatever `spell_id` names. A read also gets the checks of a cast, at the
  scroll's level: `magic.cast.unknown_target` (a target that isn't a party member and
  isn't a living creature in a group of the open encounter that hasn't fled, or a cell
  reference that doesn't name a cell of the level the party stands on),
  `magic.cast.invisible_target` (an invisible monster or NPC adventurer of the open
  encounter, while an invisible member is still a target), `magic.cast.unknown_mode`,
  `magic.cast.target_count`, `magic.cast.target_must_be_creature`,
  `magic.cast.out_of_range`, `magic.cast.caster_incapacitated`,
  `magic.cast.caster_restrained`, and `magic.cast.anti_magic_shell`.
- Devices: `items.device.inert` (no charges left),
  `items.use.target_required` (an area device used in an encounter needs a
  `target_id`), `items.use.unknown_target` (a group that isn't in the open encounter or
  has fled, or a staff of healing's target that isn't a party member and isn't in a group
  of the open encounter that hasn't fled), `items.use.target_cannot_be_healed` (a
  staff of healing used on a creature that's dead or turned to stone),
  `items.use.invisible_target` (a staff of healing used on an invisible monster or NPC
  adventurer of the open encounter that stands),
  `items.use.target_healed_today` (a staff of healing used on a creature it already
  healed today, because the OSE SRD's staff "Is effective on any individual at most once
  per day"), and `items.use.battle_only` (a staff whose only power is its strike, like the staff of
  striking, works only as a battle declaration).

**Events:**

`ItemIdentifiedEvent`, and
`CurseRevealedEvent` for a cursed item,
the first time the item is used. An
`ItemUsedEvent` records what happened:
a potion drunk, potions mixed, a scroll read, a device activated, or a cursed
scroll's curse. The events of the item's effect follow: healing, saving throws,
damage, effects attached, and a scroll's
`SpellCastEvent`, each a separate event. While
exploring, one round passes. During an encounter, the encounter round's events
follow instead. During a pursuit, a `PursuitEvent`
round follows, because the party keeps running. When a wand of fear or a scroll of
*cause fear* frightens only some of a group, a
`MonsterFledEvent` for the new group of afraid
members comes before the round's events.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"use_stairs"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

UseStairs.title: UseStairs
UseStairs.description:
Take the stairs, trapdoor, chute, or other transition on the party's cell.

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`) and standing on a cell
with an authored transition, a `TransitionSpec`.
The move uses as much movement as a step onto an unexplored cell. A passage doesn't
count, because the party walks through a passage with
`MoveParty`. On a cell with both a passage and
stairs, this command takes the stairs.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `exploration.stairs.none` - the party's cell has no transition other than a
  passage.
- `exploration.transition.gate_refused` - the transition has an
  authored condition (`GateSpec`) the party
  doesn't meet. The rejection includes the gate's authored refusal text. Like every
  refusal, it costs no movement, no time, and no toll.

**Events:**

`ItemConsumedEvent` first when
the gate takes an item as a toll, then
`LocationEnteredEvent` when the
level or dungeon changes, with the gate's success text when its author
wrote one. That arrival event records how the party crossed: `via` is the
transition's `kind`, and `transition_ref` is the cell the transition stands
on, which is the cell the party left. Leaving a level shuts the unwedged doors the
party opened on it, with a `DoorEvent` for each.

The session then runs the destination cell's entry checks, the same ones as for
`MoveParty`: a
`HoardGeneratedEvent` for area
treasure, a
`DetectionRolledEvent` and a
`TrapEvent` for a room trap with its
resolution, and the opening of an encounter with monsters keyed to that area in the adventure
(`SurpriseRolledEvent`s,
`EncounterStartedEvent`,
`ReactionRolledEvent`,
`StanceChangedEvent`, and
`BattleStartedEvent` when the monsters
attack). When the movement completes a turn on the game clock, the events of that
turn follow, as they do for a step.

adventure.description:
Player-visible info that `POST /v1/adventures` would return, with `id` and `created_at` set to
`null`.

ValidAdventure.title: ValidAdventure
ValidAdventure.description: Validation result when `POST /v1/adventures/validate` accepts an adventure document.

instance_id.title: Instance Id
instance_id.description:
The id of this piece, for example `"valuable-0001"`, allocated by
`IdAllocator`.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: `"gem"` or `"jewellery"`.

name.title: Name
name.description:
A display name for the piece. Generation sets a plain one. When you place treasure by hand in an adventure, you
can give it any name.

phrase.title: Phrase
phrase.description:
What to call the piece in the middle of a sentence, with its article and its case, like
`"the abbot's seal ring"`. The session copies it from the
`ValuableSpec.phrase` that placed the piece, as it copies `name`. It's
empty for a piece that treasure generation rolls, for a piece placed with no phrase, and for a piece from a save
that osrlib 2.9.0 or earlier wrote.

To word a sentence, read
`PlayerView.valuable_phrases`, which has this phrase when it's
set and, when it's empty or only whitespace, the phrase osrlib makes from `name`. A piece with no name of its own,
whose `name` is empty, is only whitespace, or is the one treasure generation gives its kind, has no phrase in the
view, whatever this field holds.

value_gp.title: Value Gp
value_gp.description: What it's worth in gold pieces, and what it pays when sold.

weight_coins.title: Weight Coins
weight_coins.description:
The weight in coins, taken from the treasure encumbrance rows when the piece was generated. See
`TreasureWeight`.

ValuableInstance.title: ValuableInstance
ValuableInstance.description:
One gem or piece of jewellery a character carries.

Treasure generation rolls the value once, when the piece is created, and it never
changes. `generate_treasure` returns these
alongside the coins. `SellTreasure` sells a piece
for exactly `value_gp`, with no haggling or appraisal. The SRD gives no rate at which a
town buys treasure, and selling at full value makes a piece's sale price equal to the
experience it's worth. If you want haggling or appraisal, add them yourself.

kind.title: Kind
kind.description:
Whether the valuable is a gem or jewellery. No rule in osrlib depends on it. Use it for display,
and for any rule you apply to one kind and not the other.

name.title: Name
name.description:
The name the party sees, like `"The abbot's seal ring"`. Leave it empty for an unnamed
valuable, like the ones the session rolls on the treasure tables.

phrase.title: Phrase
phrase.description:
What to call the piece in the middle of a sentence, with its article and its case, like
`"a silver altar candlestick"`, `"the abbot's seal ring"`, or `"Ossor's Eye"`. A client shows `name` in a list,
such as an inventory row, and words a sentence, such as "Wren takes the abbot's seal ring.", with the phrase that
`PlayerView.valuable_phrases` gives.

Leave it empty, and osrlib makes the phrase from `name`, as for a common noun. A name whose first word is "the",
"a", or "an" has that word in lowercase, so `"The abbot's seal ring"` reads `"the abbot's seal ring"`. Any other
name has its first character in lowercase and "an" or "a" in front, by its first letter, so
`"Silver altar candlestick"` reads `"a silver altar candlestick"`. Set the phrase when the piece has a proper name,
like `"Ossor's Eye"`, when it takes "the", like `"the Prior's chain of office"`, or when its first letter doesn't
give its article, like `"a unicorn-horn cup"`. A phrase that's only whitespace counts as empty, and the view
leaves out any spaces around a name or a phrase.

Only a piece with a name of its own has a phrase in the view. A piece whose `name` is empty, is only whitespace,
or is the name treasure generation gives its kind, `"Gem"` for a gem or `"Jewellery"` for a piece of jewellery,
is named by its kind, whatever `phrase` holds.

value_gp.title: Value Gp
value_gp.description:
What the valuable is worth in gold pieces. It sells for this much in town, and it is worth
this much experience to the party.

weight_coins.title: Weight Coins
weight_coins.description:
What the valuable weighs, in coins, for encumbrance. The default, 0, makes it weightless, as
a gem usually is.

ValuableSpec.title: ValuableSpec
ValuableSpec.description:
A gem or piece of jewellery that you place in a cache by hand.

Use it when the treasure is a particular thing with a name, not one of the gems the session
rolls on the treasure tables. Put it in the `valuables` of a `FeatureSpec`.
When the party empties the cache with `TakeTreasure`, the
session turns it into a `ValuableInstance` with an id.

label.title: Label
label.description:
The clause as the item's page prints it, for example `"+2 vs Lycanthropes"`. Show this to players. Don't parse
it.

bonus.title: Bonus
bonus.description: The attack and damage bonus that applies against a matching target, replacing the item's base bonus.

categories.title: Categories
categories.description: Monster category tags that match, for example `("undead",)`.

template_ids.title: Template Ids
template_ids.description:
Monster template ids that match, from `load_monsters` (listed in
[the monster id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/monsters/)). At least one of
`categories` and `template_ids` is non-empty.

VersusBonus.title: VersusBonus
VersusBonus.description:
A magic weapon's bonus against particular enemies, as in `+2 vs Lycanthropes`.

When the target matches, this bonus replaces the item's ordinary attack and damage
bonus rather than adding to it. Attack resolution reads the clause off the template. You
read it to show a player what a weapon is good against.

The engine never matches a clause's printed label against a monster's name. Instead, `categories`
lists tags a monster template has, like `undead` or `enchanted`, and `template_ids`
lists compiled monster ids from `load_monsters`. A clause
matches a target whose template has any of the listed tags or ids. Characters have no
monster template, so a clause never matches a character.

Visibility.title: Visibility
Visibility.description:
Who may see an event: the players, or only the referee.

Every event has one of these values, because in B/X the referee makes some rolls behind a screen. Filter
a log on it before you show anything to a player, or call
`GameSession.view`, which builds the players' view and the referee's
view for you. A narrator that plays the referee reads every event.

A serialized event contains the lowercase value. The values stay fixed within a `schema_version`, the version
stamp of the saved format.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"wait"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

Wait.title: Wait
Wait.description:
Hold for one encounter round, and let the monsters act on their stance.

An encounter must be open. The monsters' stance is their reaction to the party:
`attacks`, `hostile`, `uncertain`, `indifferent`, or `friendly`. Waiting spends a round
to see what the monsters do. Monsters whose stance is `uncertain` roll a new reaction,
and `hostile` monsters attack once their patience runs out. During a pursuit after an
`Evade`, waiting runs one round of the pursuit instead.

Modes:

`encounter`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - no encounter is open.
- `encounter.none_active` - a second check behind the mode gate, which normal
  play never reaches.

**Events:**

The encounter round's events. Monsters whose stance is `uncertain` roll a new
reaction (`ReactionRolledEvent`, and a
`StanceChangedEvent` when it changes).
Battle opens when the monsters attack, or when `hostile` monsters run out of
patience (`BattleStartedEvent`). During a
pursuit, a `PursuitEvent` round runs
instead, which can end in an
`ExhaustionEvent` at the round limit
(with an `EffectAttachedEvent`
and a `ConditionGainedEvent` for the
exhaustion) or in battle.

When the encounter ends, the session emits
`EncounterEndedEvent`, a
`MonsterDefeatedEvent` for each
monster killed or driven off, a
`LootDroppedEvent` when the slain leave
anything on the floor,
`EffectReleasedEvent`s, and, under
the immediate XP timing,
`XpAwardedEvent` and
`CharacterLeveledUpEvent`.
The round also brings the usual
`EffectExpiredEvent`,
`LightEvent`, and
`ProvisionsEvent` events for the time that
passes.

visibility.description: Referee visibility: the referee makes the check in secret, and the party sees only what it produces.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `wandering_check`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

chance.title: Chance
chance.description:
The chance in six that the check needed, limited to the range 0 to 6. It's the level's
chance, adjusted for noise, bright light, and a rest with
`hidden` set.

roll.title: Roll
roll.description:
The d6 that was rolled, or `null` when the chance came out at zero and no die was
rolled.

encounter.title: Encounter
encounter.description:
Whether the check produced an encounter. When it did, the encounter's events follow in
the same result.

WanderingCheckEvent.title: WanderingCheckEvent
WanderingCheckEvent.description:
A wandering-monster check came due and the referee rolled for it.

Emitted by `wandering_check`, which the
session runs every few turns while it's in `exploring` mode (see
`wandering_interval`). Any command that
passes those turns can emit it, most often
`MoveParty` or
`Rest`. When the check hits, the encounter opens in
the same result, and the command passes no more time.

It has referee visibility because the party can't know a check was made. It knows
only what it meets.

chance_in_six.title: Chance In Six
chance_in_six.description:
The base chance, in six, that each check brings monsters. The default, 1, is the B/X rule. The
session adjusts it for each check, within 0 to 6. Noise since the last check adds 1, and light as
bright as daylight adds 1. A rest with `hidden` set, where
the party hides while it rests, subtracts 1. With 0, a level has wandering monsters only after
noise or under bright light. Set it higher for a busier level.

interval_turns.title: Interval Turns
interval_turns.description: How many exploration turns pass between checks. The default, 2, is the B/X rule.

table.description:
An encounter table of your own for this level, or `null` to use the built-in table for the
level's number. Your table replaces the built-in one completely, so use it to give a level
different monsters. It has the same rows as the built-in tables from
`load_encounter_tables`, and
`stock_area` can roll on it too.

WanderingSpec.title: WanderingSpec
WanderingSpec.description:
A level's wandering-monster check: how often the session rolls it, and on what table.

Every `LevelSpec` has one. The default is the B/X rule, so you
write your own only to change the chance or the monsters. The session runs the check as the
party spends turns on the level. You don't roll it yourself.

kind.description:
Whether `weapon_ids` lists the weapons allowed, the weapons refused, or nothing. See
`WeaponPolicyKind`.

weapon_ids.title: Weapon Ids
weapon_ids.description:
The weapon ids the policy lists, like `("long_bow", "two_handed_sword")` for the dwarf.

Look each one up with `load_equipment().get(item_id)`, or see
[the equipment id index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/). Empty when `kind`
is `"any"`, and not empty otherwise.

manual_notes.title: Manual Notes
manual_notes.description:
Weapon rules from the SRD that osrlib doesn't check, like the dwarf's limit to "small or normal sized" weapons.

Show them to the referee, who applies them.

WeaponPolicy.title: WeaponPolicy
WeaponPolicy.description:
Which weapons a class may wield.

Read it from `ClassDefinition.weapons`.
`validate_equip` checks a weapon against it. It covers
weapons only. `validate_equip` doesn't check a piece of
gear used as a weapon, like a torch, against it. Frozen.

WeaponPolicyKind.title: WeaponPolicyKind
WeaponPolicyKind.description:
Whether a class's weapon list contains the weapons it may use or the weapons it may not.

Read it from `WeaponPolicy.kind`. With `"any"` the list
is empty and every weapon is allowed. With `"allowed"` the list contains the only weapons allowed.
With `"forbidden"` the list contains the only weapons the class may not use. The values are those three strings.

WeaponQuality.title: WeaponQuality
WeaponQuality.description:
What a weapon can do in combat, as the SRD's weapon table prints it.

Every `WeaponTemplate` and every gear
`CombatFacet` has a tuple of these, and attack
resolution in `osrlib.core.combat` reads them: they are what makes
a bow behave differently from a mace. Compiled equipment already has its qualities. You
set them yourself only when you build a weapon template to bundle with an adventure.

The lowercase values appear in the compiled equipment data and in saves.

item_type.title: Item Type
item_type.description: Always `"weapon"`. This field distinguishes the four template kinds when they are stored or loaded together.

id.title: Id
id.description:
The catalog id, for example `"sword"`. Unique across every equipment list. Get every id from
`load_equipment`, or see [the equipment id
index](https://mmacy.github.io/osrlib-python/reference/content-ids/equipment/).

name.title: Name
name.description: The display name, for example `"Sword"`.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
What to call one of these weapons in a sentence, like `"sword"` or `"two-handed sword"`.

It's lowercase unless a word is a proper noun or an abbreviation, and it has no article, so put a number or an
article in front of it: "a sword", "2 swords".
`PlayerView.item_names` gives it to the players' client.

A template you write that leaves it out gets its `name`.

display_name_plural.title: Display Name Plural
display_name_plural.description:
What to call two or more of these weapons, like `"swords"` or `"staves"`.

`PlayerView.item_names_plural` gives it to the players' client. A
template you write that leaves it out gets `display_name` with the regular English ending on the word that names the
item: the last word before the first `of`, `with`, or `vs`, a comma, a bonus like `+1`, a closing Roman numeral, or
an opening parenthesis, or the last word when the name has none of them. So `"Idol of the drowned saint"` becomes
`"Idols of the drowned saint"`, and `"Lantern (hooded)"` becomes `"Lanterns (hooded)"`. The ending is `s`, or `es`
after `s`, `x`, `z`, `ch`, or `sh`, or `ies` in place of a `y` that follows a consonant, and `staff` becomes
`staves` with its capital kept, so `"Staff of the Magi"` becomes `"Staves of the Magi"`. The connecting words count
in any case, so `"Staff Of Power"` becomes `"Staves Of Power"`, and any spaces after the word stay after the ending.
The compiled plural of every built-in template follows the same rule. Set it yourself when the name is already
plural, like `"Torches (6)"`, or when the plural is irregular.

cost_gp.title: Cost Gp
cost_gp.description: The listed price in gold pieces, for one weapon.

weight_coins.title: Weight Coins
weight_coins.description:
The weight in coins. For a missile weapon this already includes its ammunition and quiver, which is why
ammunition itself weighs nothing.

damage.title: Damage
damage.description:
The damage the weapon deals, as a dice expression, for example `"1d8"`. Ignored when the `variable_weapon_damage`
flag of `Ruleset` is off, and then every weapon deals 1d6.

qualities.title: Qualities
qualities.description: What the weapon can do. See `WeaponQuality`.

missile_ranges.description: The three range bands, present exactly when `qualities` includes the missile quality.

material.description: What it's made of, for monsters that only silver or magic can hurt. Standard unless the weapon is silvered.

overrides_applied.title: Overrides Applied
overrides_applied.description:
Which fields were corrected when this row was compiled from the SRD text, as dotted paths. Empty when none were.
osrlib doesn't read it during play.

WeaponTemplate.title: WeaponTemplate
WeaponTemplate.description:
A mundane weapon, from the SRD's weapon table.

One of the four kinds of equipment template. Get one from the compiled catalog with
`EquipmentCatalog.get`, then buy it with
`purchase`, which creates the
`ItemInstance` a character carries.
Templates are frozen and shared. Construct one yourself only to bundle a weapon of your
own in an `Adventure`.

command_type.title: Command Type
command_type.description: Always `"wedge_door"`. Pass it in every request body to select this command.

source.title: Source
source.description: Referee only. Who or what issued the command, such as a trigger id, a quest id, or the name of a subsystem in your application (at least 1 character), or `null` when unset. The session records `source` in `command_log` without changing how the command executes. A player who sets `source` gets 403 `referee_required`.

direction.description:
Which side of the party's cell the door is on, from the `door` edges in
`ExploredLevelView.edges`. Wedging holds the
door as it stands, open or shut. To keep a way back, wedge an open door before the party
walks through it.

WedgeDoor.title: WedgeDoor
WedgeDoor.description:
Wedge a door with an iron spike so it can't swing shut or be closed (takes no game time).

The party must be exploring a dungeon (see
`EnterDungeon`). The spike comes from the first
living member in marching order who carries iron spikes, and one spike is used up.
No play command removes the spike. Only the referee's
`SetDoorState` with `wedged=False` does.

Modes:

`exploring`

**Rejections:**

- `session.command.wrong_mode` - the session is not exploring a dungeon.
- `exploration.door.no_door` - no known door on that side of the cell.
- `exploration.door.wedged` - the door is already wedged.
- `exploration.door.no_spike` - no living member carries iron spikes.

**Events:**

`ItemConsumedEvent` for the spike,
then `DoorEvent` with code
`exploration.door.wedged`.

min_score.title: Min Score
min_score.description: The lowest score this row covers.

max_score.title: Max Score
max_score.description: The highest score this row covers. Equal to `min_score` on a one-score row.

magic_saves.title: Magic Saves
magic_saves.description: What to add to a saving throw against a magical effect. Negative at a low score.

WisdomRow.title: WisdomRow
WisdomRow.description:
One row of the wisdom table: a band of scores, with its saving throw modifier.

Wisdom grants no other bonus. Read the rows from
`AbilityTables.wisdom` to draw the table. To look up
one score, call
`magic_save_modifier` instead.

label.title: Label
label.description:
The Hit Dice as the SRD prints them, from `"Less than 1"` to `"21–21+"`, like `"2"`, `"2+"`, or `"9–10+"`.

A `+` after a count is for a monster with a bonus to its hit points, like 2+1, which is
worth more than the same count with no bonus. The ranges use an en dash.

base.title: Base
base.description: The experience points a monster in this row is worth, before its special abilities.

bonus.title: Bonus
bonus.description: The extra experience points for each special ability, shown as an asterisk in a stat block, as in 3*.

XpAwardRow.title: XpAwardRow
XpAwardRow.description:
One row of the table of experience awards for monsters: what a monster of some Hit Dice is worth.

`monster_xp` does the whole calculation, including the
special abilities, so read a row directly only to display the table.

XpAwardTiming.title: XpAwardTiming
XpAwardTiming.description:
When a party receives the experience points it has earned.

Set it on `Ruleset.xp_award_timing`. The choice affects
the game's pacing. With `ON_RETURN`, the party gets its experience only once it's back
in town alive. With `IMMEDIATE`, it gets experience as it earns it, which suits a game
with no trip home.

Saved games contain the lowercase values, and they stay fixed within a
`schema_version`, the version stamp that identifies a serialized model's format.

visibility.description: Player visibility: it goes on the character's sheet.

event_type.title: Event Type
event_type.description: The event type, `xp_awarded`, which identifies this class in serialized form.

character_id.title: Character Id
character_id.description: The member who received it.

award.title: Award
award.description: The award as the session handed it over, before the character's adjustment.

modified_award.title: Modified Award
modified_award.description:
The award after the class's prime-requisite adjustment, rounded down. The character gains
this much, except when it would raise them two levels: one award raises a character at most one
level, so their total stops one point short of the level after next and the rest is lost. Then
`clamped` is true and `gained` says how much the character got.

level_after.title: Level After
level_after.description: The member's level once the award was applied.

gained.title: Gained
gained.description:
The experience the character actually gained. It's less than `modified_award` when
`clamped` is true, and `null` in an event recorded before osrlib 2.7.0.

clamped.title: Clamped
clamped.description:
Whether the one-level limit cut the award, so the character gained less than
`modified_award` and the rest was lost.

XpAwardedEvent.title: XpAwardedEvent
XpAwardedEvent.description:
One character was awarded experience.

Emitted wherever an award is made: after the
`AdventureXpAwardEvent` on
`TravelToTown`, and by the referee's
`AwardXP`. When the ruleset is set to award experience
immediately, it's also emitted at the end of an encounter in which monsters were
defeated, and by a `TakeTreasure` that takes
coins, gems, or jewellery. When the award crosses a threshold, a
`CharacterLeveledUpEvent` for the same
member follows it at once.

role.title: Role
role.description: The group member's role, like `"leader"`, `"chieftain"`, or `"bodyguard"`.

XpNote.title: XpNote
XpNote.description:
What a leader or other special member of a group of these creatures is worth in experience.

Read them from `MonsterTemplate.xp_notes`. A band of
gnolls has a leader worth more than the rest, and this is that number. What else makes the
leader different is prose in the template's `abilities`, because the SRD gives it as prose.
Frozen.

modifier_pct.title: Modifier Pct
modifier_pct.description: The adjustment as a percentage, like `10` for a tenth more experience or `-20` for a fifth less.

minimums.title: Minimums
minimums.description:
The lowest score in each ability that earns this tier, keyed by ability. The character must meet every entry for
the tier to apply. There's at least one entry.

XpTier.title: XpTier
XpTier.description:
One tier of a class's experience modifier: a percentage, and the minimum scores that earn it.

A class adjusts every experience award up for a character whose prime requisites are high, and
down for one whose prime requisites are low. Read a class's tiers from
`ClassDefinition.xp_tiers`.
`xp_modifier_pct` checks them in order and returns the
percentage of the first tier whose minimums the character meets. Frozen.

HTTPBearer.description: An API key from the server's `BXAPI_API_KEYS` setting.

Idempotent-Replayed.description: `true` when the response is replayed from an earlier `POST` with the same `Idempotency-Key`. Omitted on the initial response.

ETag.description: Weak entity tag for the uncompressed response body, such as `W/"5f0c1b6de0a94d7f8f3f0f5b7a1c2d3e"`. Send it in `If-None-Match` to check whether the content has changed.

X-Request-Id.description: The request identifier, such as `req_Zk3uY0mWq1x8Jr5cTt2aLw`, which the server logs with the request. Echoes the request's `X-Request-Id` header when it contains 1 to 128 letters, digits, and `.`, `_`, `~`, or `-`. Otherwise the server generates a `req_` id.

tags.name: meta
tags.description:
Check that the server is reachable, verify an API key, and inspect the server's versions and your
client's storage usage.

- `GET /health`: returns `{"status": "ok"}` without an API key, for load balancer and container
  health checks.
- `GET /v1/meta`: checks your API key and returns `api_version`, `engine_version`,
  `schema_version` (the document format version), `auth_enabled`, your `client` name and `role`,
  and your `storage` usage and limit.

tags.name: rules
tags.description:
Read the B/X rules catalogs that osrlib loads: character classes, monsters, spells, mundane
equipment, magic items, languages, printed reference tables, session commands, and the Open Game
License. Use these endpoints to populate a class picker, a shop, a bestiary, or a command menu.

Each list operation returns a page of summaries, and each detail operation returns osrlib's full
model for one entry. Pass an entry's `id` from a list to the matching detail operation. Where a
list accepts `q`, it filters to entries whose `id` or `name` contains that text, ignoring case.
Every 200 response includes `Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600`, because the catalogs change
only when the server's osrlib version changes. Both `player` and `referee` keys can read every
entry, including details that remain hidden in play until identified, such as whether a magic item
is cursed.

- `GET /v1/rules/classes` and `GET /v1/rules/classes/{class_id}`: character classes and level
  progressions. Pass `id` as `class_id` to `POST /v1/characters`.
- `GET /v1/rules/equipment` and `GET /v1/rules/equipment/{item_id}`: weapons, armour, adventuring
  gear, and ammunition, filterable by `q` and `item_type`. Pass `id` in `purchases` on
  `POST /v1/characters` or in a session's `purchase_equipment` command.
- `GET /v1/rules/spells` and `GET /v1/rules/spells/{spell_id}`: cleric and arcane spells,
  filterable by `q`, `class_id`, and `level`. Pass `id` in `starting_spell_ids` on
  `POST /v1/characters` for a magic-user or elf.
- `GET /v1/rules/languages`: spoken languages. Pass an `id` whose `choosable` is `true` in
  `extra_languages` on `POST /v1/characters`.
- `GET /v1/rules/monsters` and `GET /v1/rules/monsters/{monster_id}`: monster stat blocks,
  filterable by `q`. Pass `id` as `monster_id` to `POST /v1/generate/monsters`.
- `GET /v1/rules/magic-items` and `GET /v1/rules/magic-items/{item_id}`: magic item templates,
  filterable by `q` and `category`.
- `GET /v1/rules/tables` and `GET /v1/rules/tables/{name}`: the printed `abilities`, `combat`,
  `encounters`, and `treasure` tables.
- `GET /v1/rules/commands` and `GET /v1/rules/commands/{command_type}`: all session commands,
  filterable by `kind` (`play` or `referee`) and `mode`, with the JSON Schema for each command's
  request body.
- `GET /v1/rules/license`: the Open Game License 1.0a text and Section 15 notice for the rules
  content.

tags.name: dice
tags.description:
Roll B/X dice expressions such as `3d6`, `d%`, or `2d6+1x10` outside a session and get every
individual die alongside the final total. The server stores nothing.

A *seed* is an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 that determines every random number osrlib draws. Any
caller may pass `seed` to repeat a roll, or omit it to let the server draw and return a new one.

- `POST /v1/dice/roll`: takes `expression`, `times` (1 to 100), and an optional `seed`, and
  returns `rolls` and the `seed` used.

tags.name: generate
tags.description:
Roll first-level characters, treasure hoards, NPC parties, stocked dungeon rooms, and monster
groups from the B/X tables without storing anything. Use these stateless endpoints for referee
tools, adventure preparation, or previews.

Every operation accepts an optional *seed* (an integer from 0 to 2^53 - 1 that determines every
random roll) from any caller and returns the `seed` it used. Sending the same request body with
that `seed` reproduces the exact result on the same osrlib version.

- `POST /v1/generate/character`: takes character creation choices and returns the character,
  derived stats, every creation roll, and `seed`. To store a character for play, call
  `POST /v1/characters` instead.
- `POST /v1/generate/treasure`: takes a `treasure_type` (`A` to `V`) and magic item `tier`
  (`basic` or `expert`), and returns rolled coins, valuables, and magic items.
- `POST /v1/generate/npc-party`: takes `kind` (`basic` or `expert`) and `count` (1 to 100), and
  returns NPC adventurers with gear and treasure.
- `POST /v1/generate/room`: takes a dungeon `level_number` (from 1), and returns rolled room
  contents, treasure presence, and any encounter.
- `POST /v1/generate/monsters`: takes a `monster_id` from `GET /v1/rules/monsters` and `count` (1
  to 100), and returns monster instances with rolled hit points.

tags.name: characters
tags.description:
Create, import, inspect, and delete stored player characters for starting game sessions. Each
session copies its party members when it starts, so play never modifies a stored character and one
stored character can start any number of sessions.

In B/X, players roll six ability scores before choosing a class. An *ability roll* stores those
six scores along with a *seed* (the integer that determines osrlib's random rolls), which the
server never reveals to players. Creating a character from that roll derives hit points and
starting gold from the same seed, so retrying after an invalid choice keeps the same rolls.

1. `POST /v1/ability-rolls` rolls and stores six scores, returning `id`, `scores`, and
   `eligible_class_ids`. `GET /v1/ability-rolls/{roll_id}` reads a stored roll again.
2. `GET /v1/ability-rolls/{roll_id}/adjustment-limits` returns how far the player can trade
   ability points for the class they pick, so your client can disable each control that can't
   change a score.
3. `POST /v1/ability-rolls/{roll_id}/preview` returns the character, hit points, and starting
   gold that the player's choices would give, without storing anything or using the roll. Call it
   as often as the player changes a choice.
4. `POST /v1/characters` creates and stores a first-level character from `ability_roll_id` (or
   freshly rolled scores) and the player's choices.
5. `POST /v1/sessions` starts a game session with the character's `id` in `character_ids`.

`GET /v1/characters` lists your client's stored characters, `GET /v1/characters/{character_id}`
returns one character with its derived stats, and `DELETE /v1/characters/{character_id}` deletes
one without affecting active sessions. A referee can import an osrlib *character document* (`kind`,
`schema_version`, `engine_version`, and `payload`) with `POST /v1/characters/import`. To roll a
character from new scores without storing it, call `POST /v1/generate/character`.

tags.name: adventures
tags.description:
List, validate, upload, inspect, and delete adventures that sessions can play. An *adventure*
defines a starting town, one or more dungeons, and their encounters, treasure, triggers, and
quests. Every server includes the built-in adventure `builtin-barrow`, so you can start a session
without uploading anything.

An *adventure document* is osrlib's versioned JSON envelope (`kind` set to `"adventure"`,
`schema_version`, `engine_version`, and `payload`), as produced by
[osr-forge](https://github.com/mmacy/osr-forge), [osr-editor](https://github.com/mmacy/osr-editor),
or osrlib. *Adventure info* is the player-safe summary shown before play: title, description,
hooks, recommended party, town, and dungeon names, with maps, monsters, and quests omitted.

1. `GET /v1/adventures` lists built-in adventures first, followed by your client's uploads.
2. `POST /v1/adventures/validate` checks an adventure document and returns `valid` without storing
   anything.
3. `POST /v1/adventures` validates and stores an adventure document, returning its `adv_` id.
4. `POST /v1/sessions` starts a game session with the adventure's `id` as `adventure_id`.

`GET /v1/adventures/{adventure_id}` returns one adventure's player-safe info,
`GET /v1/adventures/{adventure_id}/document` returns the full uploaded document to a referee, and
`DELETE /v1/adventures/{adventure_id}` deletes a client upload without affecting sessions already
started from it.

tags.name: sessions
tags.description:
Start, play, inspect, save, and delete dungeon-crawl game sessions. A *session* is one game in
progress: a party of characters playing a copy of an adventure from `town` until play reaches
`game_over` or `victory`.

- A *command* is one action sent to the session, such as
  `{"command_type": "move_party", "direction": "east"}`, which osrlib either accepts or refuses.
- A *mode* is the current phase of play (`town`, `exploring`, `encounter`, `battle`, `game_over`,
  or `victory`), which determines which commands are legal.
- An *event* is one recorded occurrence from a command, trigger, or quest, marked visible to all
  players (`player`) or to the referee alone (`referee`).
- The *revision* counts accepted command requests in the session, starting at 0.
- The *player view* is everything the players may see at the current revision, whereas the
  *referee view* exposes the hidden map, monster hit points, flags, and logs to a referee.

1. `POST /v1/sessions` starts a session in `town` at revision 0 from an `adventure_id` and
   `character_ids` (or a referee's `party_document`).
2. `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/commands` lists the commands legal in the current mode for your
   role. Read `GET /v1/rules/commands/{command_type}` for a command's body schema.
3. `POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/commands` executes one command and returns `accepted`,
   `rejections`, `events`, `messages`, `mode`, `ended`, and `revision` (plus `view` when you pass
   `include=view`).
4. `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/view` returns the player view when you didn't request
   `include=view` in step 3.
5. Repeat steps 2 to 4 until `ended` is `true`.

`GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/events` pages through the event log after a reconnect, and
`GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/referee-view` returns the full game state to a referee.
`POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/saves` snapshots the session into a save that
`POST /v1/saves/{save_id}/restore` can branch from. `GET /v1/sessions` lists your sessions,
`GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}` reads session metadata, `PATCH /v1/sessions/{session_id}` renames a
session, and `DELETE /v1/sessions/{session_id}` deletes a session while keeping its saves.

The server runs one command, view read, or event-log read at a time per session. A request that
waits longer than 5 seconds for the session lock gets 409 `session_busy`.

**Syncing, retries, and reconnects:**

- **Lost `POST` response:** Send a fresh `Idempotency-Key` with each new `POST` and reuse that key
  on retries so the server replays the stored 2xx outcome instead of running the move twice.
- **Guarding against concurrent moves:** Track `revision` from `POST /v1/sessions`,
  `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}`, `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/commands`, or `CommandOutcome`
  (standalone `PlayerView` omits `revision`, so pass `include=view` on commands or pair view reads
  with `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}`). Pass `expected_revision` on commands. On 409
  `revision_conflict`, refresh `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/view` before deciding your next
  move. On 409 `session_busy`, check `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}` first if you sent
  `expected_revision`, or retry directly if you didn't.
- **Polling:** Send the previous `ETag` in `If-None-Match` on `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}` or
  `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/view` to receive 304 with no body while state is unchanged.
- **Catching up on events:** `after` and `next_after` on `GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/events`
  count events for the requested `visibility` and advance independently of `revision`. Persist
  `next_after` from `/events` rather than adding `len(CommandOutcome.events)` whenever another
  client or referee might also act on the session.

tags.name: saves
tags.description:
List, inspect, relabel, restore, export, import, and delete saved games. A *save* snapshots a
session after its last accepted command. Restoring a save starts a new session at revision 0 from
that snapshot while leaving both the save and the original session unchanged.

A *save document* is osrlib's versioned JSON envelope (`kind` set to `"save"`, `schema_version`,
`engine_version`, and `payload`) containing the full game state, including the master seed,
unexplored map, monster hit points, and logs. Because it exposes hidden state, only a referee may
export or import a save document.

1. `POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/saves` creates a save from a session and returns its `sav_` id.
2. `GET /v1/saves` lists your saves (optionally filtered by `session_id`), and
   `GET /v1/saves/{save_id}` returns one save's metadata.
3. `POST /v1/saves/{save_id}/restore` starts a new session from the save.

`PATCH /v1/saves/{save_id}` updates or clears a save's `label`, and `DELETE /v1/saves/{save_id}`
deletes a save without affecting sessions restored from it. A referee exports a save document with
`GET /v1/saves/{save_id}/document` and imports one on any compatible server with
`POST /v1/saves/import`.
